**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 37, verses 1–3:**

**Surah al-Saffat (The Ranks)**

It is Meccan, and they reported no disagreement about that. It has 181 verses according to the Basrans and 182 according to others. It details the circumstances of the generations mentioned in His saying, in the previous surah, ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, that they will not return to them?﴾ (36:31). It also contains, concerning the believers and their disbelieving enemies on the Day of Resurrection, what serves as an elucidation of what was mentioned of that in the previous surah. It mentions something related to the stars that was not mentioned earlier. Because of the totality of what is mentioned, it was placed after it.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, by Abu Hayyan), the connection between the beginning of this surah and the end of Surah Ya-Sin is that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the Return (al-ma'ad) and His power, glory be to Him, to bring the dead back to life, and that He is the One who originates them, and that when His will is directed toward a thing it comes to be, He, mighty and majestic, mentioned here His oneness, glory be to Him, since what His will is directed toward cannot be completed, whether in bringing into existence or annihilating, except by the Willer being one, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿If there were in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ (21:22).

**In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful**

﴿By those who range in ranks﴾ is an oath by Allah, exalted is He, by the angels, peace be upon them, as was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Masruq, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Suddi. Abu Muslim rejected this and said: it is not permissible to interpret this word, and what follows it, as referring to the angels, because the word implies feminine gender, and the angels are free of this attribute. The reply to this is that this is in the sense of a plural of a plural, being the plural of saffah, meaning a group or a company that ranges in rows. It is also permissible that it is the feminine of the singular, considering that it is a self and a soul. The meaningful feminine (al-ta'nith al-ma'nawi) is what it is not fitting to apply to them, but the grammatical feminine (al-ta'nith al-lafzi) has no prohibition against it. How could it not, since they are the ones named "angels" (malaikah)! The attribute mentioned is treated as intransitive (munazzal manzilat al-lazim), on the basis that the intended meaning is the occurrence of the act itself without intending an object; that is, those who cause themselves to range in rows, or the object is omitted, i.e. the ones that range themselves, namely those who arrange themselves in the lines of rows by standing in their known stations, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ (37:164). This is in consideration of precedence of rank and nearness to the enclosure of holiness.

[p. 65]

Or it means the ones that range themselves, standing in rows for worship. It was also said: the ones that range their feet for prayer. It was also said: the ones that range their wings in the air, awaiting the command of Allah, exalted is He. It was also said: the intended meaning of "those that range" is the birds, from His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And the birds in ranks﴾ (24:41), but this is not relied upon. ﴿Ranks (saffan)⟩ is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid), and likewise ﴿driving (zajran)⟩ in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and those who drive with a driving﴾. It was also said: saffan is an object (maf'ul bihi), and it is singular but intended as plural, meaning those that range their rows, but this is not the right view.

The intended meaning of ﴿those who drive﴾ is also the angels, peace be upon them, according to the majority. Zajr in origin means repelling something by force and shouting. They cited the verse:

*Zajara Abi 'Urwata al-sibaa' idha ashfaqa an yakhtalitna bi'l-ghanam*

[My father 'Urwah drove off the beasts when he feared they would mix among the sheep.]

It is also used in the sense of driving and urging, and in the sense of prevention and forbidding even if there is no shouting. The attribute is treated as intransitive, or its object is omitted, i.e. those who drive for driving (i.e. those who carry out the act of driving), or those who drive what they are charged with driving, from the heavenly and earthly bodies and others, in a manner that befits the one being driven. Among this is driving the servants away from sins by inspiring good, and driving the devils away from whispering and seduction, and away from eavesdropping, as will come shortly, if Allah, exalted is He, wills. It was reported from Qatadah that the intended meaning of "those who drive" is the verses of the Qur'an, because they include the legal prohibitions. It was also said: everything that drives away from the disobedience of Allah, mighty and majestic is He. What is relied upon is what preceded. Likewise, the intended meaning, as was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and others, in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and those who recite the Reminder﴾ is the angels, peace be upon them.

﴿Reminder (dhikran)⟩ is in the accusative, being an object (maf'ul), and its tanwin is for magnification. It has the meaning of "that which is mentioned and recited," and it was explained as the Book of Allah, mighty and majestic is He.

Abu Salih said: they are the angels who bring the Book and the Qur'an from Allah, mighty and majestic is He, to people. So the intended meaning of their reciting it is their reciting it to others. Some explained it as the signs and the divine knowledges, and the angels recite these to the prophets and the saints. It will come, if Allah, exalted is He, wills, in the chapter on allusion (bab al-isharah), what relates to the angels' reciting that to the saints, may Allah, exalted is He, sanctify their secrets. Some said: that is, those who recite the signs of Allah, exalted is He, and His Books sent down upon the prophets, peace be upon them, and others, such as glorification, sanctification, praise and exaltation. Perhaps reciting in this sense is more general than reciting to others and other than that. It was also said: ﴿dhikran⟩ is in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun of a different root, so that the accusative terms are in one order. Qatadah said: ﴿those who recite the Reminder﴾ are the children of Adam who recite His revealed Book, glorification of Him and magnification of Him.

It is also permitted that Allah, exalted is He, swore by the souls of the diligent scholars who range themselves in the ranks of congregations or their feet in the prayers, who drive with admonitions and advice, who recite the signs of Allah, exalted is He, who study His laws and rulings. Or by groups of the commanders of warriors in the way of Allah, exalted is He, who range the rows in the places of battles, who drive the horses for jihad by urging them, or drive the enemy in battles by chasing them, who recite the signs of Allah, glory be to Him, and His remembrance and His glorification in the midst of that.

It is also permitted that He, glory be to Him, swore by groups of celestial bodies arranged like ranks set in order, one above another, and by the souls that manage those bodies by moving them and the like, and by the holy essences absorbed in the seas of holiness, glorifying night and day without slackening, and they are the cherubic angels (al-karrubiyyun) and the like. This is far, by many stages, from the way of the pious predecessors (al-salaf al-salih), and indeed from the way of the People of the Sunnah in general, as is not hidden.

The conjunctive fa' (al-fa' al-'atifah) for the attributes may be for ordering their meanings of attribute in existence when the entity characterized by them is one, as in the saying:

*Ya lahfa Zayabata lil-hadithi al-sabihi al-sabihi al-sabihi...*

[Alas for Zayabah's grief for the raider who swam, then plundered, then returned.]

That is, the one who swam, then plundered, then returned. Or it is for ordering their meanings in rank when the entity is also one, as in your saying: "The perfection of intellect is in you when you are a youth, then a man of middle age." Or it is for ordering the things characterized by them in existence, as in your saying: "I stopped at so-and-so's sons, generation after generation (batnan fa-batnan)." Or in rank, as in: "May Allah have mercy on those who shave, then those who shorten." Both of these occur with a multiplicity of the thing characterized. Ordering by rank is either in consideration of ascent or in consideration of descent. When the entity characterized by these attributes here is one, and they are all the angels, peace be upon them, together, it may be for ordering by rank in consideration of ascent: the ranging is at the first rank, because it is a deficient action (amal qasir), and driving is higher than it because of the benefit it brings to others, and reciting is higher and higher still because of the benefit to the elite spreading to the benefit of the general public with what contains the welfare of livelihood and the afterlife. Or it may be for the external ordering from the point of view of the existence of the entities of the attributes: ranging exists first, because it is a perfection of the angels in themselves; then driving for others exists after it, because it is a perfection for others, through which the person prepares himself, for one who has not perfected himself is not qualified to perfect others; then reciting exists, on the basis that it is an overflow upon others who are prepared for it, and this is not realized except after the preparation has been achieved, which is one of the effects of driving. When the entities characterized by them are multiple among the angels, in the sense that one category of them is so-and-so and another category is so-and-so, then the apparent view is that they are for ordering by rank in consideration of ascent, as in the first part. So the ranging groups are perfect, the drivers are more perfect than them, and the reciters are more perfect and more perfect still, as is known from what has preceded.

It was said: it is permissible that it is the opposite of that, by intending by the ranging ones groups of angels ranging around the Throne, standing in the station of servanthood, and they are the cherubim, the nearest ones; or other angels called, as the Greatest Shaykh (al-Shaykh al-Akbar, Ibn 'Arabi), may Allah sanctify his secret, mentioned, al-muhaymimun, those utterly absorbed in His love, exalted is He; none of them knows that Allah, mighty and majestic is He, created anything other than him. He mentioned that they were not commanded to prostrate to Adam, peace be upon him, because of their lack of awareness of their absorption in Him, exalted is He. They are the ones meant by "the exalted ones" in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Have you grown arrogant, or were you of the exalted?﴾ (38:75). By "those who drive" is meant other groups who were commanded to subject the heavenly and earthly things and to manage them for what they were created for, and they are superior to the ranging ones in terms of their benefit to the servants. By "those who recite the Reminder" are other groups who were commanded to recite knowledge to the special people of creation, and they are, because of the specific benefit they bring, superior to the drivers. Or the intended meaning of "those who drive" is those who drive people away from wrongdoing by inspiring awareness of its ugliness and what repels from committing it, and "those who recite the Reminder" are those who inspire goodness and the aspects that encourage it. Because preventing harm is better than bringing benefit, and averting corruptions is more important than bringing about benefits, this is why it was said: clearing (al-takhliyah, with the letter kha') precedes adorning (al-tahliyah). So the reciters are below the drivers. The status of the fa' in the attributes according to all the preceding views is not hidden from anyone who has the slightest reflection.

In my opinion, and Allah, exalted is He, knows best, it is permissible that the intended meaning of "those who range" is those who arrange themselves for worship, such as prayer or fighting disbelievers, for example, whether they are angels, humans, or others. And by "those who drive" is meant those who drive others away from committing sins by their words or actions, whoever they may be. And by "those who recite the Reminder" are those who recite the signs of Allah, exalted is He, to others for teaching or the like, likewise. There is no contradiction among these attributes, so they may all be combined in some individuals. Perhaps the ordering in the manner of ascent is in consideration of the attributes themselves: arranging oneself for worship is a perfection, driving away from committing sins is more perfect, and reciting the signs of Allah, exalted is He, for teaching is because it includes commanding acts of obedience, forbidding sins, freeing oneself from vices, and adorning oneself with knowledge, and beyond that there are other matters more perfect and still more perfect. Regarding the meanings of the harmonious attributes, there are possibilities other than what has been mentioned, so do not be heedless.

Whatever the case, the oath is by those groups themselves, and there is no restriction upon Allah, mighty and majestic is He; He, glory be to Him, may swear by whatever He wills. So there is no need to say that the speech is by elision of a noun in the genitive (hadhf mudaf), meaning "by the Lord of those who range," for example. **In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful**

﴿By those who range in ranks﴾ is an oath by Allah, exalted is He, by the angels, peace be upon them, as was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Masruq, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Suddi. Abu Muslim rejected this and said: it is not permissible to interpret this word, and what follows it, as referring to the angels, because the word implies feminine gender, and the angels are free of this attribute. The reply to this is that this is in the sense of a plural of a plural, being the plural of saffah, meaning a group or a company that ranges in rows. It is also permissible that it is the feminine of the singular, considering that it is a self and a soul. The meaningful feminine (al-ta'nith al-ma'nawi) is what it is not fitting to apply to them, but the grammatical feminine (al-ta'nith al-lafzi) has no prohibition against it. How could it not, since they are the ones named "angels" (malaikah)! The attribute mentioned is treated as intransitive (munazzal manzilat al-lazim), on the basis that the intended meaning is the occurrence of the act itself without intending an object; that is, those who cause themselves to range in rows, or the object is omitted, i.e. the ones that range themselves, namely those who arrange themselves in the lines of rows by standing in their known stations, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ (37:164). This is in consideration of precedence of rank and nearness to the enclosure of holiness.

[p. 65]

Or it means the ones that range themselves, standing in rows for worship. It was also said: the ones that range their feet for prayer. It was also said: the ones that range their wings in the air, awaiting the command of Allah, exalted is He. It was also said: the intended meaning of "those that range" is the birds, from His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And the birds in ranks﴾ (24:41), but this is not relied upon. ﴿Ranks (saffan)⟩ is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid), and likewise ﴿driving (zajran)⟩ in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and those who drive with a driving﴾. It was also said: saffan is an object (maf'ul bihi), and it is singular but intended as plural, meaning those that range their rows, but this is not the right view.

The intended meaning of ﴿those who drive﴾ is also the angels, peace be upon them, according to the majority. Zajr in origin means repelling something by force and shouting. They cited the verse:

*Zajara Abi 'Urwata al-sibaa' idha ashfaqa an yakhtalitna bi'l-ghanam*

[My father 'Urwah drove off the beasts when he feared they would mix among the sheep.]

It is also used in the sense of driving and urging, and in the sense of prevention and forbidding even if there is no shouting. The attribute is treated as intransitive, or its object is omitted, i.e. those who drive for driving (i.e. those who carry out the act of driving), or those who drive what they are charged with driving, from the heavenly and earthly bodies and others, in a manner that befits the one being driven. Among this is driving the servants away from sins by inspiring good, and driving the devils away from whispering and seduction, and away from eavesdropping, as will come shortly, if Allah, exalted is He, wills. It was reported from Qatadah that the intended meaning of "those who drive" is the verses of the Qur'an, because they include the legal prohibitions. It was also said: everything that drives away from the disobedience of Allah, mighty and majestic is He. What is relied upon is what preceded. Likewise, the intended meaning, as was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and others, in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and those who recite the Reminder﴾ is the angels, peace be upon them.

﴿Reminder (dhikran)⟩ is in the accusative, being an object (maf'ul), and its tanwin is for magnification. It has the meaning of "that which is mentioned and recited," and it was explained as the Book of Allah, mighty and majestic is He.

Abu Salih said: they are the angels who bring the Book and the Qur'an from Allah, mighty and majestic is He, to people. So the intended meaning of their reciting it is their reciting it to others. Some explained it as the signs and the divine knowledges, and the angels recite these to the prophets and the saints. It will come, if Allah, exalted is He, wills, in the chapter on allusion (bab al-isharah), what relates to the angels' reciting that to the saints, may Allah, exalted is He, sanctify their secrets. Some said: that is, those who recite the signs of Allah, exalted is He, and His Books sent down upon the prophets, peace be upon them, and others, such as glorification, sanctification, praise and exaltation. Perhaps reciting in this sense is more general than reciting to others and other than that. It was also said: ﴿dhikran⟩ is in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun of a different root, so that the accusative terms are in one order. Qatadah said: ﴿those who recite the Reminder﴾ are the children of Adam who recite His revealed Book, glorification of Him and magnification of Him.

It is also permitted that Allah, exalted is He, swore by the souls of the diligent scholars who range themselves in the ranks of congregations or their feet in the prayers, who drive with admonitions and advice, who recite the signs of Allah, exalted is He, who study His laws and rulings. Or by groups of the commanders of warriors in the way of Allah, exalted is He, who range the rows in the places of battles, who drive the horses for jihad by urging them, or drive the enemy in battles by chasing them, who recite the signs of Allah, glory be to Him, and His remembrance and His glorification in the midst of that.

It is also permitted that He, glory be to Him, swore by groups of celestial bodies arranged like ranks set in order, one above another, and by the souls that manage those bodies by moving them and the like, and by the holy essences absorbed in the seas of holiness, glorifying night and day without slackening, and they are the cherubic angels (al-karrubiyyun) and the like. This is far, by many stages, from the way of the pious predecessors (al-salaf al-salih), and indeed from the way of the People of the Sunnah in general, as is not hidden.

The conjunctive fa' (al-fa' al-'atifah) for the attributes may be for ordering their meanings of attribute in existence when the entity characterized by them is one, as in the saying:

*Ya lahfa Zayabata lil-hadithi al-sabihi al-sabihi al-sabihi...*

[Alas for Zayabah's grief for the raider who swam, then plundered, then returned.]

That is, the one who swam, then plundered, then returned. Or it is for ordering their meanings in rank when the entity is also one, as in your saying: "The perfection of intellect is in you when you are a youth, then a man of middle age." Or it is for ordering the things characterized by them in existence, as in your saying: "I stopped at so-and-so's sons, generation after generation (batnan fa-batnan)." Or in rank, as in: "May Allah have mercy on those who shave, then those who shorten." Both of these occur with a multiplicity of the thing characterized. Ordering by rank is either in consideration of ascent or in consideration of descent. When the entity characterized by these attributes here is one, and they are all the angels, peace be upon them, together, it may be for ordering by rank in consideration of ascent: the ranging is at the first rank, because it is a deficient action (amal qasir), and driving is higher than it because of the benefit it brings to others, and reciting is higher and higher still because of the benefit to the elite spreading to the benefit of the general public with what contains the welfare of livelihood and the afterlife. Or it may be for the external ordering from the point of view of the existence of the entities of the attributes: ranging exists first, because it is a perfection of the angels in themselves; then driving for others exists after it, because it is a perfection for others, through which the person prepares himself, for one who has not perfected himself is not qualified to perfect others; then reciting exists, on the basis that it is an overflow upon others who are prepared for it, and this is not realized except after the preparation has been achieved, which is one of the effects of driving. When the entities characterized by them are multiple among the angels, in the sense that one category of them is so-and-so and another category is so-and-so, then the apparent view is that they are for ordering by rank in consideration of ascent, as in the first part. So the ranging groups are perfect, the drivers are more perfect than them, and the reciters are more perfect and more perfect still, as is known from what has preceded.

It was said: it is permissible that it is the opposite of that, by intending by the ranging ones groups of angels ranging around the Throne, standing in the station of servanthood, and they are the cherubim, the nearest ones; or other angels called, as the Greatest Shaykh (al-Shaykh al-Akbar, Ibn 'Arabi), may Allah sanctify his secret, mentioned, al-muhaymimun, those utterly absorbed in His love, exalted is He; none of them knows that Allah, mighty and majestic is He, created anything other than him. He mentioned that they were not commanded to prostrate to Adam, peace be upon him, because of their lack of awareness of their absorption in Him, exalted is He. They are the ones meant by "the exalted ones" in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Have you grown arrogant, or were you of the exalted?﴾ (38:75). By "those who drive" is meant other groups who were commanded to subject the heavenly and earthly things and to manage them for what they were created for, and they are superior to the ranging ones in terms of their benefit to the servants. By "those who recite the Reminder" are other groups who were commanded to recite knowledge to the special people of creation, and they are, because of the specific benefit they bring, superior to the drivers. Or the intended meaning of "those who drive" is those who drive people away from wrongdoing by inspiring awareness of its ugliness and what repels from committing it, and "those who recite the Reminder" are those who inspire goodness and the aspects that encourage it. Because preventing harm is better than bringing benefit, and averting corruptions is more important than bringing about benefits, this is why it was said: clearing (al-takhliyah, with the letter kha') precedes adorning (al-tahliyah). So the reciters are below the drivers. The status of the fa' in the attributes according to all the preceding views is not hidden from anyone who has the slightest reflection.

In my opinion, and Allah, exalted is He, knows best, it is permissible that the intended meaning of "those who range" is those who arrange themselves for worship, such as prayer or fighting disbelievers, for example, whether they are angels, humans, or others. And by "those who drive" is meant those who drive others away from committing sins by their words or actions, whoever they may be. And by "those who recite the Reminder" are those who recite the signs of Allah, exalted is He, to others for teaching or the like, likewise. There is no contradiction among these attributes, so they may all be combined in some individuals. Perhaps the ordering in the manner of ascent is in consideration of the attributes themselves: arranging oneself for worship is a perfection, driving away from committing sins is more perfect, and reciting the signs of Allah, exalted is He, for teaching is because it includes commanding acts of obedience, forbidding sins, freeing oneself from vices, and adorning oneself with knowledge, and beyond that there are other matters more perfect and still more perfect. Making the mentioned attributes apply to one entity of the angels, according to what has passed, in that groups of them are ranging ones in the sense of ranging themselves in the line of rows by standing in their known stations, or standing in rows for worship, and reciting the Reminder in the sense of reciting the verses by way of revelation to the prophets, peace be upon them, does not, in my view, avoid being far-fetched, on the basis that the multiplicity of angels who recite the revelation, whether it is a separate category or not, is something that creates a problem, which is why more than one scholar mentioned that the trustee of revelation who recites the Reminder to the prophets is Jibril, peace be upon him, and no other. Yes, there are verses that descend accompanied by a company of angels, peace be upon them, and the Noble Book states the watch at the delivery of revelation. This is one matter, while reciting to the prophets, peace be upon them, is another matter. So reflect on all of that. Regarding the meanings of the harmonious attributes, there are possibilities other than what has been mentioned, so do not be heedless.

Whatever the case, the oath is by those groups themselves, and there is no restriction upon Allah, mighty and majestic is He; He, glory be to Him, may swear by whatever He wills. So there is no need to say that the speech is by elision of a noun in the genitive (hadhf mudaf), meaning "by the Lord of those who range," for example. The verse clearly indicates the view of Sibawayh and al-Khalil regarding verses such as ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ and ﴿By the day when it reveals itself﴾ (92:1–2), that the second waw and what follows it are for conjunction (lil-'atf), in contrast to the view of others, that they are for oath, because the fa' is placed there in the position of the waw, except that it conveys ordering.

Ibn Mas'ud, Masruq, al-A'mash, Abu 'Amr and Hamzah assimilated the three ta's (taa') into the following letters, because of their closeness, since they come from the tip of the tongue and the roots of the upper incisors.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verses 4–5:

﴿Indeed, your God is One.﴾ This is the response (jawab) to the oath (qasam). Their custom is to emphasize what matters by placing the oath first, so it is placed first here. It should not be said that this is speech addressed to a denier who rejects it, so the oath would be pointless. And what has been said, that the oneness of the Creator has been established by textual proof after being established by reason, so that its benefit is clear here, is not complete. This is because the speech is addressed to one who does not acknowledge monotheism. The proof has been indicated in His, the Glorified's, saying: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, and Lord of the easts.﴾ Their existence in this wondrous pattern is the clearest proof of His oneness, the Mighty and Majestic. Indeed, in every atom of the world there is a proof of this:

"In everything there is a sign for Him
that points to the fact that He is One."

"Lord" (Rabb) is a second predicate (khabar) of "indeed" (inna), according to the view of those who permit multiple predicates, or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, or the meaning is "He is the Lord of the heavens," and so on.

Abu al-Baqa' and others permitted that it be an apposition (badal) of "One," so that it is the intended referent in terms of the relation. That is, the Creator of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them of existing things. The actions of servants enter into the general scope of the relative clause (mawsul), so the verse indicates that they are created by Him, the Exalted. This does not contradict the fact that the power of the servant is effective by His permission, the Mighty and Majestic, as most of the early generations (salaf) held, even al-Ash'ari himself at the end of his life, as some eminent scholars have stated explicitly. Some have interpreted "Lord" here as "King" and as "the One who nurtures," and the first is perhaps more apparent. Regarding the indication of the verse that the actions of servants are created by Him in this way, there is a discussion. According to a group, "the easts" (al-mashariq) means the risings of the sun, because these are the well-known and common ones among them. They are equal in number to the days of the year, for in each day it rises from an east and sets in a west. So the wests are as many as the easts. It seems that the mention of only the easts suffices because it implies that, together with the fact that rising is a stronger indication of power and more complete in blessing. For this reason Abraham, peace be upon him, used it as evidence when debating Nimrod. Ibn Atiyyah reported that the easts of the sun are one hundred and eighty. Some reconciled this with what the previous count implies, namely doubling the number, by saying that its easts from the beginning of Cancer, which is the first of the summer signs, to the beginning of Capricorn, which is the first of the winter signs, are distinct from its easts from the beginning of Capricorn to the beginning of Cancer. If what it was and what it returned to is considered one, they are one hundred and eighty; if their difference is considered, they are three hundred and sixty. In this there is the dropping of the fraction, for the solar year exceeds that number by about six days, as explained in its proper place. The easts have also been interpreted as the easts of the stars, and this was preferred because it fits His saying after this: ﴿Indeed, We have adorned﴾ and so on. For the wandering stars (sayyarat), their easts vary in number. The most numerous of them, according to what is well known among the earlier scholars, is Saturn, and its easts until it completes its orbit are far more than the easts of the sun until it completes its orbit by thousands. The easts of the fixed stars until their orbit is completed are more and more. So do not be heedless, and reflect.

The dual form of "east" and "west" in His saying, ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾, refers to the east of summer and the east of winter and their two wests. The repetition of "Lord" here along with the easts is for the great manifestness of the traces of lordship in them and their renewal every day.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 6:**

﴿Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven﴾, meaning the nearest of the heavens to the people of the earth. Here *al-dunya* is the feminine of *adna* in the sense of *aqrab* (nearer), an *af'al* of comparison (*af'al tafdil*, the elative form).

﴿with an adornment﴾, wondrous and marvelous, ﴿the stars﴾. It is read in the genitive (*bi-l-jarr*) as a substitute (*badal*) for "adornment," a complete substitution (*badal kull*), on the basis that what is meant by it is the noun (*ism*), that is, that by which something is adorned, and not the verbal noun (*masdar*). For the stars themselves, and the arrangement of some of them relative to others, are an adornment, and what an adornment it is:

*"As if the bodies of the stars are shining pearls*
*scattered over a blue carpet."*

It is also permitted that it be an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*). Most readers read *"bi-zinati al-kawakib"* with the genitive construction (*idafa*), on the basis that it is explicative (*bayaniyya*), since "adornment" is indefinite and applies to everything by which something is adorned, so "the stars" serves as its explanation. It is also permitted that it be a *lam* construction (*lamiyya*), on the basis that the adornment belongs to the stars, their lights or their arrangements. Explaining it as "lights" is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. It is also permitted that *zina* be a verbal noun like *nisba*, and its idafa is then an idafa of the verbal noun to its object, meaning: We adorned the nearest heaven by Our adorning the stars within it; or an idafa of the verbal noun to its subject, meaning: We adorned it by the stars adorning it.

Ibn Wuthab, Masruq according to one report, al-A'mash, Talha and Abu Bakr read *"bi-zinatin"* with tanwin and *"al-kawakiba"* in the accusative, so *zina* may be a verbal noun and *al-kawakiba* its direct object, as in His words ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger﴾ ﴿an orphan﴾. This is not a verbal noun of the single-occurrence type (*masdar al-marra*, like *darba*, "a single blow") such that one would say its government (*'amal*, operating on an object) is invalid, as Ibn Malik stated explicitly, because it is formed with the *ta'* like *kitaba* and *isaba*, and not every *ta'* in a verbal noun denotes unity. Moreover, this form is not the form of unity. It is also possible that *al-kawakib* is a substitute of partial inclusion (*badal ishtimal*) for ﴿the heaven﴾, and the requirement of a pronoun with the substituted element when the connection of one to the other is not apparent is as they established in His words ﴿Destroyed were the people of the trench﴾ ﴿the fire﴾.

It has also been said that the *lam* is a substitute for it. It is permitted that it be a substitute for the place of the preposition and its object, or for the object alone according to the two views, and that it be in the accusative with an implied verb, "I mean." Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read *"bi-zinatin"* with tanwin and *"al-kawakibu"* in the nominative, on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are the stars; or the subject of the verbal noun. The Basrans permitted its nominative use as the subject of the verbal noun, though rarely, while al-Farra' claimed that it is not attested.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that the stars are in the nearest heaven. There is no obstacle to this, even though their movements differ and vary in speed and slowness, because they may be in their orbits (*aflak*), and their orbits are in the nearest heaven, which is motionless, and which has enough thickness to permit the arranging of those moving orbits with their varying movements and the elevation of some of them above others. Al-Nisaburi, in his tafsir of surah al-Takwir, related from al-Kalbi that the stars are in lamps suspended between heaven and earth by chains of light, and those chains are in the hands of the angels, peace be upon them. This is something the apparent text refutes, and I do not regard it as anything but a tale of superstition.

As for what most of the philosophers held, that the moon alone is in the nearest heaven, Mercury in the second, Venus in the third, the sun in the fourth, Mars in the fifth, Jupiter in the sixth, Saturn in the seventh, and the fixed stars in an orbit above the seventh, which is the Kursi (*kursi*, the Footstool) in the language of the Shari'a, this is among things for which no proof establishes certainty. Even if it were sound, it would not harm the verse, because it is enough for the nearest heaven to be adorned with stars that it appears so to the eye.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 7:

﴿And as a guard﴾ is put in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of a verb conjoined to ﴿We adorned﴾; that is, "and We guarded it with a guarding." Or it is conjoined to "adornment" (zinah) according to its meaning, for it carries the sense of an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), as if it were said: "We created the stars as an adornment for the heaven and as a guard for it." Conjunction according to meaning (al-'atf 'ala al-ma'na) is common, and it is different from conjunction according to the wording (al-'atf 'ala al-mawdu') and from conjunction by assumption (ʿatf al-tawahhum).
Page 69
It is also permitted that it be an object of purpose with the addition of the particle wa (waw), or on the basis of the postponement of the governing element (ta'khir al-'amil), meaning: "and for its guarding We adorned it." His words, exalted is He, ﴿from every rebellious devil﴾ are connected to "our guarding" which is elided, or to "guarding." Al-marid is like al-marid (the one who is stripped bare of good things), from their saying: "a tree is amrad (bare) when it has been stripped of leaves," and from this it is said: "a sandy tract is marda' (barren) when it grows nothing," and from it comes al-amrad (the beardless youth), because he is bare of hair. It has also been explained here as "one who has departed from obedience," and this has the sense of being stripped bare of it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 8:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They cannot listen to the exalted assembly﴾, means: they do not eavesdrop (*yatasamma'una*). Its original form is *la yatasamma'una*, and the *ta'* was assimilated into the *sin*. The plural pronoun refers to every devil (*kull shaytan*), because the word is in the sense of "devils" (*al-shayatin*).

The majority of readers recite *la yasma'una* with the light form. *Al-mala'* (the assembly, or the notables) originally means a group that gathers upon an opinion, so that they fill the eyes with splendour and the souls with majesty and radiance. It is applied to any group in general and to nobles in particular. The "exalted assembly" (*al-mala' al-a'la*) means the angels, peace be upon them, as narrated from al-Suddi, because they are in the direction of height. Opposite to them is the "lower assembly" (*al-mala' al-asfal*), which is humankind and the jinn, because they are in the direction of lowness. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the noblest of the angels, peace be upon them. In another narration from him, they are their scribes. On both narrations, the height is explained as a height of rank (*al-'uluww al-ma'nawi*).

On the majority's reading, the verb is transitive through *ila* ("to") because it is implicitly containing the meaning of listening attentively (*al-isgha'*). That is, *la yasma'una musghina ila al-mala' al-a'la* ("they do not hear, listening attentively to the exalted assembly"). The intended meaning is the negation of their hearing even while they are attentive. This indicates a great obstacle and a bewilderment that distracts them from perception. The same applies to the other reading, that of Ibn 'Abbas (with a variant from him), Ibn Thabit, 'Abd Allah ibn Muslim, Talha, al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs, based on what is apparent: that the *tafa''ul* form (*al-taf'ul*) does not differ from its triliteral root in transitivity. The use of *tasamma'a* with *ila* does not require that it be non-implicit. It was also said that there is no need to consider implicit meaning in this case. The *tafa''ul* form indicates seeking, so *tasamma'a* means "sought to hear." It was said that this suggests attentive listening, because seeking to hear occurs through attentive listening, and thus the two readings agree, even if implicit meaning is not stated for the intensive reading. Yet the better view is to accept implicit meaning. The negation of their seeking to hear, although it occurs from them, is such that it was said that they climb upon one another for this purpose. This is either a rhetorical assertion for emphasis in negating their hearing, or, as some have said, it refers to their state after reaching the place of danger, from fear of being pelted, so that they are bewildered from seeking to hear.

Abu Hayyan said: the negation of eavesdropping is because its fruit, which is hearing, is absent. Ibn Kamal said: in both readings the verb is transitive through *ila* because it implicitly contains the meaning of reaching (*al-intiha'*), that is, "they do not reach, by hearing or eavesdropping, the exalted assembly." But this is not so, as is not hidden from the sincere and careful reader.

In the well-known view, the clause is a grammatical resumption (*isti'naf nahwi*), and it is not permitted for it to be a qualifying clause (*sifa*) for "devil." They said: there is no sense in protection from devils who do not hear, or do not eavesdrop, and this also suggests the absence of protection from others. Nor is it permitted for it to be an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*), which is an answer to an implied question, because the question is most naturally drawn from the content of what precedes it. Its implied form would then be: "why are they not protected?", which returns the prohibited qualifying sense. Likewise it is not permitted for it to be a future circumstantial clause (*hal muqaddara*), because a circumstantial clause of this kind is determined by its subject, and devils do not determine the absence of hearing or the absence of eavesdropping, nor do they wish for it.

Ibn al-Munir permitted it to be a qualifying clause, and the meaning is the protection of the heavens from one who does not hear or does not eavesdrop, because of this protection. It is similar to ﴿Then We sent Our messengers﴾, ﴿and He subjected for you the night and the day﴾, and ﴿the sun and the moon and the stars subjected by His command﴾. For this reason some eminent scholars did not treat his (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever kills an enemy, he has his spoils" as a metaphor of the first kind. It was objected that this is contrary to what is apparent, and one hardly understands from "strike the struck man" that he is struck with this particular blow commanded, rather than with another blow before it.

Likewise the author of al-Kashf permitted it to be a qualifying clause and also an explanatory resumption. He dismissed the objection and went far in that direction, as is his habit in all his investigations. He said: the meaning is that they are not enabled to hear while listening attentively, or they are not enabled to eavesdrop, as an intensification in negating hearing, as if they, despite their intense seeking, cannot accomplish that, and it must be so. The clause is made a qualifying clause first, combining the two readings and fulfilling the right of attentive listening indicated by *ila*. In that case the qualifying clause is highly antithetical (*shadid al-tibaq*). The objection to the explanatory resumption applies if it answers the implied question "why is it protected?", but that is not the case. Rather, the question concerns what happens at the time of protection and how it is carried out, because His saying, ﴿and as protection from every rebellious devil﴾, stirs the mind toward it. So it was said ﴿they cannot listen﴾ as an answer to what happens at that time, and ﴿and they are pelted﴾ for the manner of the protection. This is better than making it the start of an incidental narrative (*iqtisas mustatrad*), so that what is not truly cut off in meaning is not cut off. End of quotation.

Al-Khafaji found this subtle, approved of it, and mentioned that its gist is that the negated hearing here is not hearing in general, so that the corruption of meaning they suspected does not follow. Since the verb is transitive through *ila* and implicitly contains the meaning of attentive listening, the meaning becomes: "We protected it from devils who do not listen attentively to it in a complete way, by which they could record what the angels, peace be upon them, say." Its outcome is: "We protected it from devils who steal hearing." His glorious saying, ﴿except one who snatches a fragment﴾, and so on, calls out for the soundness of this view. The objection from the hadith about the attributes before knowing them is that reports, if they come, do not hold completely, so the hadith is not universally applicable.

It was also said: the original is *li-an la yasma'u* ("so that they do not hear"), with the preposition related to *hifzan* ("protection"). The *lam* was deleted, as in *ji'tuka an tukrimani* ("I came to you that you honour me"), then *an* was deleted and the verb was put in the nominative, as in the poet's saying:

Indeed, O you who rebuke me, "Let me attend the battles and witness the pleasures; can you make me immortal?"

In this there is a double deletion: the *lam* was deleted, the *an* was deleted, and the verb was made nominative. Although each of these occurs in eloquent speech, the combination of the two deletions is objectionable, and the speech of God, exalted is He, is protected from it. Abu al-Baqa' permitted the clause to be a qualifying clause, a grammatical resumption, and a circumstantial clause, so do not be heedless.

﴿And they are pelted﴾, meaning they are struck and stoned, ﴿from every side﴾, from the sides of the heaven, when they intend to ascend to it. The intended meaning is not that each one is struck from every side, but it is by distribution: whoever ascends from one side is struck from that side.

Mahbub, from Abu 'Amr, read *yaqdhifuna* with the active form. Perhaps the agent is the angels. It was permitted that the agent be the stars. The reference of the pronoun for rational beings is easy.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 9:

Allah's statement ﴿dukhūran﴾ (repelled, driven away) is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl lahu*, the accusative noun giving the reason for an action) and gives the reason for the hurling, i.e. for the repelling, which means driving away and distancing. It may also be an absolute object (*maf'ūl muṭlaq*, a verbal noun in the accusative that reinforces or specifies the verb) of *yuqdhafūn* (they are hurled), as in *qa'adtu julūsan* ("I sat, a sitting"). This is because the two cognate verbs are treated as if they were a single verb, so *duḥūran* stands in place of *qadhfan* (hurling), or *yuqdhafūn* stands in place of *yudḥarūn* (they are repelled). On both readings it is a reinforcing verbal noun, or a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*, a noun describing the state of the subject) from the pronoun in *yuqdhafūn*, understood as a verbal noun in the form of the passive participle according to the common recitation (*qirā'a*). It has the sense of the plural, because it covers many, meaning *madḥūrīn* (repelled ones). It is also permitted that it be the plural of *dāḥir* in the sense of *madḥūr*, like *qā'id* and *quʿūd* (sitting and sitters). It is also permitted that it be the plural of *dāḥir* without interpretation, according to the other recitation. It is further permitted that it be in the accusative by removing the preposition, which is the *bā'* (with), taking it as the plural of *daḥr*, like *dahr* and *duhūr*, meaning that by which one is repelled; that is, they are hurled with a repelling.

Al-Sulami, Ibn Abi 'Abla and al-Tabarani, from Abu Ja'far, recited ﴿duḥūran﴾ with a fatḥah on the *dāl*. This allows that it is also in the accusative by removing the preposition, and on this recitation that is more evident, because *fa'ūl* with a fatḥah means what is done with it, often, like *ṭahūr* and *ghasūl*, for that with which one purifies oneself and washes. It is also permitted that it be an adjective, like *ṣabūr*, for an implied noun, meaning a hurling that is repelling, driving them away. And it may be a verbal noun, like *qabūl* (acceptance). *Fa'ūl* as a verbal noun is rare, and the books of morphology (*taṣrīf*) do not report from it except five words: *wuḍū'* (ablution), *ṭahūr* (purification), *walūʿ* (eagerness), *waqūd* (fuel) and *qabūl* (acceptance), as is related from Sibawayh. To these is added *wazūʿ* with the letter *zāy* marked with a dot, and *hawiyy* with a fatḥah on the *hā'*, meaning falling, and *rasūl* in the sense of message (*risāla*).

Page 71

﴿Wa-lahum﴾ (And for them), that is, in the Hereafter, ﴿ʿadhābun﴾ (a punishment), another, different from what is in this world, namely the punishment of being stoned with meteors, ﴿wāṣibun﴾ (perpetual), that is, lasting, as Qatadah, Ikrimah and Ibn 'Abbas said, and they recited for Abu al-Aswad:

I will not buy with a small praise, whose remaining for a day is blame for the whole of time, perpetually.

Some of them interpreted it as "severe". It was said that the first is the literal meaning of the word, and this is an interpretation of it by its implication. The verse, as you have heard, is like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We have prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze﴾. Abu Hayyan permitted that this punishment be in this world, namely their being constantly stoned and their failure to reach what they intend of eavesdropping on the heavens.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 10 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Except one who snatches a fragment﴾ is an exception of the connected type (istithna' muttasil) from the waw of (yassamma'un, "they listen"), and (man, "one who") is a substitute (badal) for it, according to what al-Zamakhshari and those who follow him have mentioned. Ibn Malik said: when the excepted element is separated from that from which it is excepted, the preferred reading is the accusative, because substitution is for the sake of conformity (tashakkul), and this has been lost through the separation. Abu Hayyan mentioned this in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) here as a second possibility. It has also been said that it is a disconnected exception (munqati') on the basis that (man) is conditional, its answer being the clause introduced by the fa' that follows, but this is not right.

The khatf (snatching) is taking by stealth and quickly, with lightness and speed, while the one from whom it is taken is heedless. The intended meaning is the stealthy snatching of the words of the angels, as the definite form of al-khatfah, with the definite article of prior reference (lam al-'ahd), indicates, since what is meant by it is a specific, known matter. Thus it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). It has also been permitted that it be a direct object (maf'ul bihi), on the basis that the intended meaning is "the word."

al-Hasan and Qatadah read "khittifa" with a kasrah on the kha' and a shaddah on the ta'. Abu Hatim said: it is said that this is the dialect of Bakr ibn Wa'il and Tamim ibn Murr. The original form is ikhtataf; the ta' was made quiescent for assimilation (idgham), and since before it there was a quiescent kha', two quiescent letters met, so the kha' was given a kasrah according to the original form, and the ta' was given a kasrah for harmony with it (ittiba'). The hamzat al-wasl was dropped because it was no longer needed.

It was also read "khattifa" with a fathah on the kha' and a kasrah on the shaddah ta', which Ibn Khalawayh attributed to al-Hasan, Qatadah and 'Isa. This has been regarded as problematic: the fathah on the kha' is sound, as the vowel of the ta' has been transferred onto it, but the kasrah on the ta' has no basis. It has been said in its justification that they transferred the vowel of the ta' onto the kha', dropped the hamzat al-wasl, then changed the ta' and assimilated it, and gave the ta' a kasrah according to the original rule for meeting two quiescent letters. But this, as you see, is weak.

From Ibn 'Abbas it is read "khiftifa" with a kasrah on the kha' and the ta' light (not doubled). According to al-Bahr, the vowel of the kha' was made to follow the vowel of the ta', as they say "na'am" (for "ni'm"). ﴿Then he was pursued by﴾, meaning he followed him and caught up with him, with "atba'a" being one of the verbs that means the same as the triliteral "taba'a," so that it takes one object. ﴿a flaming fire﴾ (shihab) is originally the bright flame of a lit fire. What is meant by it here is the well-known phenomenon in the atmosphere that appears as though a star were falling from the sky. ﴿piercing﴾ (thaqib) means shining, as al-Hasan and Qatadah said: it seems to pierce the air with its light.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Yazid al-Raqqashi that he said: "The devil pierces (the sky) until he emerges from the other side." This was mentioned to Abu Mijlaz, who said: "That is not so; rather its piercing is its light." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Zayd that "al-thaqib" means "the blazing one," which is close to what has preceded.

[Page 72]

He transmitted from al-Suddi that "al-thaqib" means "the burning one." The shuhub (meteors) are not the stars themselves with which the sky has been adorned, for they do not fall; otherwise the adornment of the sky would be diminished, or rather it would not remain at all. Moreover, if the falling object were the stars themselves, in the sense that it is uprooted from its place and hurled at the one who snatches, and is seen, because of the speed of its motion, like a spear of fire, then it would have to land on the earth. And if it is not larger than the earth, then at least what has fallen from the stars since the time the hurling began until today would be much larger than it, so the earth would today be covered with bodies of stars. Observation refutes this; indeed, we have never heard of the fall of the body of a star at all.

The smallest of the stars, according to the Muslim thinkers (al-Islamiyyin), is like a great mountain. According to the philosophers (al-falasifah), they are larger and larger; indeed, the small fixed stars (al-thawabit al-saghar) are in their view larger than the earth. And even if it is maintained that it is hurled until, when its aim is accomplished, it returns to its place, it has been objected: then at that point a terrible sound would have to be heard from its descent, for the meteors reach a place close to the earth. Also, the non-observation of the body of a star descending or ascending rules out the possibility that the star is uprooted and hurled itself.

And if what falls is its light, then light has no harm in it, and the earth is filled with the light of the sun, while its interior is full of devils. Moreover, if what falls is all of its light, then this would entail a diminution of the adornment or its complete disappearance; and if it is only part of its light, then the brightness of the stars would have to change, yet this has not been observed in any of them. As for the matter of its falling itself, or the separation of its light, on the assumption that the fixed stars are in the eighth sphere called the Kursi according to some Muslim thinkers, and that there is nothing in the lowest heaven except the moon, then it is further and further away. The philosophers claim that this is impossible, since they claim that the sphere does not accept tearing and rejoining, along with other matters.

Regarding the meteors, the philosophers claim that they are fine vaporous, smoky particles that reached the sphere of fire, ignited, and turned into a blazing fire. Thus they are sometimes seen extending to the edge of the smoke, then they appear as though they have been extinguished. Sometimes they remain for a time, like comets, and sometimes a soul becomes attached to them, according to what they have detailed. Yet despite all this, they do not say that devils are hurled by them; rather, they deny the account of hurling entirely. The divine texts, however, are a refutation of them.

The closest of the possibilities regarding the meteors is probably that the star emits a ray of its light, and its effect reaches air that has been conditioned in a specific manner, which is thereby able to accept ignition from what falls on it of the star's ray by its specific property, so it ignites, and what is observed of the meteors results. If you wish, you may say: when that air, conditioned in that specific manner, reaches a particular place in the atmosphere, the rays of the stars affect it by what God Most High has deposited in them of that property, so it ignites, and what results, results. The effect of rays is burning upon what is receptive to it, which is undeniable. For we see that when the sunlight is reflected by certain mirrors in a specific manner, it burns what receives it, even if a crystal vessel full of water is placed between the mirror and what receives it.

It is said that God Most High diverts that resulting effect to the devil who eavesdrops, though this can occur even when there is no eavesdropper. It is also possible to say that He, glorified be He, creates the condition by which the air accepts burning in the air that is in the direction of the devil. Perhaps the nearness of the devil to certain specific parts of air is prepared by a property that God created in it, so that He creates that condition in the air near him, even as He, glorified and exalted, creates that condition in some parts of the atmospheric air where there is no devil.

If you wish, you may say: a jet (shu'ubub) of the star's ray emerges, and the marid (rebellious devil) is harmed by it or burned. God, glorified and exalted, is capable of burning with water and watering with fire, and causes are only the occasions for effects, not their agents. All things are ascribed to Him, Most High, directly according to the Ash'arites (followers of al-Ash'ari). None of what has been mentioned entails a diminution of the star's light. And even if it is granted that on some of the possibilities there is a diminution, we say: He, glorified and exalted, creates in the star without interval what replaces what was lost from it. His command, when He wills a thing, is only that He says to it "Be," and it is.

What we have mentioned does not contradict the words of God Most High: ﴿And We have adorned the lowest heaven with lamps and made them missiles against the devils﴾. For making them missiles can be understood as follows: through the falling of rays on the air, as we have described, they produce the meteors, and so they are missiles in that respect. Making them missiles does not depend on their themselves being such by being uprooted from their places and hurled. This is like saying: God Most High made the sun such that it burns some bodies with it. It is indeed true when it burns by the intermediary of certain mirrors and the reflection of its ray onto what is receptive to burning.

Some people have claimed that meteors are fiery flames that arise from particles rising to the sphere of fire, and that these are the missiles. Because they are through the heating of the earth by the stars, the Exalted said: ﴿and made them missiles﴾, using a figurative expression in ascribing the making to them, or in their wording. It is not hidden that the sphere of fire is not something established in the speech of the early generation (al-salaf), and no report about it has come from the Truthful one (peace be upon him).

It has been said: the lamps may be the meteors, which are other than the stars, and the adornment of the sky with lamps does not require that they be in it in reality, since it suffices that they appear so to the eye. It has also been said: the sky may be meant as the direction of the height, which is adorned with lamps and meteors just as it is adorned with stars. This has been objected to on the ground that describing the sky as "the lowest" makes it unlikely that the direction is meant. And the earlier view has been objected to on the ground that the apparent meaning is that the lamps are the stars, and the words of the Exalted ﴿We have indeed adorned the lowest heaven with the adornment of the stars﴾ and His words ﴿And We have adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾ hardly convey anything but one thing. Also, that the well-known meteors should be an adornment of the sky, given their swift passing and disappearance, and given that some people are sometimes astonished by some of them, is not sound. The view that the word "star" may be applied to a meteor by similarity, so that "stars" may include the meteors and the adornment of the sky, as explained just above, has been burdened with much that is open to objection.

Yes, one may say: a star may emit a light which, when it reaches a particular place in the atmosphere, turns into fire and is seen as falling, and nothing is beyond God, glorified and exalted. It may also be said: there are very small stars in the sky that are not visible even through observatories because of their extreme smallness, and these are the ones from which the objects that are hurled are themselves. The words of God Most High ﴿And We have adorned the lowest heaven with lamps and made them missiles against the devils﴾ are of the type "I have a dirham and its half." And the verse ﴿We have adorned the lowest heaven with the adornment of the stars﴾, and ﴿and as a guard﴾, if the meaning is "and as a guard by them," then it falls under this same type; otherwise the matter is easier. So reflect.

It has been disputed whether the one who is struck by a meteor is destroyed by it, or is only harmed without being destroyed. Ibn 'Abbas said that the devils are not killed by the meteor and do not die, but they are burned and made insane (takhbal), meaning that some of their limbs become corrupted. It has also been said that they are destroyed and die, and whenever a meteor strikes one of them who has snatched a word, he tells the one next to him what happened, "such and such," before he is destroyed.

The devils' creation from fire does not preclude the meteor's effect on them, since they are not of pure fire, just as man is not of pure earth, and since strong fire, when it overpowers weak fire, destroys it. In any case, it may not be said: the devils are intelligent, so how could it be conceived that they would return to eavesdropping again and again, when the eavesdropper is destroyed or suffers severe harm? And the continuous falling of meteors is evidence of the continuation of this act on their part. For we answer: we do not grant that this act continues on their part, and the continuation of the falling is not evidence of it, since falling may occur for eavesdropping and may occur for other reasons. We have already pointed out earlier that the air may become conditioned in a specific manner so that it burns because of the rays of the stars, even if there is no eavesdropper there.

It has also been said that the meteors may be seen because of a collision and friction among the airs, from which what you see results, just as lightning results from the friction of clouds, according to what has been related from some of the early generation. The events of the atmosphere are known only to God Most High. So it is possible that they had eavesdropped at first and witnessed what they witnessed, then they stopped, and the meteors continued to occur for the reason mentioned, not because the devils eavesdrop. It is also possible that it occasionally happens to someone among them who is new and did not know what happened to those who eavesdropped before him, or to someone who does not care about harm or death out of love of being called "how bold he is" or "how brave he is," for example, just as many people are seen to advance into battles where they are certain of their destruction, out of love for such a reputation. Perhaps the description of the devil as marid contains something that supports this possibility.

As for what has been said, that the meteor may strike the one who is ascending sometimes and sometimes not, like a wave for a passenger on a ship, and that for this reason they do not desist from it altogether, this is contrary to what is transmitted (al-ma'thur). Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh have transmitted

[p. 74]

Concerning the greatness (of the meteors), Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: "When a shooting star is hurled, it never misses the one it is hurled at."

Furthermore, the possibility mentioned above, that they (the jinn) had stopped (eavesdropping) after the experiment had been confirmed to them, holds only according to what is reported from al-Sha'bi, that the stars were not hurled until the Prophet (ﷺ) was born. When they were hurled after that, the people began to let their livestock roam free and to free their slaves, thinking that it was the Resurrection. They went to 'Abd Yalil the soothsayer, who had gone blind, and informed him of this. He said: "Look: if the stars are the well-known ones, among the wandering planets and the fixed stars, then it is the Hour of Resurrection; otherwise, it is a newly occurring matter." They looked and found that the stars were unfamiliar. Not much time passed before news of the Prophet (ﷺ) reached them.

Ibn al-Jawzi agreed that it did not happen before (the Prophet's birth) in his book al-Muntazam, but he said that it occurred twenty days after his mission (bi'tha). The correct view is that the hurling occurred before the birth of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and it is frequent in the poetry of the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic period). However, it is possible that (the shooting stars) were not driving away the devils at all, or that they drove them away but not entirely, or that they drove them away completely. According to this, the previous possibility does not hold. According to the first of these possibilities, the event on the day of his birth was (the beginning of) their being driven away in this manner; according to the second, (it was) their being driven away completely. (It was also) an intensification of the matter against them, so that their affair would be cut off, their confusion would end, the revelation would be sound, and the proof would be more decisive. The more probable view is that before his birth they were driven away, but not entirely; so eavesdropping still occurred, but rarely, and it was intensified at the beginning of the mission. Accordingly, the report "they were not hurled with stars until the Prophet (ﷺ) was born" means that the hurling did not become frequent. On this basis, other such reports, if authentic, are to be understood. An example is the report transmitted in the biographies (sira) that Iblis used to pierce through the heavens before 'Isa (peace be upon him); when he was sent (as a prophet) or born, he was barred from three heavens; and when the Prophet (ﷺ) was born, he was barred from all of them, and the devils were hurled with stars. Quraysh said: "The Hour has come." 'Utba ibn Rabi'a said: "Look at al-'Ayyuq; if it has been hurled, then the Hour of Resurrection has drawn near; otherwise, it has not." Some said: "The scholars of hadith agree that it occurred before, but it became frequent and was intensified when Islam came. That is why He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They have been filled with a mighty guard and meteors﴾, and He did not say 'they have been guarded'."

In sum, we have no certainty that what falls of meteors in these eras and similar ones are missiles against the devils, and to be certain of this is to speculate about the unseen.

Furthermore, the matter of eavesdropping has been challenged with several objections. Among them: the angels in the heaven are occupied with various kinds of worship; "the heaven creaks, and it has every right to creak; there is not a space of a foot in it without an angel standing, bowing, or prostrating." Then what do the devils steal from them? And if it is said that some of them speak about worldly events, then they are at (the surface of) its convex (outer sphere), while the devils listen beneath its concave side, and between them, as is established in the reports, is a distance of five hundred years; so how can hearing be possible? Especially since the apparent situation is that they do not raise their voices when they speak of such events, since no purpose appears in raising them. And even if one supposes that there is a raising of the voice, the apparent (situation) is that it is not such that it could be heard from a distance of five hundred years. And even if it were in this manner, the sphere of air ends at the sphere of fire, and no sound is heard without air.

It has been answered that the eavesdropping is from the angels of the clouds (mala'ikat al-'anan), who speak among themselves about the worldly events they have been commanded (to report) from the heaven. And (the Qur'anic words) ﴿We touched the heaven﴾ mean "we sought its news." Or (the eavesdropping is) from the angels who descend from the heaven by command, for there are angels at the gates of the heaven, and from the place where they descend they ask them: "Where are you going?" and they inform them. Eavesdropping is not from the angels who are on the convex side of the heaven. As for the matter of the sphere of fire, it is not valid, and the air is not cut off; and the more it is thin and fine, the more it helps in hearing. Moreover, the existence of air is not something on which hearing depends, according to the principles of the Ash'ari school of theology (al-Ash'ariyya); and similarly, excessive distance is not a barrier. The apparent meaning of a report transmitted by Ibn Abi Hatim from 'Ikrima is that the eavesdropping from the angels in the heaven occurred as follows: "When Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, decrees a matter, He speaks, and all the angels fall down prostrate, so the jinn think that a matter is being decreed and they eavesdrop. When the fear is removed from the hearts of the angels, peace be upon them, and they raise their heads, they say: 'What has your Lord said?' They all say: 'The Truth, and He is the Most High, the Great.'"

[p. 75]

And there came in a report transmitted by Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir from Ibrahim al-Taymi: "When the Lord of the Throne wills a matter, the angels hear something like the dragging of a chain over rock, and they are struck senseless. When they rise, they say: 'What has your Lord said?' Whoever Allah wills says: 'The Truth, and He is the Most High, the Great.'" Perhaps after this answer the matter is mentioned in particular among the angels, peace be upon them. The apparent meaning of what has come in some narrations from Ibn 'Abbas, in interpreting al-mala' al-a'la (the highest assembly) as the scribe angels, peace be upon them, also indicates that the eavesdropping is from angels in the heaven, since the scribes are apparently in the heaven. Perhaps there is recited to them from the Preserved Tablet what is recited, and they write it down for some purpose, so the devils are tempted to eavesdrop on something of it. As for the matter of distance, it is like the matter of air; it does not harm this according to the Ash'ari principles. It is also possible to claim that the body of the heaven does not block sound, however dense it may be; and how many properties the philosophers have attributed to the celestial spheres, of which the non-blocking of sound is no stranger.

Among the objections is that the prevention of the devils from ascending to the place where hearing is eavesdropped makes protection from their eavesdropping unnecessary; or (that it would make unnecessary) the command to the angels, peace be upon them, to conceal their speech so that they cannot hear it; or to make their language different from theirs so that they cannot understand their words. It has been answered that the occurrence of the matter as it occurred is a matter of trial, and that it contains wisdoms as well. It is not hidden that a similar objection applies to many things. However, the fact that the Creator is wise, and that He, exalted is His majesty, has observed wisdom in what He created and commanded in the most perfect manner, to the point that it has been said: "There is nothing in possibility more wondrous than what exists" — this resolves the matter, and nothing remains with it except the search for the aspect of wisdom, which is among the things that Allah, the Exalted, bestows by His grace upon whomever of His servants He wills. The discussion of this matter has passed in part, so return to it. And from what is here and what is there, there results what delights the observers and pleases the verifying scholars.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 11:

﴿So ask them for a ruling (istaftihim)﴾ i.e., ask them for information (fa-istakhbir-hum). The root meaning of al-istifta' (seeking a ruling) is seeking information about a matter that has occurred, and from it comes al-fata (the young man), because of the newness of his age. The pronoun refers to the polytheists of Makkah. It has been said that the verse was revealed concerning Abu al-Ashudd ibn Kaladah al-Jumahi, who was given this kunya (teknonym) because of the severity of his strike and his strength, and whose name was Usayd. The fa' is fasihah (connecting, introducing a conditional sense), meaning: if for us there is among the created things what you have heard, or if you have come to know what has passed, then ask the polytheists of Makkah and question them by way of rebuke (tabkit): ﴿Are they the stronger in creation?﴾ i.e., stronger in makeup and firmer in structure, or more difficult to create and harder to bring into being. ﴿Or those whom We have created﴾ from the angels, the heavens, the earth, what is between them, the easts, the stars, the devils, and the piercing meteors. The definiteness of the relative pronoun (ma'rifat al-mawsul) is ahdi (referring to a known antecedent), indicating what has been mentioned before, both explicitly and by implication, and it gives precedence to rational beings over others. The interrogation is taqriri (affirmative, seeking acknowledgment), though it is permitted that it be inkari (denying). In the codex of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) it reads "am min 'adadna" (or those We counted), and this supports the claim of ahd, indeed it decisively confirms it. Al-A'mash read "amana" with the mim lightened and without "am", making it a second taqriri interrogative, so "man" is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, meaning: "Is He who created what We created stronger?" ﴿Indeed We created them from clay that is sticky (tin lazib)﴾ i.e., adhering, as Ibn Jarir and a group reported from Ibn Abbas. In another narration with the wording "multaziq" (clinging), and with this Ibn al-Azraq responded and recited for him the verse of al-Nabighah:

"So do not suppose that good has no evil after it, nor suppose that evil is a blow that does not stick."

It has been said that the meaning is that part of it clings to part, and Ibn Mas'ud explained it so, as Ibn Abi Hatim reported. It refers to good kneading and well-fermented mixing. Ibn al-Mundhir and others reported from Qatadah that it clings to the hand when touched with it. Al-Tabari said: Adam was created from earth, water, air and fire, and when all of this is mixed it becomes sticky clay that adheres to whatever is next to it. Al-lazib in this sense has the meaning of al-lazim (what is necessary/adhering), which is close to what preceded. It has also been read "lazim" with mim in place of ba' and "latib" with ta' in place of za'; the meaning is one. It is reported in al-Bahr from Ibn Abbas that he described al-lazib as al-hurr, i.e., noble and good, and in another narration he said: al-lazib is the good.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujahid that he said: lazib means lazim (adhering) and munin (foul-smelling). Perhaps his description of it as foul-smelling derives from the verse ﴿from black mud, moulded﴾. However, Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas that he said: al-lazib, al-hama' (black mud) and al-tin are one and the same; at first it was dust, then it became foul-smelling black mud, then it became sticky clay, and God Most High created Adam, peace be upon him, from it.

Whatever the case, their creation from sticky clay is either a testimony against them of weakness and softness, since what is made from clay is not described as firm and strong, or an argument against them concerning the matter of resurrection: the sticky clay from which they were created, within the creation of their father Adam (peace be upon him), is dust, so why do they deny that they could be created from it a second time, when they say ﴿When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised?﴾ This is strengthened, according to al-Kashshaf, by what follows of their denial of resurrection.

[Page 77]

Allah's words, ﴿Nay, you wonder﴾, are addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ), though it is also permitted that they be addressed to everyone who hears it. The "nay" (*bal*) is for *idrab* (a shift away from a previous statement), either away from an implied omitted clause that is suggested by ﴿So ask them﴾ and what follows, meaning: they do not acknowledge or respond with what is the truth; rather, you are like one who submits and wonders at those signs. Or it shifts away from the command to ask: meaning, do not ask them, for they are obstinate, and asking will not benefit them; they do not wonder at those signs, rather you are like one who wonders at them. ﴿And they mock﴾ means: while they mock you, your wondering, and what you show them of the signs. It is also permitted that the meaning is: "Nay, you wonder at their denial of resurrection despite these signs, while they mock the matter of resurrection." It has been preferred that the meaning is: "Nay, you wonder at Allah's power over these great creations, and at their denial of resurrection, while they mock your wondering and your affirmation of resurrection."

Some have claimed that what is meant by "those whom We created" is the past nations, but this is nothing, since no mention of these nations has preceded; the mention that preceded was of the angels, peace be upon them, and of the heavens and the earth and what you have heard. Moreover, the particle of sequence (*ḥarf al-ta'qīb*, i.e. *fa*) indicates otherwise. As for the one who says, like the author of *al-Fara'id*, and the majority of the exegetes disagree with him except the Imam, and he gave it this interpretation: when he argued against them with what they acknowledged, that He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and the Lord of the easts, and obliged them with that, and they met it with obstinacy, it was said to them: "Then wait for destruction, as those before you," because you are not stronger in creation than they were. So it was placed in its position: ﴿So ask them: are they stronger in creation?﴾ Allah's words, ﴿Indeed, We created them﴾, are a justification for why they are not stronger in creation, or an evidence for their arrogance, which produces obstinacy.
