He supported this with the indication of the *idrab* and with the dismissal of resurrection after it, because it indicates that it is not connected to what came before the *idrab*. But he overlooked that the wording is not clearly indicative of the obstinacy mentioned and of deserving destruction like the earlier nations. Justifying the negation of being stronger with what was justified is not a valid argument, since it is evident that the earlier ones were stronger in that respect, and there are many such examples in the Mighty Book. As for the *idrab*, it is from asking [them] to the point that someone like you is one who submits and wonders at those signs; therefore He followed it with ﴿and they mock﴾, and made their denial of resurrection one of their mockeries. This was said by the author of *al-Kashf*, so do not be heedless!

Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Sa'dan and Ibn Muqsim read *'ajibtu* (I wonder) with the *tā'* of the first person speaker. It is also narrated from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, Shaqiq and al-A'mash.

Shurayh the judge denied this reading and said: "Allah, the Exalted, does not wonder at anything; only one who does not know wonders." This judge's denial is among what was issued as a legal opinion (*fatwa*) on its non-acceptance, because it stands against a mass-transmitted (*mutawātir*) proof. There is also in a report: "Your Lord wonders at your despair and your despair" (*'ajiba Rabbukum min ilklum wa qunūṭikum*).

The reading has been interpreted as being in the mode of supposition (*al-farḍ*), meaning: if wondering were something that could apply to Me, I would wonder at this state. Or it is interpreted as imagery (*al-takhyīl*), so that Allah, exalted is He, regards their state as a strange matter, and then wondering at it is affirmed for Him, glorified is He. According to the first, the metaphor is imaginative and representational (*takhyīliyya tamthīliyya*), as in their saying: "The wall said to the peg: Why do you split me? He said: Ask the one who hammers me!" According to the second, it is a metonymy and imagery (*makniyya wa takhyīliyya*), as in: "The tongue of the situation speaks of such-and-such." The well-known practice regarding such expressions is to take it as the necessary consequence, so it becomes a *majāz mursal* (a metonymic figure of speech, where a related meaning is intended), and wondering is understood as *istiʿẓām* (regarding something as great), which is seeing a thing as great, i.e. extreme in beauty or ugliness. What is meant here is seeing their state as extreme in ugliness. And the regarding of something as great is not preceded by an emotion that arises in the heart upon witnessing a strange matter, as is imagined, so that it might be said that the mentioned interpretation does not cut off the root of the problem.

Abu Hayyan said: It is interpreted as an attribute of action (*ṣifat fiʿl*) which Allah manifests in the form of the one wondered at, whether in magnification or belittlement, until people become wondering at it. The meaning then is: "Nay, I wonder at their misguidance and the evil of their creed, and I have made it an object of wonder for those who look at it and at what is connected to it of My law and My guidance." Makki and ʿAli ibn Sulayman said: the pronoun in *ʿajibtu* refers to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and the speech is with an implied "say" (*taqdīr al-qawl*), meaning: "Say: nay, I wonder." In my view, if the "say" were supposed after *bal*, it would be better, meaning: "Nay, say: I wonder." What the words of the early scholars (*al-salaf*) indicate is that wondering in us is an emotion that arises in the soul upon ignorance of the cause, and therefore it is said: when the cause becomes apparent, the wondering ceases. But with Allah, the Exalted, it has a meaning that befits His essence, exalted and majestic is He; He alone knows it, so they (the early scholars) do not specify the intended meaning, whereas the later scholars (*al-khalaf*) specify it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 13:

﴿And when they are reminded, they do not remember.﴾ That is, their habit is that when they are admonished with something, they do not take admonition from it; or, that when there is mentioned to them what indicates the truth of the Resurrection (al-hashr), they do not benefit from it, owing to their dullness and their lack of reflection. The indication of continuity (al-istimrar) is drawn from the context of censure. Perhaps the use of "idha" (when) and the conjunction with the past tense supports this. Ibn Hubaysh recited "dhukkirū" (ذُكِرُوا) with the letter kaf lightened (تخفيف الكاف).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 14:

﴿And when they see a sign﴾, i.e., a miracle that points to the truthfulness of the one who admonishes them and calls them away from what they are upon toward what is better; or a miracle that points to the truthfulness of the one who speaks of the resurrection (al-hashr). ﴿They mock﴾, i.e., they exaggerate in mockery and say, "It is nothing but sorcery," or some of them ask others to mock it. It is narrated that Rukana, a man of the polytheists from the people of Makkah, who was among the strongest of people, met the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on a barren mountain where he was tending his sheep. The Messenger ﷺ said to him, "O Rukana, do you see that if I wrestle you down, you will believe in me?" He said, "Yes." So he wrestled him down three times. Then he presented him with some signs; he (peace and blessings be upon him) called upon a tree and it came toward him, but he did not believe. He went to Makkah and said, "O Banu Hashim, you have bewitched your companion to the people of the earth." So this verse was revealed concerning him and those like him. It is also read as "yastasihirun" with the unpointed ha (ḥā'), i.e., they consider them to be sorcery.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 15–16:

﴿And they say: "This is nothing but manifest magic."﴾ That is, the clear signs they see; "manifest magic" means that its being magic is evident in itself.

﴿"When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised?"﴾ That is, some of our parts have become dust and some bones. The mention of dust first is because it is what the parts that are visible turn into. As for "idha" (when), it is either conditional, in which case its answer is omitted and is indicated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿"Shall we indeed be raised?"﴾, meaning "we will be raised," and regarding its governing element there is the well-known discussion. Or it is purely temporal (ẓarfiyyah), in which case it has no answer, and its dependent element is omitted, indicated by that same phrase, but not by it, because what follows "inna" (indeed) and the lam cannot act on what precedes it. That is: "Will we be raised when we have died?" If you wish, supply it as delayed, and the fronting of the temporal phrase serves to strengthen the denial of resurrection by directing it to a state that is utterly contrary to it. Likewise the repetition of the hamza (interrogative particle) is for emphasis and intensification in this matter, and likewise the adornment of the sentence with "inna" (indeed) and the lam serves to stress the denial, not to deny the emphasis, as the apparent wording of the noble text might suggest; for the fronting of the hamza is because it demands initial position. Ibn 'Amir read with the omission of the first hamza, and Nafi', al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read with the omission of the second.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 15–16:

﴿And they say: "This is nothing but manifest magic."﴾ That is, the clear signs they see; "manifest magic" means that its being magic is evident in itself.

﴿"When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised?"﴾ That is, some of our parts have become dust and some bones. The mention of dust first is because it is what the parts that are visible turn into. As for "idha" (when), it is either conditional, in which case its answer is omitted and is indicated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿"Shall we indeed be raised?"﴾, meaning "we will be raised," and regarding its governing element there is the well-known discussion. Or it is purely temporal (ẓarfiyyah), in which case it has no answer, and its dependent element is omitted, indicated by that same phrase, but not by it, because what follows "inna" (indeed) and the lam cannot act on what precedes it. That is: "Will we be raised when we have died?" If you wish, supply it as delayed, and the fronting of the temporal phrase serves to strengthen the denial of resurrection by directing it to a state that is utterly contrary to it. Likewise the repetition of the hamza (interrogative particle) is for emphasis and intensification in this matter, and likewise the adornment of the sentence with "inna" (indeed) and the lam serves to stress the denial, not to deny the emphasis, as the apparent wording of the noble text might suggest; for the fronting of the hamza is because it demands initial position. Ibn 'Amir read with the omission of the first hamza, and Nafi', al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read with the omission of the second.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 17:

﴿Or our forefathers, the earlier ones?﴾ It is a mubtada' (subject) whose khabar (predicate) has been omitted, because the khabar of "inna" (indeed) indicates it. That is: "Or our forefathers, the earlier ones, [are also] resurrected?" The sentence is coordinated with the sentence before it. This is one of the views concerning this type of construction. The apparent meaning of Abu Hayyan's words in his commentary on al-Tashil is that omitting the khabar is obligatory, for he said: Those who adopted this view said: The original in this matter is the coordination of sentences, but when they omitted the khabar because what precedes it indicates it, they put the conjunction particle in its place, and at that time they did not state the omitted khabar verbally, lest it be a combination of the substitute and what it substitutes for. So it resembled the coordination of single words, in that the conjunction particle is followed verbally only by a single word.

The second view is that it is coordinated with the implicit pronoun in the khabar of "inna", if that khabar can bear the pronoun and the pronoun is emphasized, or if there is some separator between it and the coordinated element; otherwise the coordination is weak. Ibn Hisham attributed this view and the one before it to the verifying scholars among the Basrans. But whether it can be applied here without weakness, because of the separation by the interrogative hamza, is a matter for investigation. Abu Hayyan said: The interrogative hamza does not enter upon a coordinated element unless it is a sentence, so that the effect of what precedes the hamza does not apply to what follows it, which is impermissible because the hamza has the right of initial position. The answer is that the hamza here emphasizes the sense of improbability, so in intention it is placed first and enters upon the sentence in reality, but it has been separated from it by what has intervened. This has been examined: a particle is not repeated for emphasis without its governed element, and what is stated in grammar is that the interrogative has initial position without distinction between emphatic and originating uses. Moreover, the hamza being intended to be placed first weakens the consideration of separation by it, especially since it is a single letter, so the separation by it cannot be analogized to the separation by "la" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We did not associate, nor did our forefathers﴾.

The third is that it is coordinated with the position (mahall) of "inna" together with what it governs, and apparently in that case it is in reality coordination of sentences. The fourth is that it is coordinated with the position of the noun of "inna", because it was in the position of nominative before "inna" entered, and apparently in that case it is coordination of single words.

It was objected that the nominative was due to the mubtada' (inception), which is a meaningful (ma'nawi) governing factor, and this has been nullified by a verbal governing factor. It was answered that its existence is as good as non-existence, due to its resemblance to the superfluous particle, in that it does not change the meaning of the sentence but only conveys emphasis. It was also objected that the stated khabar, like "resurrected" in the verse, would then be a khabar about both of them, and the khabar of the mubtada' is raised by the inception, or by the mubtada' itself, or by both, while the khabar of "inna" is raised by "inna"; so two governing factors would act upon one governed element. It was answered that the grammatical governing factors are not real effective agents but are like indicators, so their acting upon one governed element does no harm; and that is as you see, and the full discussion belongs in its proper place. In any case, the preferable view is the earlier one, that it is a mubtada' whose khabar has been omitted, and Abu Hayyan said: The proponents of the last three views agree on the permissibility of the first view, and this supports the claim of its preferability. Whatever the case, the intention of the disbelievers is to increase the improbability of their forefathers' resurrection, on the basis that they are more ancient, so their resurrection is more remote according to their deficient intellects.

Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Ibn 'Amir, and Nafi' in one narration, and Qalun, read "aw" with a sukun, on the basis that it is a conjunction particle, and in it the four possibilities apply, except that coordination with the pronoun in this reading is weak, because there is no separation by anything at all.

Say, "Yes, and you will be resurrected, you and your forefathers of old," and the address in His words, Glorified is He, "while you are abased" (﴿وأنْتُمْ داخِرُونَ﴾), is to them and to their forefathers by way of predominance (taghlib). The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the subject of what is indicated by "Yes" (﴿نَعَمْ﴾), meaning: you will all be resurrected while you are abased and humbled. This circumstantial clause is an addition to the answer, similar to what occurred in his answer, upon him be blessings and peace, to Ubayy ibn Khalaf when he came with a bone that had crumbled, rubbing it with his hand and saying: "O Muhammad, do you think God will give life to this after it has crumbled?" So the Prophet ﷺ said to him, according to what is in some of the narrations, "Yes, and He will resurrect you and admit you into Hell."

Many have said: this is of the stylistic method of wisdom (al-uslub al-hakim). It has been objected that counting the addition as such does not accord with what has been established in the sciences of meaning (al-ma'ani), and although that would be a new terminology, there is no dispute over terminology. He confined the answer regarding their denial of resurrection to this extent, and no proof was established for it, relying on what precedes that indicates its permissibility in His words, Glorified is He, "so ask them (﴿فاسْتَفْتِهِمْ﴾) etc.," even though the one informing has known its truth through his miracles occurring in the external world, which His words indicate, Glorified is He, "And when they see a sign (﴿وإذا رَأوْا آيَةً﴾) etc." Their mockery and their calling it sorcery does not harm one who seeks the truth, and the claim that this is for the sufficiency of the establishment of the proof against them on the Day of Resurrection is worthless.

Ibn Wththab and al-Kisa'i read "na'im" with a kasra on the ayn, and this is a dialect form of it. It is also read "qala" (﴿قالَ﴾), i.e., God Most High or His Messenger ﷺ.

The pronoun refers to the resurrection (al-ba'tha) understood from what precedes it. It has also been said that it refers to the raising (al-ba'th), and the feminine form is due to the predicate.

Zajrah means a shout, from the verb zajara, "the shepherd shouted at his sheep." Here it means the second blowing of the Trumpet (al-Sur). Since their resurrection arises from the zajrah, the zajrah is named as the resurrection itself, as a metonymy (majaz). The fa' is either the answer to an implied conditional clause, or it expresses cause for an implied prohibition. That is, the meaning is: "If it is so, then the resurrection is only one shout," or: "Do not find it difficult, for it is only one shout." Al-Zajjaj allowed that the fa' is explanatory and detailed (lil-tafsir wal-tafsil), and that what follows it explains the resurrection. This was criticised: the explanation of "resurrection" in their speech has no basis, and the explanation given in the answer is not stated explicitly. Explaining what is alluded to by "na'am" (yes) is also something not known.

The apparent view is that it is an explanation of what was alluded to by "na'am," and this is equivalent to what was stated, especially since there is mentioned what strengthens its being present, namely the circumstantial clause. My certainty is lacking regarding the absence of a precedent for such explanation.

Abu Hayyan disputed the assumption of the conditional clause. He said: there is no necessity that calls for it, and the conditional is not omitted while its answer remains, except when the verb is in the jussive after what is described as an answer to a command or prohibition, and what is mentioned with them, according to the view of some of them. As for beginning a statement with it, its omission is not permitted. The majority hold otherwise, and the truth is with them. This sentence is either part of what was said, or it is the beginning of a statement from Him, may He be exalted and glorified.

﴿and then they will be looking on﴾: that is, then they will be standing up from their resting places, alive, seeing as they used to see in the world. Or it means they will be waiting for what will be done to them and what they will be commanded.

["And they will say"] — the subject is "those who are raised" (al-mab'uthun), and the past tense form is used to express the certainty of its occurrence.

﴿And they will say: "Woe to us! This is the Day of Recompense."﴾

"Woe to us" (ya waylana) means: O our destruction, come, for this is the time of your arrival.

﴿This is the Day of Recompense﴾ is a resumed statement from them, explaining the reason for their calling out "woe."

Al-din (ad-din, here "recompense") carries the sense of requital, as in the saying "As you judge, so you will be judged" (kama tadin tudan), meaning: this is the day on which we are repaid for our deeds. They knew this because in the world they used to hear that they would be resurrected, called to account, and recompensed for their deeds. When they witnessed the resurrection, they became certain of what comes after it as well.

This is the statement of the Most High: ﴿This is the Day of Judgment (al-Fasl) which you used to deny﴾. It is the speech of the angels, answering them by way of rebuke and reproach. It has also been said that it is the speech of some of them to others. Abu Hatim paused at ﴿Woe to us!﴾ and took what follows as the speech of Allah the Most High, or the speech of the angels — peace be upon them — to them, as though they replied to them that wailing and lamentation will not benefit them. Al-Fasl means the judgment (al-qada'), or the separation between the good-doer and the wrongdoer, and the distinguishing of each from the other without judgment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 22–23:

﴿Gather those who did wrong﴾ This is an address from God, exalted is He, to the angels, or from some of the angels to others.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, that the angels say to the zabaniyah (the guardians of Hell): "Gather..." etc. It is a command to gather the wrongdoers from their various places to the place of reckoning, and it was said [that it means] from the place of standing to the Hellfire. The context (sibaq) and the flow of the passage (siyaq) support the first view.

﴿And their spouses﴾ ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Mani' in his Musnad, al-Hakim, who graded it sound, and a group [of scholars], by way of al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir, from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "Their spouses" means their likes, those who are like them: the practitioners of usury are gathered with the practitioners of usury, the adulterers with the adulterers, and the drinkers of wine with the drinkers of wine. A group related from Ibn ʿAbbas, in one wording, "their likes (ashbahahum)," and in another, "their counterparts (nuẓaraʾahum)." This interpretation of "spouses" is also narrated from Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and ʿIkrimah. The root meaning of zawj (spouse) is "that which accompanies," like the two members of a pair of shoes; it was then applied to its necessary consequence, which is "one who is similar." It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "That is, their disbelieving women," and al-Rummani preferred this view. It was also said: "their companions from the devils," and this is narrated from al-Dahhak. The waw is for conjunction, and it was also permitted that it be for accompaniment (ma'iyyah). ʿIsa ibn Sulayman al-Hijazi read "wa-azwājuhum" with the nominative case, as a conjunction upon the pronoun in ﴿did wrong﴾ (according to al-Bahr), meaning: "and their spouses did wrong."

You know the weakness of conjoining upon a pronoun in the nominative in such a construction, and the reading is anomalous.

﴿And what they used to worship besides God﴾ — that is, idols and the like. Their gathering with them serves to increase their regret and humiliation. What has been said, that it is general to every object of worship, including the angels, the Messiah and ʿUzayr, peace be upon them, but some of them are excluded by His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the good has preceded from Us﴾ — the verse.

It was said that "mā" is a reference to idols and images, so it is only for non-rational things, since the discussion concerns polytheists who worship those. It was said that "mā" is on its general sense, and idols and the like are not included, since all polytheists only worshipped the devils who led them to worship those. This interpretation does not fit with explaining "their spouses" as "their companions from the devils," but with this restriction it is closer. In this conjunction there is an indication that those who did wrong are the polytheists, and they are the most deserving of this description, for polytheism is indeed a great wrong.

﴿So guide them to the path of the Blazing Fire﴾ — that is, show them its way and make them see it. By "al-Jahim" is meant the Fire, and it is also applied to one of its levels. It derives from al-juhmah, the intensity of the blazing of a fire. The use of "path" and "guidance" is sarcastic toward them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 22–23:

﴿Gather those who did wrong﴾ This is an address from God, exalted is He, to the angels, or from some of the angels to others.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, that the angels say to the zabaniyah (the guardians of Hell): "Gather..." etc. It is a command to gather the wrongdoers from their various places to the place of reckoning, and it was said [that it means] from the place of standing to the Hellfire. The context (sibaq) and the flow of the passage (siyaq) support the first view.

﴿And their spouses﴾ ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Mani' in his Musnad, al-Hakim, who graded it sound, and a group [of scholars], by way of al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir, from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "Their spouses" means their likes, those who are like them: the practitioners of usury are gathered with the practitioners of usury, the adulterers with the adulterers, and the drinkers of wine with the drinkers of wine. A group related from Ibn ʿAbbas, in one wording, "their likes (ashbahahum)," and in another, "their counterparts (nuẓaraʾahum)." This interpretation of "spouses" is also narrated from Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and ʿIkrimah. The root meaning of zawj (spouse) is "that which accompanies," like the two members of a pair of shoes; it was then applied to its necessary consequence, which is "one who is similar." It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "That is, their disbelieving women," and al-Rummani preferred this view. It was also said: "their companions from the devils," and this is narrated from al-Dahhak. The waw is for conjunction, and it was also permitted that it be for accompaniment (ma'iyyah). ʿIsa ibn Sulayman al-Hijazi read "wa-azwājuhum" with the nominative case, as a conjunction upon the pronoun in ﴿did wrong﴾ (according to al-Bahr), meaning: "and their spouses did wrong."

You know the weakness of conjoining upon a pronoun in the nominative in such a construction, and the reading is anomalous.

﴿And what they used to worship besides God﴾ — that is, idols and the like. Their gathering with them serves to increase their regret and humiliation. What has been said, that it is general to every object of worship, including the angels, the Messiah and ʿUzayr, peace be upon them, but some of them are excluded by His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the good has preceded from Us﴾ — the verse.

It was said that "mā" is a reference to idols and images, so it is only for non-rational things, since the discussion concerns polytheists who worship those. It was said that "mā" is on its general sense, and idols and the like are not included, since all polytheists only worshipped the devils who led them to worship those. This interpretation does not fit with explaining "their spouses" as "their companions from the devils," but with this restriction it is closer. In this conjunction there is an indication that those who did wrong are the polytheists, and they are the most deserving of this description, for polytheism is indeed a great wrong.

﴿So guide them to the path of the Blazing Fire﴾ — that is, show them its way and make them see it. By "al-Jahim" is meant the Fire, and it is also applied to one of its levels. It derives from al-juhmah, the intensity of the blazing of a fire. The use of "path" and "guidance" is sarcastic toward them.

And ﴿stop them﴾, meaning hold them at the place of standing, ﴿for indeed they are questioned﴾ about their beliefs and their deeds.

In a hadith: "The feet of a servant will not move [on the Day of Judgment] until he is asked about five things: about his youth, how he spent it; about his life, how he spent it; about his wealth, from where he acquired it and how he spent it; and about his knowledge, what he did with it." 

From Ibn Mas'ud: they will be asked about "There is no god but Allah." And also from him: they will be asked about drinking cold water, in mockery of them.

Some of the Imamiyyah (the Twelver Shi'a) narrated from Ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas: they will be asked about the guardianship (wilayah) of Ali, may God honour his face. They also narrated it from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. The most preferable of these views is that the questioning is about beliefs and deeds, and the foremost of these is "There is no god but Allah," and among the most important of them is the guardianship of Ali, may God honour his face, and likewise the guardianship of his brothers, the rightly-guided caliphs, may God be pleased with them all.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that the holding back for questioning comes after they have been guided to ﴿the path of Hellfire﴾, in the sense of making them know it and pointing them to it, not in the sense of making them enter it and reach it. It has also been permitted that ﴿the path of Hellfire﴾ is their route to it from their graves to their abode, and it is extended, so the stopping may occur in one part of it after another part. There is in this some remoteness. It has been said that the stopping for questioning is before the matter mentioned, and the conjunction "wa" (and) does not necessarily imply sequence. It has also been said that the stopping is after the matter, when they arrive at the Fire, and the questioning is about what they utter.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?﴾ That is, one of you does not help another. The address is to them and their gods, or to them alone; that is, "What is the matter with you that one of you does not help another, as you used to claim in the world?" It has been narrated that Abu Jahl said on the day of Badr: "We are a united, victorious host." The postponement of this question until that time is because it is the time of the execution of the punishment, when the need for help is most intense, the state of the cutting off of hope is present, and rebuke and reproach at that time are more striking in their impact and effect. It has also been said: the question about this is at the place of reckoning, after their account has been settled, and the command to guide them to the Hellfire is as though the angels, peace be upon them, when they were commanded to guide them to the Fire and direct them towards it, hastened to do what they were commanded. So it was said to them: ﴿Halt them, for they are to be questioned.﴾ What appears more likely to me is that the command to guide them to the Hellfire comes only after the proof has been established against them and their excuses have been cut off, and that is after their reckoning. The conjunction of (guide them) with (gather them) by the particle fa' (then/so) indicates the speed with which their reckoning takes place. As for their question, "What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?", the most fitting view is that it occurs after the realisation of what calls for mutual help, and that is only after the reckoning and the command to take them to the Fire. So perhaps the halting for this question is at the beginning of their being directed towards the Fire. And God Most High knows best. ʿĪsā (Ibn ʿUmar) read ﴿annahum﴾ with a fatḥa on the hamza, with the estimate of ﴿li-annahum﴾ (because they). Al-Bazzi, from Ibn Kathir, read ﴿lā tatanāṣarūn﴾ with two tāʾs without idghām (assimilation), and it was also read with idghām of one of them into the other.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verses 26–27:

﴿Indeed, they today are surrendering (mustaslimun)﴾ — submitting, yielding to their helplessness and to the closing of every means of escape open to them. The root meaning of istislam (surrender, submission) is seeking safety, and yielding is necessarily connected with this in common usage; for this reason the word was applied to it. Or [the meaning is] mutasalimun (mutually yielding), as if each of them surrenders the other to destruction and abandons him. It has also been permitted that the particle of turning away (al-idrab) refers to the content of what precedes it, meaning: they do not dispute about standing (before the Lord) and other matters, but rather they yield or are forsaken. Or [it refers] to His, glorified is He, statement ﴿You will not help one another﴾, meaning: none of them is able to help another, but rather they are yielding to the punishment or forsaken. ﴿And they will turn to one another﴾ — they are the followers and the misleading leaders, or the disbelievers among mankind and their jinn companions. This was narrated from Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. ﴿They will question one another﴾ — some of them ask others with a question of rebuke, in the manner of contention and disputation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verses 26–27:

﴿Indeed, they today are surrendering (mustaslimun)﴾ — submitting, yielding to their helplessness and to the closing of every means of escape open to them. The root meaning of istislam (surrender, submission) is seeking safety, and yielding is necessarily connected with this in common usage; for this reason the word was applied to it. Or [the meaning is] mutasalimun (mutually yielding), as if each of them surrenders the other to destruction and abandons him. It has also been permitted that the particle of turning away (al-idrab) refers to the content of what precedes it, meaning: they do not dispute about standing (before the Lord) and other matters, but rather they yield or are forsaken. Or [it refers] to His, glorified is He, statement ﴿You will not help one another﴾, meaning: none of them is able to help another, but rather they are yielding to the punishment or forsaken. ﴿And they will turn to one another﴾ — they are the followers and the misleading leaders, or the disbelievers among mankind and their jinn companions. This was narrated from Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. ﴿They will question one another﴾ — some of them ask others with a question of rebuke, in the manner of contention and disputation.

﴿They will say﴾ is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), as if it were said: "How do they question one another?" So it is said: "They say," meaning the followers to the leaders, or the disbelievers in general to their companions. ﴿Indeed you used to come to us﴾ in the world ﴿from the right﴾, meaning from the direction and side of goodness, so that you would forbid us from it and turn us away from it. This is the view of Qatadah. Because the right side was honoured in the Jahiliyyah and in Islam, in this world and the next, it was borrowed for the direction of goodness by a clear, actualised metaphor (isti'ara tasrihiyya tahqiqiyya). The right (yamin) was made a metaphor for the direction of goodness, even though it is itself a metaphor. Therefore this is a metaphor upon a metaphor (majaz 'ala al-majaz), because the direction of goodness, through its widespread usage, has come to resemble a literal meaning, and so a metaphor upon a metaphor is permissible in it, as they said regarding the word "masafah" (distance). Originally it refers to the place of smelling, since it derives from "saffa al-turab" (he smelled the dust). When a guide was unsure of the path, he would take some dust and smell it to know whether the road had been travelled or not. Then it was used as an expression for the distance between two places, and then it was borrowed for the difference between two statements. There is no distance there. Some scholars have preferred to interpret the speech as a metaphorical image (isti'ara tamthiliyya), and to consider the figurative usage to lie in the whole phrase ﴿you used to come to us from the right﴾, meaning "you used to prevent us and turn us away from goodness." Thus the statement is free from the claim of a metaphor upon a metaphor. It seems that the intended meaning of goodness is faith in what must be believed. It has also been permitted that the intended meaning is the goodness that the misguiders claim to be good, and that the meaning is: "You used to come to us from the direction of goodness, and you claimed that what you were upon was good and the true religion, so you deceived us and led us astray." This has been related from al-Zajjaj.

Al-Juba'i said: The meaning is: "You used to come to us from the direction of sincere counsel, blessing and good fortune, and you encouraged us to what you were upon, so you led us astray." This is close to what came before. They also permitted that the right (yamin) be a metonymy by a general relation (majaz mursal) for power and force, since it is described as strong, and through it strikes are delivered. So it is as if the place was used for the state, or the cause for the effect. It is also possible that this is by way of metaphor, likening power to the right side in precedence and the like. The meaning is: "Indeed you used to come to us through power and force, and you approached us through authority and dominance, until you drove us to error and compelled us to it." This is the view of al-Farra'. It is also possible that the right (yamin) is literal, meaning an oath. The meaning of their coming to them from it is that they would come to them swearing to them that what they were upon of falsehood was true. The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and "'an" has the meaning of "ba'" (with/by), as in His saying, ﴿nor does he speak from desire﴾ (53:3). Or it is a adverbial phrase of loose attachment (zarf laghw), but this is distant. Even more distant is to interpret "yamin" as desire and passion, because the direction of the right is the place of the liver, and this contradicts what has been related from some scholars: whoever is approached by Satan from the right, Satan comes to him from the side of religion, confusing the truth for him; whoever is approached from the left, Satan comes to him from the side of desires; whoever is approached from in front of him, Satan comes to him through denial of the Resurrection, reward and punishment; and whoever is approached from behind him, Satan makes him fear poverty for himself and for those he leaves behind, so he does not maintain ties of kinship and does not pay zakah.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 29–30:

﴿Qālū﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istinaf) in the same style as what preceded it, meaning: the leaders said, or the companions (qurana') said, in their reply, by way of idrab (a turning away from, and rejection of, what they had said to them): ﴿Nay, you were not believers﴾. This is a denial of their having misled them; that is, you misled yourselves into disbelief, and you were not believers in your own essence, not that we misled you. Their statement ﴿And we had no authority over you﴾ means: no compulsion or domination by which we could strip you of your choice. ﴿Rather, you were a transgressing people﴾, exceeding the limit in disobedience, choosing it and persisting in it. This is another answer, a concessive one (taslimi), assuming that they did mislead them: they did not compel them to it; they only invited them to it, and they responded by their own choice, because what they were invited to matched their desires. It is said: all of this is one single answer, whose essential meaning is: you characterised yourselves with disbelief without being compelled to it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 29–30:

﴿Qālū﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istinaf) in the same style as what preceded it, meaning: the leaders said, or the companions (qurana') said, in their reply, by way of idrab (a turning away from, and rejection of, what they had said to them): ﴿Nay, you were not believers﴾. This is a denial of their having misled them; that is, you misled yourselves into disbelief, and you were not believers in your own essence, not that we misled you. Their statement ﴿And we had no authority over you﴾ means: no compulsion or domination by which we could strip you of your choice. ﴿Rather, you were a transgressing people﴾, exceeding the limit in disobedience, choosing it and persisting in it. This is another answer, a concessive one (taslimi), assuming that they did mislead them: they did not compel them to it; they only invited them to it, and they responded by their own choice, because what they were invited to matched their desires. It is said: all of this is one single answer, whose essential meaning is: you characterised yourselves with disbelief without being compelled to it.

The saying of theirs, ﴿So the word of our Lord has come into effect against us; indeed we are to taste (the punishment)﴾, is a consequence (tafri') drawn from the explicit statements preceding it, namely that those opponents of theirs did not believe and that they were a transgressing people in themselves; and from what their quarrelling required and indicated, namely the disbelief of these responders and their misguidance within themselves, in relation to those transgressors. The pronouns of the plural refer to both groups. So it is as if they said: "Because all of us, in ourselves, were not believers, and were a transgressing people, the word of our Lord and Creator, who knows what we are and what our predisposition (isti'dad) requires, has become binding upon us, and His threat has been confirmed against us, that we are without doubt to taste His punishment, mighty and majestic." Their meaning is that the source of the quarrel, which in reality is the punishment, is a decreed matter from which there is no escape, and that it has been made to follow for each of us because of a state that he himself is in, which his predisposition required and which he performed by his own choice. Therefore let none of us blame another, but let each of us blame himself. They placed themselves together with them in this, for the sake of intensifying the closing of the door of blame and quarrel against those people.

The conjunction fa- in their words ﴿so we led you astray﴾ (fa-aghwaynākum), meaning fa-da'awnākum ilā al-ghayy (so we called you to error), indicates that the call is a consequence of the truth of the threatened punishment against them, not mere sequence, as some have said. The causation of this for the call is in terms of its external existence being connected to them, so that it was a consequence of that in reality, and not in terms of their issuing and carrying it out upon the addressees being with that in view, as final causes are considered in voluntary acts. This is because it is apparent that the leaders of disbelief did not know in the world that the threat against them was true. Indeed, it is not far-fetched that the companion devils knew this from their father. Likewise, calling their summons to what they summoned them to "leading astray" (ighwā') means a call to error (al-ghayy), on the basis that the aforementioned statement from the leaders is in terms of the reality that became apparent to them on the Day of Resurrection. The same applies to their words ﴿indeed we were ourselves astray﴾ (innā kunnā ghāwīn), on the basis that they only knew this on the day of mutual questioning and contention. The sentence is a resumptive (mustaʼnafa) sentence giving the reason for what precedes it. It is as if what the consequence implied, in terms of the connection of the leading astray to the addressees, is this, and this is in terms of the leading astray itself proceeding from them, which is an explicit statement of what is derived from the previous consequence.

It is permissible that it be an indication of the reason for the consequence of their leading them astray upon the truth of the threat against them, which is their love that those addressees should be characterized by something like what they themselves were characterized by of error, and that they should be like them in it. The summary of their speech is that there is nothing from us toward you, in actual truth, except the love that you be like us, and this is not harmful to you; what is harmful is the evil of your choice and the ugliness of your predisposition. That is what the truth of the threat against you and the establishment of this punishment for you is consequent upon. It is also permissible to say that they negated faith and true belief from themselves, and affirmed for them transgression and exceeding the limit in disobedience, in that they did not pay attention to what necessitates correct belief despite its abundance and clarity. They consequently connected the truth of the threat, along with what the investigation requires, and they made it a consequence of both matters together: that they called them to error, meaning disbelief, because of believing in a corrupt matter, not merely the absence of faith, that is, the absence of assent to what must be assented to without believing in another matter by which one becomes a disbeliever. They indicated the reason for this consequence, which is the love that they should be like them. So it is as if they said: you were abandoning true belief, not paying attention to it despite the clarity and abundance of its proofs, and we were all deserving of the threat, so we called you to what we ourselves were upon of corrupt belief, out of love that you be a model for ourselves. This is like their words ﴿Our Lord, these are the ones we led astray; we led them astray just as we ourselves went astray﴾. Al-Raghib said: it is an announcement from them that we have done to them the utmost that a person could do to his friend, of what he wants for himself; that is, we gave them what we had and made them a model for ourselves. On this basis, ﴿so we led you astray﴾ and ﴿indeed we were ourselves astray﴾ are as stated. It is permissible on this interpretation that ﴿so we led you astray﴾ be a consequence of an explanation of the state of the addressees, in terms of their not being believers, their being established as transgressors, and their turning away from the signs. Their words ﴿so the word has come true against us﴾ ... etc. are a parenthetical interjection to hasten the clarification that what the two groups are in is a decreed matter, in which talk, dispute, contention and argument are of no benefit. It is also permissible on this view that the plural pronoun in ﴿against us﴾ ... etc. refers to the leaders or the companions, not to what includes them and the addressees. By this they indicated that what they are in suffices in place of blame, and it hints at an increase in their punishment. It is not hidden that permitting the parenthetical interjection is not free from objection, and permitting that the pronoun in ﴿against us﴾ etc. refers to the leaders or the companions proceeds on a different possibility, so reflect.

In any case, their words ﴿indeed we shall taste﴾ (innā la-dhā'iqūn) are the words of their Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and His threat to them, glory be to Him. Had it been reported as is said, it would have been said: "indeed you shall taste," but He shifted to the first-person speaker form because they are speaking this of themselves. Similar to it is the saying of the poet:

Hawazin has claimed that my wealth is little, but do I have any wealth other than what I have spent?

Had he reported their words, he would have said: "your wealth is little." And from it is the saying of the one who makes another swear to the one swearing: "swear that I will certainly go out, and you will certainly go out." The hamza (in akhruja) is for reporting the words of the one swearing, and the ta' (in takhruja) is for the attention of the one being made to swear toward the one being made to swear. Some eminent scholars said: the word of the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, is His word, glory be to Him and exalted: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and with those among them who follow you, all together﴾. The connection according to what preceded is more apparent.

﴿"Fa-innahum"﴾ means the two groups who question one another. The discourse is a consequence of what has been explained of their condition. ”Yawma'idhin" means "on the day when they question one another," and what is meant is the Day of Resurrection. ﴿They will be sharing in the punishment﴾, just as they shared in misguidance. It has been affirmed that those who misguided others will receive greater punishment, in return for their own burdens and the burdens of those like them. Sharing does not require equality. ﴿Indeed, that is how We deal with the criminals﴾ means: in the same manner as that wondrous act which the wisdom of the legislation requires. "The criminals" means the polytheists, in keeping with His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, when it was said to them﴾ through invitation and instruction ﴿"There is no god but Allah," they were arrogant﴾ toward accepting it.

Regarding the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of this noble formula, there are several opinions.

The first is that the majestic name (Allah) is in the nominative case as a substitute (badal, a grammatical substitution or apposition) for the subject of "la" (no), based on its original position, which is the nominative as a subject. It is a partial substitution (badal ba'd min kull), and "illa" (except) dispenses with the need for a pronoun to link them. If we say that the substitute in exception constructions is a separate category, distinct from other types of substitution, then much of the dispute and argument that circulates among the grammarians on this view is dispelled. On this view, the predicate is, according to the majority, omitted, and the commonly cited estimate for it is "existent" (mawjud). The noble formula stands in opposition to the polytheists, who only claim the existence of multiple gods and do not say merely that they are possible. Moreover, negating existence in this context entails negating possibility, and similarly, negating possibility for anyone other than Him, mighty and majestic, entails the actual existence of Him, exalted.

It has also been permitted to estimate the predicate as "deserving of worship" (mustahiqq li-l-'ibadah). Negating the deservingness of worship entails negating plurality. However, this estimate does not hold if "god" (ilah) is interpreted as "one deserving of worship," as is evident.

Al-Bazili preferred to estimate the predicate as coming after "illa Allah," on the basis that estimating it before would give the impression that the noun is an exceptive construction that is "emptied" (mustathna mufarragh) from a pronoun in the predicate. This is impermissible according to the verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun), though some permitted it. This is the second opinion. The third, attributed to the Kufans, is that "illa" is conjunctive (ʿatifa), and the majestic name is coordinated with "ilah" on the basis of its position. According to them, "illa" functions like the conjunctive "la" in that what follows it differs from what precedes it, except that "la" negates an affirmation and "illa" affirms a negation. The fourth opinion is that the noble name is the predicate, and "la" has no governing effect on it according to the view of Sibawayh, who held that the predicate is raised by whatever raised it before the particle entered. On this view, there is no need for "la" to govern definite nouns, which is necessary according to other views. This opinion has been deemed weak, as has the implication that a particular term is a predicate of a general term.

That the statement is intended to negate generality and to restrict it to one of the individuals covered by the general term does not help, because this "la" is, according to the majority, one of the particles that alter the subject and predicate (nawasikh al-mubtada' wa-l-khabar).

The fifth opinion is that "illa" means "ghayr" (other than). Together with its noun, the noble name, exalted is His name, it is an adjective (sifa) of the noun of "la" by virtue of its position. The meaning is: there is no god other than Allah, exalted, in existence. There is no flaw in this grammatically, but the flaw, as has been said, lies in the meaning, because the intent is to negate divinity from anyone other than Him, exalted, and to affirm it for Him, glorified. With the exceptive construction, both points are understood from the explicit statement. On this view, the explicit statement conveys only the negation of divinity from anyone other than Him, exalted, without affirming it for Him, mighty and majestic. Taking implication (mafhum) into account is not agreed upon, especially implication of the title (mafhum al-laqab), which only the subtle scholars and some Hanbalis have held.

The sixth opinion, attributed to al-Zamakhshari, is that "la ilaha" is in the position of the predicate and "illa Allah" is in the position of the subject. The original form is "Allah is a god," but when it is intended to restrict the attribute to the one described, the predicate is fronted and the subject is linked with "illa," since the restricted element is what follows "illa," and the restricted element is what occurs within the context of negation. When the subject is linked with "illa," the predicate must precede it, as is established in its proper place. There is some strain in this view, and it also entails that the predicate is indeclinable with "la," whereas "la" only makes indeclinable the subject. Moreover, if the matter were as stated, there would be no basis for the accusative case of the noun following "illa." Some have permitted this in this order, and abandoning their speech for a single view, if you adopt it, you will find no second one in support of it.

It has been affirmed that those who misguided others will receive greater punishment, in return for their own burdens and the burdens of those like them. Sharing does not require equality. ﴿Indeed, that is how We deal with the criminals﴾ means: in the same manner as that wondrous act which the wisdom of the legislation requires. "The criminals" means the polytheists, in keeping with His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, when it was said to them﴾ through invitation and instruction ﴿"There is no god but Allah," they were arrogant﴾ toward accepting it.

Regarding the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of this noble formula, there are several opinions.

The first is that the majestic name (Allah) is in the nominative case as a substitute (badal, a grammatical substitution or apposition) for the subject of "la" (no), based on its original position, which is the nominative as a subject. It is a partial substitution (badal ba'd min kull), and "illa" (except) dispenses with the need for a pronoun to link them. If we say that the substitute in exception constructions is a separate category, distinct from other types of substitution, then much of the dispute and argument that circulates among the grammarians on this view is dispelled. On this view, the predicate is, according to the majority, omitted, and the commonly cited estimate for it is "existent" (mawjud). The noble formula stands in opposition to the polytheists, who only claim the existence of multiple gods and do not say merely that they are possible. Moreover, negating existence in this context entails negating possibility, and similarly, negating possibility for anyone other than Him, mighty and majestic, entails the actual existence of Him, exalted.

It has also been permitted to estimate the predicate as "deserving of worship" (mustahiqq li-l-'ibadah). Negating the deservingness of worship entails negating plurality. However, this estimate does not hold if "god" (ilah) is interpreted as "one deserving of worship," as is evident.

Al-Bazili preferred to estimate the predicate as coming after "illa Allah," on the basis that estimating it before would give the impression that the noun is an exceptive construction that is "emptied" (mustathna mufarragh) from a pronoun in the predicate. This is impermissible according to the verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun), though some permitted it. This is the second opinion. The third, attributed to the Kufans, is that "illa" is conjunctive (ʿatifa), and the majestic name is coordinated with "ilah" on the basis of its position. According to them, "illa" functions like the conjunctive "la" in that what follows it differs from what precedes it, except that "la" negates an affirmation and "illa" affirms a negation. The fourth opinion is that the noble name is the predicate, and "la" has no governing effect on it according to the view of Sibawayh, who held that the predicate is raised by whatever raised it before the particle entered. On this view, there is no need for "la" to govern definite nouns, which is necessary according to other views. This opinion has been deemed weak, as has the implication that a particular term is a predicate of a general term.

That the statement is intended to negate generality and to restrict it to one of the individuals covered by the general term does not help, because this "la" is, according to the majority, one of the particles that alter the subject and predicate (nawasikh al-mubtada' wa-l-khabar).

The fifth opinion is that "illa" means "ghayr" (other than). Together with its noun, the noble name, exalted is His name, it is an adjective (sifa) of the noun of "la" by virtue of its position. The meaning is: there is no god other than Allah, exalted, in existence. There is no flaw in this grammatically, but the flaw, as has been said, lies in the meaning, because the intent is to negate divinity from anyone other than Him, exalted, and to affirm it for Him, glorified. With the exceptive construction, both points are understood from the explicit statement. On this view, the explicit statement conveys only the negation of divinity from anyone other than Him, exalted, without affirming it for Him, mighty and majestic. ﴿Nay, he has brought the truth and confirmed the messengers.﴾ This is a refutation of them and a denial of their claim, by making clear that what he (ﷺ) brought, namely monotheism (tawhid), is the established truth upon which proof has been established and on which all the messengers have agreed. So where are poetry and madness from his exalted station (ﷺ)?

﴿Indeed you﴾ (will taste the punishment), for what you did of associating partners with God, denying the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and arrogance, ﴿will surely taste the painful punishment﴾. The shift (al-iltifat, a change in the grammatical person of address) serves to show the full extent of anger against them, by addressing them directly with this threat and by disregarding them, which is fitting for the arrogant. Abu al-Samal and Aban, through a transmission from Asim, read "la-dha'iqu al-'adhaba" with the accusative. This is done on the basis that the omission of the nun is for lightening, just as the tanwin (nunation) is omitted for the same reason in the verse of Abu al-Aswad:

*"So I found him not seeking to make amends, nor remembering God except a little,"*

with "dhakir" in the genitive without tanwin and the majestic Name (Allah) in the accusative. This omission is rare where the word is not a complement of al- (the definite article, as a relative-clause complement). Where it is a complement of al-, it occurs frequently, because the length of the complement calls for lightening, as in his saying:

*"The guardians of the honour of the tribe, so that no blemish comes upon them from behind them..."*

Ibn 'Atiyya relates from Abu al-Samal that he read "la-dha'iqun" in the singular with tanwin, and "al-'adhaba" with the accusative. The singular is explained as being a collective sense for dha'iq, and it was also said: it is on the assumption that "inna jam'akum la-dha'iq" (indeed your gathering will taste). It has also been read "la-dha'iquna" with the nun and "al-'adhaba" in the accusative, which is the original form.

﴿You are not recompensed except for what you used to do﴾. That is: only the recompense for what you used to do of the evil deeds, or only with what you used to do of them.

﴿Except the chosen servants of God﴾ is a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*) from the pronoun in "﴿ذائقو﴾" (those who taste). What lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (*i'tiraḍ*), introduced to hasten the affirmation of the truth by clarifying that their tasting of the punishment comes only from their own side and not from the side of anyone else at all. Thus "إلّا" (*illa*) is interpreted as "لَكِنَّ" (*lakinna*, "but"), and what follows it functions as its predicate, so the sense becomes: "But the chosen servants of God, those ﴿have provision and fruits﴾, etc."

It is also permissible that the meaning be: "But the chosen servants of God are not like that." It has been said that it is a disjunctive exception from the pronoun in ﴿you are recompensed﴾, on the basis that the meaning is: "You are recompensed with the like of what you did, but the chosen servants of God are recompensed manifold, many times over, in relation to what they did." However, its remoteness is evident. Even more remote is making the exception a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*) from the generalization of the address in "تُجْزَوْنَ" (*tujzawna*, "you are recompensed") to all the obligated persons, because of what this entails, together with its need for the artificiality found in the preceding view, namely the dismantling of the pronouns.

﴿The chosen ones﴾ (*al-mukhlasin*) is an adjective of praise, since the construction is a genitive construction (*idafah*) for honor.

﴿Those﴾, that is, the servants mentioned. This indicates that they are distinguished by the sincerity (ikhlas) with which they worshipped Him, Exalted is He, apart from all others, a very pronounced distinction. The sense of distance in the demonstrative, despite the proximity of the referent, indicates the elevation of their rank and the greatness of their station in excellence.

It is a subject (mubtada') and His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿for them﴾, is either its predicate (khabar), and His statement, glorified is He, ﴿provision﴾ is raised as the agent of the adverbial phrase (zarf). Or it is a fronted predicate, with "provision" as a postponed subject, and the whole clause is the predicate of the subject. The whole, as a predicate, corresponds to the disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati') as we have indicated, or it is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) explaining in detail what the exception had stated in general. His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿known﴾, means known in its qualities, such as being uncut and unprevented, pleasant in appearance, delicious in taste, fragrant in smell, and other desirable attributes. So one should not say that provision is not known unless it is determined by a measure. Another verse has come: ﴿They will be provided for therein without reckoning﴾, and what does not fall under reckoning is not limited or measured, and so it is not known. It has been said that the intended meaning is "known in its time," based on His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿And for them is their provision therein, morning and evening﴾. It is reported from Qatadah that "the known provision" is the Garden. This was objected to on the ground that His statement "in gardens" comes afterwards and rejects this. It was also objected that if the meaning is "they will be honoured therein," there would be no problem. It was answered that making it the abode of those who are provided for does not accord with making it provision itself. As for when it is a qualifier of provision, it is plainly rejected. That dwellings are provision for their inhabitants, so that when the designation differs there is no problem, does not remove what has been established, as is not hidden from the fair-minded.

The Qur'anic phrase ﴿fawakih﴾ (fruits) is a substitute (badal) for ﴿rizq﴾ (provision), a substitution of the whole for the whole (badal kull min kull). This indicates that, although it is distinguished by its own properties, all of it is fruit. Alternatively, it is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject, and the sentence is resumed (mustaʾnafah), meaning: "That provision is fruit." By "fruit" here is meant what is eaten merely for pleasure (al-taladhdhudh) and not for sustenance (al-iqtiyat). Everything the people of Paradise eat is like this, even meat, because they are free from needing sustenance, due to the perfection of their creation and the fact that nothing of their bodies dissolves through innate heat (al-hararah al-gharizziyyah), so that they would not need a substitute obtained from food. Thus "fruit" here means something other than what is meant by it in the verse ﴿and fruit of whatever they choose, and the flesh of birds of whatever they desire﴾, where it has its well-known meaning, so there is no contradiction. It has also been permitted that it be an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) to the known provision, so the reason for singling it out is that among provisions it is known to be fruit. It has been said that it is a substitution of part for whole (badal baʿd min kull), and that singling it out for mention is because it follows all other foods, and so it indicates the existence of the others.

﴿And they will be honoured﴾ with Allah, the Exalted, such that no humiliation will reach them, and this is the greatest of rewards and the most fitting for people of high aspirations (ulu al-himam). Perhaps this is an indication of spiritual bliss (al-naʿim al-ruhani) after physical bliss (al-naʿim al-jismani), which comes through eating.

It has been said: they are honoured in obtaining provision, in that it reaches them without earning, toil, or asking, as is the condition of worldly provisions.

It has been read ﴿mukarramun﴾ with emphasis (tashdid). ﴿In gardens of bliss﴾, meaning in gardens in which there is nothing but bliss, with the genitive construction being in the sense of the lam of specification (lam al-ikhtisas), which conveys restriction (al-hasr). The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is connected to ﴿mukramun﴾, or to ﴿maʿlum﴾, or to an omitted circumstantial clause (hal) from the implicit pronoun in ﴿mukramun﴾, or it is a second predicate for ﴿ula'ika﴾, or for ﴿lahum﴾. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿upon couches﴾, may be a circumstantial clause from the implicit pronoun in ﴿mukramun﴾ or in the adverbial phrase before it, and it may be a predicate, in which case His saying ﴿facing one another﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the implicit pronoun in it, or in ﴿mukramun﴾, or in the adverbial phrase, meaning ﴿in gardens﴾. It may also be connected to ﴿mutaqabilin﴾, in which case it is a circumstantial clause from the implicit pronoun in another word.

By their facing one another is indicated the companionship of some of them with others, so some face others for companionship and conversation. In some hadiths it is related that the curtains are sometimes raised from them, so some of them look at others.
