Everything the people of Paradise eat is like this, even meat, because they are free from needing sustenance, due to the perfection of their creation and the fact that nothing of their bodies dissolves through innate heat (al-hararah al-gharizziyyah), so that they would not need a substitute obtained from food. Thus "fruit" here means something other than what is meant by it in the verse ﴿and fruit of whatever they choose, and the flesh of birds of whatever they desire﴾, where it has its well-known meaning, so there is no contradiction. It has also been permitted that it be an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) to the known provision, so the reason for singling it out is that among provisions it is known to be fruit. It has been said that it is a substitution of part for whole (badal baʿd min kull), and that singling it out for mention is because it follows all other foods, and so it indicates the existence of the others.

﴿And they will be honoured﴾ with Allah, the Exalted, such that no humiliation will reach them, and this is the greatest of rewards and the most fitting for people of high aspirations (ulu al-himam). Perhaps this is an indication of spiritual bliss (al-naʿim al-ruhani) after physical bliss (al-naʿim al-jismani), which comes through eating.

It has been said: they are honoured in obtaining provision, in that it reaches them without earning, toil, or asking, as is the condition of worldly provisions.

It has been read ﴿mukarramun﴾ with emphasis (tashdid). ﴿In gardens of bliss﴾, meaning in gardens in which there is nothing but bliss, with the genitive construction being in the sense of the lam of specification (lam al-ikhtisas), which conveys restriction (al-hasr). The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is connected to ﴿mukramun﴾, or to ﴿maʿlum﴾, or to an omitted circumstantial clause (hal) from the implicit pronoun in ﴿mukramun﴾, or it is a second predicate for ﴿ula'ika﴾, or for ﴿lahum﴾. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿upon couches﴾, may be a circumstantial clause from the implicit pronoun in ﴿mukramun﴾ or in the adverbial phrase before it, and it may be a predicate, in which case His saying ﴿facing one another﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the implicit pronoun in it, or in ﴿mukramun﴾, or in the adverbial phrase, meaning ﴿in gardens﴾. It may also be connected to ﴿mutaqabilin﴾, in which case it is a circumstantial clause from the implicit pronoun in another word.

By their facing one another is indicated the companionship of some of them with others, so some face others for companionship and conversation. In some hadiths it is related that the curtains are sometimes raised from them, so some of them look at others.

Abu al-Simmal read ﴿surar﴾ with a fatha on the ra, and this is the dialect of some of Tamim and Kalb, who pronounce with a fatha whatever is a plural on the pattern fuul (fuʿul) of a doubled root when it is a noun. The grammarians differed concerning the adjective: some of them analogised it to the noun and so pronounced it with a fatha, saying dhulal with a fatha on the lam according to that dialect. Others restricted that to the noun, which is the locus of transmitted usage (mawrid al-sama').

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 45:**

The Most High's words, ﴿they will be served﴾, are either a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*, a new sentence) explaining what they will have in their gatherings of enjoyment, or a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring either to the pronoun in ﴿facing one another﴾ or to one of the two prepositional phrases. It is also permitted that it be a qualifier (*sifah*) of ﴿honoured﴾. The one who does the serving, according to what has been said, is those children of the polytheists who died before reaching the age of obligation. In the Sahih (the collection of al-Bukhari or Muslim), they are "the servants of the people of Paradise." This is stated explicitly in another place, namely His words, exalted is He: ﴿There will circulate among them youths of eternal youth﴾, and His words, glorified is He: ﴿There will circulate among them servants of their own﴾.

﴿with a cup﴾, i.e., with wine, as is related from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and others related from al-Dahhak, who said: "Every cup that God, exalted is He, mentions in the Qur'an, He means by it only wine." This is also transmitted from al-Habr (Ibn 'Abbas) and al-Akhfash. It is a well-known figurative usage (*majaz*), treated as equivalent to the literal sense. On this is the verse of al-A'sha:

*And a cup I drank with pleasure, and another by which I sought a cure from it.*

That he meant by it wine is shown by the metonymy of the container for its contents (*itlaq al-mahall 'ala al-hall*), namely his saying "I drank" (*shariibtu*). Estimating "I drank what was in it" is a forced reading. The indicator here is what follows. It is also permitted to interpret it by its literal meaning, which is a vessel containing wine. Most lexicographers hold that the vessel for wine is not called a *ka's* in the strict sense unless there is wine in it; if it is empty, it is a *qadah*. Wine is not specifically required. Al-Bahr (the Bahr al-Muhit of Abu Hayyan) says: "The *ka's* is what is of glass with wine in it, or similar drink of fermented beverages, and it is not called a *ka's* unless it contains that." Al-Raghib says: "The *ka's* is the vessel together with the drink in it, and each of the two is called a *ka's* on its own. One says: *ka's khali* (an empty cup), and one says: *shariibtu ka'san* (I drank a cup), and *ka's tayyibah* (a good cup)." Perhaps his statement is more evident that calling an empty one a *ka's* is figurative. It is related from some of them that he said: "The *ka's* among vessels is anything whose mouth is wide and which has no handle, and it is not considered whether it is for wine or for something else."

﴿from a flowing spring﴾ is in the position of a qualifier to *ka's*, i.e., it is made of a drink that flows (*ma'in*), or a river that flows (*ma'in*), meaning apparent to the eyes, running over the surface of the earth as rivers run, or issuing from springs and fountainheads. Its root is *ma'yun*, from *'Aana al-ma'* (the water appeared) when it became manifest or gushed forth, with its *mim* being augmentative; or it is from *ma'an*, so it is *fa'il* with the *mim* being radical.

It is applied to the wine of Paradise as a comparison to water because of its abundance, to the point that it runs as flowing rivers in the gardens. This suggests its delicacy and subtlety, and that it has not been trodden underfoot as the wine of this world is; the following verse points to its being trodden:

*A daughter of the vine, their mothers nursed her, then they debased her by treading her with the foot.*

Then they returned and made her a judge over them, woe to them from the injustice of an oppressed judge.

And his other saying:

*And a strong wine from the era of 'Ad, which has become slain, trodden under the feet of the presser.*

It was gentle to them until they became intoxicated, then it took hold of them and cried out against them with vengeance.

This is based on its being wine in reality. It is also permitted that it be water in which there is the pleasure and the essence of wine; in that case the description by it is clear. The verse indicates the description of their water as having pleasure and essence. What was mentioned first is the evident meaning. Yes, more than one (scholar) has said: there is no commonality between what is in this world and what is in Paradise except in names, so the reality of the wine of Paradise is not the reality of the wine of this world, and likewise all else that is in the two.

**Bayḍāʾ** (white) is another attribute of the cup, indicating that it is feminine. It is reported from al-Ḥasan that the wine of Paradise is whiter than milk. Ibn Jarīr transmitted from al-Suddī that ʿAbdullāh (ibn Masʿūd) read "ṣafrāʾ" (yellow). This attribute has been applied to worldly wine in this way, as in the saying of Abū Nuwās:

*Ṣafrāʾ lā tanzilu al-aḥzānu sāḥatahā*
*law massahā ḥajarun massat-hu sarrāʾu*

(Yellow wine, sorrows do not descend upon its courtyard; if a stone touched it, the stone would become joyful.)

The well-known view is that this (yellow color) refers to the state after mixing; otherwise, before mixing, it is red (ḥamrāʾ), as the poet said:

*Wa-ḥamrāʾu qabla al-mazji ṣafrāʾu baʿdahu* ∗∗∗ *atat fī thawbayi narjisin wa-shaqāʾiqi*

(And red before mixing, yellow after it, it came in garments of narcissus and anemones.)

*Ḥakat wajnata al-maḥbūbi ṣarfan fa-sallaṭū* ∗∗∗ *ʿalayhā mizājan fa-iktasat lawna ʿāshiqi*

(It imitated the cheek of the beloved in its pure state, then they applied mixing to it, and it took on the color of a lover.)

**Li-ladhdhatin lil-shāribīn** (a delight for those who drink): it is described by the verbal noun (maṣdar) for emphasis, by making it the very essence of delight. It is also permissible that *ladhdhah* is the feminine form of *ladhdh* in the sense of *ladhīdh* (delicious), like *ṭabb* in the sense of *ṭabīb* (skilled physician). They recited his verse:

*Wa-ladhdhun ka-ṭaʿmi al-ṣarkhadiyyi tarktuhu* ∗∗∗ *bi-arḍi al-ʿidā min khashyati al-ḥadathāni*

(And a delight like the taste of the Ṣarkhadī wine, which I left in the land of the enemies for fear of misfortunes.)

He means: a pleasant life, like the taste of the wine attributed to Ṣarkhad, a town in Syria. Al-Zamakhsharī interpreted it as sleep, meaning that it is an adjective (*ladhīdh*) that came to be predominantly applied to sleep, not that it is a fixed noun. And the saying:

*Bi-ḥadīthika al-ladhdhi alladhī law kallamta* ∗∗∗ *usda al-falāti bihi atayna sirāʿan*

(By your sweet speech, which if you spoke to the lions of the desert with it, they would come running.)

Page 88

In His saying, "*lil-shāribīn*" (for the drinkers), rather than "*lahum*" (for them), there is an indication that the drinker takes delight in it, whoever he may be.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 47:

﴿There is no ghawl (harm, unpleasantness) in it﴾, i.e., ghā'ilah (a harmful effect), as in the wine of this world, from ghālahu, yaghūluhu, when he corrupted it. Al-Raghib said: al-ghawl is the destruction of a thing in a way that is not perceived by it. It is said: ghālahu yaghūluhu ghawlan and ightālahu ightiyālan. From this the sie'lah (a desert demon) was named ghūl. The intended meaning here is the negation of there being any harm in it at all.

Al-Bayhaqi and a group related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said regarding this: there is no headache in it. In the narration of Ibn Abi Hatim from him: their minds are not corrupted by intoxication. Al-Tastari also related from him that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq said: "Tell me about His saying, the Exalted: ﴿there is no ghawl in it﴾." He said: "There is no stench in it, nor any repugnance, like the wine of this world." He said: "Do the Arabs know that?" He said: "Yes. Have you not heard the saying of Imru' al-Qays:"

Many a cup I drank, with no ghawl in it, and I gave my companion to drink from it, mixed.

In another narration from him, he explained it as stomach pain. This was also related from Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Jubayr. The generality is preferred, and that the specific mention of something particular is by way of illustration. The fronting of the adverbial phrase is said to be for restriction, and the meaning is: there is in it none of the ghawl that is in the wines of this world. There is discussion of this in the books of ma'ani (rhetoric).

﴿nor are they drained by it﴾, i.e., they are not intoxicated, as related from Ibn 'Abbas and others. This is an explanation of the resultant meaning. The original sense of nazf is pulling out a thing and removing it gradually. It is said: nazaftu al-ma'a min al-bi'r when I drained and pulled out all of its water, one thing after another. Nazafa al-hammu dam'ahu means it drew out all of his tears. It is said: shārib nazīf, i.e., wine drained his mind through intoxication and removed it, as a man drains a well and draws out its water. So the drinker is like a container for the mind, from which it is drawn out. Thus, ﴿لا يُنْزَفُونَ﴾ is in the passive voice, as the two Haramis and the two Arabis read it. Its meaning: their minds are not drawn out, i.e., the wine does not draw out their minds nor remove them. Or the agent is God, the Exalted, and the verb's transitivity with ʿan is said to be due to its being implicitly construed with the meaning of "emanating" (yaṣdurūn), and it is said ʿan is for causation and cause. This corruption is singled out for negation and is conjoined to what encompasses it, because of the magnitude of its corruption, as if it were a genus in its own right; for this reason wine was called the mother of all evils. The intended meaning is the continuation of the negation, not the negation of continuation.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿يُنْزِفُونَ﴾ with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the zay, and ʿĀṣim followed them in al-Waqi'ah, on the basis that it derives from anzafa al-shārib when he became possessed of nazf, i.e., of intellect, or of drink that is exhausted and gone. The hamzah in it indicates becoming. It is said it indicates entering into a thing, and therefore it became intransitive, like kabbahu, fa-akabba. It also has the meaning of intoxication, because the intellect of the drunkard is exhausted, or his drink is exhausted due to much drinking; intoxication is necessarily implied by both, and then it became a literal term for it. Al-Ubayrid al-Yarbu'i said:

By my life, if you have been drained or have sobered, you were the worst of drinking companions, the family of Abjar.

In al-Bahr it is stated that anzafa is shared between "to become drunk" and "to be exhausted," so it is said anzafa al-rajulu when he became drunk, and anzafa when his drink was exhausted. The transitivity of the verb is by implicit construal, as already mentioned. It was also permitted to intend the sense of exhaustion without the sense of intoxication, i.e., their drink does not run out or come to an end so as to spoil their life, but this is not the case. Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿يَنْزِفُونَ﴾ with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the zay, and Talhah with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the zay. In all of these, the intended meaning is the negation of intoxication, according to what is transmitted from the majority.

Among the strange reports is what Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "In wine there are four qualities: intoxication, headache, vomiting and urination. So God, the Exalted, purified the wine of Paradise from them: ﴿there is no ghawl in it﴾, their minds are not corrupted by intoxication, ﴿nor are they drained by it﴾, they do not vomit from it as the drinker of the wine of this world vomits." This is closer to the use of nazf for sensory matters, such as the draining of a well or a cistern, and the vomiting and expulsion of waste from the belly by analogy with the draining of a well and the removal of its water when it is emptied. Were it not that the majority holds the view you heard first, even Ibn 'Abbas in most of the narrations from him, you would say that this explanation is the preferable one.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 48:

﴿And with them are those restraining their glances﴾: They have restrained their eyes to their spouses, not extending their glance to anyone other than them. This is what Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said. So the object of the restraining (qasr) is omitted, because it is known. The statement is either upon its apparent meaning, or it is a metaphor (kinayah) for the intensity of their love for their spouses and their lack of inclination toward others. It has also been said that the meaning is that they do not open their eyes in coquetry and flirtation. The description, according to both opinions, is transitive. It has also been permitted that it be intransitive, meaning: their eyelids are languid and sickly. How delightful is the drooping of eyelids in beautiful young women! For this reason, the praise of this quality has been abundant, past and present. Among it is the saying of Ibn al-Azdi:

My consolation has fallen sick, and my passion has become healthy, from glances which are the sick and yet the healthy.

In all of this, the glance (tarf) is their glance. It has also been permitted that the description be transitive, with the glance being the glance of others, and the meaning: restraining the glance of others from passing beyond them to anyone else, because of the extremity of their beauty, so that the glance of the one looking at them does not pass beyond them. Like the saying of al-Mutanabbi:

And a waist in which glances are fixed, as though a girdle of pupils were upon it.

This meaning has also been mentioned by Ibn Rashiq regarding the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

Of those restraining the glance, if a tiny ant were to crawl above the nose of one of them from the dust, it would leave a mark.

By my life, this is elegant; but I say: the apparent meaning here is that the "being with them" is in the gatherings of drinking, to complete the pleasure. So perhaps the first meaning is more suitable for jealousy, even though the sanctuary is a sanctuary of holiness. The majority have restricted the glance to it, and it is not thought of them that they are among those who restrain (their glance). It has been said that the sentence is coordinated (ʿatf) with what precedes it, and it has been said that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: a cup is circulated among them while the state of their being with them is women restraining their glances. ﴿ʿIn﴾ is the plural of ʿaynaʾ, which is the one with wide eyes in beauty. From this, the wild cow is called ʿin. It has been said: ʿaynaʾ is one whose eye is wide, meaning one with many beautiful features of the eye. The truth is that "width" (siʿah) is the widening of the opening, and the restriction to beauty removes what might be objected. How subtle and how graceful is the mention of ﴿ʿin﴾ after ﴿restraining their glances﴾!

﴿As if they were hidden eggs﴾. The egg is well known, and it is a collective noun (ism jins). Its singular is bayḍah, and its plural is bayūḍ, as in the verse of the poet:

*In a barren wilderness, and the camels, as if they were*
*the sandgrouse of al-Huzn, whose eggs were once chicks.*

The intended meaning is the comparison of the women to eggs that the feathers have covered in the nest, or that something else has covered in another place. Thus no hands have touched them, and dust has not reached them. They have a clear whiteness mixed with a slight yellowness and a sheen, as in pearls. Most commentators, however, restrict the comparison to ostrich eggs in their nests, because they are more beautiful in appearance than other eggs, further from being touched by hands, and less exposed to anything that would change their colour.

The Arabs compare women to eggs and say of them "the eggs of the curtained chambers" (bayḍāt al-khudūr). From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*And an egg from a curtained chamber, whose tent is not approached,*
*I enjoyed from play with her, not in haste.*

The whiteness mixed with a slight yellowness in women is greatly desired. It has been said that the same is true of whiteness mixed with a slight redness in men. As for pure whiteness, it is not praised. For this reason it is reported in the noble description of the Prophet's appearance (ﷺ): "white, not of an albino (amhaq) complexion."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿAbbās, and others related from Ibn Jubayr, and Ibn Abi Ḥātim, and Ibn Jarir from al-Suddi, that the hidden egg is what lies beneath the hard shell, between it and the yellow inner part. The comparison is then to them after cooking, in smoothness and softness. When an egg is boiled and peeled, what lies beneath the shell appears in the utmost smoothness and perfect softness. From here you hear common people say in praise of a woman: "She is like a peeled boiled egg." Al-Ṭabarī preferred this view, arguing that the description "hidden" (maknūn) requires it rather than the well-known meaning, because the outside of an eggshell is not hidden. Against this it is said that what is understood from "egg" is the whole of the shell and what is inside it. And when one says "I ate such-and-such an egg," the verb "eat" indicates that what is meant is the contents inside the shell, not the whole, since the shell is not eaten normally. In that case what al-Ṭabarī said does not hold. The first view is therefore the accepted one, and the meaning of "hidden" in it is clear as you have heard. Al-Khafājī transmitted this meaning from some later scholars and criticised it, saying that it arises from ignorance of the language of the Arabs. It seems he had not come upon its transmission from the al-Ḥibr (scholar, a title of Ibn ʿAbbās) and those with him, for otherwise what he said would not be possible. Perhaps the transmission mentioned is not established. Likewise is what Abū Ḥayyān related from the al-Ḥibr, that the hidden egg is a well-guarded jewel, since the apparent wording does not support that.

A group said: the intended comparison is to eggs in the proportion of their parts, and the egg is among the things most proportionate in its parts, and proportion is praiseworthy. For this reason one of the men of letters said in love poetry:

*Their limbs are proportioned, so you see in them*
*no disparity, but they come in measure.*

You know, even after granting that the proportion of parts in an egg is well known among them, that the description "hidden" has no apparent relevance to the comparison. The comparison, according to what preceded, is problematic in light of the verse known as the bride of the Qur'an: ﴿As if they were rubies and coral﴾. This clearly indicates that their complexions have some redness, and how does this relate to the comparison with the hidden egg as you heard before? It is therefore necessary that the comparison be understood in terms of smoothness and softness, as was transmitted second, or in terms of the proportion of parts, as was said last. It has been answered that the things compared to the hidden egg may be different from those compared to the ruby and coral. That whiteness mixed with yellowness is the best of colours in women is not accepted without question. Rather it is good, and whiteness mixed with redness is similar in beauty. Moreover, what is most beautiful differs according to the natures of those who look:

*People have differing paths in what they love.*

And Paradise contains what the souls desire and what the eyes delight in.

It has also been said that the comparison to the hidden egg may refer to the whiteness of their bodies mixed with yellowness apart from their faces, while the comparison to ruby and coral refers to the whiteness of their faces mixed with redness. It has also been said that the comparison to these is not because their whiteness is mixed with redness, but that the comparison to ruby is in terms of clarity, and to coral in terms of smoothness and beauty of appearance.

If coral is understood as small pearls, as a group of scholars held, rather than the well-known red beads, then the comparison may be in terms of whiteness mixed with yellowness, and there is no difficulty at all.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 50:

﴿So they will approach one another, questioning each other﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon ﴿they will be served﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tira'), or it is among the complements of the first (muta'allaqat al-awwal). That is: they drink and converse over the drink, as is the custom of those gathered for it. Muhammad ibn Fayyad said:

"Of pleasures nothing remains except conversing with the noble over drink,
and your kissing of the two cheeks of a shining moon, over whose face the water of youth flows."

He expressed it in the past tense (fa-'aqbala, "they approached") although the item coordinated upon (yuTaf, "they are served") is in the present tense, to indicate the special care given to this coordinated item relative to what it is coordinated upon. How could they not turn to conversation, when it is the greatest of their pleasures which they indulge in? Moreover, there is in this an indication that the event is certain to occur, and their questioning one another about the knowledge and virtues, and what happened to them and against them in the world, and how sweet it is to recall what has passed at the ease of the state and the leisure of the mind.

﴿قالَ قائِلٌ مِنهُمْ﴾ [And a speaker among them said], in the course of their conversation, ﴿إنِّي كانَ لِي﴾ [Indeed, there was for me], in the world, ﴿قَرِينٌ﴾ [a companion], one who kept me company, ﴿يَقُولُ﴾ [who would say], to me, by way of reproach, about what I was upon of belief and affirmation of the Resurrection, which led to what I am upon today: ﴿أإنَّكَ لَمِنَ المُصَدِّقِينَ﴾ [Are you indeed among those who affirm?], i.e., of the Resurrection, as indicated by His saying, glorified is He, ﴿أإذا مِتْنا وكُنّا تُرابًا وعِظامًا أإنّا لَمَدِينُونَ﴾ [When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be recompensed?], i.e., shall we indeed be resurrected and requited? "Dīn" here means recompense (jazāʾ). It was also said that it means "lamasūsūn marbūbūn" (indeed, we shall be governed and managed), from "dānahu" (he governed him) when he governs him. From this is the hadith: "The intelligent person is the one who holds himself accountable (dāna nafsahu)."

The reading "al-muṣaddiqīn" (with a shadda on the ṣād, from taṣaddaq, to give charity) was also recited. This reading has been objected to on the grounds that the sense of it does not suit His saying, glorified is He, ﴿أإذا مِتْنا﴾ etc. It has been responded to that this contains an oversight regarding the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzūl). ʿAbd al-Razzāq and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, who said: There were two partners, and they had eight thousand dinars, and they divided them. The elder of the two went and bought land for a thousand dinars. His companion said: "O God, so-and-so has bought land for a thousand dinars, and I buy from You land in Paradise for a thousand dinars." So he gave a thousand dinars in charity. Then his companion built a house for a thousand dinars and said: "O God, so-and-so has built a house for a thousand dinars, and I buy from You a house in Paradise for a thousand dinars." So he gave a thousand dinars in charity. Then he married a woman and spent a thousand dinars on her, and said: "O God, so-and-so has married a woman and spent a thousand dinars on her, and I ask of You, from the women of Paradise, a wife for a thousand dinars." So he gave a thousand dinars in charity. Then he bought servants and goods for a thousand dinars, and said: "O God, so-and-so has bought servants and goods for a thousand dinars, and I buy from You servants and goods in Paradise for a thousand dinars." So he gave a thousand dinars in charity. Then he fell into severe need, and said: "If I go to my companion, perhaps he will give me some kindness." So he sat on his path until he passed by him with his retinue and family. He rose to him, and the other looked and recognized him, and said: "So-and-so?" He said: "Yes." He said: "What is your condition?" He said: "After you, need has befallen me, so I came to you that you might bestow some good upon me." He said: "What did you do with your wealth?" So he related the story to him. He said: "Are you indeed among those who affirm this? Go away! By God, I will not give you anything!" and he turned him away. Then God decreed for both of them that they died; the wealth of the one who gave charity became Paradise, and the wealth of the other became Hellfire. And concerning these two the verse was revealed. It was also said that they were two brothers who inherited eight thousand dinars and divided them, and what happened to them happened. The two were from the Children of Israel.

The purpose of the interrogative (al-istifhām) here is, according to what has been said, an offer (al-'arḍ) or a command (al-amr). The aim of this is to show them the wretched state of the companion, so that he might bring them a kind of comfort (īnās). It has also been said that he intends by this to demonstrate the truthfulness of what he related. But it is far-fetched to suspect him of lying. The looking of the people of Paradise upon the people of the Fire, and their knowledge of who is among them despite the distance between them, is not improbable: God Most High may create in them a keenness of sight and inform them of whom they wish to look upon. Perhaps, when they wish to do so, they stand upon the Heights (al-A'rāf), and so they look upon whomever they wish among the people of the Fire.

The speaker's knowledge that his companion is among the people of the Fire comes from his knowledge that he used to deny the Resurrection (al-ba'th), and the denier of it is definitely among them, and the default assumption is that he remained upon disbelief. Then he said to the angels who had informed him: "Will you look down?" But what is in this is not hidden.

﴿فاطَّلَعَ﴾ means: he looked down upon the people of the Fire. ﴿فَرَآهُ﴾ means: he saw his companion ﴿فِي سَواءِ الجَحِيمِ﴾, that is, in its middle (*sawa'*). From this is the saying of Isa ibn Umar to Abu Ubayda: "I used to write until my *sawa'* (middle of the page) was exhausted." The middle is called *sawa'* because the distance from it to the sides is equal (*istiwa'*).

Abu Amr, in the transmission of Husayn al-Ju'fi, read ﴿مُطَّلِعُونَ﴾ with a sukun on the *ta'* and a fatha on the *nun*, and "*fa-uṭliʿa*" with a damma on the *hamza*, a sukun on the *ta'*, and a kasra on the *lam*, as a past verb in the passive voice (*mabni li-l-maf'ul*). This is the reading of Ibn Abbas, Ibn Muhaysin, Ammar ibn Abi Ammar, and Abu Siraj. It was also read as ﴿مُطَّلِعُونَ﴾ with a *shadda* and "*fa-aṭṭaliʿa*" with a *shadda* as well, as a present verb in the subjunctive (*manṣub*) as an answer to the interrogative.

It was also read as ﴿مُطْلِعُونَ﴾ with light pronunciation, "*fa-aṭlaʿa*" with light pronunciation as a past verb, and "*fa-aṭlu'a*" with light pronunciation as a present subjunctive verb. Abu al-Barhasam and Ammar ibn Abi Ammar, as reported by Khalaf from him, read "*muṭliʿūn*" with a light *ta'* and a kasra on the *nun*, and "*fa-uṭliʿa*" as a past verb in the passive voice. Abu Hatim and others rejected this reading because it combines the plural *nun* (*nun al-jam'*) with the first-person *ya'* (*ya' al-mutakallim*). The correct form would be *muṭliʿiyya*, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Will they expel me (*awa-mukhrijiyya hum*)?" Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) justified it by treating the active participle (*ism al-fa'il*) as having the role of the present verb, so that one says *ḍāribūnahu* ("they strike him") as one says *yaḍribūnahu*. On this basis is the line of verse:

"They are the ones who command good and do it (*al-fa'iluna-hu*), when they fear, from the new-arising of time, something great."

Al-Tabari cited the line of the poet:

"I do not know, and every thought is a thought, whether he will hand me over (*a-muslimunī*) to my people, *Shirāḥī*."

Similar to it is the line of another:

"Is there a youth from the nobles of the tribe who will carry me, when there is none carrying me except the son of a porter?"

This *nun*, according to a group, is the protective *nun* (*nun al-wiqaya*), attached to the descriptive form by analogy with the verb. It is not like the *nun* in the reading and in the verse, though each is attached for the purpose of analogy. Some said: it is the *nun* of tanwin (*nun al-tanwin*), moved because two consonants met. This was refuted on the ground that it has been heard attached with the definite article (*al*), as in his saying "*wa-laysa al-muwafīnī*," and with the comparative form (*af'al al-tafḍil*), as occurred in the hadith: "Other than the Dajjal, I fear for you more (*akhwafunī*)."

From this it is known that attaching it is not restricted to poetry. Yes, outside poetry it is rare. Some weakened what Abu al-Fath had argued and said that this does not occur except in poetry. It was also interpreted as the placing of an attached pronoun in the place of a detached one. The original would be *muṭliʿūna iyyāya* ("looking down at me"), then the detached pronoun was made attached, so it became *muṭliʿūnī*. Then the *ya'* was deleted and the kasra was retained in its place, as in the Almighty's saying ﴿فَكَيْفَ كانَ نَكِيرِ﴾ ("So how was My rejection?"). The same is said of *al-fa'iluna-hu* in the previous line. Abu Hayyan rejected this, arguing that what was mentioned is not among the places of the detached pronoun, so that it could be claimed that the attached one took its place. He claimed that Abu al-Fath's interpretation has priority. It is said that the line is fabricated and cannot be cited as evidence. It is also said that the *ha'* is the *ha' al-sakt* (pausal *ha'*), moved because of necessity, and this is fleeing from one necessity into another, since moving it and keeping it in connected speech is not permissible.

On the question of retaining the *nun* with the descriptive form when it is attached to a pronoun, the grammarians have a lengthy discussion. Its summary is that for forms like *ḍāribuka*, *ḍāribākā*, and *ḍāribūka* ("striking you"), Sibawayh held that the pronoun is in the position of a genitive by annexation (*iḍafa*), which is why the tanwin and the *nun* of the dual and plural are deleted. Al-Akhfash and Hisham held that the pronoun is in the position of an accusative, and the deletion is for lightness. Both are retained, as in *al-fa'iluna-hu* and *a-muslimunī*. Thus for these two and similar forms, the *nun* is tanwin moved because two consonants met. You have heard what is in it. The view of the attachment for the sake of analogy to the verb is, among the explanations, the best said in interpretation.

This is what is said. *Ṭala'a* and *iṭṭala'a* (with the *shadda*) and *aṭla'a* (with light pronunciation) have one meaning, and all are intransitive (*lāzim*). *Al-iṭṭilā'* may also be transitive (*muta'addī*). One says *aṭla'ahu 'alā kadhā* ("he made him look down upon such-and-such"), then *fa-ṭṭala'a*. The *muṭliʿūn* in the reading of Abu Amr has the meaning of *muṭṭali'ūn* with the *shadda*. The deputy of the subject of *uṭli'a* is the pronoun of the speaker, and the agent is the addressees. Their causing him to look down is by way of causation: as if, when he wished to look down and did not want to be exclusive in it out of courtesy, he proposed to them that they look down. They were willing and looked down, and that became a means to his looking down. So they are, as it were, the ones who caused him to look down. Thus the *fa* in ﴿فاطَّلَعَ﴾ is an eloquent *fa* (*fa' fasīḥa*). The conjunction is with something understood, and the meaning according to the reading that follows it is: "Would you look down, so that I may also look down?" Then they looked down, and he looked down after that, and ﴿فَرَآهُ فِي سَواءِ الجَحِيمِ﴾. It is necessary to supply *iṭṭala'a* ("he looked down") after that, so that the sequence of ﴿فَرَآهُ﴾ upon what came before is correct. ﴿هَلْ أنْتُمْ مُطَّلِعُونَ﴾ ("Would you look down?") in this sense is a command, expressed courteously and with emphasis.

On the second reading, which is the light pronunciation in both words, the second word being a past verb, the meaning is as in the reading of the majority, and likewise for the reading that follows it. As for the reading of Abu al-Barhasam and those with him, "Would you look down upon me, so they looked down on him, and he saw him..." and so on. Their causing him to look down, if the address is to the companions, is by way of causation: as if he asked that they look down so that he might join them and look down. If the address is to the angels, peace be upon them, according to what comes first to mind, then it is different.

According to the author of *al-Lawāmiḥ*, *ṭala'a* and *iṭṭala'a* in the sense of *iṭṭilā'* mean "he approached and came." The one standing in for the subject in the reading *uṭli'a* (in the passive) is either the pronoun of the verbal noun (*ḍamīr al-maṣdar*) or a prepositional phrase (*jār wa-majrūr*) that is omitted, meaning "he was made to look down by it," because *aṭla'a* is intransitive like *aqbala* ("he approached"). You have known that *aṭla'a* also comes transitively, as in *aṭla'tu Zaydan* ("I made Zayd look down").

Abu Hayyan rejected the second possibility, arguing that the deputy of the subject may not be omitted, just as the subject may not be omitted. So reflect on all that we have mentioned, and do not be heedless!

﴿He said﴾, i.e., the speaker, to his companion: ﴿By God, you almost brought me to ruin﴾, i.e., would have destroyed me. In the recitation (qira'a) of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) it is "لَتُغْوِينِ" (*latughwinanī*, "would have led me astray"). The "in" (إنْ) is the lightened form of the emphatic "inna," and the lam is the lam that distinguishes it. In al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit*), the oath expresses wonder at his own safety from his companion, since that companion had nearly destroyed him.

﴿And had it not been for the favour of my Lord﴾ upon me, which is success (tawfiq) and protection (ʿisma), ﴿I would have been among those brought forth﴾ for the punishment, just as you and your like were brought forth.

﴿Are we then not to die﴾ etc. This returns to the dialogue with his companions after completing the speech addressed to his companion, out of exultation and delight at the great bounty and lasting bliss that God has granted him, and as a reproach directed indirectly at the companion. It is also permitted that this is part of the speech of all the questioners, and that it is part of the speech of the speaker himself, addressing his companion as a rebuke to him. The first view is preferred. The hamza (ʾa, interrogative particle) is for affirmation (taqrir), and within it is the sense of wonder. The fa (فَ) is for conjunction with an implied premise required by the structure of the speech, according to what al-Zamakhshari and his followers held, meaning: "Are we immortal, so that we are not among those whose nature is death?" as the attributive adjective (al-sifa al-mushabbaha) indicates.

It was also read as "بِمائِتِينَ" (*bi-ma'itin*, "dying," with the variant form of the active participle).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 59:

﴿Except our first death﴾ which was in the world. It is, according to the People of the Sunnah, a reference to what occurs in the grave after being brought back to life for questioning, since the life there is not counted, being neither complete nor settled, and its duration is very short. The exception is detached (mufarragh) from an implied verbal noun (masdar muqaddar), as if it were said: "Are we not dying a death except our first death?" It is also permissible that it be disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: "But the first death was ours in the world." Their knowledge that they will not die arises from the reports of their prophets to them in the world, informing them that the people of Paradise do not die, or from the words of the angels, peace be upon them, to them upon entering Paradise: ﴿You are good; so enter it, abiding forever﴾, and their saying: ﴿Enter it in peace, secure﴾. It is also said that the people of Paradise, when they first enter, do not know that they will not die; then death is brought in the form of a ram, white with black spots, and it is slaughtered, and a caller calls: "O people of Paradise, eternity without death! O people of the Fire, eternity without death!" Then they know it, and they say that out of gratitude for the blessing of God the Exalted and rejoicing in it. It is not hidden that the saying related here, spoken at the time of their knowledge that death does not occur, following its slaughter, is far-fetched in this context; the apparent meaning is that this occurs after their awareness and conversation with the companion.

﴿And we will not be punished﴾ like the companions of the Fire. The intended meaning is the continuity of the negation and its emphasis, and likewise in what precedes it. The continuity of this negation is a magnificent blessing, and it includes the negation of the cessation of their bliss, related in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For them is a known provision﴾ and the verses that follow, for the cessation of bliss is a kind of punishment, indeed one of its greatest kinds. Indeed, even imagining cessation is a punishment, with which no life is pleasant. Hence it was said:

If you wish to live a pleasant life, do not take as your own anything whose loss you fear.

It also includes the negation of senility and the deterioration of faculties, which the negation of death might suggest, for that too is a kind of punishment. And the reason why the mention was chosen for the continuity of the negation of punishment rather than affirming the continuity of bliss is that the negation of punishment comes more quickly to the mind of one who is not punished when witnessing one who is punished. It was also said that this is because averting harm is more important than securing benefit.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verses 60–61:

﴿Indeed, this is the great triumph.﴾ The apparent meaning is that the reference is to what they were told of the continuation of the negation of death and the continuation of the negation of punishment for them. It is also permissible that it refers to the bliss they are in, along with the continuation of the two negations. If the statement is part of the speech of the speaker, ﴿Then are we not to die,﴾ etc., then it implicitly contains that speaker's indication to the manifestation of bliss, and the omission of explicitly stating it is because the manifestation itself suffices.

It is also permitted that this is the speech of Allah, Exalted and Glorified be He, affirming the words of that speaker and confirming them, addressing with it His beloved (ﷺ) and his community. The emphasis is for the importance of the matter of the report. It has also been read as ﴿Indeed, this is the great provision (rizq),﴾ meaning what they were granted of supreme happiness.

﴿For the like of this let the workers work.﴾ That is, for attaining the likes of this exalted matter, the workers ought to work, not for the swiftly passing worldly pleasures mixed with various kinds of pain. Thus the fronting of the prepositional phrase (lam, "for") serves to restrict. And if this refers to a specific individual insofar as he is individualized, then "mithl" (like) is not superfluous; if it refers to the genus, then it is superfluous, as in: "Someone like you does not stint." The statement may be part of the speech of the speaker, and it is not objectionable that the Hereafter is not a place of works, since the intended meaning is not a command to work therein. It may also be part of the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Regarding His words, glorified and exalted be He, ﴿Is that better as a welcome gift, or the tree of Zaqqum?﴾: according to most scholars, this is part of His own speech, glorified and exalted be He. It is connected to His words, exalted be He, ﴿For them is a known provision﴾. The account between the two has been mentioned by way of digression (istitrad), so the reference is to the known provision.

As for the claim of some that it may be part of the speech of the previous speaker, while it is definitely part of the speech of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, that will come, God willing.

The root of nuzul (نُزُل) is the surplus and the excess of food, and it is used for what results from a thing. From this comes the phrase ﻟَيْسَ مِن أنْزالِ الأرْضِ (honey is not from the nuzul of the land), meaning, not from what is produced from it. And al-Shafi'i's statement, "Ushr (the tithe) is not obligatory on honey, because it is the nuzul of a bird," and it is also said of the provision prepared for the guest (nazil).

Zaqqum is the name of a tree with small, bitter leaves and a foul smell, which has a milky sap; when it touches a person's body, it causes swelling. It grows in Tihama and in the barren lands bordering the desert. The tree described in the verse was named after it. Both meanings of nuzul are possible here. However, on the first meaning, it is necessarily in the accusative as a tamyiz (specification accusative), meaning: "Is that provision which is known, whose result is pleasure and joy, better as nuzul and as result, or the tree of Zaqqum whose result is pain and grief?" The sense of comparing the two nuzuls is rebuke and mockery, a style that occurs frequently in the Qur'an. Treating it as a shared comparison is permissible. On the second meaning, its accusative is apparently as a hal (circumstantial accusative), and the meaning is: the known provision is the nuzul of the people of Paradise, and the nuzul of the people of Hell is the tree of Zaqqum. So which of them is better while being a nuzul? The mockery mentioned applies here too.

Parsing it as a tamyiz is not lexically prohibited, as in the phrase ﻫُمْ أكْفاهُمْ ناصِرًا (they are better in support, as in: "they are sufficient as helpers for them"). However, the meaning as a hal is stronger, because the intended comparison is between those fruits and this food in this condition, not a comparison between them in description. And this matter of being a nuzul is more fitting for the comparison than the other. Understand this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 63:

﴿Indeed, We have made it a trial for the wrongdoers.﴾ A trial (miḥnah) and a punishment for them in the Hereafter, and a test (ibtilā') for them in this world. For when they heard that it (the tree) is in the Fire, they said: "How is that possible, when the Fire burns trees?" Abu Jahl said likewise, then he said, mocking its matter and not denying its literal meaning (al-madlūl al-lughawī): "By God, we do not know zaqqūm to be anything but dates and butter. So eat it (fa-tazaqqamū)!" They did not realize that whoever is able to create an animal that lives in the Fire and takes pleasure in it is more able to create a tree in the Fire and preserve it from burning. The Fire does not burn except by His permission, or the burning is by Him at its occurrence, not by the Fire itself.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 64:

﴿Indeed, it is a tree that springs up from the root of Hellfire.﴾ Its place of growth is at the bottom of the Fire, and its branches rise up to its (various) levels (darakat). It has been read as "nabitatun fi usul al-Jahim" (a growing tree at the root of Hellfire). ﴿Its ṭal'* ﴾, that is, its fruit (hamluha). Its original meaning is the ṭal' of the date palm, which is the first thing that appears before its shamarikh (flower-stalk clusters) emerge: white, tender, elongated like an almond. This word was applied to the fruit of this tree either because it resembles it in shape or in emerging (ṭuluʿ), and perhaps the latter is preferable, given that the comparison is then implicit, making it an istiʿara taṣrīḥiyya (explicit metaphor). Or (it was applied) because the word has come to be used in the general sense of whatever emerges, in which case it is like the mursal (figurative usage by relation) for the unprecedented (al-unuf), and thus it is a majaz mursal (figurative usage by relation).

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 37, verse 65:

﴿As though they were the heads of devils﴾ (*ka-annahu ru'us al-shayatin*), meaning in extreme repulsiveness and ugliness of appearance. The Arabs liken a person of hideous appearance to a devil, and so they say: "It is as though it were the face of a devil or the head of a devil," even if they have not seen one, because it is extremely repugnant in their nature. They believe it to be pure evil with no good mixed into it, so it is imprinted in their imagination in its most hideous form. Among this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Would you kill me while the Mashrafi (sword) is my bedfellow, and whetted blue (spears) are like the fangs of ghouls (aghwal)?"

He compared them to the fangs of ghouls, which are a kind of devil, although he had never seen them, because of what was imprinted in his imagination. The opposite of this is their comparison of a beautiful form to an angel (*malak*), because they believe it to be pure good with no evil in it, so it is imprinted in their imagination in its most beautiful form. Upon this is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿This is not a human being; this is none but a noble angel﴾. By this, a response is made to some of the heretics (*malahida*) who objected to this comparison, claiming that it is a comparison to something unknown. Its essence is that it is not required that the thing be known in external reality; it is sufficient that it be fixed in the mind and imagination.

The interpretation of the comparison in the verse as mentioned is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, and others. Al-Jubba'i claimed that when the devils enter the Fire, their forms are greatly disfigured and their limbs become abhorrent, so the meaning is "as though they were the heads of the devils
Page 96
who are in the Fire." However, the objection to this is that the comparison is likewise not known in external reality upon descent. It has also been said: "the heads of the devils" is a well-known tree in the region of Yemen, hideous in appearance, called *al-astan*, and it is this that al-Nabigha meant in his saying:

"She swerves away from dark-bottomed *astan* (trees), like maidservants going out in the morning carrying bundles of firewood."

Al-Asma'i said: it is also called *al-sawm*, and he recited:

"Appointed to watch over the shade of the *sawm* tree, a lean, hollow-bellied, gap-toothed (*zarim*) one from the western lands."

It has also been said: the devils are a species of snakes with crests. Al-Farra' recited:

"A little old woman who swears when I swear, like the devil of the *hamat* tree, which has a mane."

That is, it has a mane. Al-Mubarrad recited:

"And among the herbs, if Allah does not avert their evil, are devils, some of which run upon others."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 66:

﴿Indeed, they will be eating from it﴾ is a consequence (tafrī') of its being made a trial (fitnah), i.e., a tribulation and a punishment for the wrongdoers. The feminine pronoun refers to the tree, and "min" (from) is either for the starting point (ibtida'iyyah) or partitive (tab'idiyyah). There is an implied noun (mudaf muqaddar), i.e., "from its spathes (ṭal')." It has also been said: "min" is partitive and the pronoun refers to the spathe (ṭal'), and it is feminine because it is attached to a feminine noun, or because it is interpreted as the fruit, or it refers to the tree by way of metaphor (tajawwuz). Each of these has some remoteness. ﴿Then they will be filling their bellies from it﴾ because of the overpowering of hunger, even though they dislike it, or by way of compulsion to eat it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 67:

﴿Then indeed for them over it﴾, i.e., over the tree from which they filled their bellies, ﴿is a mixture of boiling water﴾, i.e., a drink mixed with water of intense heat. This drink is al-Ghassaq (the pus-like discharge), i.e., what drips from the wounds and skins of the people of the Fire. It has also been said: this is al-sadid (pus), and as for al-ghassaq, it is a spring in the Fire into which flow the venom of snakes and scorpions, or the tears of the disbelievers therein. Their drinking of that is due to the intensity of their thirst from what they ate of the tree, so when they drink, their intestines are cut to pieces.

It has been read as "lashawban" with a damma on the shin, and it is the noun for what is mixed in with something (al-shawb, i.e., the mixture). On the first reading, it is a verbal noun (masdar) that has been named as such. As for the word "thumma" (then), it has been said that it indicates temporal sequence (al-tarakhi al-zamani), because after they fill their bellies from that tree they become thirsty, and their drink is delayed for a period so that their thirst increases and their punishment is thereby increased.

It has been objected that this is contradicted by the conjoining of drinking with "fa" (so) in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So indeed you will fill from it the bellies﴾ ﴿and then drink upon it from the boiling water﴾, so there must be no intervening time. It has been answered that it is permissible for the drinking of the drink mixed with boiling water to be delayed by a period from their filling of the bellies, but not the drinking of boiling water alone; similarly, it is permissible for the situation to vary, so that at times the drinking is delayed absolutely by a period, and at other times it is not delayed in that way. Some of them said: their filling of the bellies is an extended matter, so with regard to its beginning it is conjoined with "thumma," and with regard to its end it is conjoined with "fa."

It has also been permitted that "thumma" is for graduated sequence (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because their drink is far more hideous than their food, and the conjoining of their filling of the bellies with "fa" is because it follows what precedes it. Considering graduated difference in it is not as appropriate as it is in the drinking of the drink mixed with boiling water together with eating.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 68:

﴿Then indeed their return⦆ — i.e., their destination — and it has been read thus; and it has also been read, "Then indeed their outlet (manfadhahum)." ﴿is to the Blazing Fire (al-Jahim)﴾ — i.e., to their place of abode from the Fire. For in Jahannam there are several stations, in each of which is prepared a particular kind of affliction. So the people are taken out from their place of settlement, where the fire blazes, and are driven to another place of what Jahannam encircles, in which there is that drink, to come to it and be given to drink from it; then they are returned to their place, just as beasts are led out to the places of water in the town, for example, so that they may come to it, and then are returned to their place. Qatadah pointed to this meaning, then recited His saying, exalted is He:
Page 97
﴿This is the Fire which the guilty used to deny. They will go around between it and scalding, boiling water﴾, and the reading of Ibn Mas'ud supports it: "Then indeed their return (munqalabahum)," since "inqilab" is more evident in the sense of returning. Or the meaning is: "Then indeed their return is to the levels of the Blazing Fire," so they are moved back and forth within the Fire from one place to another nearer to it. It was also said: the drink is presented to them before entering the Fire, so they drink and then proceed to the Blazing Fire; but this requires a textual report (tawqif), otherwise it is contrary to the apparent meaning. It seems that between the people's going out to drink and their return to their dwellings there is a considerable time, during which they gulp down that drink; and for this reason "thumma" (then) is used. This drink stands in contrast to what the people of Paradise have of drink, implied by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are given to drink from a cup from a flowing spring﴾ ﴿white, delicious to the drinkers﴾ etc., just as the zaqqum stands in contrast to the fruits they have.

It has come from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that: "If a single drop of the zaqqum of Jahannam were sent down to the earth, it would corrupt the livelihoods of the people." Ibn Abi Shaybah related it. So how about one whose food and drink is al-ghassaq and pus along with scalding water? We ask Allah, exalted is He, for His pleasure and Paradise, and we seek refuge with Him, Mighty and Majestic, from His anger and the Fire. And His saying, glorified is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verses 69–70:

﴿Indeed, they found their fathers astray.﴾ ﴿So they were hastening along in their footsteps.﴾ This is a explanation (ta'lil) for their deserving the various kinds of punishment that were mentioned, through blindly following (taqlid) their fathers in the foundations of the religion, without them or their fathers having anything at all to hold on to in the first place. That is: they found them astray in reality, having nothing that could serve as a doubt, let alone being fit to be a proof. So they, without reflecting that they were upon the truth first, while it is evident that they were upon falsehood with even the slightest contemplation. And ihrā' (al-ihra') is intense hastening; it was also said: it is a hastening accompanied by something like trembling.

In the passive construction of the verb (bina' al-fi'l li-l-maf'ul) there is an indication of the greater eagerness of them hastening in their footsteps, as if they are being driven and urged on intensely toward it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 71–74:

﴿And certainly the earlier people before them went astray﴾, i.e., before these wrongdoers, for whom the Zaqqum tree was made a trial, and they are the Quraysh, ﴿most of the earlier ones﴾ among the previous nations. This is the answer to an omitted oath. Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And certainly We sent among them warners﴾, prophets who warned them of the evil outcome of the falsehood they were upon. The repetition of the oath serves to display the complete care in confirming the content of each of the two sentences. ﴿So look how was the outcome of those who were warned﴾, of the horror and dreadfulness, when they did not heed the warning and did not raise their heads to it.

The address is either to the master of those addressed, ﷺ, or to everyone who is able to witness their traces. Since the meaning is that they were destroyed with a dreadful destruction, He excepted from them the sincere ones with His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿except the servants of Allah, the sincere ones﴾, i.e., those whom Allah made sincere by granting them success in faith and in acting upon the requirement of the warning. It is also read "al-mukhlisin" with a kasra on the lam, i.e., those who made their religion sincere for Allah, glorified and exalted is He. The exception on both readings is either disconnected (munqati') if "the warners" is taken as specific, or connected (muttasil) if it is taken as general.

﴿And Noah certainly called out to Us﴾. This is an elaboration of what was stated in summary earlier, by explaining the circumstances of some of the messengers and the good end they received. It also includes an explanation of the evil end of some of those who were warned, such as the people of Noah, peace be upon him, and an explanation of the good end of some of those whom Allah purified, or who purified their religion, according to the two readings (qira'at), such as the people of Yunus, peace be upon him. The placing of the story of Noah, peace be upon him, before all the other stories needs no explanation. His call (nida') peace be upon him includes a supplication against the disbelievers of his people, a request for deliverance, and a plea for help. The lam (la-) is attached to the answer of an omitted oath, and likewise what is in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿so how excellent were the Answerers!﴾, where the object of praise is omitted, and the fa' (so) is an eloquent connector (fa' fasihah), meaning: "By Allah, Noah certainly called Us when he despaired of the faith of his people, after he had called them for ages and eons, but his supplication only increased them in flight and aversion. So We answered him in the best answer. By Allah, how excellent are We as Answerers!" So what was omitted was omitted, relying on what was mentioned as an indication of it. The plural form is for majesty and grandeur, and in it is an exaltation of the matter of answering to the extent that it contains. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed in my house and passed by this verse, ﴿And Noah certainly called out to Us, so how excellent were the Answerers!﴾, he would say: 'You have spoken the truth, our Lord. You are the nearest of those who are called upon, and the nearest of those who are sought. How excellent is the One who is called upon, how excellent is the Giver, how excellent is the One who is asked, how excellent is the Protector, our Lord, and how excellent is the Helper.'"

(p. 98)

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 76:

﴿And We saved him and his family from the great distress﴾. [It was] from the drowning, according to what is related from al-Suddi. It was also said: [it was] the harm of his people. There is no barrier to combining the two. Al-karb (distress), according to what al-Raghib [al-Isfahani] said, is intense grief. Its root is from karb al-ard (the tilling of the earth), which is turning it over by digging; so grief stirs the soul in the way that tilling stirs the earth. It may also be that it derives from karabat al-shams (the sun drew near), when it approaches setting. And the saying "inaʾun karban" (a vessel nearly full), on the pattern of "qarban" (near), means close to being filled, or close to... [the word] karb, which is a thick knot in the rope of a bucket. And grief may indeed be described as a knot upon the heart.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 77:

﴿And We made his descendants the survivors﴾, so [it was] only [that] when We destroyed the disbelievers in accordance with his supplication: ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth any of the disbelievers a dwelling-place.﴾ It has been narrated that everyone in the ship died, and they left no lasting progeny except his three sons, Sam, Ham and Japheth, and their wives; for they continued to have offspring until the Day of Resurrection.

al-Tirmidhi related it and graded it sound (hasan), and Ibn Sa'd, Ahmad, Abu Ya'la, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim related it and declared it sound, from Samurah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Sam is the father of the Arabs, Ham is the father of the Abyssinians, and Japheth is the father of the Romans." Ibn Mardawayh related a similar report from Abu Hurairah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Yes, al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Khatib in Tali al-Talkhis related from him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Noah had three sons: Sam, Ham and Japheth. The descendants of Sam are the Arabs, the Persians and the Romans, and goodness is among them. The descendants of Japheth are Gog and Magog, the Turks and the Slavs, and there is no goodness among them. The descendants of Ham are the Copts and the Sudanese." I do not know the status of this report. Most scholars hold that all people in the east and west of the earth are from the descendants of Noah (peace be upon him), and for this reason he is called "the second Adam." And if it is established that Canaan, the drowned one, had a son in the ship, it is not far-fetched to include him among the descendants, and so it is not restricted to the three sons. Some have used the verse as evidence that all people are from his descendants. A group said: Allah the Exalted preserved the descendants of Noah (peace be upon him) and extended his lineage, and people are not confined to his lineage; rather, among the nations are those who do not trace back to him. This is reported in al-Bahr. It seems this group does not hold that the drowning was universal, and Noah (peace be upon him) only prayed against the disbelievers, and he was not sent to all the people of the earth, for the universality of the mission from the beginning is among the special features of the Seal of the Messengers (ﷺ), and the arrival of news of his call, while he was in the Arabian Peninsula, to all the regions such as the land of China and others, is not known.

The restriction in the verse, with respect to those in the ship, applies to those other than his children and their wives. It is as if it were said: "And We made his descendants the survivors," not the descendants of those who were with him in the ship. This does not necessitate that the descendants of those who were not with him did not survive, and there were in some vast regions, which the call had not reached and whose people did not deserve drowning, such as the people of China, according to what they claim. It is also possible that this group holds the universality [of the flood], and makes the restriction with respect to those drowned, and commits to the view that no lineage remained for anyone from among the people of the ship who is from the descendants of any of the drowned; that is: "And We made his descendants the survivors," not the descendants of anyone else among the drowned. As for the son of Canaan, if it is established, and if the survival of his lineage is established, he entered into his descendants. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

(Page 99)

﴿And We left for him among the later generations﴾: among those who remain, for the rest of time. ﴿Peace be upon Noah﴾: a subject (mubtada') and predicate (khabar).

The subject may begin with an indefinite noun because it carries the sense of a supplication (du'a'). The statement is given as a quotation (hikaya), as in your saying, "I read ﴿a surah We have sent down﴾." According to al-Farra' and others among the Kufan grammarians, it is quoted by "tarak" (left) in a position of accusative (nasb) governed by it, meaning: "We left for him this very statement."

Others said: it is quoted by an implied utterance (qawl muqaddar), meaning: "We left for him among the later generations the saying 'Peace be upon Noah'." The intended meaning is that We kept for him the supplication and greetings of people, nation after nation. It was also said: this peace is from Him, Mighty and Majestic, and not from the later generations. The object of ﴿We left﴾ is omitted, meaning: "We left for him the good praise and kept it for him among those who come after him until the end of time." This is attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi.

The clause ﴿Peace be upon Noah﴾ is an object governed by an implied utterance, according to what al-Khafaji mentioned, meaning: "And We said: Peace..." etc. Abu Hayyan said: it is a resumptive clause (mustani'afa), God Most High having bestowed peace upon him, peace be upon him, so that mankind might take this as an example and no one would mention him with evil.

'Abdullah [Ibn Mas'ud] read "salaman" with a fatha, as the object of ﴿We left﴾.

The words of God Most High ﴿in the worlds﴾ are connected to the adverbial phrase (zarf), since it substitutes for its governing verb, or to what the adverbial phrase is connected to. It was also permitted that it be a circumstantial (hal) from the hidden pronoun within it. In any case, it is part of the preceding sentence. It was brought in to indicate complete concern for the matter of peace, in that the statement established its permanence among the worlds, of angels and of the two species (humans and jinn), or that it was—while in the worlds—upon Noah. This is like your saying, "Peace upon Zayd in all places and at all times." Some claimed it is permissible to make it a substitute (badal) for God's words ﴿among the later generations﴾, but this is nearly an error, as is not hidden.

The words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾, give the reason for what was done to him, which Allah related. He was among those known for goodness and firmly established in it, so what happened was a case of rewarding good with good. His goodness was his striving against the enemies of Allah, the Exalted, by calling to His religion and his long patience with their harm, and similar things that have been mentioned. The reference "thus" (dhalika) points to the noble honours that were bestowed on him, peace be upon him, as a reward. The sense of distance in it (indicating the far-off demonstrative) signals the lofty rank of his station and the great distance of his position in virtue and nobility. The kaf (like/thus) is connected to what follows it, meaning: "Like that complete reward, We reward those who are complete in goodness, not a lesser reward than it."

The words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants﴾, give the reason for his being a doer of good, which is understood from the context, namely the purity of his servitude and the perfection of his faith. It contains, as is clear, an indication of the great worth of both qualities. Otherwise, the station of prophethood is a great station, and a messenger does not depart from sincere servitude and perfect faith. Thus the purpose of the attribute is to praise the attribute itself, not merely to praise the one it describes.

﴿Then We drowned the others﴾, meaning those who opposed Noah, peace be upon him, and his family, namely the disbelievers of his people, all of them. "Thumma" (then) here indicates a lapse in mention (al-tarakhi al-dhikri), since the survival of him, peace be upon him, and those with him came after the drowning in time, though it is mentioned after it in the narrative.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 83:

﴿And indeed, among his followers﴾ means: among those who supported Noah and followed him in the fundamentals of the religion, ﴿was Abraham﴾, even though the derivative rulings (furu') of their two sacred laws (shari'ah) differ. Or it means: among those who supported him in steadfastness in the religion of God, the Exalted, and in enduring those who denied. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also permissible that there was a complete or majority agreement between their two laws, and the majority takes the ruling of the whole. I have seen in some books (and I do not now recall which book it is) that Noah (peace be upon him) was sent only with tawhid (monotheism) and the like of the fundamental beliefs ('aqa'id), and was not sent with derivative rulings (furu'). It has been said: between Abraham and him, peace be upon them both, there were only two prophets, Hud and Salih, and no others. Perhaps by "prophet" (nabi) is meant "messenger" (rasul), not what is more general than it. This is based on the view that Sam was a prophet. And, according to what is in Jami' al-Usul, the period between them was one thousand one hundred and forty-two years. It has also been said it was two thousand six hundred and forty years.

Al-Farra' held that the pronoun in ﴿his followers﴾ refers to our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is what we have pointed to, and it is what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi. It is rarely said of one who came earlier that he is a follower (shi'ah) of one who came later. From this is the verse of al-Kumayt al-Asghar ibn Zayd:

"I have no followers but the family of Ahmad, and I have no path but the path of truth, its path."

The mention of the story of Abraham after the story of Noah is because he is, relative to the prophets and messengers after him, like the third Adam, since they are all from his offspring, except Lot, who is in the position of his son, peace be upon them both. What adds to the beauty of the sequence is that God, the Exalted, saved Noah from drowning, and God, the Exalted, saved Abraham from burning.

﴿When he came to his Lord﴾ is in the accusative (manṣūb) governed by "remember" (udhkur), as is usual in similar constructions. It has also been permitted for it to depend on an implied verb indicated by His words, ﴿Indeed, among his followers﴾, as if it were said: "When did he follow him?" and the answer is: "He followed him when he came to his Lord." It has also been said that it depends on "followers" (shī'ah), because the word contains the meaning of following (mushāyaʿah). This has been rejected on the grounds that it would require the governing word to precede the lam of initiation (lām al-ibtidā') and operate on what follows it, and they do not permit this because of the requirement that the lam stand at the head of its clause (ṣadārah). Thus one may not say: "Indeed, a striker is coming to us, Zayd," and similarly it would require separating the governing word from the governed by an extraneous element, which is not permitted.

It has been answered that there is no objection to either, when the governed element is an adverbial complement (ẓarf), because of the latitude they allow in such cases.

﴿with a sound heart﴾: that is, free from all defects, such as corrupt beliefs, evil intentions and ugly qualities like envy, rancour and others. ʿAbdullāh (sic) — rather, Qatādah restricted soundness to being free from shirk, but the generality we have mentioned is better. Or, it means free from worldly attachments, in the sense that there is nothing in it of love for them, inclination towards them, or towards their people. It has also been said that "sound" (salīm) means "grieving" (ḥazīn), a metaphorical use from al-salīm meaning one stung by a snake or scorpion, for the Arabs call such a person "sound" optimistically, hoping for his recovery, and the word then became literal for that meaning. What precedes is more suitable to the context. The bāʾ, it has been said, is for transitivity. The meaning of his coming to his Lord with his heart is that he sincerely devoted his heart to Him, exalted is He, by way of a subsidiary, explicit metaphor (istiʿārah tabʿiyyah taṣrīḥiyyah). Its basis is the comparison of his sincere devotion of his heart to Him, glorified and exalted is He, with coming to Him, exalted is He, with a gift, in that it is a cause of attaining His good pleasure. The impossibility of the literal meaning, together with the fact that the context is one of praise, suffices as an indicator. Thus the sense of the construction is: when he, peace be upon him, sincerely devoted to God, exalted is He, his heart, sound from defects, or detached from attachments, or grieving and humbled. It has been objected that soundness of the heart from defects cannot exist without sincerity, and likewise detachment from attachments cannot exist without it. It has been answered that both may exist without that, as in hearts that are simple. In al-Muṭliʿ, the meaning of his coming to his Lord with his heart is that he sincerely devoted his heart to God, exalted is He, and God, glorified is He, knew that from him, just as an absent person and his circumstances are known by his coming and presence; so the coming was used as an example for that. End of quotation. In the statement about it there is an allegorical, representational metaphor (istiʿārah tamthīliyyah), in which the configuration abstracted from Abraham's, peace be upon him, sincere devotion of his heart to his Lord, exalted is He, and God's knowledge, glorified is He, of that sincerity in him, is likened to the configuration abstracted from bringing an absent person into the presence of someone who knows him and knows his circumstances, and then the metaphor is extended as required. To express this meaning, the expression deviated from "came to his Lord with a sound heart" to what is in the sublime composition. It has also been said that the bāʾ is for accompaniment (mulābasah), and this is perhaps the most evident reading. The meaning of his coming to his Lord is his dwelling in the station of obedience and the like. It has been mentioned that the wisdom in deviating from what you have heard to what is in the text is that it avoids the suspicion that the condition is transient, since transience is the more common state of such conditions, while it is also more clearly indicative that the soundness of the heart was his, peace be upon him, even before the coming. So let it be pondered.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verses 85–86:**

﴿When he said to his father and his people, "What is it that you worship?"﴾ is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for the first *idh* (إذ, "when"), or it is a *zarf* (adverbial complement of time or place) governed by *jaa'a* (جاء, "came") or by *Salim* (سَلِيم, "sound"). That is, "what thing do you worship?"

﴿Is it falsehood, gods other than God, that you desire?﴾ That is, do you desire gods other than God, the Exalted, as *ifkan* (إفكًا), meaning for the sake of falsehood? The direct object was placed before the verb for emphasis, because denouncing it or establishing it as a matter of fact is the point intended. This also serves the rhyme (*fasila*, فاصلة, the verse-ending). Then comes the *maf'ul li-ajlihi* (object of purpose), because the more important matter is confronting them with the fact that they are upon falsehood and vanity in their polytheism.

It is permissible for *ifkan* (إفكًا) to be a direct object, meaning "do you desire a falsehood?", with *alihatan* (آلهة, "gods") being a *badal* (substitute) from it, a *badal kull min kull* (substitute of the whole for the whole). Treating the gods as the very falsehood is hyperbole, or the speech contains an elided modifier, meaning "the worship of gods," which is a diversion of worship from its proper direction. It was also permitted for *ifkan* to be a *hal* (circumstantial state) from the pronoun in *turidun* (تُرِيدُونَ, "you desire"), meaning "lying" (*affakin*, أفّاكين), or from its object, meaning "being lied about" (*ma'fukatan*, مَأْفُوكَةً). It was objected that making a verbal noun a circumstantial state is not general, and occurs only with *amma* (أمّا), as in *amma 'ilman fa-'alimun* (أمّا عِلْمًا فَعالِمٌ, "as for knowledge, he is a knower").
