Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 87:

﴿So what is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?﴾ That is: what is your thought about the One who deserves worship because He is the Lord of the worlds? Did you doubt Him to the point that you abandoned His worship altogether? Or did you know what He is, so that you made idols partners with Him, glory be to Him and exalted be He? Or what is your thought about His punishment, mighty and majestic is He, that you dared to fabricate lies against Him, exalted be He, and did not fear? His people, peace be upon him, used to revere the well-known stars and believed that good fortune, misfortune, good and evil in the world come from them. They would take a sanctuary (haykal) for each of these stars and place in them idols that suit that star in their claim. They made worshipping and venerating these idols a means to worshipping those stars and summoning their spiritual forces (ruhaniyyat). They used to infer from their positions the cosmic events, generally or specifically. It so happened that the day of a festival of theirs drew near, on which they would go out. So their king sent to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, saying: "Tomorrow is our festival, so attend with us." He sensed an opportunity arising, through what might become a cause for their monotheism, so he wished to excuse himself from attending in a manner they would not deny him,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 88:

﴿So he glanced a glance at the stars﴾. That is, he reflected in some manner upon their conditions. In reality, it was in the manner of the reflection of those who are perfect in contemplating the creation of the heavens and the earth and in pondering that; for this is what befits him, peace be upon him. But he gave them the impression that he had reflected upon their conditions regarding conjunction, opposition and similar configurations, which by their assumption indicate events, so that he might build upon this what would lead him to his purpose, which would be a means of rescuing them from what they were in. The apparent meaning, after considering the impression, is that it was the impression of reflecting upon the judgments of the ascendant at his birth, peace be upon him, and what it indicates according to their assumption, namely the configurations that had occurred to him at that time. This is among the allusive actions (ma'arid al-af'al), like what occurred in the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him, in the searching of the bags of his brothers, the sons of his father by different mothers (bani 'illat), before the bag of his full brother. For the one searching began with their bags although he knew that the drinking cup was not in them, and delayed searching his brother's bag although he knew it was in it, as an allusion that he did not know in which bag it was, and to clear the accusation from him had he begun with the brother's bag.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 89 (part 1 of 9):

﴿So he said﴾, that is, to them, ﴿"Indeed, I am sick."﴾ He meant that he would become sick. And he spoke the truth, peace be upon him, for every human being must fall ill. The disturbance of the temperament is enough of a sickness, being the first onset of death's spreading through the body. It has also been said: he meant "I am now prone to sickness," or "my temperament is out of balance, a departure from equilibrium that few are free of," or "I am sick at heart because of your disbelief." The people understood that he meant that he was about to be afflicted with a sickness which would prevent him from going out with them to their festival. This, according to what is reported from Sufyan and Ibn Jubayr, was the sickness of plague, for both of them interpreted ﴿sick﴾ as "afflicted with plague." It was, as has been said, the most prevalent of diseases among them, and they were greatly fearful of it, because they believed in contagion. Similarly, his peace be upon him, saying ﴿"Rather, it was done by their chief, this one"﴾ and his saying about his wife Sarah, "She is my sister," belong to the category of equivocal speech (ma'arid al-aqwal), like the saying of our Prophet ﷺ to one who asked him on the road of the Hijrah, "From whom is the man?" He replied, "From water," intending to mention the origin of his creation, while the questioner understood it as a statement of his tribe. Likewise is the saying of his companion al-Siddiq, when he was asked about the Prophet ﷺ in that same matter: "He is a guide who guides me," intending one thing while the questioner understood another. Such a thing is not regarded as a lie in reality.

As for his being described with it in some sound hadiths, this is with regard to what others understood from it, not with regard to what the speaker intended. As for its being counted as a sin in the hadith of intercession, it is said that this is because it becomes evident to Abraham, peace be upon him, that it was something contrary to the better course, not that every equivocation is like that. For it may be obligatory, and the Imam, due to the narrowness of his prayer niche and sphere, denies the hadith reported on this matter, which is in the Two Sahihs, and says: "Attributing a lie to its narrator is easier than attributing it to the Friend (al-Khalil), peace be upon him." The discussion of this has already passed.

It has also been said: he had a fever which came at a specific time of the night, so he looked to know whether it was that hour, and when it had arrived he said to them, "Indeed, I am sick." None of this is among the equivocations. Similar to this is what Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: their king sent to him, peace be upon him, saying, "Tomorrow is our festival, so come out with us." He looked at a star and said, "Indeed, this star has never risen except that it rose with a sickness for me."

You know that the verb "nazara" when followed by "fi" means reflection and contemplation, and the looking referred to here does not require contemplation. From Abu Muslim it is reported that the meaning is: he looked and reflected upon the stars in order to infer from their conditions that they are created and that they are not fit to be gods; then he said, "Indeed, I am sick," meaning sick in his looking, since perfect certainty had not been achieved for him. End. By my life, this, in my view, strips Abu Muslim of Islam, and it contains such ignorance of the station of the prophets, especially the Friend, upon him and upon them peace, as indicates a sickness in his looking. We seek refuge in God, exalted, from His abandonment and His deception.

Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from Qatadah that "nazara nazrah fi al-nujum" is a phrase from the speech of the Arabs; they say, when a person reflects, "he looked at the stars." Accordingly, it is not an equivocation; rather his saying "Indeed, I am sick" alone is of that kind. This, if it is supported by a transmission from the lexicographers, is very good.

It has also been said: the meaning is that he looked into the conditions of the stars, or into their science, or into their books and their judgments, in order to infer what would happen to him. Looking into them to infer some matters is not forbidden by the Law, provided it is with the belief that God, exalted, made them signs for that; what is forbidden is inference with the belief that they have influence in themselves, and a firm conviction in the universality of their judgments. Al-Kirmani, in his Manasik, has mentioned, according to what al-Khafaji said, that the Prophet ﷺ said to a man who wanted to travel at the end of the month: "Do you wish to lose your bargain and have your effort go in vain? Wait until the crescent appears!" End.

This investigation is among the most important of investigations, for it has remained the arena of contention among scholars and wise philosophers. We have promised to establish the truth in it and to explain its turbidity and its clarity. So we say, and with God, exalted, is success, in following the most upright path:

Know that some people have denied that the stars have any influence on this world beyond the presence of light in the places where the sun and moon rise upon and its absence where they set, and similar things. This is a departure from fairness and a path of injustice and oppression. Others have said: they have an influence on what follows natural matters, such as a land of little elevation whose temperament inclines away from balance toward heat and dryness, and likewise its people's temperament, so their bodies are weak and their colors are black and yellow, like the Nubians and Abyssinians; and a land of great elevation whose temperament inclines away from balance toward cold and moisture, and likewise its people's temperament, so their bodies are stout and their colors white and their hair fair, like the Turks and Slavs; and like the growth of plants, their strengthening, and the ripening of their fruit by the sun and moon, and similar things perceived by the senses. There is no harm in attributing this to the star, in the sense that God, exalted, deposited in it a influential power, so that it has effect by God's permission, just as burning is attributed to fire and quenching to water, for example, in that sense. This is the position of the early generations (al-salaf), according to what Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani said concerning all causes and their effects, and some of the Maturidis stated it explicitly. Or it means that God, exalted, created that effect in its presence, and there is no influential power in it at all, as the Ash'aris say about every cause and effect. For them there is no difference between water and fire, for example, in that neither has in itself a power from which the result follows; the only difference is that God's custom has been that He creates burning in the presence of fire and not water, and creates quenching in the presence of water and not fire, and neither fire nor water has any part in the effect of burning or quenching except that each accompanies God's creation of the effect without an intermediary.

The apparent evidences agree with the former, and their position does not conflict with the Oneness of Actions, and that He, exalted and majestic, is the Creator of everything, as has been established in its proper place.

Some have claimed that they have an influence known to the astrologer besides that, such as good and bad fortune, length and shortness of life, breadth and narrowness of livelihood, and other things that are not hidden from anyone who consults the books on judging the ascendants of births, the ascendants of years, eclipses, and deeds, and the like. This is something that should not be relied upon or attended to, for there is no rational or transmitted proof for it; rather the evidences stand against its falsity, and they undertake to demolish its foundations. Those who hold it, although they agree that good and evil, giving and withholding, and similar things occur in the world through the stars according to their good or ill fortune, and their being in signs which are either discordant or harmonious to them, and according to the aspects of some to others by sextile, square, trine, and opposition, and according to their being in their exaltation, their fall, their detriment, their retrogression, their direct motion, and their stationing, have disagreed on many principles and spoken words at which the people of intellect laugh. For they have disagreed on the manner in which this occurs. Some of them claimed that their action is by their natures; others claimed that it is not their action but that they indicate it by their natures; others claimed that they act in some cases incidentally and in some cases essentially; others claimed that they act by choice, not by nature, except that the fortunate one among them chooses only good and the ill-fated one chooses only evil; and this is together with their saying that they may coincide upon good and may coincide upon evil, which is a matter at which one marvels. Others claimed that they do not act by choice but merely indicate, and this is a statement whose meaning is not intelligible.

They also disagreed: one group said that among the stars there are some that are fortunate and some that are ill-fated, and some of them bring good fortune to others and bring ill fortune to others. Another group said: they are in themselves one nature, and only their indication of good and bad fortune differs. This is the view of those among them who say that the sphere has a nature different from the nature of the corruptible, generable elements, and that it is neither hot nor cold, nor dry nor moist, and there is neither fortune nor misfortune in it; rather some of its bodies and parts indicate good and others indicate evil, and the connection of good and evil, fortune and misfortune, with them is the connection of signified things to their signs, not the connection of effects to their causes. This is wiser than the advocates of natural necessitation and causality, although this view, in the opinion of some eminent scholars, is also worthless, because sensory indication does not differ or contradict.

They also disagreed: one group said that they act upon both bodies and souls, and this is the view of Ptolemy and his followers; and most said that they act upon souls but not upon bodies. Perhaps the disagreement is merely verbal. Their leaders, Ptolemy, Dorotheus, Antiochus, Rimas, and others among the scholars of the Romans, the Indians, and Babylon, disagreed about the rules and other matters, and they contradicted one another in the sources from which they took their evidence. Among these is their disagreement about the Lot of Fortune. Ptolemy claimed it is computed by always taking the number from the position of the sun to the position of the moon, beginning from the ascendant, and then projecting from it the same number in succession; the endpoint of the count is the place of the Lot. Some claimed it begins from the ascendant and counts the same number in reverse order. Some Persians claimed that the Lot of Fortune is taken at night from the moon to the sun, and by day from the sun to the moon. The people of Egypt, regarding the rules, claimed it is taken from the lords of the houses, and the Chaldeans claimed it is taken from the lords of the triplicities. They also disagreed: one group arranged the masculine and feminine signs from the ascendant, counting one masculine and then one feminine, and made the beginning with the masculine. Another group divided the signs into four parts, and made the masculine ones those from the ascendant to the midheaven and those opposite them from the descendant to the nadir, and made the other two quarters feminine. And what makes the intelligent laugh is that they divided the signs into two kinds, hot in temperament and cold, and made the hot ones male and the cold ones female, beginning with Aries, saying: it is male and hot, and the one after it is female and cold, and so on to the end, so that there were six males and six females. Some said: the first is male, and the three after it are female, the fifth is male, and the three after it are female, the ninth is male, and what follows it is female. So the males are three, and after each male come three females differing from it in nature. Then this division into masculine and feminine is essential to the signs, and it has a second division by accident, namely that they begin from the ascendant to the twelfth, taking one male and another female.

[Page 107]

Some have claimed that the stars' acting by choice (ikhtiyar) entails nullifying the matters of conjunction, separation, conjunction-in-sign, descent, and the like. The state of what was mentioned as a condition for choice is not hidden. As for the claim that the stars necessitate (these effects) by the nature of their rays, which are heating and cooling, and that these two bring about the difference of bodily temperaments, and that the difference of temperaments brings about the difference of the soul's acts: this is answered by the fact that we see heating, for example, producing heat and sharpness in temperament, by which one person does the utmost good and virtuous deeds while another does the utmost evil and wicked deeds. So this difference requires a cause other than heating. Also, they say that all created events (al-hawadith al-kawniyya) are traced back to the stars, and the discussion of heating and cooling and their entailing the difference of the soul's acts does not achieve this aim.

[Page 108]

Imam al-Razi, may God have mercy on him, mentioned that those who affirm the science of judgments (ʿilm al-aḥkām, astrological judgments) and influences (al-taʾthirat) (i.e., among the Muslims) argued from the Book of God, Exalted, with verses of several kinds.

The first: verses indicating the greatness of the stars. Among them is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So I swear by the stars that recede, that run and hide﴾ (81:15–16). Most exegetes hold that what is meant are the stars that sometimes become retrograde and sometimes direct. Among them is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So I swear by the places of the stars—and indeed it is a mighty oath, if you only knew﴾ (56:75–76). He, glorified be He, has declared this oath to be great, and that indicates the utmost majesty of the places of the stars and the highest degree of their nobility. Among them is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿By the sky and the night-visitant. And what will make you know what the night-visitant is? The piercing star﴾ (86:1–3). Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The piercing star is Saturn, because it pierces the thickness of the seven heavens with its light." Among them is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars are subjected by His command. Unquestionably, to Him belong creation and command. Blessed is God, Lord of the worlds﴾ (7:54). He, glorified be He, has thus shown His divinity by making these stars under His management and subjugation.

The second kind: what indicates that He, Exalted, describes some days with misfortune, such as His saying, glorified be He: ﴿So We sent upon them a furious wind during days of misfortune﴾ (41:16).

The third kind: verses indicating that they have an influence in this world, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who arrange affairs (fa-al-mudabbirati amran)﴾ (79:5), and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who distribute affairs (fa-al-muqassimati amran)﴾ (51:4). Some said: what is meant is these stars.

The fourth: verses indicating that He, Exalted, made the motions and the creation of these bodies in a manner by which benefit is derived for the interests of this world, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light, and determined for it phases that you may know the number of years and the reckoning. God did not create that except in truth﴾ (10:5), and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations and placed therein a lamp and a luminous moon﴾ (25:61).

The fifth kind: that He, Exalted, related of Abraham, peace be upon him, that he relied on the science of the stars, so He, glorified be He, said: ﴿Then he looked a look at the stars﴾ (37:88) ﴿and said, "Indeed, I am ill"﴾ (37:89).

The sixth: that He, Exalted, said: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind, but most of mankind do not know﴾ (40:57). The meaning cannot be the largeness of the mass, because everyone knows this; so it must be that the meaning is the greatness of rank and nobility. He, glorified be He, also said: ﴿And they contemplate the creation of the heavens and the earth, [saying], "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain"﴾ (3:191). It is not permissible that the meaning be that He, Exalted, created them so that by the composition and arrangement of them one would infer the existence of the Creator, because this degree is present in the composition of a gnat; and the indication of the presence of life in the structure of animals of the existence of the Creator is stronger than the indication of the composition of the celestial bodies, because life is not capable of being produced by anyone other than Him, Exalted, whereas composition in general can be produced by others. So when He, glorified and exalted be He, singled them out with this honour—derived from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾—we know that in their creation there are lofty secrets and far-reaching wisdoms, by which the minds of humans fall short of comprehending. Close to this verse is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾ (38:27). It is not possible that the meaning be that He, Exalted, created them in a manner by which the existence of the wise Creator can be inferred from them, because their being an indication of their need for a Creator is a fact established for them in their very essence, since every spatially-occupying thing (mutahayyiz) is originated, and every originated thing needs an agent. So it is established that the indication of spatially-occupying things of the existence of an agent is a fact established for them by their very selves and essences. What is like this cannot be the cause of an act and a making. So it is not possible to take the verse in this sense, and it is necessary to take it in the sense already mentioned.

The seventh kind: it is reported that ʿUmar ibn al-Khayyam used to read the book of al-Majisti (the Almagest) to his teacher. A member of the jurists (al-mutafaqqihah, students of jurisprudence) entered upon them and said: "What are you doing?" ʿUmar said: "We are engaged in the exegesis of a verse of the Book of God, Exalted: ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them—how We constructed it and adorned it, and it has no rifts?﴾ (50:6). So we are looking at how He created the sky, how He built it, and how He preserved it from rifts."

The eighth: when Abraham, peace be upon him, argued for establishing the Creator by His saying, Exalted: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾ (2:258), Nimrod said to him:

[Page 108]

Do you claim that He gives life and causes death through the natures (tabaʾiʿ) and the elements (ʿanasir), or not through them? If you claim the first, that is something you will absolutely not find, because everything that occurs in this world is by means of the elements and the celestial motions. And if you claim the second, then such giving of life and causing death is found from me and from everyone, and that is what is meant by His saying: ﴿"I give life and cause death"﴾ (2:258). Then Abraham, peace be upon him, did not dispute that these lower events are connected to the celestial motions. Rather, he answered that God, Exalted, is the originator of those motions, so the act is truly from Him, glorified be He; and one of us cannot move the spheres contrary to the divine motion. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿"Indeed, God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west"﴾ (2:258).

When you know the method of discourse in this matter, you will know that the Noble Qur'an is full of glorifying the celestial bodies and ennobling the stellar spheres.

As for reports (akhbar), there are many. Among them is what is reported: that he (ﷺ) forbade facing the sun and the moon or turning one's back to them while relieving oneself. Among them: when his (ﷺ) son Ibrahim died, the sun eclipsed, and people said, "It eclipsed only for the death of Ibrahim." So he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed the sun and the moon are two signs among the signs of God, Exalted. They do not eclipse for the death of anyone nor for his life. So when you see that, hasten to prayer." Among them is what Ibn Masʿud reported: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When fate (al-qadar) is mentioned, refrain; when my companions are mentioned, refrain; when the stars are mentioned, refrain." Some people narrate that he (ﷺ) said: "Do not travel while the moon is in Scorpio." Some of them narrate it from ʿAli, may God honour his face, though the traditionists do not accept it.

As for narrations from the companions (athar), they are also many. From ʿAli, may God honour his face: a man came to him at the end of the month and said: "I want to go out on a trade." He said: "Do you want God to destroy your trade? Set out at the beginning of the month's crescent!"

From ʿIkrima: a Jewish astrologer said to him, Ibn ʿAbbas: "Woe to you! You tell people what you do not know?" He said: "Your son in the school will get a fever tomorrow and die on the tenth day." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "And when will you die?" He said: "At the year's end." Then he (Ibn ʿAbbas) said to him: "And you will not die until you go blind." All of that came to pass.

From al-Shaʿbi, who said: "Abu al-Darda' said: 'The Messenger of God (ﷺ) departed and left us, and there is not a bird that flies on its two wings except that we claim knowledge of it.'"

The stars are not assigned to corruption and rectitude, but in them is an indication of some events, which is known by experience. It has been reported in the narrations that the first to be given this knowledge was Adam, peace be upon him: he lived until he saw forty thousand households of his descendants, who had dispersed over the earth, and he used to grieve over the obscurity of their news. So God, Exalted, honoured him with this knowledge, and whenever he wanted to know the condition of one of them, he looked at the stars and knew him.

From Maymun ibn Mihran, who said: "Beware of denying the stars, for it is from the knowledge of prophethood." It is reported from al-Shafiʿi that he was knowledgeable in the stars. A child was born to one of his neighbours, and he judged for him that this child should have on such-and-such a limb a mole of such-and-such description; and the matter turned out as he said. Ibn Ishaq narrated that the astrologers informed Pharaoh that a boy from the Children of Israel would be born whose destruction would be at his hand. And so it was, as God, Exalted, related: ﴿He slaughters their sons and keeps alive their women﴾ (28:4).

As for what is rational (al-maʿqul): this knowledge has not been free of any religion among the religions, nor of any nation among the nations; they have always been occupied with it and relied upon it in knowing the interests. And if it were entirely corrupt, it would be impossible for the people of the East and the West, from the beginning of the construction of the world until its end, to agree upon it. The experiments in this field are more than can be counted. End of his words.

By my life, he has scattered the quiver, emptied the bag, exhausted his strength, expended his effort, dressed up falsehood and embellished it, thundered and crackled, and without any grinding, has pounded the air. He has combined what is known necessarily to be a lie upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and upon his companions, with what is known necessarily to be an error in interpreting the words of God, Exalted, and in knowing His intent, glorified be He. What he mentioned is accepted only by someone extremely ignorant or a blind follower of the people of falsehood among the astrologers.

If you want clarification and wish for explicitness, then listen to what we say: What he mentioned of the proofs is weaker than spiders' houses, and most like the fire of al-Hubahib (a fire that flares briefly and dies). As for the argument from His saying, Exalted: ﴿So I swear by the stars that recede, that run and hide﴾ (81:15–16), we do not concede that there is an oath here by the stars. It has been reported from Ibn Masʿud that what is meant by al-khunnas is wild cattle, and this is a narration from Ibn ʿAbbas; Ibn Jubayr chose it. Al-Mawardi related that they are the angels. And even if we grant that it refers to the stars, according to what the majority held, what indication is there in it of influence? God, glorified be He, has sworn by the night and the day, the forenoon, Mecca, the begetter and what he begot, the dawn, ten nights, the even and the odd, the sky and the earth, the promised day, the witness and the witnessed, the sent ones, the stormy winds, the scatterers, the separators, the drawers-out, the swimmers, the racers, the fig and the olive, and Mount Sinai, and other things besides. So if swearing by a thing were evidence of its influence, it would follow that everything God, Exalted, swore by would be influential, and they do not say this. And if it is not evidence, then arguing from it is invalid. Similar to this is the argument from His saying, Exalted: ﴿So I swear by the places of the stars﴾ (56:75), for more than one exegete interpreted "the places of the stars" as the stations (manazil) of the Qur'an and its "stars," which were revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) over a period of twenty-three years. And likewise is the argument from His saying, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿By the sky and the night-visitant﴾ (86:1).

[Page 110]

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿by those who arrange affairs﴾, none of the Companions, the Successors, or the scholars of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) said that it is an oath by the stars. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, Ibn Qutaybah, and others said that what is meant by ﴿those who arrange affairs﴾ is the angels. Ibn 'Atiyyah even said: "I do not know of any disagreement on this." Likewise, ﴿by those who distribute affairs﴾: interpreting these two by the stars is the interpretation of the astrologers (munajjimun) and those who follow their path, and it is interpretation by opinion (tafsir bil-ra'y), God forbid.

As for His exalted description of some days as ill-omened, as in the verse he mentioned, that is not due to the influence of the stars and their ill fortune, as the astrologer claims. Rather, it is because God, exalted is He, punished His enemies on those days, so they are days of ill omen for the enemies. Describing those days as ill-omened is like describing the Day of Resurrection as ﴿difficult for the disbelievers﴾.

The same applies to His saying, ﴿on a day of continuous ill fortune﴾. The word ﴿continuous﴾ here is not a description of ﴿day﴾; rather, it is a description of ﴿ill fortune﴾, meaning ill fortune that is lasting and does not lift from them, unlike the afflictions of this world, which lift from their people. The view that it describes ﴿day﴾, and that the day meant is the last Wednesday of the month and that it is perpetually ill-omened, is a mistake. The astrologer would hardly claim that the last Wednesday of the month is ill-omened forever, even if it were the month of Safar. Rather, he often judges that its fortune is at its best, according to what the celestial configurations require in his claim.

As for his use as evidence of the verses that indicate that He, glorified is He, set the movements of these bodies in a way that benefits the affairs of this world, it is a curiosity. For if the astrologer's claim were correct, the most fitting thing would be for the verse to mention what the stars require of good and ill fortune, what they bestow of happiness and misery, and what they grant of lifespans, provisions, knowledge, and insights, and all the other good and evil in the world. For the lesson in that is far greater than the lesson in mere light and illumination, or in knowing the number of years and calculation.

As for what is reported about Abraham (peace be upon him), that he relied on the knowledge of the stars when he said ﴿Indeed, I am sick﴾, that is a very sick claim. You have already heard what has been said about the verse. It is not fitting to think of the leader of the monotheists (hunafa'), the shaykh of the prophets, and the intimate friend of the Lord of the earth and the heavens, that he engaged in the science of the stars and took from it judgments about events. If this door were opened to the prophets (peace be upon them), it would be possible that all their reports about future matters came from the positions of the stars and not from revelation. And that, as you see, is untenable.

As for the use of His saying, ﴿Indeed, the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾, and the claim that what is meant by it is greatness of rank and nobility, not greatness of bulk, it is utterly corrupt. For the word ''creation'' here means the act, not the thing created. The verse serves to demonstrate the resurrection: the One who created the heavens and the earth, whose creation is greater than your creation, how could He be unable to restore you after death? A parallel to this is His saying, ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them?﴾ And where is this from the investigation of the rulings of the stars and their influences?

Similar to this is the use of His saying, ﴿and they reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth: "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain"﴾. For the creation of the heavens and the earth is among the greatest proofs of the existence of their Originator, the perfection of His power, wisdom, and knowledge, and His singularity in lordship. Whoever equates them with a gnat has been obstinate. This is why you find that weak things such as the gnat, the fly, and the spider are only mentioned in the context of parables, to emphasize their insignificance and weakness, and are not mentioned in the context of proving the greatness of the Lord of majesty, may He be exalted.

Moreover, if the verse indicated that the stars have influence, it would also indicate that the earth has influence, just like the stars. But they have not said that. As for what he mentioned afterward, that the indication of life arising in the bodies of animals is stronger than the indication of the heavens and the earth, and so on to the end of what he said, it falls within the realm of denial. A similar use is His saying, ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾. This verse also does not indicate that the stars have influence. What this verse and its like indicate is only that those creatures have wisdom and benefits in them and are not in vain, that is, empty of that. We say what it indicates, but we do not say that those wisdoms are bringing happiness and misery, granting lifespans and provisions, and so on, which the astrologers claim. Rather, they are the manifest effects in the world of nature, as you have heard, and similar things, such as the indication of the existence of the Creator and many of His attributes, which the disbelievers deny, may He be exalted in majesty. There is no objection to saying: God, exalted is He, created such and such so that its indication of such and such would be manifest. The expression he mentioned is not the only one possible, and on close examination there is nothing wrong with it. Perhaps what he said is among the branches of the view that quiddities are not created, and the discussion of that is well known.

As for what he mentioned from 'Umar ibn al-Khayyam, it is on the edge of thyme (i.e., of little worth). As for what he mentioned about Abraham's argument and the presentation of the debate as he set it out, none of the exegetes, past or present, has said it. Indeed, one may be certain that it never occurred to the idolater who was observing, and it is nothing but interpretation by personal opinion and desire. We seek refuge in God, exalted is He, from that.

As for his use of what is narrated about the Prophet's prohibition (peace and blessings be upon him) against facing the sun and the moon when relieving oneself, it is far from his purpose. Indeed, the prohibition mentioned gives no indication of the influence of the stars that they claim. Otherwise, the prohibition against facing the Ka'bah when relieving oneself would indicate that it too has influence. Moreover, some eminent scholars have mentioned that no single word has been transmitted from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning that prohibition, neither with a sound chain, nor a weak one, nor connected, nor disconnected. Rather, some jurists said, in the etiquette of relieving oneself: "one should not face the sun or the moon." It was said that this is because it is more effective in concealment; it was said that this is because their light is from the light of God, exalted is He; and it was said that this is because the name of God, exalted is He, is written upon them.

As for what he mentioned of the hadith about the eclipse of the sun on the day of Abraham's death, and the Prophet's statement (peace and blessings be upon him) that he made, it is authentic, but it does not indicate what the astrologers claim. The beginning of the hadith indicates that the sun and the moon are two signs and are neither lords nor gods, and in it there is an allusion to denying that they have any control. As for his statement (peace and blessings be upon him), "They do not eclipse for the death of anyone or for his life," there are two views. One is that the death or life of anyone does not cause them to eclipse. The other is that no death or life results from their eclipse. Rather, that is a warning from God, exalted is He, to His servants. He has established the custom that it occurs at times known by calculation, related to the rising of the crescent, its fullness, and its waning. As for the cause of the eclipse of the sun, it is the moon passing between the body of the sun and our eyes, like a cloud passing beneath it. If the moon had no latitude, it would conceal the entire sun from us; if it has latitude, then it conceals the amount that its latitude requires. As for the cause of the eclipse of the moon, it is the earth passing between it and the sun, so that it becomes prevented from acquiring light from the sun, and the darkness of the earth's conical shadow remains in its path. It may be that all of it falls into the cone, or some of it falls into it while the rest remains outside, and so on to the end of what has been established in its proper place. Nothing in the Shari'ah contradicts this. Knowing the time and extent of eclipses is an easy matter, and the astrologer's accuracy in that does not entail the accuracy of what he claims about influences. Reporting them is nothing more than reporting the time of sunrise on such a day at such an hour, or reporting the time of the crescent, its fullness, and its waning.

Furthermore, we do not deny that God, exalted is He, during the two eclipses brings about, from His decrees and destinies, what becomes a trial and calamity for some people, and He makes the eclipse a cause for that. This is why the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded, at the time of eclipse, to turn in fear to the remembrance of God, exalted is He, to prayer, to freeing slaves, and to charity. For these acts are causes for averting the consequence of the eclipse, which God, exalted is He, made a cause of what He made it a cause of. Had the cause of warning not been established, the Prophet (peace be upon him) would not have commanded the averting of its consequence through these acts of worship. For God, exalted is He, has in the days of His time moments in which He brings about whatever He wills of trial and blessing, and He decrees causes that avert the consequence of those causes for whoever is affected by them, or lessen it, or lighten it. So whoever turns in fear to those causes, or some of them, the evil that God, exalted is He, made the eclipse a cause of is averted from him, or part of it is. This is why, in the regions of the earth where faith and what the messengers brought have become hidden, few are safe from the great evil that occurs because of the eclipse. And those places in which the light of prophethood shines and what the messengers brought is upheld are safe from it, or it is very little there.

It has been related that when the sun eclipsed in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), he rose in fear, hastening and dragging his garment, and called out to the people: "The prayer is to be gathered for!" He addressed them with that eloquent sermon and informed them that he had not seen a day like that one, in good and in evil. He commanded them, when such a situation occurred, to free slaves, give charity, pray, and repent. And that was only because he (peace be upon him) was the most knowledgeable of creation about God, exalted is He, about His command, His affair, His disposal of the affairs of His creatures, and His management of them; the most sincere to the community; and the most compassionate toward the servants. The Prophet (peace be upon him) did not explain to them the causes of the two eclipses or their calculation, because ignorance of that does no harm, and knowing it does not benefit in the way that knowing what the messengers (peace be upon them) brought benefits.

It may be said: the command to pray at the time of the two eclipses is like the command to pray at the break of dawn, at sunset, and at midday, together with the inclusion in that of averting their consequence, which God, exalted is He, made them causes of. Some people have denied that the two eclipses are causes of any calamity at all, and that the cause of their occurrence is not what the astrologers have spent long discussing, part of which has passed. Rather, the cause is the manifestation of God, exalted is He, upon them. This is based on what Ibn Majah reported in his Sunan, and Imam Ahmad and al-Nasa'i reported, from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, who said: "The sun eclipsed during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), so he went out in fear, dragging his garment, until he came to the mosque. He kept praying until it cleared. Then he said: 'Indeed, some people claim that the sun and the moon do not eclipse except for the death of a great man among the great. That is not so. Indeed, the sun and the moon do not eclipse for the death of anyone or for his life. So when God manifests Himself to something of His creation, it humbles itself before Him.'" The command to pray is for the manifestation of the effects of the manifestation of majesty upon these two great bodies. Or it is like the command to pray at sunset or at the break of dawn, for example, and its wisdom is like its wisdom. Those who hold this view are being obstinate toward the philosophers regarding matters in which obstinacy is not fitting, and perhaps it harms religion and becomes a cause for the taunts of the atheists.

[Page 111]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 89 (part 5 of 9):

They are obstinate about the claims that the celestial spheres are circular, that the earth is spherical, that the light of the moon is borrowed from the light of the sun, that a lunar eclipse is the disappearance of the moon's light when the earth comes between it and the sun, insofar as its light is derived from the sun, and that a solar eclipse is the moon's body coming between the observer and the sun when the two meet at the nodes (al-'uqdatayn, the lunar nodes) at the same moment. [They also claim] the influence of perceptible causes on their effects, and the affirmation of powers (quwa), natures (taba'i'), actions and reactions, and other matters on which certain proofs rest and which definitive texts of the Sharia do not contradict. As for the hadith they cite, Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali criticised it, saying: "The addition, 'Indeed Allah...' etc., is not established by transmission, so its narrator must be deemed a liar. Even if it were authentic, its interpretation would be easier than the obstinate denial of definitive matters. How many apparent meanings have been interpreted through rational proofs that were not as clear as this! The greatest cause for the joy of the atheists is that a defender of the Sharia declares that this and its like contradict the Sharia, so it becomes easy for them to invalidate the Sharia if its conditions are such things." [End of quotation.]

The matter is not as he said, regarding the claim that it is not authentic, for its isnad (chain) is not open to criticism. Ibn Majah narrates the hadith with this addition from Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna, Ahmad ibn Thabit and Humayd ibn al-Hasan, and they narrate it from 'Abd al-Wahhab, from Khalid al-Hadhdha', from Abu Qilaba, from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir. All of these are trustworthy (thiqat) and memorisers (huffaz). Indeed, the hadith without that addition was narrated by some ten or more Companions, among them 'Ali (may Allah honour his face), Ibn 'Abbas, 'A'isha, her sister Asma', Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Samura ibn Jundub, Qabisa al-Hilali and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr. From here some of the eminent scholars feared that the addition was an interpolation (mudraja) into the hadith, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. In that case it may be said: the eclipse of the sun and the moon causes them to lose some of their authority and splendour, and this brings about in them such humility and submission before the Lord of the worlds, His greatness and His majesty, glory be to Him, that it becomes a cause for His manifestation (tajalli) to them, exalted and majestic is He. It is not objectionable that Allah, glory be to Him, should manifest Himself to them at a specific time, just as He draws near to the people of the standing place (at 'Arafat) on the evening of 'Arafa, and just as He, blessed and exalted, descends every night to the lowest heaven at the passing of half the night. That manifestation causes in them a different humility, which is not the eclipse itself, for the eclipse occurred through the cause you have learned. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not say that when Allah manifests Himself to them they eclipse; rather he said: "When Allah manifests Himself to something of His creation, it humbles itself before Him." In the narration of Imam Ahmad: "When Allah appears to something of His creation, it humbles itself to Him." So there are here two humilities: one caused by their eclipse which occurred from their particular state, and another caused by His manifestation to them, because of that humility which the eclipse caused. This is a subtle interpretation, accepted by sound reason and upright nature, God willing.

As for his citing the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, it is said that if that hadith were established, it would be a proof against him, not for him, since if the science of the stars were true, the Prophet (ﷺ) would not have ordered abstention at the mention of the stars. The apparent meaning is that he (peace be upon him) only ordered this because delving into that is delving into what the one who delves has no knowledge of. So reflect.

As for the hadith forbidding travel while the moon is in Scorpio (al-'Aqrab), it is authentic as a saying of the astrologers (al-munajjimun), not of the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds (ﷺ). Its narration from 'Ali (may Allah honour his face) is also a lie, and what is well known from him is the opposite, as you heard in the account of his going out to fight the Kharijites. As for what he cited from the report from 'Ali (may Allah honour his face) that a man came to him, etc., its authenticity from him is not known (may Allah be pleased with him), and liars often market their false wares by attributing them to him or to the People of his House. Furthermore, even if it were authentic from him, there is nothing in it indicating the establishment of the rulings of the stars in any way. The Prophet (peace be upon him) has indeed said: "O Allah, bless my nation in its early hours." The attribution of the beginning of the month to it is like the attribution of the beginning of the day to it. Sakhr, the narrator of the hadith, used to send his merchandise out at the beginning of the day, and he prospered and his wealth increased. It is not far-fetched that the beginning of the year is also like the beginning of the day; the early parts of things have the virtue of strength, as is observed in youth and old age. Allah has manifestations (tajalliyat) in times, places and persons, and that is not from the influence of the stars in anything. The same may be said of what al-Kirmani mentioned. What he mentioned from the Jew who informed Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) has already passed, and we do not accept its authenticity. Even if it were established, it is of the same kind as the soothsayers' reports of some unseen matters. Ibn al-Sayyad informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of what he informed him, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) said to him: "You are only one of the brothers of the soothsayers."

Knowledge of the introductory preface of knowledge (muqaddimat al-ma'rifa) is not restricted to what the astrologers mention. Rather, it has several causes through which a judgement may be true or false, among them: soothsaying (kihana); dreams (manamat); optimistic omens (fa'l); augury by observing birds (zajr); throwing pebbles (darb al-hasa); geomancy (khatt); scapulimancy (kataf); and spiritual unveiling (kashf) based on spiritual discipline, which is a partial unveiling of some events, shared by believer and unbeliever; and other things besides. Workers at sea and couriers and the like on land have signs by which they know the times of rain, clear weather, hail, wind and other things. They rarely err in their reports; indeed their accuracy in this is greater than the astrologer's accuracy.

As for what he mentioned from the hadith of Abu al-Darda', what is preserved in it is: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died and left us, and there was no bird flapping its wings but that he had told us knowledge of it." There are other authentic narrations of it too, and none of them contains "and the stars are not..." etc. So it is among the greatest proofs of the falsity of the claim of the astrologers, for the Prophet (peace be upon him) mentioned none of the rulings of the stars at all, and he taught them the knowledge of everything, even the matters of relieving oneself (al-khira'a).

As for his saying that it has come in the reports that the first to be given this knowledge was Adam (peace be upon him), etc., it is a lie and a fabrication against Adam (peace be upon him). This liar and fabricator has acted according to the well-known proverb: "If you lie, make your witness distant." Similar is what is related from Maymun ibn Mihran.

As for what is attributed to al-Shafi'i, it is part of an account that Abu 'Abd Allah al-Hakim mentioned in what he composed on his virtues (manaqib). The accounts related from him concerning the rulings of the stars are three. The first: al-Hakim said: It was read to Abu Ya'la Hamza ibn Muhammad al-'Alawi, and my most assured opinion is that I was present, [saying that] Abu Ishaq Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn al-'Abbas al-Azdi related to us along with others, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi Ya'qub al-Jawwal al-Dinawari related to us, 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad al-Balawi related to us, my maternal uncle 'Imara ibn Zayd told me, saying: I was a close friend of Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and I entered with him one day upon Harun al-Rashid, and he asked him [something]. Then I heard Muhammad ibn al-Hasan saying: "Muhammad ibn Idris claims that he is fit for the caliphate." He said: Harun was enraged at his words, then said: "Bring him to me!" When he stood before him, he lowered his gaze for a while, then raised his head to him and said: "O you!" Al-Shafi'i said: "Not 'O you', Commander of the Faithful! You are the one who calls and I am the one called; you are the questioner and I am the responder!" Then he recounted a long account in which he was asked about the sciences and his knowledge of them, until [Harun] said: "How is your knowledge of the stars?" He said: "I know the revolving sphere (al-falak al-da'ir), the moving star (al-najm al-sa'ir), the fixed pole (al-qutb al-thabit), the watery and fiery [signs], what the Arabs used to call the anwa' (rising and setting of stars), the mansions of the two luminaries, direct motion and retrograde motion, the unlucky and the lucky, their configurations and natures, and that by which I am guided on land and sea, and by which I am guided in the times of my prayers, and by which I know the times that have passed in my evening and morning, and my travelling on my journeys." Then he went through the sciences in this manner. Anyone with knowledge of the transmitted reports knows that this account is a fabricated lie and a false invention against al-Shafi'i, and the blame for it lies with Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Balawi, for he is a notorious liar and forger (kadhdhab wadda'). He is the one who forged the journey of al-Shafi'i and mentioned in it his debate with Abu Yusuf in the presence of Harun, though al-Shafi'i never saw Abu Yusuf nor met him at all, since he entered Baghdad only after Abu Yusuf's death. What proves its falsehood is that it indicates that Muhammad (ibn al-Hasan) informed on al-Shafi'i to Harun and wanted to kill him, and Muhammad is too exalted to be attributed with that.

[End of page 114.]

[Page 114 continues]

Its glorifying of al-Shafi'i and his love for him is well known, just as al-Shafi'i glorified him and praised him. There are other proofs of the lie that the one versed in transmitted reports will recognise once he has examined them all.

The second is the one from which I took what the Imam (al-Hakim) mentioned. Al-Hakim said: Abu al-Walid al-Faqih informed us, saying: I was told on the authority of al-Hasan ibn Sufyan, from Harmala, who said: al-Shafi'i used to constantly study the books of the stars (kutub al-nujum). He had a friend who had a slave-girl who had become pregnant, and he said: "She will give birth within twenty-seven days, and there will be a black mole on the left thigh of the child, and it will live for twenty-four days and then die." It happened as he said. He then burned those books and never looked into any of them again.

The chain of this report has trustworthy men, but the problem lies with whoever related to Abu al-Walid from al-Hasan ibn Sufyan, or with whoever related to al-Hasan from Harmala. What shows the story to be false is that, if it were sound, it would have been necessary for fingers to be pointed at this knowledge and for hands to be bound to it, not for its books to be burned and for no one to look into any of them again.

The ascendant (al-tali') according to the astrologers (al-munajjimin) is of two kinds. The first is the ascendant at the moment of the seed's drop (tali' maskit al-nutfa), which is the original ascendant that they claim indicates the time of birth. The story does not include that al-Shafi'i looked at this, and if he had, it would have been included. The second is the ascendant of birth. Al-Shafi'i's prediction came before it, since he said: "She will give birth within twenty-seven days."

The third is what al-Hakim said: Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hasan al-Qadi informed me that Zakariyya ibn Yahya al-Sajji told them, saying: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, the son of al-Shafi'i's daughter, informed me, saying: I heard my father say: "al-Shafi'i, while still a youth, used to look into the stars, and he never looked into anything without excelling in it. One day he sat while a woman was giving birth, and he calculated and said: 'She will give birth to a girl, blind in one eye, with a black mole on her private part, and she will die at such and such a time.' She was born, and it was as he said. So he made it binding on himself never to look into this again." The matter of this report is like the one before it, for the son of al-Shafi'i's daughter never met al-Shafi'i nor saw him, and the problem lies with whoever related it from him.

Also, the ascendant of the drop of the seed was never taken, and the report came before the ascendant of birth was verified. Furthermore, if the verification of this story came before the verification of the one before it, this one would hardly have been verified; and if the verification of that one came first, the other would hardly have been verified, as is not hidden from the fair-minded person.

What is established from al-Shafi'i regarding the matter of the stars is that he knew what the Arabs knew of the science of the lunar mansions (ilm al-manazil) and of guidance by the stars on roads. As for other judgments that the astrologers claim, he did not hold them. He, may Allah be pleased with him, was strongly opposed to the scholastic theologians (al-mutakallimin), disparaging them, and his ruling about them was that they should be beaten with palm-stalks and paraded among the tribes. So what do you suppose he would think of the astrologers, whose nonsense has spread and whose condition has become repugnant to people of sound intellect?

Yes, he, may Allah be pleased with him, had a supreme hand in the science of physiognomy (firasa), and he went to Yemen to gather his books. He gathered what he gathered, and he has accounts in it from which wonders may be drawn. Perhaps his prediction about the child's matter, if it is sound, was from that science, and the transmitter either confused it or attributed it to something else, saying that it was from looking into the judgments of the stars, and said what he said.

As for what Ibn Ishaq mentioned, that Pharaoh used to kill the sons of the Children of Israel because the astrologers informed him that a boy would be born to them whose destruction would be at his hand, this is, as some eminent scholars said, from the reports of the People of the Book, and it contradicts the narrations of most of the exegetes (mufassirin), for they attributed that to the reports of the soothsayers (kuhhan). Some of them narrated that his people informed him that the Children of Israel claimed that a boy would be born among them whose destruction would be at his hands. In the reports of the soothsayers there is something more wondrous than that.

Among them is their report of the emergence of the Seal of the Messengers (ﷺ) and the spread of his affair. We do not deny the knowledge of foreknowledge through causes that lead to such things, which differ in the faculties of people in grasping and attaining them. Our dispute is with the astrologers regarding the foundations of the science of judgments, the demonstration of its corruption, and the falsity of most of the judgments they attribute to it.

As for what he (al-Hakim) mentioned as an argument from reason, that no religion (milla) among the religions nor any nation among the nations has been free of this science, and that they have never ceased to occupy themselves with it, relying upon it for knowing the benefits, and so on to the end of what he said, this is a slander without doubt. How strange is his claim that the people of East and West, from the beginning of the construction of the world to its end, have agreed upon it, when they say that its foundations and rules were laid down in the time of Hurmus al-Haramisa (Hermes Trismegistus), meaning by him Idris (peace be upon him), who came long after the construction of the world. Moreover, many philosophers and a great multitude of the pillars of Islam have rejected it, to the point that more than a hundred works have been composed refuting and invalidating it.

Abu Nasr al-Farabi said: "Know that if you reversed the attributes of the astrologers, making the hot cold and the cold hot, the fortunate unlucky and the unlucky fortunate, the male female and the female male, and then judged, your judgments would be of the same kind as theirs: they would be right at times and wrong at other times." Ibn Sina exposed their matter in his two books, al-Shifa and al-Najat, and likewise Abu al-Barakat al-Baghdadi in his book al-Ta'bir. This is what some of the verifiers chose in refuting the astrologers.

I return to say: What I consider in this matter, and what appears more correct to me from the words of the eminent scholars, is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not create anything vain, free of wisdom and benefit. Rather, He created things, the heavenly and the earthly, the sublime and the lowly, containing wisdoms that cannot be counted and benefits that cannot be exhausted, even though they differ in their individuals in number and quantity. He assigned to each of them a property not found in others, while all share in indicating His existence, exalted be He, His oneness, His knowledge and His power:

"For Allah, in every movement and every stillness, there is always a witness;
and in everything there is a sign for Him that points to His oneness."

So the celestial bodies share in this indication, each having its own property. The condition of the stars in their properties and effects is like the condition of plants, minerals and animals in their properties and effects. Some of them have a property in themselves that does not depend on joining anything else to them; some have a property that depends on joining something else; and some, when something else is joined to them, cancel their property and nullify their benefit. Some of them have an effect whose mode is understood, and some whose mode is not understood. Some affect one place and not another, and one time and not another, and some affect all times and places, and so on through other states. Their being an adornment for the heaven does not require denying that they have another benefit, as on earth. Glorified is He who said: ﴿Indeed, We have made that which is on the earth an adornment for it﴾, while flowers and others include benefits that you know and benefits you do not know. Likewise, their being signs by which one is guided in the darknesses of land and sea, and their being missiles against the devils.

I do not hold that the spheres are simple, nor that the stars are simple, nor that they are confined to what is seen by sight or observation, nor that some are male and others female, and so on to much of what the astrologers claim. I say: Allah, exalted be He, has deposited in some of them an effect, just as He has deposited in the flowers of the earth and the like, and they affect only by His permission, Mighty and Majestic be He, as is the doctrine of the Salaf regarding all customary causes. And if you wish, say as the Ash'aris said about them. It is not far-fetched that some of them are signs for Allah's bringing about, exalted be He, of matters not through them, in one of the two worlds, the upper and the lower, which are known to whomever Allah, exalted be He, makes them aware of among His angels and the special of His servants. The connection of many lower things with upper things is something the great scholars have affirmed, and none denies it except the obstinate.

I do not ascribe any effect definitively to a particular star, because of the possibility of another star or another matter sharing in it. Yes, the apparent evidence indicates the great involvement of some stars in some effects, such as the moon in the tides of the seas and their ebb. Some of them begin to increase when the moon separates from the sun until the time of fullness, then they begin to decrease, and their decrease continues according to the decrease of the moon until the new moon. Some of them experience a tide every day and night with the rising and setting of the moon, such as the Gulf of Persia, the Indian Ocean and the Chinese Sea. Its mode is that when the moon reaches an eastern point of the sea, the sea begins to rise, and continues so until the moon is at the midst of the sky of that place. When it passes the western point of that place, the tide begins from beneath the earth and continues to grow until the moon reaches the peg of the earth. Then the tide reaches its limit, and then the ebb begins again, and the water returns as it was.

Like the tide and ebb are the crises of illnesses, for they follow the increase and decrease of the moon, in the sense that the involvement of that is apparent in them, in many matters. I do not say that a star has an influence on happiness and unhappiness or the like. It is not far-fetched that a star or stars, in relation to some conditions, are signs for something of this kind, known through some special properties. I have no confidence in what the judicial astrologers (al-ahkamiyyun) said. All that they say is conjecture and guesswork for which they have no proof. In the foundations on which they built their judgments, they contradict one another and differ in their schools. The Babylonians have a school, the Persians a school, the people of India a school, and the people of China a school. Some of them have refuted others, and some have testified against others regarding the corruption of their foundations and the basis of their judgments.

Their earliest ancestors and the great observers among them from the time of Ptolemy (Batlaymus), Timocharis (Tiymuharis) and Manalaris had made judgments about the stars and agreed upon their soundness. People persisted in following them and building the matter upon what they said for more than seven hundred years. Then came after them Khalid ibn Abd al-Malik al-Marwazi, al-Hasan the owner of the al-Ma'mun astronomical tables (zij), Muhammad ibn al-Jahm and Yahya ibn Abi Mansur. They tested what they had said and found them mistaken, and they agreed on their error, and they named their observation "the tested observation" (al-rasd al-mumtahan).

Then about sixty years later another group arose, whose leader was Abu Ma'shar Muhammad ibn Ja'far, and he refuted them and showed their error, as Abu Sa'id Shadhan the astrologer mentioned in his book Asrar al-Nujum (The Secrets of the Stars). In it: I said to Abu Ma'shar: "The tail (al-dhanab) is cold and dry, so why do you say it indicates femininity?" He said: "This is what they said." I said: "They have said that it is not truly dry, but cold, moist and twisted. All accidental properties (al-a'rad al-ghā'iyya) are an imagining, and none of them is certain. There is only one imagining stronger than another imagining."

[Page 115]

Whoever reflects on the circumstances of these people will know that what they have is a conjecture (tafarrus) in which they are sometimes right and sometimes wrong. Then, about seventy years after them, another group emerged, among them Abu al-Husayn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Umar, known as al-Sufi, who refuted those before him, corrected their errors, and wrote a book in which he set out the mistakes he had identified. He presented it to 'Adud al-Dawla ibn Buwayh, who admired it and gave its author a generous reward. Then, about thirty years later, another group came, among them Kushyar al-Daylami, who wrote *al-Mujmal fi'l-Ahkam* (The Summary on Judgments), in which he declared ignorant those who argue for judicial astrology (ahkam) among the practitioners of judgments (al-Ahkamiyyun). He said of the art of astrology (tanjim) that it is an art that is not demonstrated, and that conjecture and speculation have room in it. He went on to say: Among those who specialize in the science of judgments are some who support its particulars with arguments by way of speculation and disputation, and so they think these are demonstrations, because of their ignorance of the method and nature of demonstration.

Then another group emerged, among them the astrologer of al-Hakim in the land of Egypt, known as al-Fikri, who together with his companions established another observatory (rasad) that they named the Hakimi Observatory. They disagreed in it with the people of the tested observatory (al-rasad al-mumtahan), and built the matter of judgments upon it.

Then another group emerged, among them Abu al-Rayhan al-Biruni, author of the book *al-Tafhim li-Sina'at al-Tanjim* (The Instruction in the Art of Astrology). He came about forty years after Kushyar. He opposed those who preceded him, and brought from their contradictions and his refutations of them what indicates the corruption of their art. He concluded his book with his statement on hidden things and the inner thoughts: How often astrologers are exposed in this matter, and how often the fortune-tellers (al-zajirin) are correct, by means of what is said at the time of the question, and what they see as manifest from the traces and actions of the questioner, to the end of what he said.

Then another group emerged, among them Abu al-Salt Umayya ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz al-Andalusi, who came about eighty years after al-Biruni. He was a leading figure in the art, yet despite this he acknowledged that the statements of the astrologers are delirium (hadhayan).

Then another group emerged in the Maghrib, among them Abu Ishaq al-Zarqali and his companions, who came about a hundred years after Abu al-Salt. He opposed the earlier and later scholars in both the observational and judicial arts.

The most recent of what we know to have emerged is the Zij of Lalinet and al-Qusini (the Lalande and Cassini tables?), and in it there is much of the disagreement with the astronomical tables (azyaj) that came before it. It mentions the Herschel ephemeris and the measure of his motion; he is a wandering star (kawkab sayyar) that Herschel, one of the philosophers of the Franks (al-Ifranj), discovered and named after himself, and no one had discovered it before him. This zij is, according to what the astrologers claim today, the most precise of the tables. The Franks, despite the great skill of many of them in the science of observation, do not hold any of what the early and later judicial astrologers hold, and they mock them. A trustworthy writer has mentioned aspects that indicate the corruption of what they possess of this knowledge and that it cannot be relied upon:

The first: knowing all the astral influences (al-mu'aththirat al-falakiyya) is not attainable. Firstly, because there is no way to know the stars except through the visual faculties; when the object seen is small or extremely distant, its seeing is impossible. The smallest of the stars in the sphere of the fixed stars, which is the one by which the power of sight is possible, is about ten times the size of the Earth, and the Earth is so many times greater than Mercury. So if we suppose that many stars have come to exist in the outermost sphere, each of them the size of Mercury, how would they be seen? The negation of this possibility requires a proof, and even if it were granted, certainty about the knowledge of all the influences would not be achieved. If they say: it is possible, since the effects of this star are weak because of its smallness and do not reach this world, we reply: smallness of body does not necessitate weakness of effect, for you have attributed strong effects to Mercury despite its smallness compared with the other planets; indeed you have attributed strong effects to the Head and Tail (of the dragon) and the Lot of Fortune and the Lot of the Unseen, which are imaginary matters. Secondly, what has been observed of the visible stars is a very small amount compared with what has not been observed, so from where do they get their knowledge of the nature of what has not been observed? Thirdly, because knowledge of the natures of all the observed stars has not been reached either, and they have rarely spoken about knowing the stars other than the fixed stars of the first and second magnitudes. Fourthly, the observing instruments are not sufficient to measure seconds, thirds and beyond; and there is no doubt that one second is a thousand times the size of the Earth or less or more. With this enormous disparity, how can the goal be reached? It has been said that a man running swiftly, between lifting one foot and placing the other, moves the body of the outermost sphere three thousand miles; if that is so, how can these influences be measured? Fifthly: even if they had known the natures of these stars in their simple state, have they known their natures when some of them are mixed with others? The mixtures arising from the natures of a thousand stars or more, according to the celestial degrees, reach such a multiplicity that the intellect cannot master them. 

Sixthly, it is said: suppose we knew those mixtures that occur at that time; there is no doubt that we cannot know the mixtures that existed before it, while we certainly know that the earlier configurations may have been obstructing and preventing the requirements of the configurations present now. And there is no doubt that we observe many individuals of plants, animals and humans that come into being at the same ascendant, although each of them differs from the others in most matters; this is because the prior conditions relating to each one differ from the prior conditions relating to the other. This shows that there is no reliance upon the requirement of the ascendant of the moment; rather, one must encompass the earlier ascendants, and that is beyond reach, for those earlier ascendants may have been repelling the requirements of this present ascendant. On this basis Ibn Sina relied in his two books *al-Shifa'* and *al-Najat* to refute this science.

The second: the influence of the stars varies according to their magnitudes. What is of the first magnitude has its effect by its position in the degree, even if the minute is not fixed. What is of the last magnitude has no effect except by fixing the minute. There is no doubt that the magnitudes of all the stars are unknown, so how can the effects be fixed?

The third: the corruption of their principles, the contradiction of their opinions, and their great disagreement without evidence. Whenever statements conflict and preference among them cannot be made, nothing from them can be relied upon.

The fourth: their observations are never free from some kind of defect, and these are the foundation of their judgments. Abu 'Ali ibn al-Haytham wrote an eloquent treatise on the types of defect that occur in observing instruments, and he explained that it is not within human power to repel or remove it. Their accuracy at times of eclipses and solar eclipses, despite that defect, does not require their accuracy at other times with it.

The fifth: we observe a great number of people killed in one hour in a battle, and a great multitude drowning in one hour, although their ascendants differ and, according to you, require different conditions. This shows that what you considered first has no weight.

If you say: the ascendants may be stronger or weaker than one another, so perhaps the ascendant of the moment is stronger than the ascendant of the origin, and therefore the judgment follows it.

We reply: this very argument invalidates your reliance on the ascendant of the child at birth, for the ascendants after it are many and different, and perhaps some of them are stronger than it; so relying on it benefits nothing.

The sixth: the intellect has no basis for affirming that a particular star or particular position necessitates a specific influence, and experience, with its own limitations, is contradicted by another experience that required the opposite, along with other aspects.

Abu al-Barakat al-Baghdadi, although he rejected what they hold, nonetheless accepts some of the judgments. He said, after mentioning some of their statements for which they have no evidence: These are statements that someone said, that a receiver accepted, and that a transmitter transmitted; the listener's opinion of them was good, and those without expertise or ability to reflect were deceived by them. Then judges judged by them, whether good or bad, negative or positive, fortunate or unlucky. Some of it coincided with what exists, so it came true, and the deceived were deceived by it, and did not pay attention to the falsehood in it, but rather excused him and said: he is an astrologer, not a prophet, so that he should be right in everything he says. They made excuses for him, saying that knowledge is too vast to be encompassed, and that if he had encompassed it he would have been right about everything.

By the might of God, Most High, if he had encompassed it with true knowledge he would have been right. But the matter is that one encompasses it in reality, not by supposing a supposition, imagining an imagining, transferring it into existence, establishing it in what exists, attributing it to something, and analogizing upon it. What is valid and what intelligent people pay attention to is other than these fables that have no root, things that were attained through revelation or genuine experiment, such as conjunctions, transits, oppositions, the passage of a planet among the wandering stars beneath a fixed star, the retrogradations, stations, retrogressions in the north, descents in the south, and other such things. It seems I wish to shorten the discussion here and to comply with your indication, and to act according to your choice, by writing a treatise on this in which I will mention what has been said in it about the science of the judgments of the stars, of true or metaphorical or imaginary or erroneous principles, and branches of results produced from those principles. I will mention what is permissible of that and what is impossible, what is near and what is far. I will not reject the science of judgments from every angle as those who ignore it have rejected it, nor will I accept every statement in it as those who do not understand it have accepted it; rather I will clarify the place of acceptance and rejection, the place of verification and conjecture, what belongs to the astrologer, what belongs to astrology, and what belongs to both. I will make clear to you that if it were possible for a human to encompass by knowledge the form of everything in the sphere, he would encompass everything the sphere contains, because from it come the origins of causes. But it is not possible, and it is very far from possibility; and the possible part of it does not guide to some judgment, because the other unknown part may contradict the known in its judgment and nullify what it necessitates. Thus the relation of the known to the unknown in judgments is like the relation of the known to the unknown in causes, and that is distance enough. End of quotation. In it is support for some of the aspects mentioned earlier, and there is much in it.

I say: the encompassing of the secrets deposited in the celestial bodies is not far-fetched to occur to some privileged people of holy souls, but by way of unveiling (kashf) or the like, not by rational inference or observational works, for example. This is what the words of al-Shaykh al-Akbar (Ibn 'Arabi), may his secret be sanctified, indicate. He said in the seventy-third chapter of *al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya*: Among the saints are the nuqaba' (chiefs), who are twelve in every age, neither more nor fewer, corresponding to the twelve zodiac signs. Each naqib knows the property of each sign, and what God, Most High, has deposited in its station of secrets and influences, and what is given to its dwellers from the wandering planets and the fixed stars.

Then he said: Among them are the nujaba' (the noble), who are eight in every age... to his saying: They have a firm foot in the science of the courses of the stars from the standpoint of unveiling and disclosure, not from the standpoint of the known method among the scholars of this discipline.

The nuqaba' are those who have attained the knowledge of the ninth sphere, and the nujaba' have attained the knowledge of the eight spheres below it, which are every sphere in which there is a star. From this statement one understands the influences, and that they are diffused from the sign onto the star that descends into it.

This passage is a long, complex classical commentary. Translating it faithfully in full:
