He (al-Alusi's source, Ibn al-'Arabi, in al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya) has repeatedly alluded to this. In the third chapter of the three hundred and seventy-first section of al-Futuhat (the text says "al-Futuhat"), he states that God Most High created within the interior of the Kursi a transparent, circular body—meaning the outermost sphere (al-Falak al-Atlas)—and divided it into twelve parts, which are the zodiacal signs (al-buruj), and He settled in each sign an angel... until he said: And He made for each deputy of these twelve angels, in each sign, a dominion over thirty storehouses, each storehouse containing various sciences, from which they bestow upon whoever comes to them what their rank grants. These are the storehouses of which God Most High said: ﴿And there is not a thing but its treasuries are with Us, and We send it down only in a known measure﴾. These storehouses are called by the people of the sciences of the celestial "degrees" (darajat al-falak), and those who descend upon them are the al-Jawari, the manazil, and their 'Ayyuqat from the fixed stars. The knowledge obtained from these divine storehouses is what appears in the world of the elements (alam al-arkan) of influences—indeed, what appears from the concave of the sphere of the fixed stars down to the earth. He also made for these twelve a gaze upon the Gardens and their people and what is in them, unveiled without any veil. So whatever judgment there is in the Gardens comes through these directly, as an honor to the people of Paradise. As for the people of this world and the people of Hell, they do not carry out what judgment is theirs except through the deputies, namely those who descend upon them, whom we have mentioned.

He—may his secret be sanctified—also said in the fourth chapter: God Most High made for each of these planets portions in the outermost sphere, so that from those storehouses which are in its signs and in the hands of its twelve angels there may be obtained from the knowledge of influence what the reality of each planet gives, and He made them of differing realities. End of what is meant from him.

He—may his secret be sanctified—has other statements besides this as well, and he explicitly stated something similar to what the astrologers state, regarding the differing natures of the signs, and that each three of them are of one degree in temperament. As for me, I do not go beyond saying that the celestial bodies—their planets and their spheres—have secrets, wisdoms and influences that are not essential but are bestowed upon them from the side of the Truth and the Absolute Overflowing One—exalted is His majesty and great is His dominion—and among them are those that are signs of what God Most High wills. No proof for negating what has been mentioned is complete, nor is the quantity or quality of that known, nor that the influence of such-and-such from such-and-such a planet is a sign of such-and-such in reality, except God Most High, the All-Knowing, the All-Seeing: ﴿Does He not know who created? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾. However, He—glory be to Him—may inform some of His special servants, from among humans and angels, of some of that, and it is not far-fetched that He—glory be to Him—may inform some of them of all of it, and the occurrence of that to our Prophet ﷺ is something I can hardly doubt.

Some of our Sufi masters—may their secrets be sanctified and their lights shine upon us—have stated that the knowledge of his (ﷺ) that was granted to him is of three kinds: a kind that he was obliged to make manifest and convey, which is the knowledge of the Shari'ah and the divine obligations, and the words of God Most High: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message﴾ refer to that and not to the absolute generality, or to the specific matter of the caliphate of 'Ali—may God honor his face—as the Shi'a say. And a kind that he was obliged to conceal, which is the knowledge of the divine secrets that no power other than his holy power can bear—upon him be prayers and peace. Just as God Most High has a knowledge that He has reserved for Himself, to the exclusion of any of His creation, so too for His Beloved, the Greatest (ﷺ), there is a knowledge that he has reserved, after his Lord—glory be to Him—but it is overflowed to him from Him—exalted is He. Perhaps this is alluded to in the words of God Most High: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾. Between the lover and the beloved there may be secrets that are withheld from strangers, and from here it has been said:

"And one who asks about the secret of Layla—I left him in blindness regarding Layla, without certainty.
They say: 'Inform us, for you are its trustee,' and I am not trustworthy if I inform them."

And a kind in which God Most High gave him the choice between the two matters: of this, some he made manifest to whoever he saw as fit for it, and some he did not make manifest for some reason. So perhaps what was granted to him—upon him be prayers and peace—of knowledge of the subtleties of the secrets of the celestial bodies, their wisdoms, and what God Most High intended by them, which he did not make manifest to people, is like the knowledge of the Shari'ah, since it is something that cannot be governed by a single rule, and detailing the matter of it is hardly possible, and some of it is linked to some of it. Despite this, the one who knows it cannot make residence into travel, nor defeat into victory, nor a contract into dissolution, nor a firm decision into annulment, nor despair into hope, nor an enemy into a friend, nor a distant one into a near one, nor... nor... nor...

And if its matter were to spread and its sweet and bitter become apparent, it would likely weaken the trust in God of many of the common people, their devotion to Him, and their desire for what is with Him, and they would be distracted by it from other things, and would reject the beneficial sciences other than it for its sake. Each would wish to know the unseen, to be informed of it, to perceive what will happen tomorrow, or to find a way to it. Indeed, perhaps that would become a cause for some individuals, leading to corrupt belief and manifest polytheism. Some of that existed among the Arabs. So if this door were opened, the breach would widen and the evil would grow great.

The Prophet ﷺ left the demolition of the Ka'bah and its rebuilding upon the foundations of Abraham—upon him be peace—for something like this consideration.

For it is narrated that he—upon him be prayers and peace—said to 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her: "Were it not that your people are recent in disbelief, I would have demolished the Ka'bah and rebuilt it upon the foundations of Abraham."

It is also not far-fetched that it may be in the knowledge of God Most High that making that manifest, and people's knowledge of it, would be a cause for the disruption of worldly benefits and contrary to the divine wisdom, so He obligated His Messenger ﷺ to conceal it and to refrain from teaching it, just as He taught him the laws.

It is also possible that he ﷺ knew that knowledge of that is among the bestowed sciences which God Most High grants by favor to whomever He wills of His servants, and that whoever among his community God Most High has given a holy power, God will give him what his power can bear of it. You have heard what you have heard concerning the nuqaba' and the nujaba'. It is also possible that he—upon him be prayers and peace—taught that to their likes and to one higher in rank than them, such as the Amir 'Ali—may God honor his face—who is the gate of the city of knowledge, by a way of teaching, and among these is the overflow that some of the Sufi path-people mention. It may be said that the secret of the mission is only guiding creatures to what brings them near to Him—glory be to Him—and there is no nearness to God Most High in knowing celestial influences and cosmic events. The Prophet ﷺ spared no effort in calling creatures and guiding them to what brings them near to Him—glory be to Him—and benefits them on the day they come before Him—exalted is His majesty. As for what depends on the stars in their religious matters, such as knowing the qibla and the times of worship, he has guided whoever he guided to it, and he left what they need of that in their worldly affairs, such as agriculture, to their customs and what each people has tested in their places. He alluded in a general way to some cosmic events of some planets in some of their states, as in the hadith of the eclipse mentioned earlier, and guided them to what benefits them when the like of that appears. The general allusion also includes His command—Most High—to seek refuge from the evil of the moon in some of its states, which is in the words of God Most High: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾ ﴿from the evil of what He created﴾ ﴿and from the evil of the darkness when it settles﴾, according to what came in the hadith of 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her. And in some respects his (ﷺ) matter approaches his matter regarding plants and the like: he explained to them what is lawful and unlawful of that, and pointed to the benefit of some things, of plants and others, and did not elaborate on their properties, and left people regarding what they eat and drink, of what is lawful, to their customs, except that he said: "Eat and drink, and do not be extravagant."

Yes, the Prophet ﷺ forbade delving into the science of the stars in order to seek knowledge of future events through arrangements which, according to the astrologers' claim, depend on knowledge of the natures (of the planets), in order to block the door to evil and to falling into falsehood; for knowledge of that in its verified sense is not acquired like knowledge of the properties of plants and the like, and the acquired knowledge which the astrologers claim is not knowledge at all; it is merely conjecture for which they have no proof, as has been previously mentioned and as Aristotle also stated explicitly at the beginning of his book Physics (al-Sama' al-Tabi'i): that there is no path to certainty in knowing the influence of the stars. Something similar is related from Ptolemy. That what is forbidden is this is what some eminent scholars have stated explicitly, and the report of Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah is understood in this sense: "Whoever acquires a branch of knowledge from the stars has acquired a branch of sorcery." As for delving into the science of the stars to obtain what is known by it of the times of the prayers, the direction of the qibla, how much of the night or day has passed and how much remains, the beginnings of the solar months and the like, and among it—in my view—what is known by it of the times of eclipses and solar and lunar events, that is not forbidden; rather, the knowledge that leads to some of what has been mentioned is a collective obligation (fard kifaya). Indeed, if the science of the stars is an expression for the science that investigates the stars with regard to what befalls them of conjunction, opposition, trine and sextile, the manner of their motion, the measure of their movements, and the like of what is studied in the astronomical tables (zij), or if it is an expression for what encompasses that, and the science by which one reaches knowledge of the rising and setting of a planet, knowledge of the passed part of the night and day, knowledge of longitudes and latitudes and the like, which is contained in the science of the astrolabe, the quadrant and the like, then I see no harm in learning it absolutely. But if it is an expression for the science that investigates their judgments and influences which their arrangements and natures require, according to what the judgment-astrologers claim, then this is what has been disputed. Some said its learning is forbidden, based on the report of Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah mentioned above, and the one who says this is one who says that learning sorcery is forbidden. This is one of the opinions on the matter, in which there is excess and deficiency. The second is that it is disliked; the third, that it is permissible; the fourth, that it is a collective obligation; the fifth, that it is disbelief. The majority hold the first, and because it involves promoting falsehood and exposing the ignorant to believing that the judgments of the stars known among their people are true, and that the planets have influence in themselves. It was also said: learning it is forbidden because it is abrogated; al-Kirmani said in his Wonders: "The science of the stars was a prophetic science, then it was abrogated." This was critiqued on the grounds that there is no meaning to abrogating knowledge itself; and if the statement is taken to mean "its learning was permissible, then that was abrogated to prohibition," then the argument would be begging the question! Some said: there is no prohibition in learning it; the prohibition lies only in believing in the validity of the judgments and the influences of the planets in the manner which the ignorant judgment-astrologers claim, not absolutely. The report mentioned above was answered by saying that it is to be understood as learning some of the science of the stars with a view to taking care of its matter, as the word "iqtabasa" (acquired) indicates; and that cannot be achieved without believing in the validity of its judgment and that the planets are influencing agents. Learning it in this manner is forbidden, and without that it is permissible; and there is discussion in this.

It was also said in response: the report refers to one who claims knowledge of a judgment among the judgments, taking it from the stars, saying: "The matter is such-and-such, and there is no doubt, because the star necessarily requires it." Such a person is certainly sinful, and his claim is forbidden, since proofs have established its falsehood. And this is as you see. And the statement of some

**[Page 123]**

...the eminent scholars, is explicit in permitting its study, provided one believes that God Most High has established the custom that such and such occurs when a particular star reaches such and such a mansion (manzil), for example, while allowing for the possibility that the custom may not hold. Some scholars have concluded that studying it is forbidden absolutely whenever it encourages the ignorant to pursue this knowledge and leads them into the prohibited belief in its causal influence, or when it involves other harms. Disliking it, if it is free of these harms, is due to the waste of time on what has no benefit, and its foundation is conjecture, delusion, and imagination. It is not far-fetched to say that it is permissible for a firmly grounded scholar to examine its books in order to become acquainted with what its practitioners have said, to learn of their contradictions and disagreements, some of which you have heard, so as to deter people from them and turn away those who cling to them. Just as he may examine the books of all the other people of falsehood, such as the Jews and Christians, for this purpose. Indeed, if it were said that it is recommended (sunnah) for this purpose, it would not be far-fetched. But you know that the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-salih) did not approach any part of it except to condemn it and condemn its people, and they did not seek out any of its books to examine them in any manner whatsoever. Attributing the opposite to any of them is not valid. Therefore, prudence lies in following them in this and taking their path, for by my life, it is the most upright of paths.

And this: the claim that he (ﷺ) had knowledge of what has been mentioned concerning the heavenly bodies has been objected to on the grounds that it opens the door to doubt about whether his (ﷺ) reports of the unseen come from revelation, since they may be among the judgments of the stars according to that view. It has been answered that the doubt arises only if it is established that he, peace and blessings be upon him, observed a star, even once, determined its position, and reported an unseen matter on that basis. For mere knowledge that a certain star has a certain judgment when it arrives at a certain mansion is not restricted, without knowing that it has actually arrived at that mansion. Therefore, since it has not been established that he (ﷺ) did such a thing, it does not open the door to doubt. In this answer there is evident weakness. And it has been answered that his (ﷺ) knowledge of what the configurations indicate, according to those who hold this view, is only through revelation. So the most that follows from that doubt is that his report of the unseen was through the medium of knowledge of the judgments of the stars, which he knew by revelation. And what harm would result from this for his prophethood, peace and blessings be upon him? Rather, this doubt presupposes that he is a prophet, just as its absence does.

It has been criticized: once it is granted that celestial configurations have an indication of unseen matters, and that he (ﷺ) knows what they indicate, confusion arises between him and other scholars of that science who report the unseen, when their reports come true as they said. The distinction, that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was revealed this knowledge and they were not, depends on his being a prophet, and that is the very first point of the question. In the answer, it has been preferred to say: if his (ﷺ) report of the unseen came after his prophethood was established by a miracle other than this, the doubt does not arise, provided it conveys that his report was through revelation; and it does no harm if it does not convey this. For the most that can be said in this matter is that he is a prophet because the miracle appeared at his hand before he reported an unseen matter through a celestial configuration, and others shared with him in that. If, however, it came before his prophethood was established by a miracle other than this, that is, if the challenge was made by that report and the occurrence of what he reported, then what removes the doubt at that point is the inability to produce an equal. No astrologer can truthfully report the like of that by virtue of his knowledge of configurations and their implications. So reflect!

Then, the apparent view, as mentioned by the Greatest Shaykh (al-Shaykh al-Akbar, Ibn al-Arabi), may God sanctify his secret, in *al-Nuqaba' wa al-Nujaba'*, is that each of the prophets, peace be upon them, has knowledge of this, since the rank of a prophet is above the rank of a saint (wali), and his knowledge is above theirs, for he is the greatest pillar in excellence.

There is no proof in the story of Musa and al-Khidr, peace be upon them, against this. As for those who hold that al-Khidr, peace be upon him, was a prophet, it is obvious. Likewise, for those who hold that he was a saint and that he did what he did by the command of God Most High through a prophet. As for those who hold that he was a saint and that he did that by a knowledge given to him without a prophet as intermediary, then this indicates only that Musa, peace be upon him, lacked knowledge of those three matters, and that al-Khidr had knowledge of them. It does not follow from this that al-Khidr was absolutely more knowledgeable than him, as is obvious. And on this basis, it has been deemed permissible to keep the verse on its apparent meaning, so that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, looked at the stars as God Most High had taught him of the affairs of the higher kingdom...

**[Page 123]**

...and he inferred that he would fall ill from what he inferred. Perhaps his observation was of the rising sign (tali') of the hour or the like, or of the rising sign of his birth, or of the rising sign at the falling of the drop from which he was created. His knowledge of this was through revelation, or through knowledge of the rising sign of birth. As for the objection to this, that it would imply that he strengthened them, peace be upon him, in the falsehood they held concerning the matter of the stars, it also applies to interpreting what is in the verse as an allusion (ta'ridh). The answer is the same answer. This is what I have. And if you have comprehended fully all that I have mentioned to you on this matter, then reflect well on what it contains of refutation and affirmation! I have gathered for you what I do not know to have been gathered in any single exegesis. I do not absolve myself of error, forgetfulness, and shortcoming. God, glorified be He, is the Giver of success, and in His hand, mighty and majestic, are the reins of verification.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 90:

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So they turned their backs and went away﴾ is a consequence (tafri') of his saying, peace be upon him, ﴿Indeed, I am sick﴾. That is: they turned away from him and left his vicinity. The meaning is that they went off to their place of festivity (ma'id) and left him. "Mudbirin" (turning their backs) is either a confirmatory circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkidah) or a restrictive circumstantial clause (hal muqayyidah), based on the view that what is meant by "sakim" (sick) is "mat'un" (afflicted with plague), or that they imagined he had a disease that is contagious (lahu 'adwa), such as the plague or otherwise. For the disease that is contagious, according to the claim of the physicians, is not restricted to the plague. So it is as if it were said: they turned away from him, fleeing for fear of contagion (al-'adwa).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 91–93:

﴿So he turned to their gods﴾ — he went secretly to their idols which they worshipped. The root of al-rawaghan (turning aside) is the inclination of a person to one side in order to deceive whoever is behind him, and it is used figuratively here for what has been mentioned, because it is the fitting sense in this context. ﴿Then he said﴾ to the idols, mockingly, ﴿Will you not eat?﴾ of the food that is before you. The polytheists used to place food before the idols on their festival days so that it would be blessed by them. He used the pronoun for rational beings (ʿuqalāʾ) because he, peace be upon him, treated them as they treated him. ﴿What is wrong with you that you do not speak?﴾ in answer to me. ﴿Then he turned upon them﴾ — he inclined toward them, overpowering them. The phrase ﴿striking﴾ (darban) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of "rāgha ʿalayhim" according to the meaning, since what is intended by it is striking them; or it is the object of a hidden verb which, together with its subject, is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from its subject, meaning: he turned upon them striking them with a strike; or it is a circumstantial clause from it, taking it as a verbal noun in the sense of the agent, meaning striking; or it is an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), meaning: for the sake of striking. Al-Hasan read "safqan" and "ṣafqan" as well. ﴿with the right hand﴾, meaning with the right hand, as is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. Restricting the striking to the right hand serves to indicate its severity and strength, because the right hand is generally the stronger and more powerful of the two limbs, and the strength of the instrument requires the severity and strength of the action; or it means with strength, taking "the right hand" as a metaphor for it.

It is reported that he, peace be upon him, would gather his two hands on the instrument with which he struck them, which was the axe, and strike with his full strength. It is also said: what is meant by "right hand" is the oath, and an oath is called a yamin (right hand) either because the custom was that when a person swore to another he would place his right hand in the other's right hand and then swear, or because an oath strengthens and affirms speech. What is meant by "the right hand" is his, peace be upon him, saying: ﴿And by God, I will surely plot against your idols﴾. The preposition "bi" (with) here indicates causation, meaning: a striking because of the oath he had sworn before; and it is, as previously stated, for instrumentality (istiʿānah) or accompaniment (mulābasah).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 91–93:

﴿So he turned to their gods﴾ — he went secretly to their idols which they worshipped. The root of al-rawaghan (turning aside) is the inclination of a person to one side in order to deceive whoever is behind him, and it is used figuratively here for what has been mentioned, because it is the fitting sense in this context. ﴿Then he said﴾ to the idols, mockingly, ﴿Will you not eat?﴾ of the food that is before you. The polytheists used to place food before the idols on their festival days so that it would be blessed by them. He used the pronoun for rational beings (ʿuqalāʾ) because he, peace be upon him, treated them as they treated him. ﴿What is wrong with you that you do not speak?﴾ in answer to me. ﴿Then he turned upon them﴾ — he inclined toward them, overpowering them. The phrase ﴿striking﴾ (darban) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of "rāgha ʿalayhim" according to the meaning, since what is intended by it is striking them; or it is the object of a hidden verb which, together with its subject, is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from its subject, meaning: he turned upon them striking them with a strike; or it is a circumstantial clause from it, taking it as a verbal noun in the sense of the agent, meaning striking; or it is an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), meaning: for the sake of striking. Al-Hasan read "safqan" and "ṣafqan" as well. ﴿with the right hand﴾, meaning with the right hand, as is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. Restricting the striking to the right hand serves to indicate its severity and strength, because the right hand is generally the stronger and more powerful of the two limbs, and the strength of the instrument requires the severity and strength of the action; or it means with strength, taking "the right hand" as a metaphor for it.

It is reported that he, peace be upon him, would gather his two hands on the instrument with which he struck them, which was the axe, and strike with his full strength. It is also said: what is meant by "right hand" is the oath, and an oath is called a yamin (right hand) either because the custom was that when a person swore to another he would place his right hand in the other's right hand and then swear, or because an oath strengthens and affirms speech. What is meant by "the right hand" is his, peace be upon him, saying: ﴿And by God, I will surely plot against your idols﴾. The preposition "bi" (with) here indicates causation, meaning: a striking because of the oath he had sworn before; and it is, as previously stated, for instrumentality (istiʿānah) or accompaniment (mulābasah).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 94:

﴿Then they came hastening toward him﴾, i.e., toward Ibrahim (peace be upon him), after returning from their festival and questioning him about the smasher (al-Kasir) and saying, ﴿Bring him before the eyes of the people﴾. ﴿Hastening﴾ (yazifFun) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the wa of "aqbalu," meaning they are hurrying. It is said: "zaffa al-na'am" (the ostrich ran quickly), since it combines flying with walking; its verbal noun is al-zaff and al-zafif. It was also said that ﴿yazifFun﴾ means they walk with deliberation and calm, from the "zifaf" (wedding procession) of the bride, since they were at ease that the idols would not be harmed by anything, due to their (the idols') honor. But this is not correct.

Hamza, Mujahid, Ibn Waththab, al-A'mash read "yuziffun" with a damma on the ya', from "azaffa," meaning he entered into zafif; the hamza then is not for transitivity. Or it means he caused another to perform zafif, so the hamza is for transitivity. This is what al-Asma'i said. Mujahid also read, as did Abdullah ibn Yazid, al-Dahhak,

and Yahya ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Muqri and Ibn Abi Abla, "yazifun," the imperfect of "wazafa," meaning "asra'a" (hastened). Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: "We do not know wazafa to mean zaffa." But the trustworthy transmitters have confirmed it, so the fact that they do not know the two does no harm. It was also read "yuzaffun" in the passive voice, and "yazfun" with a sukun on the zay, from "zafa-hu" when he drove him (hadahu), as if some of them were driving others toward him because of their eagerness to come to him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 95–96:

﴿"He said"﴾ after they had brought him (peace be upon him), and after the exchange that had taken place, in the form of rebuke and denunciation directed at them: ﴿"Do you worship what you carve?"﴾ That is, that which you carve of idols. So "mā" (what) is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah) whose returning pronoun has been omitted, and this is the apparent and immediately understood reading. It has also been permitted that it be a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), meaning: "Do you worship your carving?" Their rebuke for worshipping carving, even though they worship idols, which are not the carving itself, is an indication that in reality they worshipped the carving, because the idols before it were stones and they did not worship them; they worshipped them only after they had carved them. So in reality they worshipped nothing but their own carving. And in this there is what there is.

﴿"And Allah created you and what you do"﴾ This is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relative to the pronoun in "you worship," to emphasise the denunciation, rebuke and argument that such worship is not fitting. And "mā" is also a relative pronoun whose returning pronoun has been omitted: that is, He created you and created that which you make, namely the idols, as is the apparent meaning. They are a reference to materials, which are the stone substances, and forms that came to them through carving. That the materials are created by Him, glorified and exalted, is evident; and that the forms and shapes are likewise created by Him, although they are by their action, is by the consideration that the power to act and the creation of what depends upon it, of motives and causes, is from Him, exalted is He. And that the idols, which you have heard about, are made by them with respect to their formal part, is by the consideration that it, while being made by them, is created by Allah, exalted is He, by that consideration. So there is no difficulty.

In the complementary treatise on this important question by Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani (may God have mercy on him), the clear statement indicates that Allah, exalted is He, is the Creator of the idols with all their parts, of which the shapes are one; and it is known that the shapes came about only through their shaping, so the shapes are created by Allah, exalted is He, and made by them, because their carving and shaping is the very same as the creation by Allah, exalted is He, of the shapes through them.

There is no impossibility in this, because the servant has no power except through Allah, exalted is He, by the text; and whoever has no power except through another, the power belongs to that other and not to him. So there is no power, in reality, except for Allah, exalted is He. It is known that there is no act of the servant except by power; so there is no act for him except through Allah, exalted is He; so there is no act, in reality, except for Allah, exalted is He. And whatever is so, the carving and shaping is the very same as the creation by Allah, glorified is He, of the shapes through them and in them essentially, and other than that by consideration. So the made is the very same as the created essentially, and other than it by consideration. For Allah's bringing into being, glorified and exalted is He, relates to the act itself as such, while the servant's act in the verbal-noun sense relates to the act in the sense of what is achieved by the verbal noun, insofar as it is obedience, disobedience or permissible, because he is accountable; and Allah, exalted is He, has absolute freedom, and no judge over Him, glorified is He. End of quotation. So understand.

Al-Zamakhshari also took "mā" as a relative pronoun, except that he made the created thing belonging to Allah the substances, and what they make the form and shape; either on the basis that the speech contains an omitted genitive, meaning "and what you make of its shape and form," or on the basis that this is the common usage, for they say "the carpenter made the door," "the goldsmith made the anklet," and "the builder made the building," meaning nothing but the making of the shape, without any shape being supposed in the wording; as if the making's relation to the thing is this relation and not the relation of bringing into existence. This is built upon his corrupt belief that the acts of servants are created by them. The argument in the verse on the first reading is that He created the worshipper and the worshipped, in matter and form; so how does the created worship the created? On the second reading, that He created the worshipper and the matter of the worshipped, so how does the created worship the created, given that the worshipper is the one who made the form of the worshipped? The first is more evident.

He departed from the pronoun in "what you carve" or from using it, rather than "what you do," to indicate that the createdness of the idols by Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is not merely from the aspect of their carving by them, but from the aspect of all their other works too, such as the painting, the adornment and the decoration. In al-Kashshaf, the benefit of the deviation is to show that their influence upon them is not the carving alone; then the action falls upon the carving and upon the trace resulting from it, and carving does not fall upon the second; so a deviation is necessary for this point, and with it the argument is complete. That is, it is said upon Zamakhshari's reading. It has also been permitted that the relative pronoun be general, covering idols and other things, and the idols enter primarily; but the deviation hadith cannot apply to this. It has been said that "mā" is a verbal-noun particle, and the verbal noun is interpreted as the passive participle so as to match "what you carve," as is apparent in it, and the meaning unites with what preceded on the possibility of the relative reading. It has also been permitted to keep the verbal noun in its verbal-noun sense, meaning by it the resulting thing from the verbal noun, namely the trace; and this is often meant by it, so much so that it has been said that it is shared between it and influence and bringing about; that is: He created you and created your work. The verse has been cited as evidence against the Mu'tazilah. It was objected that this is not valid, because citing it to show that the worshipper and the worshipped are both the creation of Allah, exalted is He, so how does the created worship the created? If it were said that the worshipper and his work are from the creation of Allah, exalted is He, the harmony and the argument would be lost. Also, because "mā" in the first is a relative pronoun, so in the second it is likewise, so that the wording does not break apart. What al-Qadi al-Baydawi said, that the argument is not lost but is even more forceful in it, since when their action is by the creation of Allah, exalted is He, their object which depends upon their action is more deserving of that; and this is supported by the claim that the style becomes a kind of metonymy, which is more forceful than explicit statement, and there is no benefit in deviating from the apparent meaning except this; so it is obligatory, in safeguarding the speech of Allah, exalted is He, from futility. Al-Kashshaf objected to this, saying that it is not complete, because the implication is disputed by the people; do you not see that they acknowledge that the servant, his power and his will are from the creation of Allah, exalted is He? Then what depends upon these two, namely the act, they make the creation of the servant; and the verification is that it indicates its dependence upon Him, exalted is He, and they do not deny this; the dispute is only about bringing into existence and origination. Then he said: More evident than this is to say: because the made, in terms of matter, they did not deny was from the creation of Allah, exalted is He; so it was said: it is also from the aspect of its form that He created it; so it is created in every respect, like you, without difference; so why do you equate it with the Creator? And your action has increased it only in distance from deserving worship. And since this meaning in Zamakhshari's exposition is in the most forceful form, this construction collapses however it is established. Moreover, the benefit of the deviation has become clear to the utmost clarity, so the restriction also falls away. It has been said against this: the intended meaning of the act is the resulting thing from the verbal noun, because in the other sense, namely bringing about, it is among the relations that do not exist according to them; and the dependence of the resulting thing upon the power and will of the servant is a remote dependence, unlike its dependence upon the bringing about which has no existence; so what he mentioned as evidence coincides with the disputed premise and so is not fit to serve as evidence. The intended meaning of "their made" is the forms of the idols, which depend upon that meaning subsisting in them. If that is by His creation, exalted is He, then that which does not subsist in them but in what is separate from them is by His creation, exalted is He, all the more so.

The opponent has no room to refuse this implication, since he has affirmed the creation of consequential things absolutely for the servants through their creation of what subsists in them, and the absence of the first entails the absence of the second. So reflect. In al-Taqrib, in support of those who said the verbal-noun reading: the substances are created by Him, exalted is He, by consensus, and the actions are also created, because of the generality of the verse; so how is what has no part in creation worshipped? So the claim that the argument is lost is false, and likewise the dismantling of the wording and its scattering. Al-Kashshaf also objected to this, saying: if the consensual premise is unavoidable and is not known from this context, the argument is lost; as for interpreting it through predominance in address, that is a justification, not a preference, and the discussion concerns the second reading.

Then he said: As for the claim that the verbal-noun reading is better so that the deletion of the pronoun is not required, it is countered by the claim that the relative reading is more common in usage, and it is more fitting to the preceding context. Moreover, it is necessary to suppose their work upon the carved thing, so the deletion increases.

It was objected: we do not accept that it is more common, nor that it is more fitting to the context, given what you have heard, that the style on that reading is metonymy, which is more forceful than explicit statement; and the stated supposition is not necessary, since the speech may be left in its general sense, including the carved thing by the first way, or it may be supposed to be a verbal noun added with a known annexation. Some of them made it a relative pronoun as a metonymy for the work, so that the wording does not break apart and the Companions' argument on the creation of human actions appears. It was objected to this as well: it is worse than the first, because of its complexity and the loss of the argument; and that the relative in the first refers to bodies and in the second is a metonymy for meanings, and the breaking apart of the wording is not due to the specific relative or verbal-noun reading, but to the difference between the two meanings, which remains. The author of al-Intisaf said that it is necessarily to be taken as the verbal-noun reading, because they did not worship the idols as stones, but worshipped them as shapes; so in reality they worshipped their work, and by that the proof is made clear against them: that they and their work are both created by Allah, exalted is He; so how does the created worship a created thing like itself, when the worshipped is the acquisition and work of the worshipper? He answered the objection about the breaking apart of the wording by saying that we may take the first also as the verbal-noun reading, since in reality they worshipped their carving. Yet the claim of necessity is open to discussion. It has been permitted that the second "mā" be an interrogative for denunciation and contempt, meaning: and what do you do in your worship of idols that you carved? That is, you have no work that is considered. And it has been permitted that it be a negation, meaning: and you do nothing at the time of your creation, nor are you able to do anything. It is not hidden that both possibilities go against the apparent meaning; rather, the revelation should not be read in that way. The most apparent of the aspects is that it is a relative pronoun, and the explanation of that according to what the Companions say; then that it is a verbal noun, and the argument from the verse on it is evident. As for the words of the author of al-Kashshaf: "The fairness is that the Companions' argument from this verse is not complete if it is meant to prefer the argument of the Mu'tazilah," this is outside the bounds of fairness. Then, even if it is not evidence for them, it is not evidence for the Mu'tazilah either, as is not hidden from the fair-minded.

This is so. When Abraham (peace be upon him) overcame them with the argument, they resorted to overpowering by force of might.

The most apparent of the aspects is that it is a relative pronoun, and the explanation of that according to what the Companions say; then that it is a verbal noun, and the argument from the verse on it is evident. As for the words of the author of al-Kashshaf: "The fairness is that the Companions' argument from this verse is not complete if it is meant to prefer the argument of the Mu'tazilah," this is outside the bounds of fairness. Then, even if it is not evidence for them, it is not evidence for the Mu'tazilah either, as is not hidden from the fair-minded.

This is so. When Abraham (peace be upon him) overcame them with the argument, they resorted to overpowering by force of might.

﴿They said: Build for him a structure﴾, a wall in which you kindle the fire. It was also said: a catapult (manjaniq).

﴿Then throw him into the Blazing Fire﴾, into the intense fire. Al-Jahim comes from al-juhmah, which means the intensity of blazing and kindling. The اللام (al-lam, the definite article) here is either a substitute for the genitive complement (al-mudaf ilayhi, the noun that follows the construct) or indicates prior reference (al-'ahd). What is meant is the blaze of that structure, the fire that is in it or near it.

﴿And they intended a scheme against him﴾, an evil act by deceit. **Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verses 99–101:**

﴿And he said: Indeed I am going to my Lord.﴾ To wherever He has commanded me, or to where I may devote myself to His worship, Mighty and Majestic is He. He made going to the place to which his Lord commanded him to go a going to Him, and likewise going to a place where He, exalted is He, is worshipped. This is not because the speech contains an elided noun (muda") but... [The text reads: "لا أن الكلام بتقدير مضاف"], meaning it is not that the speech implies an omitted genitive. The intended place is al-Sham (Syria). It was also said Egypt. It seems the purpose was to express despair of their faith and dislike of remaining with them, i.e., "I am leaving you and migrating from you to my Lord." ﴿He will guide me﴾ to that which is good for my religion, or to my destination.

The sin (السين, *sin*) in ﴿سيهدين﴾ is for emphasizing that the action will occur in the future, because it stands in opposition to *lan* (لن, "never"), which is the emphatic particle of negation, as Sibawayh mentioned. Abraham, peace be upon him, stated the matter definitively, either because of the prior promise of guidance God had given him when He commanded him to go, or because of the intensity of his reliance upon God, peace be upon him, or because of building upon God's established practice with him.

Page 127

Moses, peace be upon him, did not say the same thing but said: ﴿Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way﴾ (28:22), using the form of expectation. It was said this is because there had been no prior promise and no established precedent, and because his station required observing courtesy toward God, not to decide anything about Him before it occurred. Placing the observance of courtesy before the expression of intense reliance is not a contradiction, since the stations of the prophets vary and all of them are lofty. It was also said that Moses said what he said before his mission (ba'tha), while Abraham said it after. It was said that Abraham was concerned with a religious matter, so firmness suited him, while Moses was concerned with a worldly matter, so the absence of firmness suited him. Among the strange views is what was said and inclined to by Qatadah: that Abraham's intention in his saying "Indeed I am..." etc. was not migration; rather he meant meeting God after the burning, supposing that he would die in the fire when thrown into it, and by his saying ﴿He will guide me﴾ he meant guidance to Paradise. This view is refuted by his supplication for a child, where he said: ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] of the righteous﴾ (37:100), meaning some of the righteous who would help him in the call and in worship and keep him company in his estrangement. The implied meaning is: a son from among the righteous. It was omitted because the word "grant" (هب) indicates it; in the Qur'an and Arabic speech, its usage is predominantly with rational beings regarding children. God's saying ﴿And We gave him from Our mercy his brother Aaron as a prophet﴾ (19:53) is contrary to the common usage, or what is meant there is the granting of his prophethood, not the granting of his person, which is something else. Also, God's saying ﴿So We gave him good tidings of a forbearing boy﴾ (37:101) is apparent that what he was given good tidings of is the very thing he asked to be granted. Moreover, such a phrase is customarily used regarding children. By this statement, the good tidings combined that the child is male, because the word "boy" (غلام, *ghulam*) is specific to him, and that he will reach maturity, or that maturity is by the known age, for forbearance necessarily implies that age according to custom, since it is rare to find among children breadth of chest and goodness of patience, and that is tolerance in every matter. It is also permissible that this is understood from God's saying "boy" (غلام), for it may be specific to what comes after maturity, even though it came in general form and custom supports it, as the jurists have mentioned. He will be forbearing, and what forbearance is like his forbearance! When his father proposed to him the slaughter while he was an adolescent, he said: ﴿You will find me, God willing, among the patient﴾ (37:102). So consider what he would be after reaching maturity. It was said that God described no prophet with forbearance, for its rarity and abundance, except Abraham and his son, peace be upon them both, and their condition mentioned afterward indicates what has been said about them.

The *fa'* in His words, ﴿So when he reached with him the striving﴾, is *fasiha* (a particle that signals an omitted clause), pointing to an implied element that has been deleted. It was omitted because the context makes it evident, and to indicate that there is no need to state it explicitly, since failure to fulfil it is impossible. The implied sense is: "So We granted him to him, and he grew up. When he reached the level of being able to strive with him in his affairs and needs..." *Ma'a* ("with") is an adverb of place for *al-sa'y* ("striving"). It indicates the sense of companionship and its beginning. It is connected to an implied element that is indicated by what is mentioned, because the complement of a verbal noun (*masdar*) cannot precede it. When it functions as a verbal noun, it is interpreted as a verb with the *an* (*an al-masdariyya*, the particle that turns a verb into a verbal noun), and the verb together with the complement of its relative clause cannot precede the relative pronoun. This is either because it is like the precedence of a part of a thing whose parts are arranged in sequence, or because of its weakness in governing. There is discussion on this point. Firstly, the interpretation mentioned is established according to the well-known view regarding an indefinite verbal noun, not a definite one. Secondly, even if its generality is accepted, not everything that is interpreted as something has the same ruling as that to which it is interpreted. Thirdly, the element put forward here is an adverb, and it is well known that leniency is permitted with adverbs what is not permitted with other things.

They have stated that the mere scent of the verb suffices for it. On this basis, the view prohibiting it is weak because of the weakness of the governing element. The correct position is that in such a case there is no need for an implied element, whether the verbal noun is definite or indefinite, as in His words, ﴿And let not pity for them take hold of you﴾. This is the position chosen by al-Radi and held by the scholar al-Thani (al-Allama al-Thani). The author of *al-Fara'id* chose that it is connected to an implied element that functions as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from *al-sa'y*. That is: "So when he reached the striving, with that striving being with him." In this there is an objection: being "with him" in striving means that they both share it, so the companionship is between the two persons in it. What he has implied requires companionship between the striving and Ibrahim (peace be upon him), which does not fit the context. It was also permitted to connect it to *balagha* ("reached"), but this was rejected because it would require that both of them reached the limit of striving together, due to the meaning of *ma'a* that you have heard. This is not correct. It was answered that *ma'a* in this case is merely for companionship, and may be synonymous with *'inda* ("at"), as in: "So-and-so sings with the sultan," meaning "at him." The resulting meaning is: he reached [adulthood] at his father's side and in his company, taking on his character and conforming to his nature. This requires the father's complete love for him. According to this, it is also permissible to connect it to an implied element functioning as a circumstantial clause from the subject of *balagha*.

Among the instances of *ma'a* used merely for companionship is the statement of God, relating from Bilqis: ﴿And I have submitted with Solomon to God, Lord of the worlds﴾. So let what we are dealing with be like it in that verse. This was objected to: that meaning is figurative, and the figurative interpretation there is due to a barrier, and there is no barrier in our case, so it should be taken in its literal sense. Moreover, there it is not necessarily the case that it means the companionship of the subject, since it is possible that the meaning intended is "I submitted to God and to His Messenger," for example. The placement of *ma'a* at the front indicates that she thought she had been upon a religion before, and that she was submitting to God in what she used to worship from the sun. This shows that it is a submission that is valued, derived from following His prophet, not a submission like the first which is corrupt. The author of *al-Kashf* said: this is a correct meaning, and interpreting the verse in this way is preferable. If it is interpreted as the companionship of the subject, then an implied element is necessary, such as: "with the arrival of his call and the manifestation of his miracle," because the difference between the restricted and the unrestricted sense of togetherness is known necessarily. Some claimed that there is no barrier to intending the literal sense and the beginning of their both embracing Islam together, in the sense that he (peace be upon him) agreed with her or taught her. This is nothing, as is not hidden. It was also said that, if *ma'a* is connected to *balagha*, then *al-sa'y* means the place of striving, which is the mountain to which one walks. This is an artificial stretch that should not be resorted to.

In general, the preferable view is that it is connected to *al-sa'y*, and the specification is because the father is more complete in gentleness and in guiding him to proper conduct, so he does not make him strive before his time. Or it is because he (peace be upon him) had asked for him for this purpose. On the first view, it indicates his proper time, and that in the freshness of his youth there was in him what there was of firmness of intellect and gravity of forbearance, such that he answered as he answered. On the second view, it indicates the granting of his supplication (peace be upon him). The boy was thirteen years old on that day, and a son is most beloved to his father at an age when he is able to help his father and fulfil his needs, and is not able to disobey.

﴿He said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you."﴾ It is possible that he (peace be upon him) saw in his dream that he performed the slaughter, so he took it to mean what is most common in the dreams of the prophets (peace be upon them), namely that they come true exactly. It is also possible that he saw something whose interpretation was that, but he did not mention it and mentioned the interpretation instead, as one who is tested says when he sees himself riding in a ship: "I saw in a dream that I am saved from this trial." It was also said that he saw the act of slaughtering in progress but did not see the blood flowing, so "that I am slaughtering you" means "that I am working at slaughtering you." The practice of some of them suggests the choice that he (peace be upon him) was visited in a dream, and it was said to him: "Slaughter your son." The dreams of the prophets are revelation, like revelation in waking. In a report it is said that he saw on the night of *al-Tarwiya* (the eighth of Dhu al-Hijja) as if someone was saying, "Indeed God commands you to slaughter your son." When morning came he reflected on that and thought from morning until evening: is this dream from God or from Satan? Therefore that day was named the Day of *Tarwiya* (reflection). When evening came he saw the same, and he knew that it was from God, so that day was named the Day of 'Arafa (knowledge). Then he saw the same on the third night, and he resolved to slaughter him, so that day was named the Day of Sacrifice (*al-Nahr*). It was also said that when the angels gave him the good news of a forbearing boy, he said: "Then he is the sacrificed one of God." When he was born and reached the limit of striving with him, it was said to him: "Fulfil your vow." Perhaps this statement was in the dream, otherwise what would be the function of his words, ﴿Indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you﴾? In the Torah that is in the hands of the Jews today there is something that hints that the command to slaughter was at night. For after mentioning God's words to him (peace be upon him), "Take your son and go to the land of worship and offer him there as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains that I will show you," it says: "So Abraham rose early in the morning..." etc. So the command was either in a dream or in waking, but it occurred as an affirmation of what was in the dream. For there is no escape from believing in what God has related to us, in what He has made the two worlds (humans and jinn) unable to produce, in the Qur'an. The firm position is the certainty that it was in a dream only, since no reliance is placed on what is in the hands of the Jews, and there is nothing in the authentic reports that indicates it also occurred in waking.

[Page 129]

Perhaps the secret in its being in a dream and not in waking is that the swiftness of compliance demonstrates more clearly complete submission and sincerity.

It was also said: that occurred in a dream and not in waking, in order to show that the states of the prophets, whether waking or sleeping, are equal in truthfulness. The first view is preferable. The emphasis (with *inna*) is because of the improbability in the reality of what is reported. The use of the present tense in both places was said to be for evoking the image of the past for a kind of strangeness. It was also said: in the first place it is for the repetition of the dream, and in the second place for the aforementioned evocation, or for the repetition of the slaughter according to the repetition of the dream, or for correspondence (*musha kala*, matching the form of the preceding statement). Whoever considers this further will find something other than that.

﴿So look, what do you see?﴾ That is, from opinion. He consulted him about this, although it was a decisive matter, in order to know what he had in mind regarding what had descended of God's trial (mighty and majestic is He), so that he might strengthen his foot if he was distressed, and be assured of him if he submitted. And so that he could prepare his soul for it, so that it would be easier for him, and to earn reward by submitting to God's command before it descended. And so that it would become a precedent for consultation. For it was said: if Adam had consulted the angels about eating from the tree, that lapse would not have occurred from him. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *"Mādhā tura"* with a pure *ḍamma* on the *tā'* and *kasra* on the *rā'*, meaning: what is it that you show me of patience and other things? Or: what thing do you show me? In this reading *mā* is the subject, *dhā* is a relative pronoun that is its predicate, and the two objects of *tara* ("see") are omitted. Or *mādhā* is like one thing, a second object of *tara*, and the first object is omitted. It was also read *"Mādhā turā"* with a *ḍamma* on the *tā'* and a *fatḥa* on the *rā'*, in the passive voice, meaning: what does your own self show you of opinion? And *unzur* ("look") in all the readings is suspended from operating, and in *mādhā* there are the two possibilities. So do not be negligent.

﴿He said, "O father, do what you are commanded."﴾ That is, "what you are commanded," so the prepositional phrase was deleted all at once, or the preposition was deleted first so that the verb took the object directly, as in "I commanded you the good," and then the object was deleted after it had become the second accusative. The first deletion is common with *al-amr* ("command") to the extent that it almost counts as transitive without a preposition, so it is as if two deletions had not been combined. Or the meaning is: "do your command," on the basis that *mā* is a verbal noun, and what is intended by the verbal noun is the thing resulting from the verbal noun, that is, the commanded thing. There is no difference, in permitting this meaning from the verbal noun, between it being explicit and it being a verbal noun with *an* (*maslūk*, a clause formed with *an*).

Its being annexed to the pronoun of Ibrahim is an annexation to the object, and the distance of this interpretation is not hidden. This statement requires that the command had preceded it, and it is not mentioned. So either it was understood from his (peace be upon him) words that he saw that he would slaughter him as one commanded, or he knew that the dreams of the prophets are true and that they do not undertake such a thing except by command. The use of the present tense is to signal the strangeness of that, similar to its use in Ibrahim's words in one respect. In this there is an indication that what he said did not come except from a dream not mixed with ignorance of the state of the one commanded. It was said: it is for indicating that the command is connected to him, directed at him, continuing until the time of compliance with it. It was said: it is for the repetition of the dream. It was said: it was brought in that form because no command had yet come, but there was only the dream of slaughter, so he informed him of it, and he knew, because of his knowledge of his father's standing, and that he was among those whom Satan cannot reach with false imaginings in dreams, that this would happen and would only happen by divine command. So he said to him: "Do what you are commanded afterwards of the slaughter that you saw in your dream." And since the father's address was "O my son" as an expression of tenderness, he replied "O father" as an expression of reverence and honour. Along with that, he gave a wise answer, for he entrusted the matter to God when he consulted him, so he answered that he was not going beyond it, and that what was obligatory was to carry out the command.

﴿You will find me, if God wills, of the patient.﴾ In submission to God's decree, whether it is slaughter or something else. It was said: it is in submission to the slaughter. The first is preferable because of its generality, and the slaughter enters it as a primary instance. In His words "of the patient" rather than "patient," although the endings of the verses would require that, there is so much humility in it. It was said, and perhaps he was granted success in patience through its blessing together with the blessing of the exception. When Moses (peace be upon him) did not follow this path of humility in his words, "You will find me, if God wills, patient," in that he did not place his noble self in the row of the patient, but phrased the statement in a way that does not indicate the existence of another patient, patience was not made easy for him, although he did not neglect the matter of the exception. In it there is also an encouragement to his father (peace be upon him) towards patience, since he knows his father's compassion for him together with the greatness of the trial, in that he indicated that God has servants who are patient. And this is a spring flower that cannot bear rubbing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 103:

﴿When they both submitted﴾ — i.e., they surrendered and yielded to the command of God, the Exalted; so the verb is intransitive (lazim). Or: the sacrificed one (al-dhabih) submitted himself, and Ibrahim his son, on the basis that it is transitive (muta'addin) and its object is omitted.

ʿAli (may God honour his face), Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAbd Allah, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, al-Aʿmash and al-Thawri read "sallama" (they both caused [themselves] to submit). It has been construed according to what you have heard. It is also permissible that the meaning is that they both entrusted the matter to Him, the Exalted, in His decree and His destiny. It has also been read "istaslama." The root of the three verb forms is salima hadha li-fulan, meaning: this became pure and unchallenged for him, for he was safe from being disputed over it.

﴿And He threw him down upon his forehead﴾ — he felled him onto his side, so that his forehead fell upon the ground. The original sense of al-tall is throwing [someone] onto the tall (talla), which is the heap of earth, and then it was generalised to every kind of felling. Al-jabin is one of the two sides of the forehead. Its plural "ajbun" is anomalous; the regular plural for paucity would be "ajbinah," like kathib and akthibah, and for abundance "jubnan" and "jubun," like kuthban and kutub. The lam here indicates the place upon which he fell, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they fall down upon their chins﴾ [17:107], and the line of verse:

"He fell prone upon his two hands and his mouth."

It is not for transitivity (ta'diyah). It has been said that the intended meaning is that he laid him on his face, and that this was by a gesture from him. Several transmitters related from Mujahid that he said to his father: "Do not slaughter me while you look at my face, perhaps you will be merciful to me and not finish me off. Tie my hands to my neck, then place my face upon the ground." He did so, and what happened, happened. It is not hidden that this meaning from the verse is remote; yet it is not far that the sacrificed one himself said this.

In the reports there are also narrations of other statements besides this. Among them is what is in a report from al-Suddi that he said to his father, peace be upon them both: "O father, tighten my bonds so that I do not thrash about, and draw your garments back so that none of my blood splashes upon them and my mother sees it and grieves; and hasten the passage of the knife over my throat, so that death is easier for me. When you come to my mother, convey my greetings to her." Then Ibrahim approached him, kissing him, and both of them were weeping. Among them is what is in a hadith related by Ahmad and a group from Ibn ʿAbbas, that he said to his father, and he was wearing a white shirt: "O father, I have no garment to shroud me in other than this, so take it off so that you may shroud me in it." He began to take it off, and what God, Mighty and Majestic, related occurred. That took place at the rock that is in Mina; and from al-Hasan, at the place overlooking the mosque of Mina; and from al-Dahhak, at the place of sacrifice where sacrifice is made today. It has also been said that it was in Bayt al-Maqdis, and this is related from Kaʿb. And al-Imam (al-Razi) related, alongside this view, that it was in al-Sham.

[Page 131]

﴿And We called to him, "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision."﴾ It was said that a angel called to him from behind, from before Allah (exalted is He) with that. The *an* here is *mufassirah* (an explanatory *an*, meaning "that is"). Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿قَدْ صَدَّقْتَ﴾ without the particle ﴿قَدْ﴾ [that is, without *qad*]. It is also read ﴿صَدَقْتَ﴾ with the light (unstressed) pronunciation. Fayyad read ﴿الرِّيّا﴾ with a kasrah on the *ra'* and with assimilation (*idgham*). His (peace be upon him) fulfilling the vision (*taṣdīq*) means that he gave it its due of action and exerted his utmost effort to bring it about. This is by resolve and by taking the preliminary steps. It does not necessarily follow that what he saw actually occurred exactly as he saw it. It was also said that it means bringing about its interpretation, and its interpretation is what took place. It is understood from the words of the Imam that it is an acknowledgment of the obligation to act upon it, and it does not indicate carrying out everything that he saw in the dream.

Did he (peace be upon him) pass the knife over his throat or not? There are two opinions. Many of the eminent scholars held the second of them. Imam Ahmad narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that when he (peace be upon him) took the knife and wanted to slaughter him, he was called from behind: "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision." He, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* also narrated from him that he (peace be upon him) was working at his shirt to take it off when he was called with that.

Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated through the route of Mujahid from him as well: "When he put his hand [with the knife] to slaughter him, he did not raise the blade until he was called, 'O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision,' so he held back his hand." 'Abd ibn Humayd and others narrated from Mujahid: "When he put his hand to slaughter him, he was called, 'O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision,' so he held back his hand, raised his head, and saw the ram descending toward him until it fell upon it, and he slaughtered it." In another narration from him, which 'Abd ibn Humayd also related, and Ibn al-Mundhir, that he passed the knife but it turned back. The Jews also held the view of non-passage, because of what is in their Torah: "Abraham stretched out his hand and took the knife. Then the angel of Allah called to him from heaven, saying, 'Abraham! Abraham!' He said, 'Here I am.' He said, 'Do not stretch out your hand against the boy, and do not do anything to him.'"

A group held the first view. Among them are those who said that he did pass it, but it did not cut, despite the absence of an obstacle, because cutting is by Allah's creation in it, or it is customary with it, and Allah (glorified is He) may not create it. Among them are those who said that he did pass it but it did not cut because of an obstacle. Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Ata' ibn Yasar that he (peace be upon him) came toward him with the knife, and he lay down on him, so Allah (exalted is He) made what was between his nape and his throat [i.e., the area of the neck] of copper, on which the knife had no effect.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi that he (peace be upon him) drew the knife across his throat but it did not cut, and Allah (exalted is He) placed a sheet of copper over his throat.

al-Khatib in *Tali al-Talkhis* narrated from Fudayl ibn 'Iyad, who said: "He laid him down and placed the knife, but Jibril (peace be upon him) turned it over."

al-Hakim narrated, through a chain containing al-Waqidi, from 'Ata': "He cut into his throat, and behold, he had cut into copper. Then he sharpened the knife twice or thrice on a stone." All of this has been deemed weak. It was also said that he (peace be upon him) did slaughter, but whenever he cut a part of the throat, Allah (exalted is He) restored it. They claimed that this is reported in some reports, but it is hardly authentic. What is related to this matter will come up shortly, if Allah (exalted is He) wills.

The answer to ﴿لَمّا﴾ [*lamma*, "when"] is omitted and understood after ﴿صَدَّقْتَ الرُّؤْيا﴾, meaning: "what happened happened, of what the state expresses but speech cannot encompass": their joy and their gratitude to Allah (exalted is He) for what He bestowed upon them, namely the removal of the trial after it had descended, the granting of success in what He did not grant to anyone else like it, the manifestation of their virtue together with the securing of great reward, and so on. This is better than estimating ﴿فَإذا﴾ [*fa-idha*, "then suddenly"] or the like. Some of the Basran grammarians estimated it after ﴿وَتَلَّهُ لِلْجَبِينِ﴾ [and He laid him down on his brow], meaning: "We multiplied their reward." It is narrated from al-Khalil and Sibawayh that its estimate is before ﴿وَتَلَّهُ﴾. Al-Bahr [*Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit*] says: the estimate is "when they both submitted, they both submitted, and He laid him down." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is, according to them, like the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"When we crossed the courtyard of the tribe and he turned aside,"*

meaning: "we crossed and he turned aside." This, as you see, is [weak]. The Kufans said: the answer is affirmed, namely ﴿وَنادَيْناهُ﴾ [And We called to him], with the *waw* being extra. A group said it is ﴿وَتَلَّهُ﴾, also with the *waw* being extra. Perhaps the first, what was mentioned earlier, is better.

As for His (exalted is He) saying: ﴿Indeed, that is how We reward the doers of good﴾, it is the beginning of a statement not included in the calling. It is the cause (*ta'lil*) for relieving that hardship, which is understood from the estimated answer or from the stated answer, namely "We called to him…" etc., according to the view that this is the answer or part of it. Even if the answer and the cause are not, in meaning, their excellence, and its being a cause for the gratitude contained in the answer is not worth anything.

Indeed, this is the manifest trial (al-bala' al-mubin), namely the clear test and examination (al-ibtila' wal-ikhtibar al-bayyin) in which the sincere one (al-mukhlis) is distinguished from others. Or it is the evident ordeal (al-mihnah al-bayyinah), that is, the ordeal whose difficulty is apparent, and nothing is more difficult than what occurred, and its severity is hardly hidden from anyone. It belongs to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to test whom He wills with what He wills, and He, glory be to Him, is the All-Wise, the Doer of whatever He intends. Perhaps this sentence serves to show that the two of them (Abraham and Ishmael) were among the good-doers (al-muhsinin). It has also been said that it serves to explain the wisdom behind what befell them. Under both interpretations the sentence is resumptive (mustaanifah), a explanatory resumption (isti'nafan bayaniyyan), so let it be reflected upon.

Page 132

﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾: with an animal that is slaughtered in his place, ﴿great﴾. It was said: that is, great in body and fat. It is a white ram, with horns and large eyes. In another report, " amlah" (speckled or black-and-white) replaces "abyad" (white). From al-Hasan it is related that it was a wild goat sent down from Thabir. The majority hold the first view, and al-Hasan agreed with them in a report transmitted from him by Ibn Abi Hatim, in which its name is given as Hariri. The Jews also hold that it was a ram.

Al-Mu'azzim (the one who exalts) explained "great" as great in rank. This is based on what is reported from Ibn Abbas: it was the ram that Habil (Abel) offered, which was accepted from him, and it remained grazing in Paradise until the day of this ransom. In a report from him and from Ibn Jubayr, they both said: its greatness lay in its being one of the rams of Paradise, which grazed there for forty autumns.

Mujahid said: it was described as great because its acceptance was certain. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: because it came from God, mighty and majestic. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: because it was not produced by procreation but by direct creation. Amr ibn Ubayd said: because a practice was established through it and it became a lasting religious rite until the end of time. It was also said: because through it a prophet and the son of a prophet was ransomed. Its descent from Thabir is as al-Hasan said concerning the wild goat, and this is related in a report from Ibn Abbas.

In a report from Ali, may God honour his face, that he found it (peace be upon him) tied by a sumrah (acacia tree) at the base of Thabir.

«From Ata ibn al-Sa'ib, who said: I was sitting at the place of sacrifice (al-Manhar) when a man from Quraysh told me, from his father, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: "The ram descended upon Ibrahim in this very place."»

In a report from Ibn Abbas: a ram from Paradise came out to him, one that had grazed there for forty autumns. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) sent his son and followed it. He struck it with seven pebbles and drove it to the first Jamrah (pillar), and it escaped. He struck it with seven pebbles and drove it to the middle Jamrah, and it escaped. He struck it with seven pebbles and drove it to the greatest Jamrah, and then brought it to the place of sacrifice in Mina, and slaughtered it. It was said: this is the origin of the sunnah of stoning the pillars (ramy al-jimar). The well-known view, however, is that the origin of the sunnah is the stoning of Satan there. In a report from Qatadah, Satan wished to achieve his aim with Ibrahim and his son on the day he was commanded to sacrifice him. He took the form of a friend of Ibrahim and tried to turn him from this, but he could not. Then he confronted the son, but he could not. Then he came to the Jamrah and swelled up until he filled the valley. With Ibrahim was an angel, who said to him: "Throw, O Ibrahim!" So he threw seven pebbles, saying "Allahu akbar" after each pebble, and the way was opened for him. Then he went on until he came to the second Jamrah, and Satan again filled the valley. The angel said: "Throw, O Ibrahim!" So he threw as he had done the first time. The same happened at the third.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that the ransom was one animal, and this is the well-known view. Abd ibn Humayd related from Ibn Abbas that he was ransomed with two speckled, horned, large-eyed rams, but I know of no soundness in this report. "Dhibh" (sacrifice) here, even if the report were sound, is to be understood as a genus. The one who actually ransomed was Ibrahim (peace be upon him). God, glorified is He, said "fadaynahu" (We ransomed him) using the word figuratively for ransoming, meaning "We commanded" or "We gave," or on account of its attribution to Him, exalted is He. It is also permitted that there is a metaphor here of the implicit kind. The purpose of departing from the original usage is glorification.

We left upon him among later generations: "Peace be upon Abraham." (37:108–109)

The explanation of its meaning has already been given when discussing its counterpart at the end of the story of Noah (Nuh). Perhaps the mention of "among the worlds" (fi al-'alamin) there, and its omission here, is because Noah (peace be upon him) has a fame that Abraham (peace be upon him) does not have, being like a second Adam to mankind, and because the salvation of those who were saved from the people of the Flood came through his blessing.
