Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 110:

﴿Thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ That (dhalika, "thus") is a reference to the perpetuation of his good remembrance among the nations, not to what it referred to earlier, so there is no repetition. Here the phrase "Innā" (indeed, We) has been omitted. It has been said that this is for emphasis in repelling the suspicion that it is one and the same with what preceded, especially since the first was brought as a justification for the recompense of Ibrahim and his son, peace be upon them both, for what was indicated before, while this one is brought as a justification for the recompense of Ibrahim alone, by what is contained in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We left for him...﴾ etc. How subtle is the omission here, for brevity, since in what came before there was something similar, in not mentioning the son and restricting it to Ibrahim.

It has also been said that perhaps this is for the sake of sufficiency with mentioning "Innā" once in this story. Some of the eminent scholars said: it is to indicate that the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was not complete, for what follows His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac...﴾ etc., is a completion of what pertains to him, peace be upon him. This differs from the other stories, in which ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good⁠

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verses 111–112:

وقَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿إنَّهُ مِن عِبادِنا المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾
صفحة 133
الكَلامُ فِيهِ كَما تَقَدَّمَ.

"His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants﴾. The discussion of it is as has preceded."

﴿وبَشَّرْناهُ بِإسْحاقَ نَبِيًّا﴾ حالٌ مِن إسْحاقَ، وكَذا قَوْلُهُ تَعالى ﴿مِنَ الصّالِحِينَ﴾ وفي ذَلِكَ تَعْظِيمُ شَأْنِ الصَّلاحِ، وفي تَأْخِيرِهِ إيماءٌ إلى أنَّهُ الغايَةُ لَها لِتَضَمُّنِها مَعْنى الكَمالِ والتَّكْمِيلِ والمَقْصُودُ مِنهُما الإتْيانُ بِالأفْعالِ الحَسَنَةِ السَّدِيدَةِ وهو في الِاسْتِعْمالِ يَخْتَصُّ بِها.

"﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet﴾: 'a prophet' is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action) of Isaac. Likewise His saying ﴿from among the righteous﴾. In this there is the magnifying of the rank of righteousness. Placing it last indicates that it is the goal of prophethood, because prophethood includes the meanings of perfection and completion, and what is intended by them is the performance of good and upright deeds, and this word (ṣalāḥ, righteousness) in usage is specific to such deeds."

وجُوِّزَ كَوْنُ (مِنَ الصّالِحِينَ) حالًا، وكَوْنُ (نَبِيًّا) حالًا مِنَ الضَّمِيرِ المُسْتَتِرِ فِيهِ، وقُدِّمَ في اللَّفْظِ لِلِاهْتِمامِ، ولِئَلّا تَخْتَلَّ رُءُوسُ الآيِ، وفِيهِ مِنَ البُعْدِ ما فِيهِ، عَلى أنَّ في جَوازِ تَقْدِيمِ الحالِ مُطْلَقًا أوِ اطِّرادِهِ في مِثْلِ هَذا التَّرْكِيبِ كَلامًا لا يَخْفى عَلى مَن راجَعَ الألْفِيَّةَ وشُرُوحَها، وفِيهِ ما فِيهِ مِن بُعْدٍ، وجُوِّزَ أيْضًا كَوْنُهُ في مَوْضِعِ الصِّفَةِ لَـ”نَبِيًّا“، والكَلامُ عَلى الأوَّلِ - وهو الَّذِي عَلَيْهِ الجُمْهُورُ - أمْدَحُ كَما لا يَخْفى، والمُرادُ كَوْنُهُ نَبِيًّا وكَوْنُهُ مِنَ الصّالِحِينَ في قَضاءِ اللَّهِ تَعالى وتَقْدِيرِهِ أيْ مَقْضِيًّا كَوْنُهُ نَبِيًّا مَقْضِيًّا كَوْنُهُ مِنَ الصّالِحِينَ، وإنْ شِئْتَ فَقُلْ: مُقَدَّرًا، ولا يَكُونانِ بِذَلِكَ مِنَ الحالِ المُقَدَّرَةِ الَّتِي تُذْكَرُ في مُقابَلَةِ المُقارَنَةِ؛ بَلْ هُما بِهَذا الِاعْتِبارِ حالانِ مُقارِنانِ لِلْعامِلِ وهو فِعْلُ البِشارَةِ، أوْ شَيْءٍ آخَرَ مَحْذُوفٍ أيْ بَشَّرْناهُ بِوُجُودِ إسْحاقَ نَبِيًّا... إلَخْ، وأوْجَبَ غَيْرُ واحِدٍ تَقْدِيرَ ذَلِكَ مُعَلِّلًا بِأنَّ البِشارَةَ لا تَتَعَلَّقُ بِالأعْيانِ بَلْ بِالمَعانِي. وتُعُقِّبَ بِأنَّهُ إنْ أُرِيدَ أنَّها لا تُسْتَعْمَلُ إلّا مُتَعَلِّقَةً بِالأعْيانِ فالواقِعُ خِلافُهُ كَـ ﴿بُشِّرَ أحَدُهم بِالأُنْثى﴾، فَإنْ قِيلَ إنَّما يَصِحُّ بِتَقْدِيرٍ وِلادَةٍ ونَحْوِهِ مِنَ المَعانِي فَهو مَحَلُّ النِّزاعِ فَلا وجْهَ لَهُ، والَّذِي يَمِيلُ إلَيْهِ القَلْبُ أنَّ المَعْنى عَلى إرادَةِ ذَلِكَ، ورُبَّما يُدَّعى أنَّ مَعْنى البِشارَةِ تَسْتَدْعِي تَقْدِيرَ مَعْنًى مِنَ المَعانِي، وقِيلَ هُما حالانِ مُقَدَّرانِ كَقَوْلِهِ تَعالى ﴿فادْخُلُوها خالِدِينَ﴾ وفِيهِ بَحْثٌ.

"It is also permissible for ﴿from among the righteous﴾ to be a ḥāl, and for ﴿a prophet﴾ to be a ḥāl from the hidden pronoun within it. It was placed first in wording for emphasis, and so that the verse-endings (ru'us al-ay, the rhyming final words of verses) would not be disrupted. Yet there is in this much remoteness (from the correct construction). Moreover, regarding the permissibility of fronting a ḥāl absolutely, or its being consistent in such a construction, there is a discussion that is not hidden from one who has consulted the Alfiyya (Ibn Malik's poem on Arabic grammar) and its commentaries, and in it is much remoteness too. It is also permitted that it (﴿from among the righteous﴾) occupies the position of an adjective of ﴿a prophet﴾. The discussion on the first view, which is the one held by the majority, is more laudatory, as is not hidden. What is meant is that his being a prophet and his being among the righteous were decreed in God's Exalted decree and determination, i.e., his being a prophet was decreed, his being among the righteous was decreed. If you wish, say: 'determined.' Yet they are not, by this consideration, among the ḥāl muqaddara (the anticipated circumstantial state) which is mentioned in contrast to the ḥāl muqārana (the concurrent state). Rather, by this consideration they are two concurrent ḥāls relative to the governing element, which is the verb of giving good news, or to something else omitted, i.e., 'We gave him good news of the existence of Isaac as a prophet…' etc. Several scholars made it obligatory to posit such an omission, giving the reason that good news does not relate to concrete entities but to meanings. It has been objected that if it is meant that it is never used except related to concrete entities, then the reality is contrary to this, as in ﴿when one of them is given good news of a female﴾. If it is said that it is valid only with an implied birth or similar meanings, then that is the point of dispute, so there is no basis for it. What the heart inclines to is that the meaning is according to that intention. Perhaps it is claimed that the meaning of good news requires positing some meaning. It was also said that both are anticipated ḥāls, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Enter it, abiding therein forever﴾, but in this there is a discussion."

الكَلامُ فِيهِ كَما تَقَدَّمَ.

[p. 133]

﴿And We blessed him﴾, that is, Ibrahim (peace be upon him), ﴿and Ishaq﴾, that is, We bestowed upon both of them the blessings of the religion and of the world, by multiplying their offspring and making among them prophets and messengers.

It is recited as (barrakna) with shadda, for emphasis. ﴿And from their offspring is one who is a doer of good﴾ in his deeds, or [one who is good] to himself, through faith and obedience. ﴿And one who wrongs himself﴾ through disbelief and sins, and the wrongdoing toward others (zulm al-ghayr) is included in this. ﴿Manifestly﴾, evidently, his wrongdoing being apparent.

In this there is an indication that lineage has no effect on guidance and misguidance, and that wrongdoing among descendants does not return to the forefathers as a defect or blemish. This is what [needs to be said].

* * *

Further discussions remain concerning these verses. (The first) is that they differed concerning the one who was sacrificed (al-dhabih). According to what al-Jalal al-Suyuti mentioned in his treatise *al-Qawl al-fasih fi ta'yin al-dhabih* (The Eloquent Statement on Identifying the One Sacrificed), ʿAli, Ibn ʿUmar, Abu Hurayra, Abu al-Tufayl, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Shaʿbi, Yusuf ibn Mihran, al-Hasan al-Basri, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi, Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib, Abu Jaʿfar al-Baqir, Abu Salih, al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas, al-Kalbi, Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others said that it was Isma'il (peace be upon him), not Ishaq (peace be upon him). This is one of the two narrations from Ibn ʿAbbas. A group preferred this view, especially most of the later scholars of hadith (muhaddithun). Abu Hatim said: "It is the correct [view]." In al-Huda [it is stated] that it is the correct view according to the scholars among the Companions, the Successors and those after them.

Abu Saʿid al-Darir was asked about this and recited:

*Indeed the one sacrificed, may you be guided, is Isma'il; the Book and the Revelation explicitly affirm this.*
*It is an honour with which God singled out our Prophet, and the explanation (tafsir) and interpretation (ta'wil) have brought it.*
*If you are his nation, do not deny him a honour with which preference (al-tafdil) has singled him out.*

But his claim of an explicit text (nass) is open to question. It was also well known among the Arabs before the prophethood, as verses that al-Tha'alibi transmitted in his tafsir from Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt indicate. [Isma'il's view] is supported by the argument that he is the one who was granted to Ibrahim (peace be upon him) after the migration (athar al-hijra), and that the glad tidings of Ishaq
[p. 134]
afterwards are conjoined (ma'tufa) to the glad tidings of this boy, and the apparent meaning is that they are different, so it is necessarily Isma'il. [It is also supported by the argument] that he was given glad tidings that he would come into existence and be made a prophet, so it is not permissible for Ibrahim (peace be upon him) to be tested by slaughtering him, since [Ibrahim] knew that the condition for its occurrence was absent.

The reply that the first [glad tiding] was a glad tiding of existence, and this [later one] was a glad tiding of prophethood, but after the sacrifice, is weak, said the author of al-Kashf. This is because the structure of the verse does not indicate that the glad tiding is of his prophethood, but rather that the glad tiding is of a matter restricted to prophethood. So either it is to be understood as the existence of Ishaq after the sacrifice, for which the wording gives no indication, or the existence is to be understood absolutely, which is what is sought. If you say: "The earlier glad tiding of existence is sufficient for the indication," I reply: "That is against you, not for you. And who grants that the earlier [glad tiding] was a glad tiding of Ishaq, so that the purpose is established for you?"

[The argument is also supported] that the glad tiding of him was given together with the birth of Yaʿqub from him, according to what is apparent in the words of the Exalted in Hud: ﴿So We gave him glad tidings of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Yaʿqub﴾. And when one is given glad tidings of a son and a grandson at once, how can the command to slaughter the son while he is an adolescent (muraheq), before his own son is born, be conceived? To deny that he was then an adolescent, on the grounds that he could have been an adult, as the Jews claimed, when Yaʿqub had already been born to him, and similar [claims], is obstinacy that should not be heeded. [It is also supported by the argument] that the Exalted described Isma'il (peace be upon him) with patience, in His words: ﴿And Isma'il, and Idris, and Dhu al-Kifl, each of them was among the patient﴾. And that He, the Mighty and Majestic, described him with truthfulness of promise, in His words: ﴿Indeed he was true to the promise﴾. He did not describe Ishaq with either of these. So [Isma'il] is the more fitting, not [Ishaq], since the speaker says: ﴿O my father, do what you are commanded; you will find me, God willing, among the patient﴾, one who fulfils his words by his deed.

[It is also supported by the argument] that what happened took place in Mecca, and Isma'il is the one who was there. [It is also supported by the argument] that the two horns of the ram were hung in the Ka'ba until they burned with it during al-Hajjaj's siege of Ibn al-Zubayr, may God be pleased with him. The Quraysh had inherited them from one generation to the next. The apparent [reason] is that they did this only out of pride, and this would not hold for them if the ram was a ransom for Ishaq rather than for their forefather Isma'il.

[It is also supported by the argument] that al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak, Ibn Jarir in his tafsir, al-Umawi in his Maghazi, and al-Khil'i in his Fawa'id narrated, through the chain of Isma'il ibn Abi Karima, from ʿUmar ibn Abi Muhammad al-Khattabi, from al-ʿUtbi, from his father, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Saʿid al-Sunabihi, who said: "We attended the gathering of Muʿawiya, and the people discussed Isma'il and Ishaq: which of them was the one sacrificed? Some of the people said: 'Isma'il,' and some of them said: 'Rather, Ishaq.' Muʿawiya said: 'You have fallen upon one who knows (ʿala al-khabir saqattum). We were with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when a Bedouin came to him and said: "O Messenger of God, I left the pasture dry and the water sour; the dependants have perished and the wealth is lost, so return to me from what God has granted you, O son of the two sacrificed ones (ya ibn al-dhabihayn)." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) smiled and did not object to him.' The people said: 'Who are the two sacrificed ones, O Commander of the Faithful?' He said: 'When ʿAbd al-Muttalib was commanded to dig Zamzam, he vowed to God that if its matter was made easy, he would sacrifice one of his sons. When he finished, he cast lots among them, and they were ten. The lot fell upon ʿAbd Allah, so he wanted to sacrifice him, but his maternal uncles, the Banu Makhzum, prevented him and said: "Ransom your Lord and redeem your son." So he ransomed him with a hundred camels.' Muʿawiya said: 'This is one, and the other is Isma'il.'"

[It is also supported by the argument] that it is mentioned in the Tawrah that God tested Ibrahim, and said to him: "O Ibrahim!" He said: "Here I am!" [God] said: "Take your son, your only one (wahidaka), whom you love, and go to the land of worship, and offer him up there as a sacrifice upon one of the mountains that I will show you." The meaning of "your only one" is one who has no other [son]. This cannot apply to Ishaq at the time of the command to sacrifice, because Isma'il was then existing, for he was born to Ibrahim according to the Tawrah when he was eighty-six years old, and Ishaq was born, according to the same [Tawrah], when he was a hundred years old. Also, the phrase "whom you love" is more fitting for Isma'il, since the first son usually holds a love that is not held for those who come after him.

It is known from what has been mentioned that what is in the Tawrah now in the hands of the Jews today, of the mention of "that is Ishaq" (huwa Ishaq) after "whom you love," is among their additions and falsehoods which they inserted into the words of God the Exalted, since it hardly fits with what precedes it. Some of the Jews replied to this by saying that the application of "only one" to Ishaq is because Isma'il was then in Mecca. This is a distortion and a false interpretation, because "only one" is not used as a description of a son unless he is the sole [son] in sonship and has no partner in it. Some of them told me: "The application of this to him is because he was the only one of his mother, and she had no other son." I said: "That is excluded in every way, because of its attribution to the pronoun of Ibrahim (peace be upon him)." What supports what we have said is what Ibn Ishaq related: Muhammad ibn Kaʿb mentioned that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz sent to a man who had been a Jew, then became Muslim and whose Islam was good, and who had been one of their scholars, and asked him: "Which of Ibrahim's two sons was he commanded to sacrifice?" He said: "Isma'il, by God, O Commander of the Faithful. The Jews know this, but they envy you, O Arabs."

Ibn Kathir mentioned that in some copies of the Tawrah the word is (bikrak) (your firstborn) instead of (wahidak) (your only one), and this is more evident for the purpose. It was also said that it is Ishaq. al-Qurtubi attributed this to the majority. al-Baghawi and others attributed it to ʿUmar, ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud, al-ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Shaʿbi, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, Abu Maysara, Zayd ibn Aslam, ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaqiq, al-Zuhri, al-Qasim ibn Yazid, Makhul, Kaʿb, ʿUthman ibn Hadir, al-Suddi, al-Hasan, Qatada, Abu al-Hudhayl, Ibn Sabit, Masruq, ʿAta', Muqatil, and it is one of the two narrations from Ibn ʿAbbas. Abu Jaʿfar ibn Jarir al-Tabari chose this view, and al-Qadi ʿIyad in al-Shifa and al-Suhayli in al-Taʿrif wa al-Aʿlam definitively affirmed it. They argued for it by saying that God did not mention that He gave glad tidings of Isma'il before his existence, so [the sacrificed one] is Ishaq, since this is established by explicit text. And because Hagar, the mother of Isma'il, was not married to him, so the one called [to be sacrificed] was born of Sarah.

It is answered that this verse is itself sufficient proof that [Isma'il] was also given glad tidings of, because God's words: ﴿And We gave him glad tidings of Ishaq﴾, after the completion of this story and its concluding with what it concludes, is clearly indicative that there were two distinct glad tidings there. Then the absence of mention does not indicate the absence of existence. It does not follow that he had asked for a son from Sarah, nor is it known that he (peace be upon him) prayed for that before Hagar was given to him, because she was presented to him at Harran before arriving in Syria. Moreover, the glad tiding of Ishaq was explicitly given in Syria, so the apparent [meaning] of this verse is that it [came] before their arrival there, because the glad tiding followed the supplication, and that was before arriving in Syria. So said the author of al-Kashf.

[It is also supported] by what Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Kurayb, from Zayd ibn Habbab, from al-Hasan ibn Dinar, from ʿAli ibn Zayd ibn Juda'an, from al-Hasan, from al-Ahnaf ibn Qays, from al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The one sacrificed is Ishaq."

This was objected to on the ground that al-Hasan ibn Dinar is abandoned (matruk) and his teacher is one whose narrations are rejected (munkar al-hadith).

[It is also supported] by what al-Daylami in Musnad al-Firdaws narrated through the chain of ʿAbd Allah ibn Naji'a, from Muhammad ibn Harb al-Nasa'i, from ʿAbd al-Mu'min ibn ʿAbbad, from al-Aʿmash, from ʿAtiyya, from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed Dawud asked his Lord a request, saying: "Make me like Ibrahim and Ishaq and Yaʿqub." God the Exalted revealed to him: "I tested Ibrahim with the fire and he was patient; I tested Ishaq with the sacrifice and he was patient; I tested Yaʿqub and he was patient."'"

[It is also supported] by what al-Daraqutni and al-Daylami in Musnad al-Firdaws narrated through his chain, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Katib, from al-Husayn ibn Fahm, from Khalaf ibn Salim, from Bahz ibn Asad, from Shuʿba, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'The one sacrificed is Ishaq.'"

[It is also supported] by what al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Ibn Abi Hatim in his tafsir narrated through the chain of al-Walid ibn Muslim, from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, from ʿAta' ibn Yasar, from Abu Hurayra, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed God the Exalted gave me the choice between forgiving half of my nation or my intercession, and I chose my intercession, and I hoped that it would be more general for my nation. Had it not been for what the righteous servant (al-ʿabd al-salih) preceded me to, I would have hastened my supplication. Indeed when God the Exalted relieved Ishaq of the distress of the sacrifice, it was said to him: "O Ishaq, ask, and you will be given." He said: "By God, I will hasten it before the incitements of Satan. O God, whoever dies without associating anything with You, has done well, so forgive him."'"

This was objected to on the ground that ʿAbd al-Rahman is weak. Ibn Kathir said: "The hadith is strange and rejected (gharib munkar), and I fear that there is an inserted addition in it, namely his words: 'Indeed God the Exalted, when He relieved...' etc. And even if it is preserved, the more likely [reading] is that the context concerns Isma'il, and they altered it to Ishaq, along with other reports. Among them are many that are attributed to Companions (mawquf), weak (da'if), and fabricated (mawdu')." And whenever a raised (marfu') hadith is authenticated that it is Ishaq, we accept it and place it upon the eye and head.

The commentators who hold this view claim that some of these reports are authentic in this regard. Some of the arguments used by the first view have been answered. It is not accepted that the story took place in Mecca. Rather, it happened in Syria. The hanging of the two horns in the Ka'bah does not prove that the event occurred in Mecca, since they may have been transported from the lands of Syria to Mecca and hung there. Even if the event is granted to have occurred in Mecca, there is no barrier to Abraham having traveled with him from Syria to it. Indeed, the view has been related: 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad reported in *Zawa'id al-Zuhd* from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "When Abraham saw in a dream that he was slaughtering Isaac, he traveled with him from his dwelling to the place of sacrifice at Mina, a distance of a month, in a single morning. When the slaughter was averted from him and he was commanded to slaughter the ram, he slaughtered it, and then he returned with him to his dwelling in a single evening, a distance of a month, the valleys and mountains having been folded up for him." As for the boast, even if it is granted, using it as evidence is not much of a boast. The report containing "O son of the two sacrificed ones" is rare, and in its chain of narration is someone whose condition is unknown. Its content clearly shows that it is not authentic, in the words: "When he finished, he cast lots among them; they were ten, and the arrow fell upon 'Abd Allah." For 'Abd Allah, by the consensus of the historians, had not yet been born at the time of digging Zamzam. The story of 'Abd al-Muttalib's vow to slaughter one of his sons is related in another form: that he vowed to sacrifice one of his sons when his sons reached ten. When they reached that number with the birth of 'Abd Allah, what happened, happened.

As for what has spread of the report, "I am the son of the two sacrificed ones," al-'Iraqi said: "I have not found it." The previous report, after its condition has been known, is not sufficient to establish it as a hadith. There is no need to interpret it as meaning by "the two sacrificed ones" Isaac and 'Abd Allah, on the basis that the word "father" may be applied to a paternal uncle; or as meaning by them the two who sacrifice, namely Abraham and 'Abd al-Muttalib, by taking the form *fa'il* in the sense of the active rather than the passive. These (scholars) have also taken the verse ﴿وبَشَّرْناهُ بِإسْحاقَ نَبِيًّا﴾ ("And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet") to mean good news of his prophethood, and what preceded the good news as meaning that he would come into existence before it. Since the announcement there was before birth, and naming usually occurs after birth, he was not named there, but was named here because it was after birth. They also found support for the unity (of the two accounts) in the description of him as being among the righteous, because that was what Abraham had sought. It is as if it were said to him: "This boy about whom you were first given good news is the one you sought when you said: ﴿رَبِّ هَبْ لِي مِنَ الصّالِحِينَ﴾ ('My Lord, grant me [a son] from among the righteous')." Yet you know that interpreting it as good news of prophethood is contrary to the apparent meaning, since the apparent meaning would be to say: "If that were intended, We would have given him the good news of his prophethood," or similar. The supposition that he would come into being as a prophet does not remove this difficulty, as is not hidden. Likewise, describing him with the righteousness that was sought (by Abraham) (does not remove it). So reflect.

Some scholars saw the strength of the evidence on both sides, and none of it seemed preponderant to them, so they suspended judgment on the specific identity, like the great al-Jalal al-Suyuti, may God have mercy on him. He said at the end of his earlier treatise: "I had inclined to the view that the sacrificed one is Isaac, in the tafsir, but I am now suspending judgment on that." Some of them said, as al-Khafaji related: "There are many proofs that it was Isaac, and the People of the Book in general hold this view, and nothing has been transmitted in hadith to oppose it. Perhaps it happened twice: once in Syria, to Isaac, and once in Mecca, to Isma'il, peace be upon them both." My suspension of judgment is better than this statement. What I incline to is that it was Isma'il, peace be upon him, on the basis of the apparent meaning of the verse, which requires it, and because it is what is related from many of the imams of the Ahl al-Bayt. I have not found certain authentic a raised (marfu') hadith that requires the opposite. The condition of the People of the Book is not hidden from people of understanding.

* * *

[p. 137]

(The third discussion): It has been used as evidence from the story for the permissibility of abrogation before the act is performed. This is the position of many of the jurists of legal theory (*usuliyyun*, scholars of the foundations of jurisprudence), and the Mu'tazilah and al-Sayrafi disagreed with it. The line of argument, as stated by some eminent scholars, is that Abraham, peace be upon him, was commanded to slaughter his son, as shown by the words ﴿افْعَلْ ما تُؤْمَرُ﴾ ("Do what you are commanded"), and because he, peace be upon him, proceeded to the slaughter and the terrifying of the child. Had he not been commanded to do it, that would have been forbidden by the Law and by custom. And it was abrogated before the act was performed, because he did not do it. Had he left off the act while the time had arrived, he would have been disobedient.

It was objected to this: We do not accept that if he had not acted while the time had arrived he would have been disobedient, because the time may be extended (*muwassa'*), so that the capacity is attained, and he would not be disobedient by delaying, and then it is abrogated. It was answered: First, if it were extended, the obligation would be attached to the future, because the command remains upon it with certainty; so when it is abrogated, the attachment of the obligation to the future is abrogated, and that is what they hold prevents abrogation. For they say: When the obligation is attached to the future while the command remains on it, it is impossible to remove that attachment by a prohibition against it, otherwise the command and the prohibition would both be directed at one thing, which is impossible. So when they permit abrogation in an obligatory act whose time is extended, before its performance, even though the obligation in it is attached to the future and the command remains upon it, they have acknowledged the permissibility of what they had forbidden, and that is what is sought. Second, if it were extended, he would have postponed the act and would not have proceeded to the slaughter and the terrifying of the child, as is customary, either hoping that it would be abrogated from him, or hoping that he would die, so that it would lapse from him because of the gravity of the matter, and such things are usually postponed. This was answered: The custom of the prophets, peace be upon them, is to hasten to comply with God the Exalted's command, contrary to the custom of most people, and extraordinary habits are not improbable from them, and Abraham is among the most exalted of them in rank. Even granting that custom, even with respect to the prophets, requires delay, how is it known that he, peace be upon him, did not delay until the end of the time in accordance with custom? So the reliance is upon the first answer, and by it the argument is complete. They have also repelled it with other considerations, among them: that he was not commanded with anything, but merely imagined it through the showing of a dream; and if that is granted, he was not commanded to slaughter, but only to its preliminaries: bringing out the boy, taking the knife, and laying him down on his brow. This was answered: This is nothing, because of what has passed in the words ﴿افْعَلْ ما تُؤْمَرُ﴾, and his proceeding to the slaughter and the forbidden terrifying, were it not for the command. How so? And the verse indicates the opposite: God the Exalted said: ﴿إنَّ هَذا لَهو البَلاءُ المُبِينُ﴾ ("Indeed, this is a clear trial"), and He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿وفَدَيْناهُ بِذِبْحٍ عَظِيمٍ﴾ ("And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice"). Were it not for the command, it would not have been a clear trial, nor would the ransom have been needed. That the ransom was because of his supposition that he was commanded to slaughter is a matter whose state is not hidden. According to the principle of the Mu'tazilah, it would involve implicating Abraham, peace be upon him, in ignorance of something that appears to be a command but is not a command, and that is not permissible. And whoever does not permit a corrupt assumption about the prophets, peace be upon them, for him this is, in his view, less than nothing. Another is that we do not accept that he did not slaughter; rather it is related that he did slaughter, and that whenever he cut something it joined together immediately after the cut, and that a plate of copper or iron was created that prevented the slaughter. This was answered: This is not to be heeded, because first, it is contrary to custom and to what is apparent, and it has not been transmitted in a reliable manner. It was answered: The report is a basis for the prevention, and weakness does not contradict it, and possibility is sufficient in the context, and there is no doubt about its permissibility, like the sending down of the ram from Paradise. Second, if he had slaughtered, the ransom would not have been needed. That it was because the killing had not taken place is not a valid point. And if the slaughter with the plate were prevented despite the command to it, that would be an obligation to the impossible, and they do not permit that. Then it has been abrogated from him; otherwise he would have sinned by leaving it, and so it would be abrogation before the possibility of performance, which is in our favor, not against us.

Among the eminent Hanafi scholars, some have said: What we are discussing is not abrogation, because it is the lifting of a ruling without a replacement; but here there is a replacement standing in its place, like the expiation (*fidyah*) for fasting in the case of the aged person who is unable to fast. Thus it is known that the ruling of the commanded act was not lifted. In the *Talwih* it is said: If it is said: Grant that the substitute stood in the place of the original, yet it entailed the prohibition of the original, that is, the slaughter of him, and the prohibition of a thing after its obligation is abrogation without doubt, since its ruling is lifted. It is answered: We do not accept that it is abrogation, and it would only follow if it were a legal ruling, and it is [p. 138] prohibited, for the prohibition against slaughtering the son is established in the original; it was removed by the obligation, then returned by the standing of the sheep in place of the son. So it is not a legal ruling, such that its establishment would be abrogation of the obligation. End of quote. It was objected: This is based on what has been established, that the lifting of original permissibility is not abrogation. But if it is abrogation, as some Hanafis have committed to (since there is no permissibility or prohibition except by a legal source, as they have established), then the lifting of original prohibition would be abrogation; and if its lifting is abrogation too, the aforementioned objection remains without answer, as established in the commentary on the *Sharh al-Tahrir*. This is enough, and the full discussion of the arguments of both sides is detailed in the principles of jurisprudence; and this amount is sufficient for the purpose of the exegete.

(The third discussion): Abu Hanifa used the story as evidence that if someone vows to slaughter his son, then he must give a sheep. Muhammad (al-Shaybani) agreed with him in this, and al-Qurtubi, the imam, related it from Malik. In *Tanwir al-Absar* and its commentary *al-Durr al-Mukhtar*: "If he vowed to slaughter his son, he must give a sheep, on account of the story of the Friend (Khalil, Abraham), peace be upon him." Abu Yusuf dropped this, and al-Shafi'i held it to be like a vow to kill him. al-Jassas related that a vow to kill is like a vow to slaughter. It was objected to the Imam (Abu Hanifa): that this is a vow of disobedience, and it has come: "There is no vow in disobedience to God the Exalted." He himself said: In the law of Abraham, peace be upon him, that refers to the slaughter of a sheep, and its abrogation has not been established, so it is not disobedience. Some Shafi'is said: There is nothing in the glorious text which indicates that it was a vow made by Abraham, peace be upon him, such that one could use it as evidence. It was answered: It is related in the transmitted tafsir that he vowed that, and that is in the status of an explicit text; and for this reason it was said to him when the son reached the age of striving with him: "Fulfill your vow." And because when the sheep was substituted for what God the Exalted had obligated upon him, it is known that its substitution for what he obligated upon himself is more fitting, so it is established by the indication of the text. The truth is that the basis of al-Shafi'i and Abu Yusuf, may God have mercy on them both, is more apparent and stronger than the basis of the great Imam, may God the Exalted be pleased with him, in this issue. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verses 114–116:

﴿And We certainly bestowed favour upon Moses and Aaron.﴾ We bestowed upon them both prophethood and other benefits, both religious and worldly. ﴿And We delivered them and their people from the great distress.﴾ This and what follows is of the type of mentioning the specific after the general (ʿatf al-khāṣṣ ʿalā al-ʿāmm). The great distress is the domination of Pharaoh and those with him from the Copts; it was also said to be drowning, but that is not correct. ﴿And We helped them﴾: the pronoun refers to both of them together with the people; it was also said that it refers to both of them alone, and it was expressed with a plural pronoun to magnify them both. ﴿So they were the victorious﴾ over Pharaoh and his people by means of that. The word "hum" (they) may be a separating pronoun (faṣl), an emphatic (tawkīd), or an appositive (badal). Although the deliverance (tanjiyah), in terms of existence, coincides with the victory mentioned, yet, since in terms of meaning it is an expression for rescue from what is disliked, it was begun with; then with the victory, whose meaning is realized by the mere deliverance of the one who is helped from his enemy without dominating him; then with the overcoming, so that the station of bestowing favour is given its due by showing that each of these three levels is a magnificent blessing in its own right.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verses 117–123:

﴿And We gave them the Book that makes things clear﴾, meaning the one that is eloquent in clarification and detail, as the added emphasis of its form suggests. This is the Torah. ﴿And We guided them to the straight path﴾, which leads to the truth and what is right, through the details of the laws and the branches of the rulings it contains. ﴿And We left for them among later generations﴾ ﴿Peace be upon Moses and Aaron﴾ ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers﴾ ﴿Indeed, they were among Our believing servants﴾. The discussion of this is similar to what preceded in its counterpart. ﴿And indeed Elias was among the messengers﴾. Al-Tabari said: he is Elias son of Yasin, son of Finhas, son of al-Ayzar, son of Harun, brother of Musa, peace be upon them both. So he is an Israelite from the tribe of Harun. Al-Qutaybi related that he was from the tribe of Yusha. Page 139. Al-Tabarsi related that he was a cousin of al-Yasa', and that he was sent after Hizqil. In al-Kirmani's *al-Aja'ib* it is stated that he is Dhu al-Kifl. From Wahb: he was given a long life as al-Khidr was, and he will remain until the end of the world.

Ibn Asakir narrated from al-Hasan that he is entrusted with the deserts, while al-Khidr is entrusted with the seas and islands, and that they meet each year at the season. As for the report of his meeting with the Prophet ﷺ on some journey, and his eating with him from a table that descended upon them both from the sky, peace and blessings be upon them both, consisting of bread, fish and celery, and their praying the afternoon prayer together, it was narrated by al-Hakim from Anas, who said: this is a hadith with a sound chain. All of this belongs to the matter of extended lifespan, and what follows it is not to be relied upon. The hadith of al-Hakim was declared weak by al-Bayhaqi. al-Dhahabi said: it is fabricated; may God Most High disfigure whoever fabricated it. Then he said: I would not have thought, nor do I allow, that ignorance would drive al-Hakim to declare this sound.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Asakir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that Elias is Idris. It is also reported from him that he recited: ﴿And indeed Idris was among the messengers﴾. The widely transmitted reading from him is like that of the majority. Indeed, Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, al-Minhal ibn Amr and al-Hakam ibn Utayba al-Kufi recited in the same way.

It has been read as ﴿Idras﴾, which is a dialect form of Idris, like Ibrahim pronounced as Ibrahaam. If Elias is explained as Idris, on the basis that one of the two names is a proper name and the other a title, then if the intended persons are those whose lineage you have heard, there is no harm in it. But if the intended one is the well-known Idris whom God Most High raised to a lofty station, who, as some have said, is Ukhnukh son of Yazd son of Mahlayil son of Anush son of Qaynan son of Shith son of Adam, and who, as the historians mention, lived before Nuh, then in al-Mustadrak it is narrated from Ibn Abbas that between him and Nuh there were a thousand years, and from Wahb that he was the grandfather of Nuh. The matter becomes problematic in God Most High's words: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave to Ibrahim against his people. We raise in degrees whom We will. Indeed your Lord is Wise and Knowing﴾ ﴿And We gave him Ishaq and Ya'qub, each of whom We guided; and Nuh We guided before, and among his descendants Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, Yusuf, Musa and Harun. Thus do We reward the good-doers﴾ ﴿And Zakariyya, Yahya, Isa and Elias, each of them among the righteous﴾ ﴿And Isma'il, al-Yasa', Yunus and Lut, and each of them We preferred over the worlds﴾. This is because the pronoun in "his descendants" either refers to Ibrahim, since the discussion concerns him, or refers to Nuh, since he is nearer. Also, Yunus and Lut are not among the descendants of Ibrahim. Under either assumption, it is not possible to place Elias, meaning Idris who comes before Nuh as you have heard, within the list of descendants. Applying the view of identity absolutely also conflicts with the apparent meaning, so do not be heedless.

Ikrima, al-Hasan according to one of two reports from him, al-A'raj, Abu Raja, Ibn Amir and Ibn Muhaysin recited ﴿Wa-inna al-Yas﴾ with a connected hamza. This allows that they connected a hamza of cutting, or that his name is Yasa', with the definite article attached to it, as was said regarding al-Yasa'. It is also found in the letter of Ubayy and in his codex: ﴿Anna Iliyas﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, followed by a yā' that is also sakin, then a lam with a kasra, followed by a yā' that is also sakin, and an unpointed sīn with a fatha.

Then it was named by what became known through the form of compounding (al-tarkib al-mazji, the compounding of two words into one name), and "idh" (when) according to a group is an object of an omitted verb, meaning: remember the time of his saying to his people: ﴿Will you not be wary (of God)?﴾, (i.e., of the punishment of God Most High and His vengeance) by complying with His commands and avoiding His prohibitions.

[p. 140]

﴿Do you call upon Ba'l﴾, that is, do you worship him, or do you seek your needs from him? Ba'l is the name of an idol for them, as al-Dahhak, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said. In some copies of the al-Qamus (a classical Arabic lexicon), it is stated that he belonged to the people of Yunus (Jonah). There is no barrier to his belonging to both, or that is a distortion. It was said: he was made of gold, twenty cubits in length, and had four faces. They were tempted by him and exalted him until [p. 140] they assigned to him four hundred attendants (sadan, the keepers of the idol), and they made them his prophets. The Devil would enter into his belly and speak the law of error, and the attendants would memorise it and teach it to the people. It was also said: Ba'l is the name of a woman who came to them with an error, and they followed her. As support for this, some of them read (Ba'la') with a long vowel on the pattern of (Hamra'). The apparent reading of its being declined (ṣarf) shows that it is Arabic on both views, so do not overlook this.

Ikrimah and Qatadah said: al-ba'l means "the lord" in the dialect of Yemen. In another narration from Qatadah, in the dialect of the Azd Shanu'ah and the Astam of Ibn Abbas: "the she-camel of a man from Himyar." He was asked, "Are you its owner?" He said, "Its ba'l (master)." Ibn Abbas then said, "Do you call upon Ba'l?" meaning: "Do you call upon a lord, of whom you are?" He said, "From Himyar." The intended meaning according to this is: "Do you call upon some of the ba'ls," that is, the lords, and by them are meant the idols or the false objects of worship. Thus the indefiniteness (tankir) is for partiality (tab'id), and it returns to what was said before it.

﴿And you forsake the best of creators﴾, that is, and you abandon His worship, exalted is He, or you abandon seeking all your needs from Him, mighty and majestic is He, on the basis that the speech contains an elided mudaf (an omitted genitive term). It was also said: the intended meaning of their abandoning Him, glorified is He, is their abandoning His worship, mighty and majestic is He. The intended meaning of "creator" is whoever may be so described, and in this sense the word is singular, even though the mode of application differs in it. There is then no difficulty in the construction of the comparative (af'al) with what follows it.

Here there is a well-known question: what is the reason for shifting from (tada'ūna) with a fatha on the ta and the dal, the present tense of (wada'a), meaning "to leave," to "tadharūna" (you forsake), despite its relation and paronomastic affinity with the (tad'ūna) before it, rather than (tadharūna)? Several answers have been given:

First: in this there is a kind of artificiality, and artificial paronomasia (al-jinas al-mutakallaf) is not praised by the eloquent. They do not praise what does not come effortlessly by way of natural suggestion, and therefore they censured its artificial practitioner, saying:

"The nature of the one who makes paronomasia contains a kind of compulsion; do you not see how he assembles the letters?"

This was said by al-Khafaji. Whether this verse applies specifically to the artificial is open to doubt, and its remoteness has its own problems.

Second: in (tad'ūna) there is confusion for one who reads from the codex without memorisation, from among the common people, who may read it like the first (tad'ūna) and suppose that the intended meaning is a denial that makes a distinction between calling upon Ba'l and calling upon the best of creators. This is not the right view, since it is not the custom of writers to avoid what confuses the common people, as is not hidden from the elite.

Also, the Companions did not take them into account; otherwise they would not have written the codex without dots and without vowel marks, as is known today. The persistence of the Uthmanic script as an authority until the end of the Companions' era supports what we have said.

Third: paronomasia is an embellishment, and it is used only in a context of approval and kindness, not in a context of anger and terror. The reply to this is that it has occurred in what it denies. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And on the day the Hour is established, the criminals will swear that they tarried but an hour﴾, and He, glorified is He, says: ﴿Its lightning nearly takes away the sight﴾ and ﴿God alternates the night and the day; indeed in that is a lesson for those who have sight﴾. In both there is perfect paronomasia (al-jinas al-tamm), and the state of the context is not hidden.

Fourth: what is reported from the Imam (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi): he was asked about the reason for the shift from (tad'ūna) to "tadharūna," and he said: it was changed because they took idols as gods and abandoned God, exalted is He, after they knew that God, glorified is He, is their Lord and the Lord of their earliest forefathers, out of arrogance and denial. For this reason it was said "tadharūna" and not "tad'ūna." In this view there is the claim that (da') is an imperative of abandonment before knowledge, and (dhar) is an imperative of abandonment after it, but language and derivation do not support this.

Fifth: the denial of each of the two acts, calling upon Ba'l and abandoning the best of creators, has a cause different from the cause of denying the other. Therefore the paronomasia was dropped as a signal of the strong contrast between the two acts.

Sixth: since there was no affinity between the two objects in any respect, the paronomasia was dropped in the two verbs governed by them, even though the negated affinity between the objects is one thing and the affinity we are concerned with between the verbs is another. Both answers, as you see, are not convincing.

Seventh: the Arabs used (wada'a) for abandonment whose doer is not blamed, because it derives from (da'ah), meaning "ease" or "rest." (Dhar) is the opposite, because it implies humiliation and disregard, since it derives from (wadhar), a small piece of meat that is not esteemed. It has been objected that what is evident from his statement "the opposite" is that the Arabs used (dhar) for abandonment whose doer is blamed. This is refuted by God's words, ﴿So leave them and what they fabricate﴾ and His words, ﴿And leave what remains of usury﴾, and others. This needs reflection.

Eighth: (wada'a) is more specific than (dhar), since it means leaving a thing together with care for it, as is evident from the derivation, as in (īdā'), the depositing of a trust, which is leaving the deposit while caring for its condition, and that is why one who is trustworthy is chosen for it. Similar is the farewell of loved ones (muwādaʿat al-aḥbāb). As for (dhar), its meaning is leaving in general, or leaving with aversion and total rejection. Al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) said: one says "So-and-so dhara the thing," meaning he casts it away because of its low esteem, and from this comes al-wadhar, which is what you have just heard. There is no doubt that the context suits this meaning and not the first, since the intended purpose is to condemn their condition in turning away from their Lord. This is close to the previous answer, but it is free of some of its problems.

Ninth: in (tad'ūna), with a fatha on the ta and the dal, there is a heaviness that is not hidden from one with a sound taste and a straight disposition, while (tadharūna) is free of it. For this reason it was chosen over it. So reflect. God, exalted is He, knows best.

He, glorified and exalted is He, has indicated by His words ﴿the best of creators﴾ the factor that requires the denial, which is expressed by the interrogative hamza, and He stated it explicitly for the sake of emphasising its matter in His words, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 126:

﴿Allah, your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old﴾ is read in the accusative (naṣb) as a substitution (badal) from ﴿the best of creators﴾. Abu Hayyan said: It is also permissible for that to be an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan), if we say that the annexation (iḍafa) of the superlative (af'al al-tafḍil) is genuine (maḥḍa). Several of the Seven Readers read it in the nominative (raf'), with the noble Name (al-ism al-jalil) as the subject (mubtada'), and (﴿your Lord﴾) as its predicate (khabar); or it is the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada' maḥdhuf), and (﴿your Lord﴾) is an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan) or a substitution (badal) from it. It is narrated from Hamza that when the verse is continued (wuṣil) he read it in the accusative, and when he paused (wuqif) he read it in the nominative. The mention of His lordship (rububiyya) over their forefathers of old serves to emphasize the denial of their abandoning Him, the Exalted, and to indicate the invalidity of the opinions of their forefathers as well.

﴿So they denied him﴾ concerning what his speech contained of God Most High's obligation of monotheism (tawhid), His prohibition of associating partners with Him (shirk), and His punishment for it. It is also permitted that their denial refers to what his statement contained: "God is your Lord." ﴿Indeed they, because of that, will be brought forth﴾, meaning into punishment. He stated it absolutely because of the indicator (qarinah), or because bringing forth (ihdar) in general usage is specific to evil, or because when it is used in the Qur'an it implies compulsion (jabr). ﴿Except the sincere servants of God﴾ is a continuous exception (istithna' muttasil, an exception connected to what precedes it) from the waw in "they denied him." It indicates that among his people there were sincere ones who did not deny him. It has been prohibited that it be a continuous exception from the pronoun in "brought forth," because that pronoun refers to the deniers. If it were excepted from that pronoun, it would imply that they denied him but were not brought forth, and its corruption is evident. It has been said: because if it is not excepted from the pronoun in "they denied," they would all have been deniers, so there would be no sincere one among them, let alone sincere ones. Its outcome is what has been mentioned. However, Ibn Kamal objected to this, saying that there is no corruption in it, because their exception from the people who are brought forth is due to their not denying him, as indicated by the description "the sincere," not from the deniers, so the meaning of the outcome is one.

It is refuted that the pronoun in "brought forth" refers to the people, like the pronoun in "they denied." Al-Khafaji said: It is not hidden that the restriction of bringing forth to punishment, as explicitly stated by more than one scholar, determines that the pronoun in "brought forth" refers to the deniers, not to the people in general. If this is not accepted, then it is another matter. In al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's al-Bahr al-Muhit): It does not fit that it be a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati', an exception not connected to what precedes it), since the meaning would become: "But the sincere servants of God from other than his people are not brought forth into punishment." And in this there is a discussion.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verses 129–132:

﴿And We left for him among later generations﴾ ﴿Peace be upon Ilyasin﴾ ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾ ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants﴾. The discussion regarding it is like that regarding its counterpart, except that it is said here: Ilyasin is a dialectal form of Ilyas (Ilyas), and they often alter non-Arabic names. In al-Kashshaf: perhaps the addition of the yā' and the nūn has a meaning in the Syriac language, and of this type are Sinā' and Sinīn; and he chose this language here out of regard for the fawāṣil (verse-endings). It was also said: it is the plural of Ilyas, by way of taghlīb (predominance), applying it to him and his people and followers, like al-Muhallabiyyun for al-Muhallab and his people.

This was held to be weak, based on what the grammarians mention: that a proper noun, when made plural or dual, must be made definite with the lām, as compensation for what it has lost of its proper-nounness. There is no difference in this between a case where there is taghlīb and other cases, as Ibn al-Hajib explicitly stated in his commentary on al-Mufassal. However, this is not agreed upon. Ibn Ya'ish said
Page 142
in his commentary on al-Mufassal: it is permissible to use it as an indefinite after the dual and plural, such as: Zaydani karimani, and Zaydun karimun. This is the preference of Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir, and they have elaborated on this at length in the detailed works of grammar. Moreover, this discussion arises only with one who does not take the lām of Ilyas as definite article; as for one who takes it so, the discussion does not arise with him. It was also said: it is the plural of Ilyasi, with the ya' of relation, and it was lightened because the yā's gathered in the genitive and accusative cases, as it was said: a'jamin for a'jamiyyin and ash'arin for ash'ariyyin. The intended meaning of "al-Yasin" is the people of Ilyas who are sincere, for they are the most worthy of being attributed to him. This was held to be weak because of the rarity of this, and its confusion with Ilyas when pluralized; and even if it is said that deleting the lām of Ilyas removes the confusion, it is also not suitable to the context and the preceding context, since the family of none of the prophets is mentioned.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Ya'qub, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read "Ala Ali Yasin" with the idafa (construct). It was written separately in the 'Uthmanic codex, so there is a kind of support for this reading. It departs from the view that Yasin is the name of the father of Ilyas, and the "family" is taken to refer to Ilyas. In referring to him in this way there is exaltation of him, as in "the family of Ibrahim" referring to our Prophet ﷺ. It is also permissible that the "family" is superfluous, with Yasin being Ilyas himself.

It was also said: Yasin in it is a name of Muhammad ﷺ, so "Ali Yasin" are his family, upon him be blessings and peace.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said regarding "Peace be upon the family of Yasin": "We are the family of Muhammad, the family of Yasin."

This is clear in making Yasin a name for him ﷺ. It was also said: it is the name of the well-known surah; and it was said: it is a name of the Qur'an, so "Ali Yasin" is this Muhammadan community or its elite. It was also said: it is a name for books other than the Qur'an. You should know that context and the preceding context reject most of these sayings.

Abu Raja' and al-Hasan read "Ala al-Yasin" with the hamza of wasl; its explanation is known from what has passed. Ibn Mas'ud, and those who read with him in the earlier passage concerning Idris, read "Salamun ala Adrasin"; and it is narrated from Qatadah "wa-inna Idris", and he read "Ala Idrisin"; and Ubayy read "Ala Ilyasin", just as he read: "wa-inna Iblisa lamina al-mursalin".

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said regarding "Peace be upon the family of Yasin": "We are the family of Muhammad, the family of Yasin."

This is clear in making Yasin a name for him ﷺ. It was also said: it is the name of the well-known surah; and it was said: it is a name of the Qur'an, so "Ali Yasin" is this Muhammadan community or its elite. It was also said: it is a name for books other than the Qur'an. You should know that context and the preceding context reject most of these sayings.

Abu Raja' and al-Hasan read "Ala al-Yasin" with the hamza of wasl; its explanation is known from what has passed. Ibn Mas'ud, and those who read with him in the earlier passage concerning Idris, read "Salamun ala Adrasin"; and it is narrated from Qatadah "wa-inna Idris", and he read "Ala Idrisin"; and Ubayy read "Ala Ilyasin", just as he read: "wa-inna Iblisa lamina al-mursalin".

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 133–138:

﴿And indeed, Lot was among the messengers.﴾ ﴿When We saved him and his family, all of them,﴾ ﴿except an old woman among those who remained behind.﴾ ﴿Then We destroyed the others.﴾ Its explanation has preceded in Surat ash-Shu'ara'. ﴿And indeed, you﴾ O people of Makkah ﴿pass by them﴾ at their dwellings, on your trading journeys to al-Sham, for Sodom lies on your route ﴿in the morning﴾ entering the morning ﴿and at night.﴾ It has been said: meaning also in the evening, by taking "the night" to mean its beginning, since that is the time of travel, and because it is placed opposite "the morning." It has also been said: meaning by day and by night. This is an interpretation given before any need for it, and so the first was preferred. The reason for restricting it to this is that Sodom perhaps lay near a station that the one departing passes in the morning and the one heading there passes in the evening. Some eminent scholars said: if it is kept on its apparent meaning, because the lands of the Arabs, due to their heat, are travelled through at night until morning, it is free of the artificiality of forcing the antithesis. ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ Do you witness that and yet not reason, so that you take heed from it and fear that there will befall you the like of what befell them? For the source of that was their opposing their messenger, and opposing a messenger is a common ground between you all.
