Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 139:

﴿And indeed, Yunus was among the messengers.﴾ It is related, according to what is in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit of Abu Hayyan), that he (peace be upon him) was made a prophet when he was twenty-eight years old. It is also reported in al-Bahr that he lived in the time of the Tawaif kings (muluk al-tawa'if) of the Persians. He was the son of Matta, with a fatha on the mim and a shadda on the taa' (with a dot above), and it is a maqsur (a name ending in an alif that does not change its form). Was this the name of his mother or of his father? There is a difference of opinion about this. It was said that it is the name of his mother, and this is what is mentioned in the tafsir of Abd al-Razzaq. It was also said:
Page 143
that it is the name of his father, and this, as Ibn Hajar said, is the more sound view. Some of the People of the Book call him Yunan ibn Mai, and some call him Yunah ibn Imtayai. We have not found, in any of the reports, a confirmed connection of his lineage. His name has six dialectal forms among the Arabs, with the nun taking three vowels together with waw, ya', and hamza. The well-known reading is with a damma on the nun together with the waw. Abu Talhah ibn Musarrif read it with a kasra on the nun. It was said: he intended to make it an Arabic word derived from anisa (to be friendly/at ease), and that, as you see, is [unsound].

﴿Idh abaqa﴾ means "when he fled." Its basic sense is fleeing from one's master (*ibaq*). But since his fleeing from his people was without the permission of his Lord, which is the most fitting description of the state of the prophets, peace be upon them, the term was applied to him. This is either a *isti'arah* (metaphor) or a *majaz mursal* (loose metonymy, using the restricted for the unrestricted). The first is more eloquent. Some of the perfected scholars (*al-kummal*) said: *al-ibaq* is fleeing from one's master in such a way that the seeker cannot find him, that is, with this intention. Peace be upon him fled from his people without the permission of his Lord, glory be to Him, to a place where they sought him and did not find him. So *al-ibaq* was used metaphorically for his flight, based on this condition and not on the first condition. Yet even granting this condition as some lexicographers (*ahl al-lughah*) mentioned, there is no barrier to considering that condition as well, so denying its consideration carries no weight.

﴿ilā al-fulk al-mashḥūn﴾: "to the laden ship," meaning the filled one.

﴿Then he drew lots﴾, and he (peace be upon him) cast lots (qur'ah) with those in the ship. Those who hold that casting lots is lawful (mashru'iyyah al-qur'ah) cite this as evidence.

﴿And he was among the losers﴾: he became one of those defeated by the lot. Its root is al-mazlaq, a passive participle, meaning one who has been moved from the place of victory.

It is related that he promised his people the punishment and told them it would come upon them within three days. When the third day came, Yunus left before Allah the Exalted had given him permission. His people missed him, so they went out with the old and the young and the animals, and they separated every mother from her child. The punishment was about to descend upon them, so they cried out to Allah the Exalted, turned in repentance, and asked for its removal. Allah the Exalted accepted their plea and turned the punishment away from them. When Yunus did not see the punishment descend, he was ashamed to return to them, and he said: "I will never return to them as a liar." He went off in the direction he had taken, came to a ship, and boarded it. When it reached the deep water, it stopped and would not move. Its captain said: "Nothing is keeping it from moving except that there is among you a man bringing ill omen." So they cast lots to throw into the water whoever the lot fell upon. The lot fell upon Yunus. They cast again, and it fell upon him again. They cast a third time, and it fell upon him again. When he saw this, he threw himself into the water.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 142:**

﴿Then the fish swallowed him﴾, meaning it swallowed him, taking him in one gulp (min al-luqmah).

In a report narrated by Ahmad and others from Ibn Mas'ud, he came to a people in a ship. They carried him and recognised him. When he boarded it, the ship stopped moving while the other ships were sailing right and left. He said: "What is the matter with your ship?" They said: "We do not know." He said: "But I know. There is a slave in it who has run away from his Lord, and by Allah it will not sail until you throw him overboard." They said: "As for you, by Allah, O Prophet of Allah, we will not throw you overboard." He said to them: "Draw lots, and whoever is chosen must be thrown." They drew lots three times, and each time the lot fell on him. So he threw himself into the sea, and what Allah related took place.

The manner of their drawing lots over what was in the sea, according to Ibn Mas'ud, was that they took a lot (sahm) for each person on the condition that whoever's lot floated would be the one, and whoever's lot sank would not be him. Yunus's lot floated.

It is also reported that when he stood at the edge of the ship in order to throw himself into the sea, he saw a fish, whose name, according to what Ibn Abi Hatim and a group narrated from Qatadah, was Najm, its head raised out of the water about three cubits, watching him and lying in wait for him. He went to another side, and the fish moved to face him; he moved to another side and found it there again.

He continued like this until he had gone all the way around the ship. When he saw this, he knew that it was a command from Allah, so he cast himself down and the fish seized him before he reached the water. ﴿And he was blameworthy﴾, meaning he had entered into blame (dakhil fi al-malamah). The form af'ala here (as in ahrama, "he entered the sacred precinct [haram]") indicates entering into a state; or it means that he had done something deserving blame. Alternatively, the hamzah in it indicates becoming (as in aghadda al-ba'ir, "the camel developed a gland [ghuddah]"), so that the meaning is that when he did what deserved blame, he became one who is blamed. Or it means one who blamed himself (mulim nafsih), with the hamzah being transitive (as in aqdamtuhu, "I made him advance"), the object being omitted. What Ibn Abbas and Mujahid reported in explaining it as "the one who does evil and the sinner" is an explanation of the general sense. The good deeds of the righteous are the bad deeds of those brought near (to Allah).

It was read as ﴿malim﴾ with a fatha on its first letter, as an ism maf'ul (passive participle). Its regular form would be *malum* (مَلُومٌ), because it is derived from a root with waw (*lawm*), and one says lamtuhu, *alumuhu*, *lawman*. But it has come in the pattern *lim* (لِيمَ), just as they said *mashib* and *mad'iyy* in place of *mashub* and *mad'uw* (the passive forms) based on *shib* and *du'iya*. This is because when the waw was changed to ya' in the passive, it was treated as if it were original, and so the adjective was formed on that basis.

[p. 144]

﴿So had he not been of those who glorify﴾, meaning: of those who remember Allah, exalted is He, much, through glorification (tasbih), as has been said. The words of Qatada contain an indication that the sense of frequency is intended, and that it is derived, as al-Khafaji stated, from the phrasing "min al-musabbihin" (of those who glorify) rather than "musabbihan" (glorifying). This phrasing indicates that he was firmly established among them, ascribed to them, and counted among them, and such a status necessarily implies frequency. It has also been said that the word is from the form taf‘il (intensive form, "sabbaha"). This was rejected on the grounds that the meaning of sabbaha (to glorify) does not take that into account, since it means only saying "Subhan Allah" (Glory be to Allah). It may be said that the form implies the sense of permanence, from "al-musabbihin," because it indicates that glorification was a constant habit for them. The meaning of tasbih here is its literal sense, which is the aforementioned utterance or what is similar to it, and this was narrated from Ibn Jubayr.

According to some, this state occurred before the whale swallowed him, during the days of ease. Abu Hayyan favoured the view that it occurred in the belly of the whale, and that the glorification is what Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in His saying: ﴿Then he called out in the darknesses: "There is no god but You; glory be to You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers."﴾ Some interpreted it as remembrance in general, others as worship in the same manner, and a group of them, including Ibn Abbas, interpreted it as prayer. Indeed, it is narrated from him that he said: "Every instance of tasbih in the Qur'an means prayer (salah)." And you know that if the word in what has been mentioned is a legal technical meaning (haqiqah shar‘iyyah), and tasbih has no other legal technical meaning, then it does not need a contextual indicator (qarina). If it is a figurative usage (majaz), or if tasbih has another legal technical meaning, then a contextual indicator is needed. If one is found, then well and good; otherwise, the matter is not hidden from you.

Just as there is disagreement about the time of the tasbih in the earlier sense, there is disagreement about its time in the other meanings. Ahmad in al-Zuhd and others narrated from Ibn Jubayr, regarding the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿So had he not been of those who glorify﴾, that he said: "Of those who prayed before he entered the belly of the whale." Ahmad and others also narrated from al-Hasan regarding the verse that he said: "It was nothing but a prayer he initiated in the belly of the whale." This was mentioned to Qatada, who said: "No, he was only doing it in times of ease." Other than what has been mentioned was also narrated from al-Hasan.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Bayhaqi in Shu‘ab al-Iman, and al-Hakim narrated from him that he said concerning the verse: "He used to pray much during times of ease. When he was in the belly of the whale, he thought it was death, so he moved his legs, and they moved. So he prostrated and said: 'O Lord, I have taken for You a place of worship in a location where no one has prostrated before.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from al-Dahhak ibn Qays that he said: "Remember Allah, exalted is He, in times of ease, and He will remember you in times of hardship. Indeed, Yunus (peace be upon him) was a righteous servant, mindful of Allah, exalted is He. When he fell into the belly of the whale, Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So had he not been of those who glorify﴾, etc. And indeed, Fir‘awn (Pharaoh) was a rebellious servant, forgetful of the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He. When drowning overtook him he said: ﴿I believe that there is no god except He in whom the Children of Israel have believed, and I am of the Muslims﴾, and it was said to him: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before, and you were among the corrupters.﴾"

The more appropriate view is to interpret the time of his being of those who glorify as encompassing both the time of ease and the time he was in the belly of the whale. This is because his being characterized by it in both periods has a bearing on his release from the belly of the whale, which is understood from the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿So had he not been of those who glorify﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 144:

﴿He would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected.﴾ This is indicated by what is in a report (ḥadīth) narrated by ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh, "from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that when the whale swallowed him and plunged with him until it reached what it reached of the earth, he (peace be upon him) heard the glorification of the earth, and he called out in the darknesses: 'There is no god but You, glorified are You, indeed I have been of the wrongdoers.' Then the supplication ascended toward the Throne. The angels said: 'O our Lord, we hear a weak voice from a land of strangeness.' He, Glorified is He, said: 'And do you know what that is?' They said: 'No, O our Lord.' He said: 'That is My servant Yunus.' They said: 'The one for whom we have never ceased raising an accepted deed and an answered supplication?' He said: 'Yes.' They said: 'O our Lord, will You not show mercy to what he used to do in ease, and save him in the time of trial?' He said: 'Indeed.' Then Mighty and Majestic commanded the whale, and it spat him out."

Abu Hayyan favoured the view that the meaning of His words, Glorified is He, ﴿He would have remained in its belly﴾ etc., is that he would have remained alive in its belly until the Day of Resurrection, and I say this too. It was objected that this contradicts what is reported, that no living being of mankind or of animals on land and sea will remain alive at the first blast. It was answered, after granting that this is reported or indicated by it, that it is an exaggeration of the length of the period, and it is within the scope of "law" (a conditional), so the objection does not arise at all. Or, the intended "time of resurrection" includes the time of the blast, since it is among its preliminaries, so it is as though it were part of it. And from Qatadah: "The belly of the whale would have been a grave for him." Its apparent meaning is that what is intended is that he would have remained dead in its belly until the Day of Resurrection. There is no obstacle to the whale's body remaining as his body does, without the affliction of decay reaching it until that day. The pronoun in ﴿they are resurrected﴾ refers to something not mentioned, and this is evident,

[Page 145]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 145:

﴿So We cast him forth﴾ by causing the fish to throw him up from its mouth, so the attribution is metaphorical. According to the Qamus (the lexicon al-Qamus), *nabdh* (casting away) means that you throw a thing forward or backward, or it is general in meaning.

Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: *nabdh* is the throwing down of a thing and discarding it because of the little regard held for it. What is intended here is casting out and hurling. The qualifier that al-Raghib mentioned I do not favour, for although he (peace be upon him) absconded and left without the permission of his Master, and was afflicted by the discipline of the Exalted, the Lord, Exalted and Majestic is He, is merciful toward His prophets, and for Him, glorified is He, in every matter there is great regard for them. Thus he (peace be upon him) was held in regard at the time of the casting out, even though it was ﴿onto the barren shore﴾, that is, onto a place empty of anything that covers it, such as trees or plants.

It is related that the fish swam along with the ship, raising its head to breathe, while Yunus glorified God, until they reached the land, and it cast him out. It has been objected that the words of the Exalted, ﴿and he called out within the darknesses﴾, contradict this. It is answered that merely raising its head to breathe does not take it out of them. Furthermore, this (raising the head) was so that Yunus would not suffocate or have his breath confined by the normal course of things, not so that water would be prevented from entering the belly of the fish, so that it might be said that fish have no need of that. Nevertheless, we do not affirm the soundness of the report. It has also been related that he (the fish) carried him around all the seas, then cast him onto the bank of the Tigris near Nineveh, with the first *nun* pronounced with a kasra and the second with a damma, as in the al-Kashf, in the land of Mosul. The swallowing was also in the Tigris, as some have stated explicitly, though the People of the Book disagreed concerning this. God willing, their account of this story will be cited for you later, so that you may take note of what it contains.

It is apparent that the fish was also one of the fish of the Tigris, and we have seen in it very large fish indeed. It was said that it was one of the fish of the Nile. Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Wahb that he sat with Tawus and others of that era, and they discussed which of God's commands is swiftest. Some of them said: the saying of God, ﴿like the blink of an eye﴾. Some of them said: the throne when it was brought to Sulayman. Wahb said: the swiftest of God's commands is that Yunus was on the edge of the ship when God, glorified is He, inspired the Nun in the Nile of Egypt, and he did not fall from its edge before he was in its belly. There is no doubt that the power of God, Exalted and Majestic is He, is greater than that, but the doubt lies in the soundness of the report.

It is as if you are saying: there is no doubt that it is unsound. The duration of his stay (in the fish) has been disputed. Abdullah ibn Ahmad, in the Zawa'id al-Zuhd, and others, related from al-Sha'bi who said: the fish swallowed him in the forenoon and cast him out in the evening, and it seems he meant when the night grew dark. Abd ibn Humayd and others related from Qatadah who said: he remained in its belly three (days). In the books of the People of the Book it is three days and three nights. From Ata' and Ibn Jubayr: seven days. From al-Dahhak: twenty days. From Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jurayj, Abu Malik, al-Suddi, Muqatil ibn Sulayman, al-Kalbi and Ikrimah: forty days. In the al-Bahr there is what indicates that no report concerning the duration of his stay (peace be upon him) in the belly of the fish has been authenticated. [p. 146] ﴿while he was ailing﴾ from what had befallen him. Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi said: his body returned to be like the body of a child when it is born. From Ibn Jubayr: that he (peace be upon him) was cast out with no hair, no skin, and no nail. Perhaps that, by the course of custom, implies that his stay in the belly of the fish was of some considerable length.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 146:

﴿And We caused a tree of gourd (yaqtin) to grow over him.﴾ That is, We caused it to grow overhanging him, providing shade for him like a tent. So ﴿عَلَيْهِ﴾ (alayhi, "over him") is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to ﴿شَجَرَةً﴾ (shajaratan, "a tree"), and it was placed before it because the noun is indefinite (nakira). Yaqtin is of the pattern yaf'il, from qatana bi-l-makan, meaning "he stayed in the place" when he remained there. Al-Tabarsi added that it means a temporary stay, not a permanent residence. What is meant by it, according to what has been reported from al-Hasan, al-Sudda, Ibn 'Abbas in one narration, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayra, 'Amr ibn Maymun, Qatada, 'Ikrima, Ibn Jubayr, and Mujahid in one of the two narrations from them: it is the pumpkin (al-dubba'), which is the well-known gourd (al-qar'). The Prophet (ﷺ) used to love it. Allah caused it to grow overhanging him, because it combines qualities: the coolness of its shade and its smooth touch, the largeness of its leaves, and that flies do not settle on it, as it has been said. The peace be upon him, because of the delicacy of his skin from his remaining in the belly of the fish, was harmed by flies and by contact with anything rough, and the heat of the sun pained him, and he found pleasure in cool shade; so Allah, Exalted, showed him kindness in this way. It is also mentioned that the leaves of the gourd are the most beneficial thing for one whose skin has peeled off. It is well known that a shajar is that which stands on a stalk of wood, so interpreting the shajara here as a pumpkin poses a difficulty.

Abu Hayyan answered that it is possible that Allah, Exalted, caused it to grow on a stalk so as to shade him, as a breach of normal custom. Al-Kirmani said: the common usage restricts shajar to that which has a stalk, but among the Arabs, everything that has a root that persists is a shajar, and other things are najm. The saying of the most eloquent of the eloquent (ﷺ), "the tree of garlic (shajarat al-thum)," supports this. End of quotation.

Some of the eminent scholars said: You may say that the original meaning of the word is that which has a root (arumah), but it came to dominate in the usage of the people of the language to mean that which has a stalk and branches. So when it is used without qualification, the second meaning is immediately understood; and when it is qualified, as here, the original meaning returns, and this is the apparent sense. Then he mentioned that what Abu Hayyan said is a far-fetched contrivance in a matter where opinion has no room.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Jubayr that he said: every tree that has no stalk is of the yaqtin, and what grows on the surface of the earth, such as the watermelon and the cucumber. In another narration from him, he was asked about the yaqtin: is it the qar'? He said: No, but it is a tree that Allah, Exalted, named yaqtin, which shaded him.

In a narration from Ibn 'Abbas: it is everything that grows and then dies within its year. In another: everything that spreads over the surface of the earth.

It was said: the tree of yaqtin is the banana tree, which covered him with its leaves, shaded him with its branches, and he broke his fast on its fruit. It was said: the fig tree. The most correct is what has preceded.

It is reported from Qatada that he, peace be upon him, used to eat from that gourd. It came in a narration from Abu Hurayra that he said: he was cast out into the open, and Allah caused a yaqtina to grow over him. He was asked: what is the yaqtina? He said: the shajarat al-dubba'. Allah, Exalted, prepared for him a wild doe that eats from the herbs of the earth; it would come close to him and feed him with its milk every evening and morning, until it grew. It was also said that he used to take shade under the tree, and the doe would come to him, and he would drink from its milk. In some reports: it grew and shaded him on the same day.

Ahmad in al-Zuhd and others reported from Wahb: when he came out of the sea he slept a sleep, and Allah caused a tree of yaqtin to grow over him, which is the dubba'. It shaded him and reached its full growth in one day. He saw that it had shaded him and saw its greenness, and it pleased him. Then he slept another sleep, and when he awoke, behold, it had dried up, and he began to grieve over it. He was told: You who did not create it, did not water it, and did not cause it to grow, do you grieve over it? And I who created one hundred thousand people, or more, then had mercy on them, and that was hard for you; and these are the people of Nineveh, those meant by the saying of the Exalted:

Page 147

﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand, or they were more.﴾ The sending, according to what Ghayr Wahid transmitted from Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatadah, is the first sending, which was before the fish swallowed him. The conjunction is then with His Exalted saying ﴿And indeed Yunus﴾ etc., by way of explanation, because it indicates the beginning of the state and its end, and the aim of the sending, which is faith. Between the two, the story of him was interposed, out of concern for it because of its strangeness. It was objected to this that it refuses to take it as the first sending.

[Page 148]

The fa' in His saying, ﴿So they believed﴾, [poses a problem], since those people did not believe immediately after his first sending, but only after he had left them. It has been answered that this is a customary sequence (ta'qib 'urfi, "consequence in customary usage"), like the saying: "He married, and a child was born to him." It has also been said: the more likely view is that the fa' is for elaboration (al-tafsil, "explanation of detail"), or for causation (al-sababiyya, "indicating cause"). And it has been said: this is a second sending to them after what befell him had befallen him, so the conjunction is upon what is before it.

It has been objected that what is related is that after he had parted from them, they saw the punishment, or feared it, and so they believed. Thus the words of the Exalted, ﴿So they believed﴾, in this sublime discourse, refuse to take it as a second sending. It has been answered that the belief joined with the particle of sequence may be a particular kind of belief, or that "they believed" is to be understood as "they made their belief sincere and renewed it," because the first was the belief of [facing] calamity. It has also been said: it is a sending to others besides them. And it has been said: the first people, after they believed, asked him to return to them, but he refused, because a prophet who has emigrated from his people does not return to them to reside among them; and he said to them: "Indeed God, Exalted is He, will send to you a prophet."

In a long report transmitted by Ahmad in al-Zuhd (Kitab al-Zuhd), and by a group [of compilers], from Ibn Mas'ud, that he, peace be upon him, after he had been cast out onto the open ground, and God caused a tree to grow over him, and his condition improved, went out and found a boy tending sheep. He said: "Whose are you, boy?" He said: "From the people of Yunus (Jonah)." He said: "When you return to them, convey my greetings to them and inform them that you met Yunus." The boy said to him: "If you are Yunus, then you know that whoever lies and has no clear proof is killed. So who will testify for me?" He said: "This tree will testify for you, and this plot of earth." The boy said to Yunus: "Command them." So Yunus said to them: "When this boy comes to you, testify for him." They said: "Yes." So the boy returned to his people, and he had brothers, and he was secure among them. He went to the king and said: "I met Yunus, and he sends you his greetings." The king ordered that he be killed. He said: "I have a proof." So the king sent [men] with him, and they reached the tree and the plot of earth. The boy said to them: "I adjure you by God, did Yunus make you witnesses?" They said: "Yes." So the people returned in alarm, saying: "The tree and the earth testify for him!" They came to the king and told him what they had seen. The king took the boy's hand, seated him in his own place, and said: "You are more worthy of this position than I am." And that boy managed their affairs for forty years.

This, by its outward meaning, indicates that he, peace be upon him, did not return to them after what had befallen him. If it is sound, then the sending here is either the first sending which is contained in the saying of the Exalted, ﴿And indeed Yunus was among the messengers﴾, or another sending to other than those people. And what is known among the People of the Book is that he, peace be upon him, was sent only to the people of Nineveh (Ninawa). The detailed account of his story according to them will come, God willing, shortly.

[Regarding] "aw" (or): according to what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, it has the meaning of "bal" (rather). It has also been said that it has the meaning of "wa" (and), and Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with them both, recited it this way. It has also been said that it is for vagueness toward the addressee. Al-Mubarrad and many of the Basrian [grammarians] said it is for doubt, considering the viewer among mankind, in the sense that whoever saw them doubted their number and said: "A hundred thousand, or more." The purpose is to express their multitude, or that the excess is not excessively great, as one says: "They are a thousand and something." Ibn Kamal said: the meaning is that they increase in another respect, namely that the obligated ones among them in actuality were a hundred thousand, and when those approaching obligation (al-murahiqun, "adolescents nearing maturity") are added to them, they became more. And from here appears the reason for expressing it with the form of renewal (al-tajaddud) rather than permanence. It was objected that although the appropriate particle for this would be "wa," it is a weak contrivance; and closer to it is that the increase is according to the second sending, and the form of renewal suits it, even though it is for the rhyme (al-fasila, "rhyming pause"). And it is conjoined to the clause ﴿We sent him﴾, with their estimate being "they increase," not upon ﴿a hundred thousand﴾ with the estimate of "persons who increase," or [the word] is stripped for the verbal noun sense; but this is weak. And the increase beyond what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas is thirty thousand. In another report from him: "some thirty thousand." In another: "some forty thousand." And from Nawf and Ibn Jubayr: seventy thousand. And al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "I asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾, and he said: 'They increase by twenty thousand.'"

And if this report is sound, then all else is invalidated.

﴿So We gave them enjoyment﴾, in life, ﴿for a time﴾, until their appointed terms which were decreed in eternity. This was said by Qatada and al-Suddi. But some claimed that their enjoyment of life lasts until the time of al-Mahdi (the rightly guided one), and that when he appears among his helpers, they are alive today in the mountains and deserts, not seen by everyone, like al-Mahdi according to the Imamiyya (the Twelver Shi'a), and like al-Khidr according to some scholars and Sufis. Sometimes it is revealed to some people, so they see one of them. This is a false fabrication. Perhaps the reason this story was not concluded like the rest of the stories, with the saying of the Exalted, ﴿And We left upon him among the later [generations]﴾ "Peace..." etc., is to distinguish the matter of Lut and Yunus, peace be upon them both, from the matter of the possessors of great laws and the resolute messengers (Ulu al-'Azm), while confining them both to the comprehensive greeting of peace for all the messengers mentioned at the end of the surah; and because they are mentioned close to him in order. And God, Exalted is He, knows best.

What is mentioned in the matter of Yunus, peace be upon him, in the books of the People of the Book, is that God, Mighty and Majestic, commanded him to go to call the people of Nineveh. At that time it was exceedingly great, not crossed except in about three days. Their evil had grown great and their corruption had multiplied. So he considered the matter grave and fled to Tarsis (Tarshish). He came to Jaffa and found a ship whose people wished to go with it to Tarsis. He hired [passage], paid the fare, and boarded the ship. A great wind arose, the waves multiplied, and the ship was about to sink. The sailors panicked and threw some of the cargo into the sea to lighten the ship. At that point Yunus went down into the bottom of the ship and slept until his breathing became loud. The captain approached him and said: "Why are you sleeping? Arise, call upon your God; perhaps He will deliver us from what we are in, and not destroy us." Some of them said to others: "Come, let us cast lots, so that we may know whose sin has brought this evil upon us." So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Yunus. They said to him: "Tell us what you have done, where you came from, where you are going, what your country is, and what your tribe is?" He said to them: "I am a servant of the Lord, God of heaven, who made the dry land and the sea." He told them his story, and they feared a great fear. They said to him: "Why have you done what you did?" They blamed him for that. Then they said to him: "What shall we do with you now, so that the sea may be calm for us?" He said: "Throw me into the sea, and it will calm, for because of me this great wave has come." The men exerted themselves to bring the ship back to land, but they could not, so they took Yunus and threw him into the sea for the deliverance of all who were in the ship. The sea became calm. God, Exalted is He, commanded a great fish, which swallowed him. He remained in its belly three days and three nights, and he prayed in its belly to his Lord and cried out to Him. God, Glorified is He, commanded the fish, and it cast him onto dry land. Then God, Mighty and Majestic, said to him: "Arise, go to Nineveh, and proclaim among its people as I commanded you before." So he, peace be upon him, went and proclaimed, saying: "Nineveh will be overthrown after three days." The men of Nineveh believed in God, Exalted is He, and they proclaimed a fast, and they all put on sackcloth. The news reached the king, who rose from his throne, removed his robe, put on sackcloth, and sat on ashes. It was proclaimed: "Let no one among the people or the animals taste food or drink." They cried out to God, Exalted is He, and turned back from evil and injustice. So God had mercy on them and did not send down the punishment upon them. Then Yunus grieved and said: "My God, it was from this that I fled, for I knew that You are the Merciful, the Compassionate, the Patient, the Relenting. O Lord, take my soul, for death is better for me than life." He said: "O Yunus, are you grieved this greatly?" He said: "Yes, O Lord." Yunus went out and sat facing the city, and he made for himself a shelter there, and sat beneath it until he would see what would happen in the city.

[Page 149]

Then God, Exalted is He, appointed a gourd plant, which rose over his head to give him shade from his distress, and he rejoiced over the gourd with great joy. God, Exalted is He, commanded a worm, which struck the gourd so that it dried up. Then a scorching wind blew, and the sun shone upon the head of Yunus, peace be upon him, so the matter weighed heavily upon him, and he longed for death. The Lord said to him: "O Yunus, are you grieved greatly over the gourd?" He said: "Yes, O Lord, I am greatly grieved." He, Glorified is He, said: "You are grieved over it, though you did not labor over it and did not grow it; rather, it came up in a single night and perished in a single night. So shall I not have compassion on Nineveh, the great city, in which there are more than a hundred and twenty thousand persons who do not know their right hand from their left, and many animals?" Here ends [the report]. In it is much of what contradicts the truth. I have quoted it to you so that you may be acquainted with its condition, and how much falsehood there is in the People of the Book.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 149:

﴿So ask them: "Does your Lord have daughters while they have sons?"﴾ At the beginning of this noble surah, God commanded His Prophet ﷺ to rebuke the Quraysh (tabkit, rebuke) and to refute their doctrine of denying the resurrection (ba'th) by way of questioning (istifta'), and He presented the proofs that clearly establish that it will inevitably occur. He explained its occurrence and the various kinds of punishment they will face at that time. He excepted from them His sincere servants, and He described in detail the everlasting bliss prepared for them. Then He mentioned that most of the earlier peoples had gone astray before them, and that He had sent warners to them in general terms. Then He related the stories of some of the Prophets, peace be upon them, in some detail, each story containing what shows their excellence and their servitude to Him, mighty and majestic. Then He commanded His Prophet ﷺ here to rebuke them by way of questioning about the aspect of something that the intellects utterly reject, namely the false division that is necessary given the deviant belief they held. They used to say, like some tribes of the Arabs, Juhayna, Sulaym, Khuza'a and Banu Malih, "The angels are the daughters of God," exalted is He far above what they say.

Then He rebuked them for what their aforementioned disbelief implies of contempt for the angels, peace be upon them, by making them females. Then God nullified the root of their disbelief, which contains these two disbeliefs, namely the attribution of offspring to Him, exalted is He far above that. He did not include this in the series of rebuke because they share it with the Jews who say, "Uzayr is the son of God," and with the Christians who believe that Jesus is the son of God, exalted is God far above that.

It has been said that the particle (al-fa') is for arranging the command upon what is known from what preceded: that those messengers were the prominent figures of creation, peace be upon them, the servants of God. For this strengthens the rebuke and makes clear the falsehood of their corrupt doctrine. So it is as if it were said: "If the messengers of your Lord are those whose condition you know, then ask these disbelievers about the matter of the existence of daughters, who in their claim are the lowest of the two kinds for Him, and of sons, who are the highest of the two for them. For they cannot establish any aspect for that, since it is utterly false and no one who has the slightest amount of intellect would say it."

Some eminent scholars said: the discourse is connected to His saying, exalted is He, at the beginning of the surah: ﴿So ask them: are they stronger in creation?﴾ (37:11), with the (al-fa') here being a conjunction (lil-'atf) upon that, and the sequence (al-ta'qib) because He commanded both of them without interval. There, it is a consequent (jaza'iyya) in response to an assumed condition. I say with this view. Abu Hayyan raised an objection against it, that it involves a long separation (al-fasl al-tawil), and the grammarians have found the separation by a sentence, such as: "I ate meat, and I strike Zayd, and bread," to be objectionable. So what do you think of separation by sentences, indeed by what approaches a whole surah? It was answered that what was mentioned concerns the conjunction of single words, but as for sentences, because of their independence, that is tolerated in them. The discourse here is such that its meanings are interlaced and its structures are linked, and some of them hold onto the waistbands of others, so that all of it is as if it were one word. Distance is not counted as distance, as it has been said:

"The distance between our bodies does no harm, when what lies between the hearts is near."

The way in which the conjoined element is ordered after what precedes it is like the way in which the element it is conjoined to is ordered. For His being the Lord of the heavens and the earth, and those great creations, indicates, as it indicates His oneness and His power, mighty and majestic, that He is exempt from having offspring. Do you not see His saying, majestic is His glory: ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth, how could He have a child?﴾ (6:101). The connection between the refutation of those who deny the resurrection

[Page 150]

and the refutation of those who affirm offspring is evident. The questioner and the one questioned, and the command, are the same in both sentences. Some have permitted that the pronoun in (istaftihim, "ask them") refers to the messengers mentioned, peace be upon them, and the rest to the Quraysh, and that the intended questioning is of those who know their reports among those who are trusted, and from their books and scrolls, meaning that none of them fails to exalt God above such things, even Yunus, peace be upon him, in the belly of the fish. By my life, this man has reached the extreme of over-elaboration without any need for it. Perhaps, had he dispensed with committing the figure of speech (tajawwuz) by holding that the questioning is directed at the messengers mentioned, in which case the Messenger of God ﷺ would gather with them in a spiritual gathering, as Shaykh Muhyi al-Din, may his secret be sanctified, claims for himself with more than one of the Prophets, peace be upon them, and claims that the command to ask, which requires such a gathering, is also in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you: did We appoint gods to be worshipped besides the Most Merciful?﴾ (43:45), in this manner the matter would have been easier, though that is a Sufi tendency.

The Lord was attributed to His pronoun, peace and blessings be upon him, rather than to their pronoun, as an honour to His Prophet ﷺ, and as an indication that they, in their saying that He has daughters, are like those who deny His lordship over them, exalted is He,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 150:

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Or did We create the angels as females?﴾ is a turning away (idrab) and a transition (intiqal) from rebuke by the earlier question (istifta') to rebuke by this matter. That is, "Rather, did We create the angels, who are among the most noble of creatures, the most powerful of them, and the most exalted in their holiness above natural deficiencies, as females?" Femaleness is among the most base attributes of animals.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while they were witnesses﴾ is a mockery of them (istihza') and a charge of ignorance against them (tajhil), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾ For such matters are known only through direct witnessing (mushahada), since there is no way to know them through reason (aql) alone in the absence of transmitted report (naql), which is beyond doubt. Therefore the one who claims their femaleness must have been a witness at the time of their creation. The clause is either a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "We created," meaning: "Rather, did We create them as females, while they were present at that time?", or it is a conjunction (atf) upon "We created," meaning: "Rather, were they witnesses?"

Al-Alusi's commentary on Qur'an 37:151–152:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Behold, it is from their own lie that they say﴾ ﴿"God has begotten a son"﴾. The phrase is a resumptive statement (*istinaf*, a new independent clause) from Him, may He be exalted. It does not fall under the inquiry (*istifta'*, the question put to them in the preceding verse). It is brought to refute the root of their corrupt doctrine by showing that its foundation is nothing but a plain lie and a shameful fabrication, with no proof or even a doubtful argument behind it. ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾ in what they profess as religion in general, or in this particular claim. This contains an emphasis on His saying: ﴿from their own lie﴾.

It has also been read as "*Walad Allah*" (with *walad* in the nominative), with the genitive construction, and with *walad* in the nominative as the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*, the topic of the sentence). The meaning is: "They say: the angels are the sons of God." The word *walad* (وَلَد) is of the *fa'al* pattern in the sense of a passive participle (*maf'ul*, "that which is begotten"). It applies to the masculine and the feminine, the singular and the plural. For this reason it is used here as the predicate of the implied "the angels," which is understood from context.

The meaning is: "They say: the angels are the sons of God." The word *walad* (وَلَد) is of the *fa'al* pattern in the sense of a passive participle (*maf'ul*, "that which is begotten"). It applies to the masculine and the feminine, the singular and the plural. For this reason it is used here as the predicate of the implied "the angels," which is understood from context.

﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾ The first letter is a hamza with a fatha, which is the interrogative particle. The connective hamza (hamzat al-wasl) that follows it has been dropped, and the interrogative is used for denunciation (inkar). The purpose is to affirm their lie and to establish their falsehood. Al-istifa' (choosing) means taking the best part (safwa) of a thing for oneself.

Nafi', in the transmission of Isma'il, and Ibn Jammaz and a group, and Isma'il, from Abu Ja'far and Shayba, read "اِصْطَفى" with a kasra on the hamza. This is the connective hamza, which takes a kasra when the word is begun with it. It is construed as the interrogative particle having been omitted, with the sense of "am" (or) following. Although this "am" is disjunctive (munqati'a) and not equivalent (mu'adila) to it, the construction is accepted because it is commonly used with it. It is also permitted to keep the sentence as a declarative, either by supposing an implied verb of saying, meaning "they are indeed liars in their saying 'He has chosen...'", or "they say, 'He has chosen...'", as has been said, or as a substitution (badal) for their saying, "God has begotten," or "the angels are God's offspring." This is not an intrusion between two related elements. However, the better construction is the one with the particle omitted, and the matter is settled, so reflect on this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verses 154–157:

﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ With this judgment, whose falsity the primary intuitions of minds decide, and the turn (from third person to second person) is for increased rebuke.
Page 151
﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ By deleting one of the two taa's from (tatadhakkarun). And Talhah ibn Musarrif read (tadhkurun), with the dhal sukun and the kaf damma, from (dhakara).

The fa' is for conjunction with an assumed (omitted) element, meaning: you observe that, so you do not remember its falsehood, for it is inscribed in the intellect of every clever and dull person. ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ This is a turning away and a transition from rebuking and censuring them for what was mentioned, to imposing upon them something that does not enter existence at all. That is, rather, do you have a clear proof that came down from heaven that the angels are His daughters? This is necessary, since the judgment of that must have a sensory or rational basis, and since both are absent, there must be a transmitted basis. ﴿Then bring your Book﴾ which speaks to the truth of your claim, ﴿if you are truthful﴾ in it. The command is for incapacitation (taʿjiz), and the attribution of the Book to them is for mockery. In these verses there is an indication of great wrath and terrible denunciation of their sayings, severe rejection of their falsehoods, and the disparagement of their intellects and understanding, together with ridicule of them and wonder at their ignorance, which is not hidden from one who reflects upon them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 158:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ is a shift to the third person (iltifat ila al-ghaybah), to indicate that they have been cut off from replying, have fallen from the rank of being addressed, and that their condition calls for them to be turned away from and for their crimes to be related to others. It has been deduced (istuzhira) that by "the jinn" is meant the devils (al-shayatin), and by the "kinship" that was made is meant marriage by alliance (al-musaharah).

Adam ibn Abi Iyas, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Mujahid, who said: The disbelievers of Quraysh said: "The angels are the daughters of Allah, Exalted is He." Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said to them, meaning as a rebuke: "Then who are their mothers?" They said: "The daughters of the chieftains of the jinn." Ibn Abi Hatim narrated this from Atiyyah, or it is meant: "They made between Him, glorified be He, and between them a relationship (munasabah), in that they associated them with Him, Exalted is He, in the entitlement to worship." This was also narrated from al-Hasan. It has been said that a group of the zindiqs (heretics) say: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and Iblis, may the curse of Allah be upon him, are two brothers; Allah, Exalted is He, is the Good and Generous, and Iblis is the Evil and Base." This is what is meant by His saying, glorified be He: "And they made..." etc. Al-Tabarsi related this from al-Kalbi. Imam al-Razi said: "This view is, in my opinion, the closest of the sayings, and it is the doctrine of the Magians who speak of Yazdan and Ahriman, and they express these two by Light and Darkness. What makes this view unlikely in my opinion is that the apparent reference of the pronoun in 'they made' is to Quraysh, as with the preceding pronouns, and this was not known of them, nor of any tribe among the tribes of the Arabs; and the context is not one of refuting disbelievers in general."

Several narrators, including Mujahid, Abd ibn Humayd, from Ikrimah, and Ibn Abi Shaybah from Abu Salih, narrated that by "the jinn" is meant the angels. Al-Tabarsi in Majma' al-Bayan related it from Qatadah, and al-Jubba'i chose it. The "making" mentioned refers to what is contained in their saying: "The angels are the daughters of Allah," and it is repeated as a preparation for what follows. This is based on the view that the jinn and the angel are one genus created from one element, which is fire; but whoever is of its dense smoky part is a devil, and that is evil and rebellion, while whoever is of its pure light is an angel, and that is entirely good. The reason for the name "jinn" is concealment from our eyes; thus "jinn" and "jinnah" carry the meaning of the passive participle from janna-hu, meaning he concealed it. On this view, the restriction of the name "jinn" to one of its two kinds is an incidental restriction, like the restriction of the word "dabbah" (beast), and the original usage is what occurs here. It is reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that a type of angels, peace be upon them, is called the jinn, and Iblis is among them. The angels are called "jinnah" to belittle them, despite their great station in themselves, so that they would not reach the level of the kinship which they attributed to them in their saying. It may also be said that concealment was, as it were, the motive for them to that false claim, based on their supposition that it befits only females; so they said: "Had they not been His daughters, glorified and exalted be He, He would not have concealed them from the eyes." Therefore He referred to them as "the jinnah."

﴿And the jinnah have certainly known that they will be brought forth﴾, meaning: by Allah, the devils, that is their kind, have certainly known that Allah, Exalted is He, will surely bring them forth and punish them with the Fire; and had they been related to Him, or partners in the entitlement to worship or in governance, He, glorified be He, would not have punished them. So the pronoun in "innahum" refers to the jinnah on the views other than the last of the preceding views; but on that last view, it refers to the disbelievers, meaning: by Allah, the angels who attributed a kinship between Him and themselves, and said they were His daughters, have certainly known that the disbelievers will be brought forth to the Fire and punished in it, for their lying and fabrication in their saying that. The purpose of this is to emphasize the refutation, by showing that those to whom these people attribute that kinship know better than them the reality of the matter, and they deny it and judge that they will be punished on account of it with an emphatic judgment. On the first view, it is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the disbelievers, and the meaning is along the lines mentioned. The angels' knowledge that the disbelievers are punished is evident; and the devils' knowledge that they themselves, and likewise the rest of the disbelievers, are punished is because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, threatened Iblis, may the curse of Allah be upon him, with what indicates that.

Al-Alusi's commentary on Surah 37, verses 159–160:

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they describe﴾, is, in accordance with all the previously mentioned aspects, a declaration of His transcendence, on His own part, above the attribute that is not befitting to Him. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except the sincere servants of Allah﴾, is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', an exception that is not of the same category as what precedes it) from "those brought forward," and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraḍ). The meaning is: "But the sincere ones are saved." It has also been permitted that it be a connected exception (istithna' muttasil) from it, and the pronoun in "indeed they" would then be interpreted as referring to something more general, though this is contrary to the apparent meaning.

It has also been permitted that it be a disjunctive exception from the pronoun in "they describe," and that it be a connected exception from it, which is also contrary to the apparent meaning.

It has also been permitted that it be an exception from the pronoun in "they made" [i.e., "they made between Him and the jinn a kinship"], on the basis of disjunction only, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection. Al-Wahidi chose the first aspect. Al-Tayyibi said: "It is most excellent when al-jinnah is interpreted as the devils, and the pronoun in 'indeed they' refers to the disbelievers, so that its meaning returns to His exalted saying, related from the accursed one: ﴿I will surely mislead them all﴾ ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾. That is: indeed they will be brought to the Fire and punished, since they obeyed us in our misleading them. But those who sincerely devoted their obedience to Allah, the Exalted, and purified their hearts from the filth of polytheism, the impurities of disbelief and the vices, our scheme had no effect upon them, so they will not be brought forward. This would be a praise of the sincere ones, an allusion against the polytheists, a humbling of their pride, and an increase in their rage; that is, they are the opposite of what they are upon of foolish minds, ignorance of souls and feebleness of intellects." End of quotation. And in explaining the meaning there is a kind of deficiency.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verses 161–163:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So indeed you, and what you worship﴾ ﴿are not able to lead [anyone] astray from Him﴾ ﴿except him who is to burn in the Blazing Fire﴾. This is a return to their address. The fa' (the "so") is the response to an implied conditional clause, meaning: "if you know this," or "if the sincere ones are saved." ﴿So indeed you﴾ ... and so on. The waw is for coordination. ﴿and what you worship﴾ is coordinated with the pronoun in ﴿indeed you﴾. The pronoun in ( عَلَيْهِ ) ("upon Him") refers to God, Mighty and Majestic, and the prepositional phrase is attached to fatinin ("those who lead astray"). It takes ʿala ("upon") because it includes the sense of domination (istila'), and this is a metaphor drawn from their saying: "He led his slave or his wife astray against him" (fatana ghulamahu aw imra'atahu 'alayhi), meaning he corrupted him. The ba' is extra (za'idah), and the phrase is the predicate of ma, and the whole clause is the predicate of inna. The exception is a restrictive exception (istithna' mufarragh) from the implied object of fatinin. ( وَأَنْتُمْ ) ("you") is addressed to the disbelievers and their objects of worship, by way of tahghib (the masculine plural form predominating over the other party, i.e., the grammatical second person prevailing), like your saying: "You and Zayd will go out," meaning: you and your objects of worship will not lead anyone astray against God, Mighty and Majestic, by your misguidance, except him who was foreknown in God's knowledge, Exalted is He, to be among the people of the Fire, who will burn in it and enter it without fail.

It is also permitted that the waw here be like it in their saying: "Every man and his estate" (kullu rajulin wa diy'atuhu). Then the clause ﴿what you are upon﴾ etc. is an independent clause, not the predicate of inna. The pronoun in ( عَلَيْهِ ) refers to ma, with an implied noun (muḍaf) understood. It is also attached to fatinin, by implying the sense of sending or driving. There is no tahghib in the address. It is as if it were said: "Indeed you and your gods are companions, not ceasing to worship them." Then it was said: "You are not those who will send [anyone] to the worship of what you worship, or drive [anyone] onto the path of temptation and misguidance, except him who was foreknown in His knowledge, Exalted is He, to be among the people of the Fire." The apparent practice of some of them is that the matter of tahghib in ﴿you﴾ remains as it is according to this view. You know that the apparent reading is the connection. It is also permitted that the meaning intended be accompaniment (ma'iyyah). The predicate of inna is the clause ﴿what you are upon﴾, etc., and the speech is in the style of the saying of al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'it, may God deal with him according to what he deserves, urging Mu'awiyah to fight the Amir 'Ali, may God ennoble his face:

"Indeed you, and the Book (concerning) 'Ali, are like the tanner (dābighah) when the hide has become rotten."

Al-Kashshaf says: The meaning of the verse, upon Him, is that you, O disbelievers, together with your objects of worship, will not be able to lead astray anyone except one who is astray like you. This is a statement of the essential meaning. Abu Hayyan preferred the coordination, that the pronoun refers to the worship, that fatinin includes the sense of carrying (haml), that the second person predominates over the third in ﴿you﴾, and that the negated clause is the predicate of inna. It is related from some of them that ʿala ("upon") means ba' ("with"), and the pronoun attached to it refers to what you worship. So reflect.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ( صَالُو الجَحِيمِ ) with a waw, according to what is in the book al-Kamil of al-Hudhali. In the book of Ibn Khalawayh, from both of them, it is ( صَالُ ) with a damma and without a waw. In al-Lawami' and al-Kashshaf, from al-Hasan: ( صَالُو الجَحِيمِ ) with a damma on the lam. So, according to the reading with the waw, it is a sound masculine plural (jam' salamah) whose nun has dropped because of the idafah (genitive construction). In the speech there is observance of the wording of man first, and observance of its meaning second, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in God and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾.

As for the reading without it, there are three aspects. The first is that it is a plural from which the nun was dropped because of the idafah, then the waw of the plural was dropped because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn), and the script followed the pronunciation.

The second is that it is a singular whose final radical, which is the ya', was dropped for lightness, and it was treated like the one forgotten, and the i'rab (case inflection) was applied to its middle radical, just as it was applied to the middle radical of yad ("hand") and dam ("blood"). On this basis is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the fruit of the two gardens is near﴾ (dān), and His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And His are the ships raised high﴾ (al-jawār), with a damma on the nun of (dānun) and on the ra' of (al-jawāru). And the saying "I did not care about it, not at all" (ma bālaytu bihi bālatan): the original of bālatan was bāliyatun, on the pattern of 'āfiyah, its final radical was dropped, so the i'rab was applied to its middle radical, and when the ha' (of the feminine) was attached to it, the i'rab moved to it.

The third is that it is also a singular, and its original form was ṣā'il, by metathesis (al-qalb al-makānī), with the lam placed before the 'ayn. Then the first lam, which is the ya', was dropped, so ṣāl remained on the pattern of fā'il, and it became inflected like bāb. Its parallel is shākin, whose i'rab is applied to the kāf in one dialect.

In the speech there is observance of the wording of man first, and observance of its meaning second, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in God and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾.

As for the reading without it, there are three aspects. The first is that it is a plural from which the nun was dropped because of the idafah, then the waw of the plural was dropped because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn), and the script followed the pronunciation.

The second is that it is a singular whose final radical, which is the ya', was dropped for lightness, and it was treated like the one forgotten, and the i'rab (case inflection) was applied to its middle radical, just as it was applied to the middle radical of yad ("hand") and dam ("blood"). On this basis is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the fruit of the two gardens is near﴾ (dān), and His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And His are the ships raised high﴾ (al-jawār), with a damma on the nun of (dānun) and on the ra' of (al-jawāru). And the saying "I did not care about it, not at all" (ma bālaytu bihi bālatan): the original of bālatan was bāliyatun, on the pattern of 'āfiyah, its final radical was dropped, so the i'rab was applied to its middle radical, and when the ha' (of the feminine) was attached to it, the i'rab moved to it.

The third is that it is also a singular, and its original form was ṣā'il, by metathesis (al-qalb al-makānī), with the lam placed before the 'ayn. Then the first lam, which is the ya', was dropped, so ṣāl remained on the pattern of fā'il, and it became inflected like bāb. Its parallel is shākin, whose i'rab is applied to the kāf in one dialect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 164:

Allah's words, ﴿There is none of us but has a known station﴾, are a report of the angels' acknowledgment of servitude, in response to someone who claims otherwise about them. So it is from His speech, Exalted is He, but it is related in their own words. Its underlying form is: "And there is none of them but..." That is, "And there is none of us but has a known station in worship and in submission to the command of Allah, Exalted is He, in the governance of the world, restricted to him, which he does not go beyond, and he cannot deviate from it, out of submission to His greatness, humility before His majesty, Glorified is He, and humbleness before His exaltedness, Majestic is His affair," as it is narrated: "Among them is one who bows and does not straighten his spine, and one who prostrates and does not raise his head."

al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as fair (hasan), Ibn Majah, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Dharr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I see what you do not see, and I hear what you do not hear. The heaven has creaked, and it has right to creak. There is not a space of four fingers in it except that there is an angel in it, placing his forehead in prostration to Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazi in the Book of Prayer reported from Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is not a place the size of a foot in the heaven except that there is an angel on it, either prostrating or standing, and that is the saying of the angels: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ ﴿And indeed, we are the ones who line up﴾."

From al-Suddi: ﴿but has a known station﴾ refers to nearness and direct witnessing.

Some scholars took this as part of the speech of the jinn, in the sense of the angels, connected to what precedes it of their speech, which is from His words: ﴿Glorified is Allah above what they describe﴾ up to ﴿the glorifiers﴾. Having interpreted the jinn as the angels, he said: "That ﴿Glorified is Allah above what they describe﴾ is a report of the angels' declaring Allah far above what the polytheists attribute to Him, after their denial of them in that, by supposing a verb governed by 'they knew' (ʿalimat) in conjunction, and ﴿except the sincere servants of Allah﴾ is a testimony from them to the innocence of the sincere from describing Him with that, which includes their own exoneration by virtue of their inclusion in the group of the sincere in the most eloquent and emphatic manner. It is also an exception of the disjunctive kind (istithnaʾ munqati') from the waw of ﴿they describe﴾, as if it were said: 'The angels certainly knew that the polytheists will be punished for their saying that, and they said: Glorified is Allah above what they describe, but the servants of Allah, of whom we are part, are innocent of that description.' And ﴿Indeed, you﴾ etc. is a justification and confirmation of the innocence of the sincere from what was mentioned, by explaining their inability to seduce and mislead them. The shift to address (iltifat ila al-khitab) serves to show complete care in establishing the content of the statement. ﴿what you worship﴾ refers to the devils who misled them, and in it is an announcement of their disavowal of them and of worshipping them, as in His saying: ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾. And their saying: ﴿There is none of us but has a station﴾ etc. is a clarification of the clear state of their affair and a specification of their place in the station of servitude, after what was mentioned of the disbelievers' denial of what they said, and the declaring of Allah far above that, and the exoneration of the sincere from it, and a demonstration of the limitedness of their own rank. The interpretation of the jinn as the angels was taken as the preferred view because it requires connecting and orienting the verses with what was mentioned. There is something in the justification, yes. This verse strongly strengthens the view of whoever says that what is meant by the jinn earlier is the angels, peace be upon them, a very clear strengthening, and the connection mentioned is most excellent."

It was also said that it is from the speech of the Messenger (peace be upon him), meaning: "And there is none of the Muslims but has a known station according to the measure of his deeds on the Day of Resurrection." This is connected to His saying: ﴿So ask them﴾, as if it were said: "So ask them, and say: 'There is none of us but...'" in the sense of: rebuke them with that and blame them for their disbelief, and enumerate the opposites of it with which you and your companions are characterized. If you wish, you may hold it as not compelling, saying, after your knowledge that the meaning leads to it: "This is distant, so understand." And Allah knows best.

"Minna" is a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and the subject is omitted because its description is sufficient. The description is the clause "lahu maqam" (he has a station), meaning: "﴿There is none of us﴾ who is [not] one who has a known station." Omitting the modified noun with a clause or something similar is permitted when it is part of what precedes it, governed by "min" (of), or in a common usage. This is the view preferred by al-Zamakhshari.

Abu Hayyan said: "Minna" is a description of an omitted subject, and the mentioned clause is the predicate, meaning: "And there is no one existing among us except that he has a known station."

What has been stated was objected to, on the grounds that no complete sentence is formed from "ma minna ahad" (there is none of us one), and His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿but has a known station﴾ is the place of the benefit, so it is the predicate. Even if one imagines that "illa" (except) means "ghayr" (other than), and that it is a description, that is not valid, because it is not permitted to omit the noun it describes. "Illa" differs from "ghayr" when used as a description in this respect, since "ghayr" is fully established as a descriptor, while "illa" is rarely established in that function. Another scholar said that it also involves the unrestricted use of description (tafrigh fi al-sifat), and they prohibited that. It is answered that a meaningful sentence fitting the context is formed from it, since its meaning is: "There is none of us who is characterized by any attribute except the attribute that he has a known station which he does not exceed." The intended restriction is for emphasis. Or it may be said that it is a description of an omitted substitute (badal), meaning: "There is none of us, except someone who has a known station," as Ibn Malik said in a similar case. In that there is an acknowledgment that the intended benefit is that clause, and this entails that it is more appropriate for it to be the predicate. As for what was mentioned about the possibility that it is a description of an omitted substitute, it is not valid, because it involves omitting both the substituted noun and the noun it substitutes for, and there is no parallel for that. In sum, what Abu Hayyan mentioned is safer from dispute and debate. Yes, it was said: "It is permissible to say that the aim here is not to convey the content of the predicate, but the refutation of the disbelievers, and for this reason the adverbial phrase was made the predicate and placed first. So the meaning is: 'There is none among us who exceeds the station of servitude to other than Him, unlike you, for what has come from you has removed you from the rank of obedience.'" And there is consideration in this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 165:

﴿And indeed, we are truly those who stand in ranks.﴾ (That is, ourselves, or our feet, in prayer.) Nasir al-Din said: that is, in the performance of obedience and in the stations of service. It was also said: those who stand in ranks around the Throne (al-'Arsh), awaiting the divine command. In al-Bahr (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit): calling down blessings upon the believers. It was also said: standing with our wings spread in the air, awaiting what we are commanded.

Page 155

Ibn Abi Hatim related through the chain of Ibn Jurayj, from al-Walid ibn 'Abdullah ibn Mughith, who said: "They did not form rows in prayer until this was revealed: ﴿And indeed, we are truly those who stand in ranks.﴾"

Muslim related from Hudhayfah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "We have been favoured over the people in three ways: our rows have been made like the rows of the angels, the earth has been made a place of prostration (masjid) for us, and its dust has been made a means of purification (tahur) for us when we do not find water."

Muslim also related, and so did Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah, from Jabir ibn Samurah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Will you not form rows as the angels form rows before their Lord?"

These reports and others like them favour the first interpretation.

And We are indeed the ones who glorify (al-musabbihun), meaning those who declare God, exalted is He, free of whatever is unbefitting of Him, glorified is He. This includes what the disbelievers attributed to Him, exalted is He. It has been said: meaning, those who say, "Glory be to God" (subhan Allah).

Abd ibn Humayd and others transmitted from Qatadah that he said: "al-musabbihun" means those who pray (al-musalluna). This is supported by what is narrated from Ibn Abbas: that every instance of tasbih (glorification) in the Qur'an carries the meaning of prayer (salah). The apparent meaning is what preceded. Perhaps the first (the declaration of freedom from the unbefitting) points to the outward courtesy of their conduct toward their Lord, mighty and majestic is He, and the second (the prayer) points to the perfection of their knowledge of Him, glorified is He.

Nasir al-Din said: Perhaps the first points to their ranks in obedience, while this (the first) concerns their knowledge. What is found in inna (indeed), the lam (emphatic lam), and the placement of the separating pronoun (al-fasl) conveys emphasis and exclusivity, because they are the ones who persist in this constantly, without interruption, whereas the elite of mankind are not free from being occupied with livelihood. Perhaps the statement does not lack an allusion (ta'rid) to the disbelievers. The apparent view is that the three verses, I mean His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And there is none of us﴾ up to here, were revealed just as their companion verses were revealed.

It is related from Hibat Allah al-Mufassir (the exegete) that they were revealed neither on earth nor in the heavens. He counted with them two verses from the end of Surat al-Baqarah, and a verse from al-Zukhruf: ﴿Ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you﴾, the verse. Ibn al-Arabi said: Perhaps he meant in the space between the heavens and the earth.

Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti said: I have not found a basis for what he mentioned except the end of al-Baqarah. It may be supported by what Muslim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, he reached Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary)," and the hadith continues, and in it: "He was given the five prayers, and he was given the final verses of Surat al-Baqarah, and whoever among his community does not associate anything with God was forgiven the sins that cast into the Fire." End of quote. So do not overlook this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verses 167–170:

﴿And indeed, they used to say﴾: "in" here is the light (mukhaffafah) form of "inna," the "lam" is the distinguishing lam (al-lam al-fariqah, which separates it from the negation "in"), and the pronoun refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, who used to say before the Prophet's ﷺ mission: ﴿"If only we had with us a reminder from the former peoples"﴾, that is, a Book of the same kind as the books that were revealed to them, and similar to them in being from Allah, the Exalted: ﴿"we would surely have been sincere servants of Allah"﴾, meaning, we would have devoted worship to Him, the Exalted, and we would have been better guided than they were. The fa' in His words, the Exalted, ﴿"So they disbelieved in it"﴾, is the fa' of fasihah (the fa' that expresses an implied condition), like its use in His words, the Exalted: ﴿"Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted"﴾. That is, there came to them a reminder, and what a reminder: the master of reminders, and a Book that watches over all other books and reports. ﴿So they disbelieved in it﴾, ﴿"but soon they will know"﴾, that is, the outcome of their disbelief and the retribution that will befall them. It has also been said that "reminder" here means knowledge, that is: if we had knowledge from those who came before us, and of what Allah, the Exalted, did with them after they died, whether He rewarded them or punished them, we would surely have devoted worship to Him, the Exalted. Then that came to them in the Mighty Qur'an, ﴿so they disbelieved in it﴾. But its remoteness is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verses 171–173:

﴿And indeed Our word has preceded for Our servants, the messengers.﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming the threat, and its opening with an oath serves to give the utmost emphasis to establishing its content. That is: "And by God, indeed Our promise to them of victory and triumph has preceded," namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, they are the ones who will be given victory﴾ and ﴿And indeed, Our soldiers, they are the victorious﴾. In that case it is an explanation (tafsir), or it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿Our word﴾. It is also permissible that it be a new resumptive clause, and the promise is what is found in another place in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I will surely prevail, I and My messengers﴾. The first is more apparent. By "the soldiers" is meant the followers of the messengers, and He attributed them to Himself, exalted is He, to honor them and to elevate their rank.

Page 156

Some of the eminent scholars said: this is generalization after specification, and there is in it as much emphasis as there is. According to al-Suddi, what is meant by the victory and triumph is that which is by proof (hujjah). Al-Hasan said: what is meant is victory and triumph in war, for no prophet among the prophets was killed in war; rather, whoever of them was killed was killed by treachery (ghilah), or in some other manner outside of war. And if a prophet dies before victory, or is killed, God, exalted is He, has established that his people will be given victory after him, so that the victory of his people is a victory for him. Close to this is what has been said: the two restrictive forms (qasrayn) are with regard to the outcome of the matter and the consideration of the final end. Nasir al-Din said: they are with regard to what is predominant and what is decreed in essence, because the good is what He, exalted is He, wills in essence, while other things are decreed secondarily, for a wisdom and another purpose, or for the desert of what proceeds from the servants. For this reason it was said: "In His hand is the good," and evil is not mentioned, although all is from Him, mighty and majestic is He. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father: if they are not given victory in this world, they will be given victory in the Hereafter. The apparent context requires that this be in this world, and that it is by way of subjugation, domination, and gaining the upper hand over the enemies, whether by killing them, dispersing them, expelling them from their homelands, taking them captive, or the like. The two clauses indicate permanence and continuity, so it must be said that the continuity of this is customary. It was also said: it is on its apparent meaning, and the continuity of victory for the soldiers is conditional upon what the idafah (annexation) implies; so the followers of the messengers are not defeated in a war except through their failure in what the annexation implies, by some inclination toward the world, or weakness of reliance upon Him, exalted is He, or the like. And it suffices for the victory of the messengers that their word be raised and the creation be unable to oppose them, and that they be protected from being killed in wars and from fleeing in them, even if great distresses occur there. Understand this. The wording (bi-mansurun) with "the messengers," and (bi-l-ghalibun) with "the soldiers," is not hidden in its significance, so do not be heedless. God, mighty and majestic is He, called His promise by that a "word" (kalimah), and they are "words" (kalimat), because when they gathered, united, and were bound together in the closest connection, they became as one thing, so this is by way of metaphor (isti'arah). The well-known view is that applying the term "word" to speech is a sent metaphor (majaz mursal) from applying the part to the whole. Some scholars said: it is a literal linguistic usage (haqiqah lughawiyyah), and the restriction of the term "kalimah" to a single word is a convention of the grammarians; according to this, no interpretation is needed. Al-Dahhak read "kalimatuna" in the plural, and it is permissible that by it be meant "Our promises." Understand. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, "ala 'ibadina" (upon Our servants), by way of including "sabaqat" the meaning of "haqqat" (became binding),
