According to al-Suddi, what is meant by the victory and triumph is that which is by proof (hujjah). Al-Hasan said: what is meant is victory and triumph in war, for no prophet among the prophets was killed in war; rather, whoever of them was killed was killed by treachery (ghilah), or in some other manner outside of war. And if a prophet dies before victory, or is killed, God, exalted is He, has established that his people will be given victory after him, so that the victory of his people is a victory for him. Close to this is what has been said: the two restrictive forms (qasrayn) are with regard to the outcome of the matter and the consideration of the final end. Nasir al-Din said: they are with regard to what is predominant and what is decreed in essence, because the good is what He, exalted is He, wills in essence, while other things are decreed secondarily, for a wisdom and another purpose, or for the desert of what proceeds from the servants. For this reason it was said: "In His hand is the good," and evil is not mentioned, although all is from Him, mighty and majestic is He. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father: if they are not given victory in this world, they will be given victory in the Hereafter. The apparent context requires that this be in this world, and that it is by way of subjugation, domination, and gaining the upper hand over the enemies, whether by killing them, dispersing them, expelling them from their homelands, taking them captive, or the like. The two clauses indicate permanence and continuity, so it must be said that the continuity of this is customary. It was also said: it is on its apparent meaning, and the continuity of victory for the soldiers is conditional upon what the idafah (annexation) implies; so the followers of the messengers are not defeated in a war except through their failure in what the annexation implies, by some inclination toward the world, or weakness of reliance upon Him, exalted is He, or the like. And it suffices for the victory of the messengers that their word be raised and the creation be unable to oppose them, and that they be protected from being killed in wars and from fleeing in them, even if great distresses occur there. Understand this. The wording (bi-mansurun) with "the messengers," and (bi-l-ghalibun) with "the soldiers," is not hidden in its significance, so do not be heedless. God, mighty and majestic is He, called His promise by that a "word" (kalimah), and they are "words" (kalimat), because when they gathered, united, and were bound together in the closest connection, they became as one thing, so this is by way of metaphor (isti'arah). The well-known view is that applying the term "word" to speech is a sent metaphor (majaz mursal) from applying the part to the whole. Some scholars said: it is a literal linguistic usage (haqiqah lughawiyyah), and the restriction of the term "kalimah" to a single word is a convention of the grammarians; according to this, no interpretation is needed. Al-Dahhak read "kalimatuna" in the plural, and it is permissible that by it be meant "Our promises." Understand. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, "ala 'ibadina" (upon Our servants), by way of including "sabaqat" the meaning of "haqqat" (became binding),

﴿So turn away from them﴾, i.e., turn away from them and be patient, ﴿for a time﴾, until the time when the period of refraining from fighting ends. According to al-Suddi, it means until the Day of Badr, and al-Tabari preferred this view. It was also said: until the Day of the Conquest (al-Fath). Before it there was the truce (muhadanah) of al-Hudaybiyyah. Ibn Jarir and others transmitted from Qatadah that he said: until the day of their death. Al-Tabarsi also related this from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Zayd said: until the Day of Resurrection. This view, and the one before it, make it evident that in the non-restriction of victory to what occurred in this world,

"And observe them" — for they are then in the worst of states and the most dreadful of punishments; there has befallen them what has befallen them of captivity and slaughter. Or, observe their affliction, with the understanding that the speech contains an omitted modifier (muḍāf), and the command is to witness that, which is not yet occurring — to indicate that, because of its great nearness, it is as though it were present before him and in his sight, especially if it is said that the command is for the present time or for immediacy.

"So they will soon observe" — what will be for you of support and victory. It has also been said: the meaning is, "Observe what will befall them on the Day of Resurrection of punishment; so they will soon observe what will be for you of increased reward." And "soon" (sawfa) here is for threat, not for postponement and distancing, which is its real meaning. The nearness of what has befallen them necessitates the nearness of what will be for him — upon him be prayers and peace — so this is an indication that distancing is not intended by it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verses 176–177:

﴿Will they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ This is a rhetorical question of rebuke (tawbikh, a reproachful question). Juwaybir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: They said, "O Muhammad, show us the punishment with which you threaten us, and hasten it for us," so this was revealed. It is also narrated that when ﴿Then they will see﴾ was revealed, they said, "When will this be?" So this was revealed: ﴿But when it descends﴾, that is, the promised punishment

(Page 157)

﴿upon their courtyard﴾. The saha (courtyard) is the wide open space near the houses, and any wide place in general. Its plural is suhuf (courtyards). The poet said:

"It was all the same whether they did not release their camels, or released them, while the courtyards were dusty."

In the pronoun there is an implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah, a metaphor in which only the comparing element is mentioned). The punishment is likened to an army that suddenly attacks a people in their homes, so it alights upon them. The "descending" is an imaginative depiction (takhyil).

Ibn Mas'ud read nuzila with light stress and in the passive voice. This is intransitive, so the prepositional phrase serves as the deputy subject. It is also read nuzzila with a shadda (doubled consonant) and in the passive voice, and this is transitive, so the deputy subject is the pronoun referring to the punishment. ﴿So evil is the morning of those who were warned﴾, that is, "so evil is the morning of those who were warned, their morning," on the basis that sa'a here means ba'isa (evil, wretched). This reading was also used by 'Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud). The thing being dispraised is omitted, and the lam in "al-mundharin" (those who were warned) is for the class (jins), not for a specific group, since they stipulate generality afterward. So it is based on dispraise and praise, so that the explanation follows the ambiguity and the detail follows the summary. If sa'a is taken in its original meaning of qabuha (to be ugly), it is permissible to take the lam as referring to a specific group without a supplied element. The word "morning" (sabah) is used metaphorically for the time when the punishment descends, that is, the time that was of the morning of an army which launches a dawn raid on an enemy. That army travels to it at night in order to attack it while it is heedless in the morning. They often call a raid a "morning," because it most commonly occurs at that time. This is a metonymic metaphor (majaz mursal) in which time is named and what occurred in it is meant, as one says "the days of the Arabs" for their battles.

It is permissible to interpret the morning here in this way. In al-Kashshaf: "It is like the punishment that descended upon them after they had been warned, by an army that gave warning of its attack upon a people after their morning, so they did not heed its warning, nor did they take their precautions, nor did they plan their affairs in a way that would save them, until it halted at their courtyard suddenly, raided them, and cut off their last remnant. Their habit was to raid at dawn, so the raid was called a morning, even if it occurred at another time." And this verse would not be eloquent, nor would it have the awe that one feels, nor would its source please you in yourself and your nature, except because it came in the manner of an image (tamthil). End of quotation. Its apparent meaning is that the discourse is based on the metaphor of image (isti'arah tamthiliyyah), and its superiority over others is too famous to mention and too great to deny.

It has also been said: the pronoun in "nazala" refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), and what is meant then is his descent on the day of the conquest, not the day of Badr, because he did not come to their courtyard except by interpretation, nor to Khaybar, according to his saying (ﷺ) when he attacked it at dawn: "Allah is greatest, Khaybar is ruined. Indeed, when we descend upon the courtyard of a people, evil is the morning of those who were warned." This is because his recitation (peace be upon him) was complete with his citing it as evidence, while the discourse here is with the polytheists. And it is not hidden that the pronoun referring to him (peace be upon him) is remote.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verses 178–179:

﴿So turn away from them for a time.﴾ ﴿And watch, for they will [soon] see.﴾ This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) following an earlier consolation, and an affirmation of the fulfilment of the promise after an earlier affirmation. Moreover, the omission of the object from the two verbs (lit. "they see" / "you see") indicates clearly that what he (peace and blessings be upon him) will see at that time of the varieties of joys, and what they will see of the varieties of harms, cannot be encompassed by description and explanation. It is also permissible that what was mentioned earlier refers to the punishment of this world, and this (the second) to the punishment of the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 37, verse 180:

﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe.﴾ This is a declaration of the transcendence of God, exalted is His majesty, above everything the polytheists attribute to Him, whatever is not fitting for the sanctity of His greatness and His dominion, of what is related about them in this noble surah, and of what is not related, among which is the failure to fulfil the promise according to the requirement of His previous word, exalted is He. This is especially so with regard to the Messenger (ﷺ), as is indicated by the mention of the title of lordship (rubbubiyyah), which expresses nurturing (tarbiyah) and perfecting (takmil), and of universal ownership (malikiyyah), together with its addition first to his pronoun, upon him be blessings and peace, and second to might. It is as if it were said: Glory be to Him who is your Nurturer and Perfecter, and the Owner of might and dominance absolutely, above what the polytheists attribute to Him, among which is the abandonment of your victory over them, as is shown by their demand for the punishment. The meaning of His, exalted is He, owning might absolutely is that there is no might for any of the kings or others except that He, mighty and majestic, is its owner.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The Lord is annexed to might because of His exclusive possession of it, exalted is He, as if it were said: the One possessing might, just as you say: a companion of truthfulness (sidq), because of his exclusive attachment to truthfulness. He then mentioned the permissibility of intending the meaning we have mentioned. The difference is that the annexation according to what we have mentioned is on the basis that He, glorified is He, is the one who bestows might, and according to the other it is on the basis that He, mighty and majestic, is the Mighty in Himself. Each has an aspect of emphasis (mubalaghah) that the other lacks.

[Page 158]

The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And peace be upon the messengers﴾, honour all the messengers after His being declared free of what was mentioned. They also bring their status to attention and indicate that they are safe from every hardship and attain every aim. The words of Allah, glorified is He, ﴿And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, point to His being described by His noble affirmative attributes, after the reminder that He is characterised by all His negative attributes (*sifat salbiyya*). They also indicate that these attributes entail praiseworthy acts, among which is His bestowing upon the messengers various noble honours and lofty perfections, both religious and worldly, and His showering upon them and upon those who follow them various kinds of blessings, both outward and inward, which call for His praise, exalted is He. They also signal that what He promised His servant (peace be upon him) of victory and triumph has been realised. The purpose is to alert the believers to the manner of glorifying Him, may He be glorified, and of sending peace upon His messengers, peace be upon them, who are intermediaries between Him and them in the overflow of perfections upon them without restriction. This clearly shows that it is not disliked to send peace upon them individually. Perhaps the placing of the greeting of peace upon the messengers between His glorification and His praise is to conclude the noble surah with praise of Him, together with what it indicates, namely that His granting success to offer the greeting of peace is one of His blessings that call for praise. So said *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim* (the Guidance of the Sound Intellect).

It may be said: the glorification (*tanzih*) is placed first because of its importance, both in essence and in standing. Since the glorification is from what the polytheists describe Him with, and since He, exalted is He, mentioned the guidance of the messengers to them and their warning them against describing Him, may He be glorified, with what is not befitting to Him, and included in that an indication of the evil state of those people and the grimness of their final end, He followed this with an indication of the good state of the messengers who call to His glorification from what the polytheists describe Him with. In this there is what there is of concern for the matter of glorification. And He, exalted is He, brought in the praise to indicate that He, glorified is He, is characterised by affirmative attributes just as He is characterised by negative attributes. Although this would call for the praise to follow the glorification directly, as in their saying, "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Allah," which is what is mentioned in the reports and is well known in the litanies, the separation between them here by the greeting upon the messengers is due to what the context of mentioning them required, as passed earlier. It also renewed attention to them, the placing of the glorification from what those to whom they are sent describe Him with. Perhaps one who examines carefully will see that the greeting here is more important than the praise, in view of the context, although in essence the praise is more important. Importance judged by the context is more deserving of consideration among them. That is why you find them placing the less excellent before the more excellent when the context requires attention to it. Perhaps it is part of the sentence of glorification. In this way is resolved what is said, that His praise is greater than the greeting upon the messengers, peace be upon them, so it would have been fitting to place it before the greeting, following the well-known method in books and sermons. It is not necessary to resort to what has been said: that the praise here means thankfulness for blessings, which are what move one to it, and because of them the sending of messengers takes place, which is a means to the good of both abodes; so it was placed before it, because that which prompts a thing precedes it in existence, even if it is prior to the prompter in rank. So reflect.

This verse is one of the comprehensive and complete verses, and its occurrence in this place calls out with an eloquent tongue that it is the speech of One to whom belongs magnificence, and from Him is might, may His majesty be exalted and His bounty be general.

Al-Khatib narrated from Abu Sa'id, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say after he had given the greeting: 'Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe. And peace be upon the messengers. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.'"

[Page 159]

Al-Tabarani narrated from Zayd ibn Arqam, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever says after every prayer: 'Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe, and peace be upon the messengers, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds,' three times, has indeed measured with the fullest measure of reward."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Sha'bi, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever would like to be given the fullest measure of reward on the Day of Resurrection, let him say at the end of his gathering, when he intends to rise: "Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might," to the end of the surah.'" Al-Baghawi narrated it through another connected chain from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, as a statement of his own (*mawquf*).

Other than this has come concerning closing a gathering with glorification, and perhaps it is more authentic than this.

Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'There are words that no one speaks in his gathering when he rises, three times, except that his expiation is made by them, and no one says them in a gathering of goodness and remembrance except that it is sealed for him by them, just as a seal is stamped upon a page: Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You. There is no god but You. I seek Your forgiveness and turn to You in repentance.'"

However, what is well known today among people is that at the close of a gathering of recitation, or of remembrance, or the like, they recite the mentioned verse: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe﴾, ﴿And peace be upon the messengers﴾, ﴿And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾.

* * *

(Among the subtle indications in the verses) is what they said about ﴿By those who arrange themselves in ranks﴾: they are the perfected, completed souls from the first rank, which is the rank of the prophets (peace be upon them), and the second rank, which is the rank of the chosen ones (*asfiya'*); ﴿and those who drive away with reproof﴾ from disbelief and sinfulness, by proofs, admonitions, and holy aspirations; ﴿and those who recite the reminder﴾: the verses of Allah and His laws, exalted is He. It has been said: the ones who arrange themselves in ranks are the multitude of angels who are absorbed in contemplation; the ones who drive away are the multitude of angels who drive away the heavenly bodies and the lower bodies by management; and the ones who recite are the multitude of angels who recite the verses of Allah and the manifestations of His holiness upon His prophets and His saints (*awliya'*). The descent of angels upon the saints is among what the Sufis have affirmed, may Allah sanctify their secrets. The basis of the descent upon them is established by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, the angels descend upon them, saying, "Do not fear and do not grieve, and receive good tidings of the Paradise that you were promised."﴾ They sometimes call some of the saints "prophets of the saints."

Al-Sha'rani said in *Risalat al-Fath* (The Treatise of Opening), in interpreting what is uttered by the perfected ones of ecstatic utterances (*shatahat*): The prophets of the saints are every saint whom the Truth, exalted is He, has established in a manifestation from the manifestations of His self-disclosures, and for whom Muhammad (ﷺ) and the locus of Gabriel (peace be upon him) have been established. The spiritual locus causes him to hear the discourse of the legislated rulings, which were prescribed for the locus of Muhammad (ﷺ). When he finishes his address and that saint's heart is relieved, the possessor of this vision understands all that discourse contained of the legislated rulings manifest in this Muhammadan community. The saint takes them as the Muhammadan locus took them, and they are returned to his sense perception. He has retained what the Muhammadan locus addressed to the Spirit, and he knows its soundness with certainty of knowledge, indeed with the certainty of sight. Such a person acts upon whatever hadiths he wishes, and he pays no heed to the authentication or weakening of others. For what some hadith scholars declared sound may not have been said by the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), and what they called weak may have been heard by this saint from the Trustworthy Spirit, who conveys it to the reality of Muhammad (ﷺ), just as some of the Companions heard the hadith of Gabriel concerning the explanation of Islam, faith, and excellence. These are the prophets of the saints, and they never single out a law, nor do they have an address with it except by making known that this is the law of Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him), or they witness what was revealed to His Messenger (ﷺ) in the presence of the imaginal representation (*tamaththul*), which is outside their essence and inside what is expressed, concerning the good tidings in the case of the sleeper. Except that the saint shares with the Prophet in perceiving what the common people perceive in sleep while in the state of wakefulness. These in this community are like the prophets among the Children of Israel, in the rank of Aaron's worship according to the law of Moses, despite his being a prophet. They are the ones who preserve the sound law, about which there is no doubt, for themselves and for this community. They are the most knowledgeable of people about the law. However, most scholars of the law do not accept this from them, and they are not obliged to establish proof of their truthfulness, because they are not lawgivers. They are the guardians of the prophetic state, of the divine knowledge (*'ilm ladunni*), and of the divine secret, while others are the guardians of the outward rulings. We have expounded on this at length in *al-Mizan*. End of quotation. He said shortly after this, in the said treatise: Know that some scholars denied the descent of an angel upon the heart of other than the Prophet (ﷺ), because they have not tasted it. The truth is that it does descend, but according to the law of its Prophet (ﷺ). So the disagreement should be only about what the angel descends with, not about the angel's descent. When he descends upon one other than a prophet, he never appears to him during speech; he only hears his speech, or he sees his person without speech. Only a prophet combines speech and vision. And peace. End of quotation. A portion of discussion about the vision of the angel has previously passed for you, so recall it.

﴿Indeed, your God is One﴾: an announcement of this so that they may know it, and not take besides Him, exalted is He, gods from the world, from desire, and from Satan. The meaning of His, exalted and glorified is He, being One is His being singular in essence, attributes, and acts, and the absence of any partner with Him, glorified is He, in any of things. They applied most of the verses afterward to what is in the souls. It has been said concerning His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾, that there is an indication that for the wayfarer in every station there is a halting that suits that station, and he is questioned about fulfilling the rights of that station. If he comes out of the obligation of its answer, he is permitted to pass over; otherwise he remains held back, detained by his states until he fulfils its rights. Likewise they applied what came of the stories of the messengers afterward to what is in the souls. It has been said concerning His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾, that it indicates that the angel does not exceed his station to what is above it, nor descend from it to what is below it. This is unlike the human species, for among its individuals is one who journeyed to the station of "two bow-lengths" (*qaba qawsayn*), indeed flew to a dwelling or nearer, and there trailed robes: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾.

Among them is one who fell down to the lowest of the low, and descended to the bottom of Sijjin: ﴿And recite to them the report of him to whom We gave Our signs, but he detached himself from them, so Satan pursued him, and he became of the misguided﴾. They mentioned that the human may rise until he reaches the station of the angel, then pass beyond it to a station of nearness through supererogatory acts and a station of nearness through obligatory acts. And he may descend to the level of animality and what is below it: ﴿Those are like livestock; rather, they are further astray﴾. We ask Allah, exalted is He, to elevate us to a station that He is pleased with, to grant us His pleasure on the Day of meeting Him, to make us among His victorious soldiers and His sincere servants, by the sanctity of the lord of the messengers (ﷺ), and upon his family and all his companions. Peace be upon the messengers, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

So said *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim* (the Guidance of the Sound Intellect).

It may be said: the glorification (*tanzih*) is placed first because of its importance, both in essence and in standing. Since the glorification is from what the polytheists describe Him with, and since He, exalted is He, mentioned the guidance of the messengers to them and their warning them against describing Him, may He be glorified, with what is not befitting to Him, and included in that an indication of the evil state of those people and the grimness of their final end, He followed this with an indication of the good state of the messengers who call to His glorification from what the polytheists describe Him with. In this there is what there is of concern for the matter of glorification. And He, exalted is He, brought in the praise to indicate that He, glorified is He, is characterised by affirmative attributes just as He is characterised by negative attributes. Although this would call for the praise to follow the glorification directly, as in their saying, "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Allah," which is what is mentioned in the reports and is well known in the litanies, the separation between them here by the greeting upon the messengers is due to what the context of mentioning them required, as passed earlier. It also renewed attention to them, the placing of the glorification from what those to whom they are sent describe Him with. Perhaps one who examines carefully will see that the greeting here is more important than the praise, in view of the context, although in essence the praise is more important. Importance judged by the context is more deserving of consideration among them. That is why you find them placing the less excellent before the more excellent when the context requires attention to it. Perhaps it is part of the sentence of glorification. In this way is resolved what is said, that His praise is greater than the greeting upon the messengers, peace be upon them, so it would have been fitting to place it before the greeting, following the well-known method in books and sermons. It is not necessary to resort to what has been said: that the praise here means thankfulness for blessings, which are what move one to it, and because of them the sending of messengers takes place, which is a means to the good of both abodes; so it was placed before it, because that which prompts a thing precedes it in existence, even if it is prior to the prompter in rank. So reflect.

This verse is one of the comprehensive and complete verses, and its occurrence in this place calls out with an eloquent tongue that it is the speech of One to whom belongs magnificence, and from Him is might, may His majesty be exalted and His bounty be general.

Al-Khatib narrated from Abu Sa'id, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say after he had given the greeting: 'Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe. And peace be upon the messengers. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.'"

[Page 159]

Al-Tabarani narrated from Zayd ibn Arqam, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever says after every prayer: 'Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe, and peace be upon the messengers, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds,' three times, has indeed measured with the fullest measure of reward."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Sha'bi, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever would like to be given the fullest measure of reward on the Day of Resurrection, let him say at the end of his gathering, when he intends to rise: "Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might," to the end of the surah.'" Al-Baghawi narrated it through another connected chain from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, as a statement of his own (*mawquf*).

Other than this has come concerning closing a gathering with glorification, and perhaps it is more authentic than this.

Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'There are words that no one speaks in his gathering when he rises, three times, except that his expiation is made by them, and no one says them in a gathering of goodness and remembrance except that it is sealed for him by them, just as a seal is stamped upon a page: Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You. There is no god but You. I seek Your forgiveness and turn to You in repentance.'"

However, what is well known today among people is that at the close of a gathering of recitation, or of remembrance, or the like, they recite the mentioned verse: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe﴾, ﴿And peace be upon the messengers﴾, ﴿And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾.

* * *

(Among the subtle indications in the verses) is what they said about ﴿By those who arrange themselves in ranks﴾: they are the perfected, completed souls from the first rank, which is the rank of the prophets (peace be upon them), and the second rank, which is the rank of the chosen ones (*asfiya'*); ﴿and those who drive away with reproof﴾ from disbelief and sinfulness, by proofs, admonitions, and holy aspirations; ﴿and those who recite the reminder﴾: the verses of Allah and His laws, exalted is He. It has been said: the ones who arrange themselves in ranks are the multitude of angels who are absorbed in contemplation; the ones who drive away are the multitude of angels who drive away the heavenly bodies and the lower bodies by management; and the ones who recite are the multitude of angels who recite the verses of Allah and the manifestations of His holiness upon His prophets and His saints (*awliya'*). The descent of angels upon the saints is among what the Sufis have affirmed, may Allah sanctify their secrets. The basis of the descent upon them is established by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, the angels descend upon them, saying, "Do not fear and do not grieve, and receive good tidings of the Paradise that you were promised."﴾ They sometimes call some of the saints "prophets of the saints."

Al-Sha'rani said in *Risalat al-Fath* (The Treatise of Opening), in interpreting what is uttered by the perfected ones of ecstatic utterances (*shatahat*): The prophets of the saints are every saint whom the Truth, exalted is He, has established in a manifestation from the manifestations of His self-disclosures, and for whom Muhammad (ﷺ) and the locus of Gabriel (peace be upon him) have been established. The spiritual locus causes him to hear the discourse of the legislated rulings, which were prescribed for the locus of Muhammad (ﷺ). When he finishes his address and that saint's heart is relieved, the possessor of this vision understands all that discourse contained of the legislated rulings manifest in this Muhammadan community. The saint takes them as the Muhammadan locus took them, and they are returned to his sense perception. He has retained what the Muhammadan locus addressed to the Spirit, and he knows its soundness with certainty of knowledge, indeed with the certainty of sight. Such a person acts upon whatever hadiths he wishes, and he pays no heed to the authentication or weakening of others. For what some hadith scholars declared sound may not have been said by the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), and what they called weak may have been heard by this saint from the Trustworthy Spirit, who conveys it to the reality of Muhammad (ﷺ), just as some of the Companions heard the hadith of Gabriel concerning the explanation of Islam, faith, and excellence. These are the prophets of the saints, and they never single out a law, nor do they have an address with it except by making known that this is the law of Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him), or they witness what was revealed to His Messenger (ﷺ) in the presence of the imaginal representation (*tamaththul*), which is outside their essence and inside what is expressed, concerning the good tidings in the case of the sleeper. Except that the saint shares with the Prophet in perceiving what the common people perceive in sleep while in the state of wakefulness. These in this community are like the prophets among the Children of Israel, in the rank of Aaron's worship according to the law of Moses, despite his being a prophet. They are the ones who preserve the sound law, about which there is no doubt, for themselves and for this community. They are the most knowledgeable of people about the law. However, most scholars of the law do not accept this from them, and they are not obliged to establish proof of their truthfulness, because they are not lawgivers. They are the guardians of the prophetic state, of the divine knowledge (*'ilm ladunni*), and of the divine secret, while others are the guardians of the outward rulings. We have expounded on this at length in *al-Mizan*. End of quotation. He said shortly after this, in the said treatise: Know that some scholars denied the descent of an angel upon the heart of other than the Prophet (ﷺ), because they have not tasted it. The truth is that it does descend, but according to the law of its Prophet (ﷺ). So the disagreement should be only about what the angel descends with, not about the angel's descent. When he descends upon one other than a prophet, he never appears to him during speech; he only hears his speech, or he sees his person without speech. Only a prophet combines speech and vision. And peace. End of quotation. A portion of discussion about the vision of the angel has previously passed for you, so recall it.

﴿Indeed, your God is One﴾: an announcement of this so that they may know it, and not take besides Him, exalted is He, gods from the world, from desire, and from Satan. The meaning of His, exalted and glorified is He, being One is His being singular in essence, attributes, and acts, and the absence of any partner with Him, glorified is He, in any of things. They applied most of the verses afterward to what is in the souls. It has been said concerning His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾, that there is an indication that for the wayfarer in every station there is a halting that suits that station, and he is questioned about fulfilling the rights of that station. If he comes out of the obligation of its answer, he is permitted to pass over; otherwise he remains held back, detained by his states until he fulfils its rights. Likewise they applied what came of the stories of the messengers afterward to what is in the souls. It has been said concerning His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾, that it indicates that the angel does not exceed his station to what is above it, nor descend from it to what is below it. This is unlike the human species, for among its individuals is one who journeyed to the station of "two bow-lengths" (*qaba qawsayn*), indeed flew to a dwelling or nearer, and there trailed robes: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾.

Among them is one who fell down to the lowest of the low, and descended to the bottom of Sijjin: ﴿And recite to them the report of him to whom We gave Our signs, but he detached himself from them, so Satan pursued him, and he became of the misguided﴾. They mentioned that the human may rise until he reaches the station of the angel, then pass beyond it to a station of nearness through supererogatory acts and a station of nearness through obligatory acts. And he may descend to the level of animality and what is below it: ﴿Those are like livestock; rather, they are further astray﴾. We ask Allah, exalted is He, to elevate us to a station that He is pleased with, to grant us His pleasure on the Day of meeting Him, to make us among His victorious soldiers and His sincere servants, by the sanctity of the lord of the messengers (ﷺ), and upon his family and all his companions. Peace be upon the messengers, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
